Config files run arbitrary JavaScript (!!js through eval inside with(ctx)) with the full authority of the host process
Code hot reload depends on Node's private module loader (expose-internals or a native addon) and tracks two incompatible internal API shapes
The loader writes a .cordis/resolve.mjs helper and a .gitignore into the user's project to resolve modules there
A runtime write-back serialises parsed data instead of the parsed document, so comments and layout of a hand-edited config file are lost
Five schema systems coexist (schemastery, zod, the in-house tool schema language, typert-generated zod, ajv) joined by four lossy converters

reason: The config becomes the Go struct acpserver.Config with the same three fields: an optional default provider and model, and sessionListPageSize with default 100 and bounds 1 to 1000, decoded strictly.
Replaced by the Go struct defaultmodel.Config with provider and model required and reasoningEffort optional, all live fields.

Replaced by the Go struct instructions.Config: maxBytes per chain as a floor, maxSourceBytes, the new maxTotalSourceBytes, projectRootMarkers, candidates, localCandidates and agentsHome, decoded strictly.

Replaced by the Go struct driver.Config: maxParallelToolCalls moves to the tools component as maxParallel (live, default 10) so that the cap has one owner, agents[] gains a required start mode and an optional preset, and the budget and flush bounds are added.

The schema becomes the Go struct agentpreset.Declaration: ID (required, unique), Name, Description, Order, Extends, and Children as a map from child id to component, disabled switch and config. The upstream plugins list becomes that map, and each child's config is decoded strictly against its component's type by the declaration's validator.

The schema becomes the Go struct agentpreset.Config with Default (required, checked against the declarations as a static issue) and SelectedDefault (a live field saved through the config service of area A21).
Replaced by the Go struct team.Config: maxTasks (256) and defaultEnabled (false) as upstream, plus releaseOnOwnerFailure (true).
The schema has one field that selects between native schemas and the run_code form. With one tool form left there is nothing to configure, so no Go struct exists.

Replaced by the Go structs stream.Config (Heartbeat, WriteTimeout, MaxAge, ReplayLimit, PageEvents, StreamsPerPeer, InterestsPerTab, TabGrace) and web.Config (MaxFormBytes, HandlerTimeout). The socket heartbeat, inbox, outbox and compression fields have no counterpart because the multiplexed socket is gone.
Replaced by routes/jobs.Config with OutputFlush (100 ms) and MaxFrameBytes (65,536), the same two values under Go names.

Replaced by conversation.Config: the history window minima and cap that upstream fixes in code. nativeOpen is dropped with the desktop application and listWorkSliceMs with the single thread it served.
Upstream's schema has no fields. The settings routes need no configuration of their own; they are present when their component is mounted.

Replaced by userterm.Config with upstream's defaults for shell choice, caps, input and buffer limits, the unattended timeout, the activity poll and the cleanup retry, plus ExitedKept. Scrollback, the stop grace and the agent terminal cap move to area A09.
Replaced by routes/workspaces.Config with DocumentsDirectory and DocumentsLookupTimeout (10 s), used by the first-use workspace route.

Replaced by wsfiles.Config with upstream's caps for pages, byte reads, lines, entries and search, plus PollInterval for the watch fallback. The process grace and stderr cap of the packaged search binary have no counterpart.

Replaced by the Go struct attachments.Config with the same nine image limits and defaults; the home override is gone, the concurrency count becomes a decoded-pixel budget, and limits for generic files and the request cache are added.

Replaced by the Go struct shell/bash.Config: Path, Timeout, MaxTimeout, TailBytes, SpillBytes and Grace with upstream's defaults. The default directory is the session's current directory, not a config field.
The sandboxing executor's config is the local executor's fields verbatim; with one bash provider there is one struct, shell/bash.Config.
The config struct of connector.cli keeps commandTimeout and adds interactiveTimeout and maxStdoutBytes, each of which a registration may override.

The schema splits three ways. recovery becomes shell.Config.Reconnect with the same caps, rendered into the page for the stream client. trustedHosts is area A18's listen.Config.TrustedHosts. maxRequestBodyBytes becomes A19's web.Config.MaxFormBytes for form bodies and area A07's attachment limit for uploads.

pollIntervalMs sets how often rebuilt bundles are looked for. Nothing is rebuilt under a running Go host. The development equivalent is shell.Config.DevDir, which re-reads templates and assets from a directory on each request and needs no interval.

enabled, which defaults to true upstream, is replaced by area A18's report.Config.Analytics.Enabled, which defaults to false and is shown in settings. appVersion comes from the binary. The two environment-query fields are gone because nothing samples the machine.
The one field, stopSequenceMs, becomes keys.Config.StopSequence, a live duration with the same 500 ms default, rendered into the shortcut table so that the script can time the double-Escape sequence.

The poll interval configured a browser poller. Polling is done by area A17's account component under its Notifications setting, off by default; the interval is requested of that area's config and this area declares no struct.

resolutionTimeoutMs (default 1000, volatile) becomes menu.Config.ResolveTimeout, a live duration with default one second and a minimum of one millisecond, read by the host that now resolves the menu; MaxItems bounds one menu.
The three fields tune the probe that races two npm registries. No registry is contacted because plugins are local directories.

The schema holds the progress of the desktop introduction and the address of a third-party questionnaire. The introduction is dropped with the desktop application, and a questionnaire prefilled with account and device data is data leaving the machine with no preview.

The credentialOnboarding switch decided whether the browser offered a first-run key step. First run is area A25's host-rendered setup page, whose setup.Config.Enabled turns it off for a deployment provisioned by configuration; the models section has no such field.

The schema carries spreadsheet limits (excel.maxBytes 16 MiB, maxCells 250000, timeoutMs 15000) and the browser-side office conversion cache limits (packages/client/ui-sidebar-documentpreview/README.md:83-87, :102-106). The Go struct preview.Config keeps the spreadsheet bounds as SheetMaxBytes, SheetMaxCells and SheetTimeout and adds page size, a Markdown bound and the HTML preview limits. The office cache fields have no counterpart because the conversion cache belongs to the host's office service, and nothing is synced to a browser.

The seven volatile config fields (preference, three font sizes, three font lists) become the preference type theme.Appearance, stored per principal and validated by the schema package with the same ranges (text 10 to 22, code 10 to 16, terminal 10 to 20). The config struct theme.Config keeps one live field, Default, which is what a principal with no stored preference gets.

The one field maxResultsPerSession (default 1000, at least 1) is kept as values.Config.MaxResultsPerSession. Two byte bounds are added, MaxValueBytes and MaxBytesPerSession, because a count bound alone lets a thousand large values pin memory.

Replaced by the Go struct basic.Config with upstream's fields and defaults, plus automatic headroom for small windows, the summariser's reasoning effort, maxConsecutiveFailures and per-route modelPolicies.
Replaced by the Go struct prune.Config with thresholdChars, headChars and tailChars at upstream's defaults and the rule that head, marker and tail fit the threshold.

The two fields are replaced by the Go structs host.Config (limits, deadlines, restart budget, whether model-authored plugins may be attached) and plugin.Entry (directory, digest, grants, credential mapping). vmTimeoutMs becomes the start-up and call deadlines of a process; clientInspectTimeoutMs has no successor because no inspect query crosses to a page.
Replaced by the Go struct secret.Config: backend auto, keychain or file, the two .env layers, watch, debounce and lock wait; the store path is no longer configurable because the home layout fixes it.

The schema configures the Swift helper: its path, signing, build and permission-poll timings, clipboard and drag settings, and the program runtime. None of it exists without the helper. The two tree-read limits have a counterpart in the adapter's snapshotMaxNodes and snapshotMaxDepth.
The schema holds the consent mode and workspace of the served cua-mcp profile, which is not built.
The schema configures the .NET helper: its path, build and connection timings and tree-read limits. None of it exists without the helper.

Replaced by the Go struct account.Config with the three origins, timeouts and logout retries as upstream, header values as text or credential references and a notifications setting that is off by default; the desktop platform field is gone.
chatimport.Config replaces it: MaxSessions 1,000, MaxArchiveBytes 512 MiB and MaxEntryBytes 256 MiB. maxTitleBytes has no counterpart because the title service's own limit applies.

The two limits, maxAudioBytes (4 MiB) and maxDurationSeconds (120), are fields of the x.speech component's Go config struct with the same defaults, enforced on the request body and on the validated recording.

The schema's headless and executablePath fields move to the x.browser.mcp config with a recipe selector, command, args and serverEntry; its mode and endpoint are fields of A16's browser component, because launch or attach is a property of the seam and not of one provider.

The schema's headless and executablePath fields move to the x.browser.mcp config with a recipe selector, command, args and serverEntry; its mode and endpoint are fields of A16's browser component, because launch or attach is a property of the seam and not of one provider.

The schema's core is the second model's name, key and headers, dropped with the Stagehand layer. Its executablePath, headless and operation timeout have counterparts in the x.browser.cdp config (path, headless, startTimeout, callTimeout).

The bridge's settings (hook and process timeouts, band size, tool aliases) configure a component that is not built. The one idea kept is the alias table from Claude Code tool names to harness tool names, which becomes hooks.Config.toolAliases.

view.Config replaces it with the same two fields, Provider and TargetLanguage (default auto). Provider has no default: upstream's preselected bing is not kept, so that turning the feature on chooses no receiver.

Replaced by the struct forgeui.Config with gitCommand, gitTimeout, grace, maxOutputBytes, readinessTimeout, maxBranches and maxUntrackedFiles at upstream's defaults, plus the new refreshThrottle (10s, upstream's fixed value). Not carried: the fifteen fields for diffs, review caches, lenses, annotations and review lists, whose features are not built; worktreePrefix is merged into worktree.Config.namePrefix so that the prefix has one owner.

command (default cua-driver), args (default mcp), the per-call timeout and the reconnect overrides are fields of the x.computer.mcp Go config struct, passed to the MCP fleet's entry. New fields: recipe, confinement and the two snapshot limits.
Replaced by the struct forge.Config with activeInterval 30s, idleInterval 120s, maxBackoff 10m and fetchTimeout 30s, the same defaults and the same rule that maxBackoff is at least activeInterval.

Replaced by the struct github.Config with command, hosts, timeout, maxOutputBytes and maxReviewThreads at upstream's defaults. Not carried: maxCommits, maxViewedFiles and maxViewerItems, which bound reads that are not built.
Replaced by the struct bind.Config with discoveryTimeout 30s as upstream, plus the new maxScanBytes that bounds how much of a settled command's output is scanned for change-request addresses.

Six of the 24 fields map onto inspect.Config (MaxExchanges, Bodies, MaxBodyBytes, MaxTotalBytes, MaxTreeNodes, plus LogPageSize which is new); the other 18 size the worker thread, the CDP bridge, client sources and reconnects, none of which exists. profile.Config (MaxSeconds, Kinds) is new and belongs to a separately disabled entry.

defaultProvider and language (default auto) are fields of the x.speech Go config struct. They are written by the selection route into the writable layer and take effect live; defaultProvider has no shipped value.

The schema's provider id, queue bound, recording limit and inference deadline survive as id, maxPending, the shared byte limit and timeout of the x.speech.command config, which adds command, args, languages and output. The model directory, precision, download origin, probe, thread, voice-activity and idle-worker fields are not carried, because the operator's program owns them.

Replaced by the Go struct oar.Config: name, runtime, node, package, model, effort, launchArgs, allowPermissionBypass, env, maxDuration and stopGrace. Changed: a permission posture must be stated or the instance does not load, and the time limit is required instead of optional.
Its two fields, the alias-to-provider map and the tool name, are the targets list and tool field of area A12's delegation tool configuration; no struct of its own exists.

Three structs replace the one schema, one per component: translate.Config (MaxTextRunes 4000, Timeout 10 s), model.Config (Route, Model, MaxOutputTokens 8192, Timeout 60 s) and web.Config (the two endpoints, MaxResponseBytes 1048576, and a new Enabled field that is the sender's own setting, default false). The provider field moves to the view's config.

Replaced by the struct worktree.Config with retainOnArchive (a live field), directory, namePrefix, gitCommand, timeout, grace and maxOutputBytes at upstream's defaults. Not carried: nodeCommand, because no Node helper is started.
Replaced by the Go struct fileref.Config: maxResults, maxEntries, excludedDirectories and the new respectIgnoreFiles.

Replaced by the struct gitlab.Config with command, hosts, timeout, maxOutputBytes, statusBatchSize and maxConcurrentRequests at upstream's defaults. Not carried: maxReviewThreads, maxCommits and maxCachedVersionBytes, which bound review and diff reads that are not built.
Replaced by the Go struct local.Config (baseDir, textMaxBytes); the diff basis bound moves to ops.Config as size limits for the diff package.
The fence has no configuration of its own in Go. It is part of the local provider, and its mode and write roots come from the policy resolver for each call.
Go struct goal.Config: defaultMaxRounds 256 as upstream, plus defaultMaxTokens, defaultMaxDuration (both none by default) and maxObjectiveBytes.

No config struct replaces it. The task, session id, output mode, permission preset and approval policy are words of the command line that area A24's cli.headless component parses with its own option specification; the upstream row existed only to carry those values from the start-up provider to the runner.

Replaced by the Go struct reload.Config with one field, Debounce (100 ms). The module watch fields base, root and ignored and the watcher options are gone with module replacement, and disabling the boot.reload entry is the switch for applying changes at the next start.

Folded into the one struct hooks.Config. configPath, pluginRoot and projectDir become fields of a source entry with dialect claude-code; defaultTimeoutMs becomes the timeouts table and stderrSummaryMaxChars becomes stderrSummaryBytes.

Folded into hooks.Config as a source entry with dialect codex. The static model field has no counterpart because the payload carries the session's own model; the timeout and summary fields are shared with the other dialect.
The schema's one field is an in-memory function that reads the desktop shell's private credential. With no desktop application there is no component to configure.
cookieMaxAgeDays becomes auth.Config.CookieMaxAge with the same 30-day default and one-day minimum; LaunchTokenTTL is added for one-time tokens.
maxEntries becomes dirbrowse.Config.MaxEntries with the same default of 1,000; Roots is added to scope what may be listed and created.
The schema's one field points at the built front end's index file on disk. Assets are embedded in the binary, so the assets component has no config and nothing on disk to point at.

probeTimeoutMs and launchWatchMs become openpath.Config.ProbeTimeout and LaunchWatch, now with defaults. iconTimeoutMs has no counterpart because icons are not extracted. Enabled, RefreshAfter and operator-defined Apps are added.

The queue, batch, interval and timeout fields become report.Config with the same count defaults, plus a byte bound and a three-second drain. The endpoint default is empty instead of the upstream vendor's collector, the channel header becomes a list of credential references, and each kind has its own live Enabled field that defaults to false.

host, port, tls and the three compression fields become listen.Config with the same meaning: one address literal, the unspecified address refused, TLS as a pair, compression off by default. Added: the explicit insecure-remote flag, trusted hosts, a public URL, timeouts and a shutdown grace period.

Go struct local.Config: maxConcurrentJobsPerOwner 10, retainBytes 262144, settledRetainBytes 16384 as upstream, plus maxSettledPerOwner 50 and stopGrace 10s. pumpPollMs is dropped because producers push output.
The url and tool-loading fields become the url and disclosure fields of the generic connector row, which names the linear preset.
Replaced by the Go struct deepseek.AccountConfig: the same connection, listing and image fields, a keyed model overlay instead of modelOverrides, and the per-route Send settings.
Replaced by the Go struct deepseek.APIKeyConfig with a credential reference, a keyed model overlay, a listing mode and the per-route Send settings.

Replaced by the Go struct keyed.Config, a map of routes each with one protocol, an endpoint, a credential reference, headers, a model overlay, deviation switches and a retry policy; it is empty by default.

Replaced by the Go struct replay.Config with Scenario (one directory instead of three file paths), Mode and Pace; the provider catalog comes from the recorded request headers and no environment variable supplies a default.
Upstream's executor config is empty; the Go struct retry.Config adds the one cap on attempts per step, and the policy itself stays on each route.
The config struct of lsp.stdio keeps the servers map with command, mapping and byte limits as durations and sizes, and adds write roots, a network setting, a concurrency limit and an idle timeout.

The Go struct mcp.Entry replaces the plugin schema: transport fields, scope, expose, disclosure, tool filters, confinement, a revision pin, deadlines for every operation, the reconnect policy and OAuth options, with templates always expanded and redacted.
The config struct of the mcp component holds the servers map of entries, operator overrides for registered entries, the schema size limit and the probe caps.
Replaced by the Go struct feedback.Config with a default note limit of 8192 bytes, a text limit and a cap on feedback events per session.
The url and tool-loading fields become the url and disclosure fields of the generic connector row, which names the notion preset.

Replaced by two Go config structs: office.Config (queue, reader, source-byte, cache, timeout, input, output, archive and font-file limits with upstream's defaults, plus the new queueWait) and the engine's config (path, confinement, reprobeInterval, minVersion). Not carried: maxBackgroundConversions (no priorities), the three output-store fields (no output store), and fontFallbacks and maxLoadedFontBytes, which configure the kit's own font loader.
Replaced by the Go struct preset.Config holding the preset table and the default preset as live configuration, validated so that the default names an entry.

Go struct plan.Config: section stays required and non-empty and unknown keys stay a load error; enforcement (read-only by default), allowTools and maxPlanBytes are new.

Every field configures the index reader (sources, fetch limits, caches, Git timeouts, file hosts). The reader is not built.

No Go config struct replaces the Node provider's schema because the provider is not built. Evaluation mode, script persistence, scoped REPL, heap size, control-message size and launch choice have no meaning without a JavaScript guest. The limits a user still feels live in other areas' config: elapsed defaults and grace on the shell tools (A09), pending calls and byte bounds on the tool endpoint (A03). Replaced by the config struct of the guard.repeat component: thresholds, include, exclude and argumentsPreviewChars as upstream, plus repeatEvery and blockAt.

The glue plugin is not built in this area. Opening the browser, printing the URL and the advertised public URL are fields of area A18's launch and listener config; the surfaceContext switch becomes whether the web layer registers the DSH_WEB_URL variable with the shell environment component.

Replaced by the Go struct github.Config with the same four fields: source, path, a credential reference for the secret that is resolved for every request, and maxBodyBytes, which gains a default of 1 MiB.

The Go struct workflow/engine.Config keeps provider, maxConcurrentAgents and maxTotalAgents with upstream's defaults, drops maxItemsPerCall and syncTimeoutMs (combinators and the vm slice no longer exist), and adds what the host now enforces: defaultRuntime, maxRuntime, settleTimeout, script and args size bounds, spill size, narration ring size, an optional token budget and extra interpreters.
workdir.Config replaces it with the one field DefaultDirectory, which must be absolute and defaults to the launch directory.
Replaced by the Go struct changes.Config: the Git limits and file caps as upstream, new budgets for snapshot, manifest and turn diff, and no diff time limit because the diff bound is input size.

The launcher stays the root of the command tree. Changed: options (--home, --profile, --layer, --safe) are written before the command or profile name instead of ending at the first unknown word; --patch is renamed --layer; --dump-config, --dump-default-config and --dump-config-schema become dsh config show, dsh config show --defaults and dsh config schema; --from-default-profile becomes dsh profile new and dsh profile reset; -V and help are kept.

dsh acp is kept with no options: it serves the Agent Client Protocol on stdio until the client disconnects, with the same launch form and exit statuses as dsh sdk. The protocol itself belongs to the SDK and ACP area.

dsh headless is kept: one task, the final assistant text on standard output, diagnostics on standard error, exit 0 only for a completed turn, --json for one event per line, --permission-mode, --approval-policy and --add-dir unchanged. Changed: --session-id is renamed --session, --command runs one human command, the JSON lines use the session export line format, approvals are asked on a controlling terminal through the cli answerer or refused when there is none, and Ctrl-C closes the turn in the log before exit 130.

Upstream forwards its arguments to pnpm in the profile directory because plugins are npm packages. Go plugins are local directories the operator placed, so the command becomes nested verbs (list, inspect, add, remove, grant, revoke, enable, disable) whose meaning the plugin area supplies; nothing is forwarded to a package manager and nothing is downloaded.

dsh sdk is kept with no options: standard output carries only protocol frames and the process ends on end of input, shutdown or a signal. The command-line area fixes the launch form programs use (dsh --home <dir> --profile sdk) and the three exit statuses the SDK area asked for: 0 clean, 125 stalled client, 124 forced.

Upstream ships a fifth profile that serves the same SDK protocol over a standalone minimal tree. The Go design keeps it as the built-in profile sdk-minimal, which area A27 defines as the bundles core, minimal and sdk (DH-ADR-BUNDLE-2) and which the launcher starts by name under rule 2 of the grammar like every other profile; there is no bundle of that name. The minimal agent preset is also selectable under dsh sdk when a session is created.

dsh web is kept as the one launch command: it starts the host, prints the launch URL as the only line on standard output and opens the system browser. All seven upstream options survive (--host is renamed --bind to match the host area) and --insecure-remote is added. New behaviour: a second dsh web for the same home and address reuses the running host, and one with listener-changing flags is refused.

The file records 42 existing reads of the cordis root context in 27 files; the Go port has one accessor, Context.Root, and a checker restricts its callers before any harness code calls it, so there is nothing to record.

The file lists nine heavy suites that run without instrumentation so the per-file 100% gate stays affordable; Go coverage is compiled in, cheap and covers child processes, and the Go rule is one uniform package floor with no list of exempt suites or files.
The baseline for the empty-catch rule is already empty upstream; the Go analogue, a discarded error value, is rejected by a checker from the first commit unless the site carries a reason.

The file records 1,204 existing type assertions to unknown in 477 files that the no-new-unknown-casts gate tolerates; in Go the analogous checker (unchecked type assertions and unsafe) is required from the first commit with inline reasoned exceptions, so no baseline is created.

The deprecated page entry point is kept upstream for existing web callers. The Go design has one history route, session.history, and UI routes carry no compatibility promise, so no second entry point exists to deprecate.
The deprecated Config type of the presentation selector has no Go counterpart because the selector component is not built.
The deprecated runtime schema of the presentation selector has no Go counterpart because the selector component is not built.
The deprecated selector module is not carried into Go; presets compose the executor directly, which is what the deprecation notice asks upstream users to do.
The deprecated apply function that mounts one of two executors has no Go counterpart because the selector component is not built.

The deprecated agent/request waterfall is not built. Model and effort use Model().Select, output cap and sampling use the controls in ModelSelection, model-switch detection uses PreStepRequest.Previous, and observers use step/start and the Start frame.
The deprecated synchronous reader eventAt has no Go counterpart: the live session does not hold the event list, and an old event is read through the paged, cancellable Read that may go to storage.

The deprecated synchronous reader snapshotEvents has no Go counterpart: there is no resident log to snapshot, ranges are read in pages, and fork reads its prefix from storage instead of from a snapshot of a live session.
The deprecated synchronous reader ownEvents has no Go counterpart: the header stores the inherited count, and the events a session owns are read in pages starting at that offset.
The untyped keyed read kept for old plugins has no Go counterpart: state is read only through the typed handle returned by Register.
A read that returns only cells some other read happened to compute does not exist: a snapshot returns every requested key with an explicit state of current, behind or pending.
The writerless working-directory/change event is not registered in the Go event vocabulary, so there is nothing for readers to ignore.

The inventory matched a regular expression in the generator that reads @deprecated tags out of doc comments; nothing at this line is deprecated, and the TypeScript generator it belongs to is not built.
The deprecated setTimeout alias is not part of the Go timer, which has one name per operation (Timeout).
The deprecated setInterval alias is not part of the Go timer, which has one name per operation (Interval).
The Go design has one store, and its persisted-type catalogue is generated from the running registry, so a hand-written note cannot disagree with what the code ships.
There is one store and therefore one implementation of the lease and of the platform lock calls.
A settings edit writes a merge operation that holds only the edited fields, so every other field of the entry keeps following the lower layers.
Spill files always live under the harness home in a directory derived from the session, so a locator written by an earlier process still resolves after a restart.
A default is a Go value and the configuration catalog is generated from the running registry, so a document cannot state a default the product does not have. The Go default follows the note.
Each tool's description states its own rule for hidden and ignored files, and a golden test pins the description and the behaviour together.
One operation service performs path resolution, policy, intent, the provider call and the observation for every file tool; a tool holds only its schema and its result text.
The intent event returns a closed decision where the strictest answer wins whatever the registration order, and observation is a notify event whose listener failures are contained.

A local child does not settle while a child it created with parent delivery is unsettled; the notice then wakes it, so the end-turn guidance is true at every depth. A result that still finds no resident creator is in the ledger and is delivered when that creator resumes.

The host starts every stdio MCP server through the one starter under a policy from the sandbox resolver, by default workspace-write with only its state directory and declared roots; an unconfined server needs an explicit operator setting and is reported as unconfined.

A generation whose schemas exceed maxSchemaBytes is registered with summary disclosure, allowTools and denyTools narrow what is registered at all, and server instructions are refused above maxInstructionBytes and labelled as third-party text.

The Go codec answers a malformed line with a parse error and a stderr line, bounds the frame size and the outbound queue, ends a connection whose pipe accepts nothing for the stall deadline, and reports failures by a domain/reason code with no internal text.
Only session/create creates a session; every other method that names a session the connection has not created or resumed fails with sdk/session-not-owned or session/not-found and creates nothing.

The Go launch environment is an immutable snapshot with a recorded source per name and is never written into the process environment. Each child environment is built explicitly by the execution area, so a discovered file's values reach a child only if they are passed by name.

Upstream's tool asked for its own approval inside its body. The Go tool asks nothing and changes nothing durable: by owner decision DH-ADR-30 it has list, inspect, attach and detach only, and it never writes the profile. The one consent an attachment needs is an interaction that the extension area asks through the interaction registry (DH-ADR-EXT-8), so no action can forget a gate. Test DH-T-BOOT-21 checks through the real pipeline that the profile layer is byte-identical after every action.

Schemas are derived from compiled-in Go config types, so dsh config schema runs as a read-only admin command that starts no component and no plugin process; there is no imported code that could hang or hold a handle.

A secret is a redacting type in every text, JSON and log form, so an error chain cannot carry its value into a report; the report itself is the host area's bounded and pruned fatal diagnostic, and this area supplies the exit statuses and the commands that list and show it.

The stop function cancels running turns with a typed cause, waits for the agent teardown's bounded final flush, and only then applies a configurable exit deadline; when the deadline does pass the exit is reported as forced (status 124) and handled as a crash on resume.

Dropped by DH-ADR-18 (no desktop application). The limit describes the Electron welcome window's sign-in button and the native window material on Windows; first run is a host-rendered setup page (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-3), and account sign-in opens in the system browser.
Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (no plugin market; the generator is not built, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8). The limit concerns how the generator fetches Git commits.
Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (no plugin market; the generator is not built, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8). The limit concerns the generator's npm registry access; the Go design reads no npm registry.
Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (no plugin market; the generator is not built, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8). The limit concerns the generator's Git credential handling.

The rule exists only because of TypeScript: host and client code merge the cordis Context type under the same keys with different services, so one compiler program cannot hold both and browser tests must be listed in two projects by hand. Go has one module and one type system. The one import boundary that remains (which packages may import the browser driver) is a test, requirement DH-LIB-PLAYWRIGHT-R6.

A macOS Developer ID signature with notarization and a Windows code signature can be produced only with the real certificates inside the protected release environment, so that part of a release cannot be rehearsed elsewhere.
justification: Apple's notarization service and Windows Authenticode vouch for a publisher through certificates the publisher must hold; no design of the harness changes that. DH-ADR-ELECTRONBUILDER-2 keeps signing in the tag-triggered release workflow. The other half of upstream's limit is removed: the update path is qualified against a private feed with a test key (DH-ADR-ELECTRONUPDATER-1). Which certificates and where the keys are kept is still open with the owner.

reason: The limit exists only because desktop plugins are npm packages installed by a bundled pnpm whose lifecycle scripts may run. In the Go design a plugin is a local directory that runs as its own process under operator grants (DH-ADR-13, DH-ADR-4); nothing installs dependencies or runs install scripts.

The split existed because two installations (the Electron application and an npm-installed dsh) carried different package trees while sharing one data root. The Go product is one binary with no package state, and several dsh processes share one harness home under per-session leases (DH-ADR-12), so there is nothing to keep separate and no reserved desktop profile.

Dropped by DH-ADR-18 and DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8: no desktop application and no bundled Python, Node and pnpm payload. The limit is about that payload's architecture on win32-arm64; the dsh binary is cross-compiled per target, windows-arm64 included.

Dropped by DH-ADR-24 (the vendor release publisher is not built). The limit describes how that private tool is installed from the pnpm workspace; publication is a job of the release workflow (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8).

Dropped by DH-ADR-24 (the vendor release publisher is not built) and DH-ADR-ELECTRONBUILDER-3 (no installer). The limit states what the publisher's own tests do not prove about installers; whether a real binary is replaced correctly is proven by the dsh update scenarios of the update library specification.
Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (no plugin market or discovery; the market index generator is not built, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8). The limit concerns the generator's GitHub metric requests.
Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (no plugin market; the generator is not built, DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8). The limit concerns the generator's cache, which still needs the network on every run.

The guarantees of patch V6 (no effects while unloading, joined cleanup, pending effects drained, a child fiber owned before it is announced) become behaviour of the Go port with their own tests instead of a patch to re-apply at each sync.
The Go port gains EffectiveConfig, ResolveConfig, RetainConfig and a fiber-owned config hook as first-class API, with the publication rules of the upstream spec files as tests.
A Notify dispatch verb calls every listener and contains and logs each failure, so no caller enumerates callbacks by hand and no deprecated API is relied on.
Every loaded fiber exposes a standard cancellation context that is cancelled the moment the fiber is asked to unload, before the unload waits for the running body.
The Go context is not a proxy and never swaps a service's context for the caller's; a method that registers on behalf of a caller takes the owner context explicitly or the service implements Scoped.
The Go port is first-party code with one recorded upstream revision and a sync table; harness requirements are implemented in it directly, so there is no patch log to re-apply.

The debt is a vendored helper package that drifted from its upstream by gaining a reference type and a changed equality. The Go design has neither: there is no helper package and no reference type (a live setting reaches a component through its update hook), and config equality is plain structural equality with no special case.
Expressions become side-effect-free data reads in a restricted language with a fixed set of names, checked at parse time; no code from a config file runs in the host.
The dependency exists only because Node has no public module-cache API; Go components are compiled in and code is never replaced in process.
The helper exists only because of Node ESM module resolution; the Go loader resolves component names in a table registered at compile time.
The YAML codec applies runtime changes to the kept node tree and re-encodes it, so comments on untouched nodes survive a write.
A shape is declared once as a Go type and converted into exactly one derived form, JSON Schema, by one module, so there is no converter between schema libraries.
The Go type is the only declaration and the schema is derived from it by reflection, so no second declaration exists to cross-check or cast.
With one mechanism based on Go types there is no schema-building vocabulary from two libraries to collide.
The one schema module is imported by a single harness package, so a version change touches one go.mod line and one package.
Field metadata is read from the Go config type by reflection and never through the schema interface, cross-field rules are a Validate method, and the Go interface is synchronous by signature.
Nothing is forked; a derived schema is immutable data without callbacks and decoding never writes into its input.
The JSON Schema document is derived from the same Go type that config is decoded into, so there is no translation step and defaults are checked when the schema is derived.
Go types are available at run time through reflection, so schemas and fingerprints are computed in the running program and no generated artifact exists to go stale.

The Go harness imports one YAML module from one package, which defines the dialect and the !expr tag once; a test over the import graph fails if a second YAML module or a second importing package appears.

All globs go through one helper with one written dialect that has no regular-expression pass-through and matches dot names everywhere; case folding and base-name matching are the only options and are named at the call site.
One helper parses versions with the module's strict parser only and passes a version type instead of strings, so a version cannot be accepted by one check and rejected by the next.

Apps describe their options with a harness Spec type and get values, a help request or a usage error back; the parsing library is hidden inside one package and one binary links one copy of it, so no private field or error shape is inspected.

The Go algorithm policy makes SHA-256 the only hash for content identity and an import check forbids crypto/sha1 outside the packages that speak an outside format that fixes it, so a constructed SHA-1 collision can no longer make two different files share one stored copy.

Minute and hour rules accept no BY part and are fixed intervals; the Go evaluator advances them in elapsed time from the start instant, so they keep their spacing through a daylight-saving transition, while daily and longer rules stay in wall time.

The dependency is fetched from one vendor host outside the package registry, so its integrity and availability depend on that host. The Go design drops the legacy .xls parser and converts such files with the Office engine, so nothing is fetched from that address.

Upstream scans HTML by hand to refuse deep nesting because its bundled parser becomes very slow. The Go HTML parser stops with an error when its open-element stack passes 512, so the scanner is not written and the tool maps the error to the same omission text.

The copy exists only because the native binding is loaded into a Node runtime hosted by Electron, whose memory cage forbids JavaScript views onto native memory. The Go design loads no binding into a JavaScript runtime; recognition runs in a separate native process.
The flags exist so that Stagehand's browser extension can connect to the browser. The Go provider drives a launched browser over an inherited pipe with no listening port and never passes either flag.

The Go project publishes no computer-use helper for any platform, so no unsigned helper ships and no second, weaker packaging path exists; a desktop driver is a program the operator installs, and its signature is its vendor's.
Code that reads or controls the desktop runs only in a separate process, so a crash fails pending calls and not the host, and the operating-system permission belongs to that program's own identity.

There is no update library whose internals could be imported: the dsh update command owns the download and its inactivity deadline, and no downloaded release is kept between runs, so there is no hidden state to clear.
No installer is built, so there is no installer script and no packaging engine whose internal classes could be imported or altered.
Signing steps run only in the tag-triggered release workflow inside a protected environment with required approval, where pull-request code never runs, and the key stays in hardware.

The Go output reader uses the shared incremental decoder: it holds back an incomplete trailing character, reports offsets that count only emitted bytes, and starts retained windows on a character boundary (DH-LIB-NODEPLATFORM-R5 and -R6).

The Go binary is already one static file cross-compiled for every target, so the wheel carries the release binary unchanged and the packer, closure manifest, deploy step, bootstrap and sidecars are not needed.
The Python types and method stubs are generated from the one protocol schema, and a test fails when the generated file is stale.
The host scopes notifications and sends the run result, and the client is held to a rule of no product logic in Python, so the interval, tree and pairing code is not rebuilt.
Every host request is dispatched to a typed handler on a bounded number of worker threads, and each run and subscription has a bounded buffer whose overflow fails only that consumer.
The wheel holds the ordinary dsh binary with no Python-specific entry point, and the Python package downloads nothing and manages no cache.
The second carrier exists only because the runtime is a Node program that can also run unpacked on a system Node; a Go binary has one form, and a developer points dsh_bin at a local build.
One pure-Go binary per release target is built from one runner, the wheel set follows the release targets, and a test refuses a tag that does not match the binary's header.

The option lists, provider metadata and serialized request become the harness's own code and data, so there is no outside library to drift from, and the request-prefix digest is computed over the bytes actually sent.

Both causes are npm rules: a package that embeds a library must re-declare what the bundle leaves outside, and a consumer must supply peer packages. A Go module requires only the packages its code imports, and go mod tidy removes the rest.
One Go module in one version serves the client role, the server role and the fixtures, and Go has no peer-dependency mechanism that could force a second generation into the build.
Exactly one harness package imports the SDK and exposes harness types; stored OAuth records are validated by harness types, so an SDK upgrade is neither a data migration nor a change to callers.
The harness process service starts the one child and passes only its pipes to the SDK; the Go SDK negotiates the revision on that same connection, so no probe process is started.

The harness interface returns a closed set of error kinds and an explicit close result, every request carries a harness deadline so deadline and cancellation are told apart locally, and stdout cleanliness is a test instead of a workaround.

The Go SDK's ordinary server supports adding and removing tools at run time, and a consent question returned as an input request is served to clients on revision 2026-07-28 and on older revisions, so no deprecated API is needed.
The browser MCP server leaves the harness's dependency graph: it is an external program with its own dependencies, found on the operator's machine and version-checked when it connects.
The Go harness does not build or ship the Chrome DevTools interface, so there is no source snapshot to track and no substitute build inputs to maintain.

The Go harness owns the PTY master descriptor and reads the foreground process group with one ioctl (TIOCGPGRP) on Linux and macOS, replacing a /proc read on Linux and a ps child process per query on macOS.

The Go design uses the operating system's ConPTY by default and recognises a prompt from the emulated screen, where the two byte forms that differ between console hosts give the same text. A different console host is operator configuration, not a bundled requirement. The reasoning is an inference to be confirmed on Windows Server 2022.

A statically linked Go binary contains the PTY code, so the manylinux rebuild and glibc symbol check, the macOS deployment-target check of spawn-helper, the -spawn-helper sidecar beside each executable, the archive unpack rules and the per-platform conpty file policy have no counterpart.

The Go harness creates the terminal's process itself and keeps its handle: exit is observed by waiting on the handle and termination is TerminateProcess or a job object, so no exit notification from a library is needed (DH-LIB-NODEPTY-R6).

In the Go design one harness process package is the only non-test importer of os/exec, enforced by a source check (DH-LIB-NODEPROC-R14), so lookup, Windows command lines, environment scrubbing, tree ownership and cleanup are the same for every program the harness starts.

A Go wrapper takes typed arguments, accepts nil where Windows does and returns the error of the same call, and the standard library passes an explicit environment block to CreateProcessAsUser, so none of the four workarounds for the foreign-function layer is needed.

The structures come from golang.org/x/sys as compiled Go types maintained per architecture by the Go project, so there are no layout strings, no load-time size assertions and no separate header probe to keep in step.

There is no native artefact in the Go design: the launch stage and the lock are Go source compiled for every target by go build from one machine, so the build matrix, the platform packages and the pack and release scripts have nothing to build or publish.
The launch stage is part of the one dsh binary, which is also the remote SSH helper, so a remote host has the stage without a second file and without a resolution hook.
A WebSocket dial takes its http.Client from the one outbound client factory, so the proxy policy and certificate authorities apply to it as to every other request.
Go has no process-global dispatcher to patch; every client is constructed from the resolved policy, so no cross-version coupling exists.
The error is a property of undici combined with Node's uncaught-error handling; Go's HTTP/2 client closes idle connections without raising an error to the program (JavaScript runtime behaviour).
net/netip parses the dotted-tail spelling as the address the listener binds and reports only the all-zero address as unspecified, so one parser serves both classification and binding.
The pin exists because of how pnpm installs an npm dependency twice; Go's certificate generation is in the standard library and has no such dependency (npm packaging).
The client factory provides a connect-time destination guard and the security decision requires the fetch tool to use it, so the documented refusal of private addresses becomes real behaviour.
The host starts the operating system's launcher itself with a scrubbed environment and observes its exit code, so no second runtime or library-timing workaround is needed.
One media-type table in one Go package answers every lookup, and the UI is rendered by the host, so there is no second table in a client bundle.
The Go design links no OpenTelemetry SDK, so there is no coordinated release train or experimental API to follow; the exporter is harness code on the standard library.
The own exporter has one transport on net/http, where the request context cancels both the request in flight and the retry wait, so a second cancellable transport is not needed.

The exporter owns the encoder, so each record is encoded once and counted exactly, every channel is bounded by count and bytes, and the per-request deadline cancels the request instead of only warning.

The Go exporter implements the logs signal only and reads no setting from the environment, so there is no unused meter or tracer to switch off and no ambient variable that can change where or how data is sent.

One watch service owns the watcher and defines one close contract (close returns only after the callback can no longer run, late errors are discarded inside the service), so consumers carry no workaround and one module version is used.
Search is Go code inside the one release binary, so there is no executable to find, unpack, sign or stub in any packaging.
All diffs are computed by one host package whose bound depends only on the size of the two texts, so the same inputs always give the same stored result.
The Go scorer searches word-start alignments directly and keeps no global state, so neither workaround is needed.
One harness helper replaces files with an explicit durability argument on every platform, and its Windows calls go through golang.org/x/sys without a foreign-function bridge.
The harness is unaudited, and its sandbox, approvals and permission controls reduce risk but do not guarantee isolation, as upstream says of itself.
justification: Re-examined by debt reviewer K1 after the fix pass: now a scope boundary stated by two records. DH-ADR-SANDBOX-11 (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner) states in its own words that the sandbox, approvals and permission controls reduce risk and are not a guarantee of isolation and that the design has had no security review; it puts that statement in dsh sandbox status, the permissions page, the first-run notice and the website's security page (test DH-T-SANDBOX-17), and makes an independent review a release criterion for the first stable release. DH-ADR-SECURITY-12 states the same and forbids any product text that calls the harness secure without the qualification (test DH-T-SECURITY-1). Neither the audit nor the review can be supplied by a design: the cause is removed only when the review is done, which the gate requires. Note for the coordinator: the two records overlap and name slightly different places for the statement; one should refer to the other.

reason: Upstream requires a real-model counter-test whenever the model-visible policy text changes, because one wording made a model give up before its first tool call in five of twelve runs. The Go design now has that check: scenario DH-E-SANDBOX-7 runs twelve tasks, six denied first and escalatable, three times on each platform's policy text against a real model, asserts at least one tool call per task and an escalation rate no lower than the previous text's and never below ten of eighteen, and states that a change to the policy text is not merged until it has passed on the new text. The text is produced by the policy resolver of DH-D-SANDBOX-1, whose completion condition includes the scenario. Re-examined by debt reviewer K1; nothing has run.

Examined by the debt reviewer (K2) after the fix pass. Upstream's debt is a browser test of the model picker switched off for WebKit, so a WebKit defect there would reach users unseen. ui-chat.md now marks step (5) of scenario DH-E-UICHAT-2, the model picker, as engine-sensitive: under owner decision DH-ADR-39 it also runs in current Firefox and Safari, and 'a crash in any engine is recorded as a failed step, never as a skip, and keeps the scenario open'. The picker of DH-D-UICHAT-7 is also filtered on the host, which removes upstream's client-side filtering of grouped rows. What is resolved is the skipped check; whether WebKit renders the picker correctly is what the scenario will show when it runs.

The exclusion list exists because the per-file 100% rule cannot be met where V8 coverage cannot see child processes or browser code. DH-ADR-TOOLCHAIN-7 replaces the rule with one uniform package floor measured across processes, with exclusions by rule only and never by a list of files, so there is no list to keep or to work off. The inventory missed the six markers because the file is at the repository root, outside its scan roots, and three of them sit in the middle of a comment line.

Upstream's main-branch workflow carries a switched-off macOS job. In the Go design macOS is one of three operating systems of the required harness job (DH-ADR-TOOLCHAIN-12), and the acceptance workflow fails when a listed scenario skips or does not run (DH-ADR-TOOLCHAIN-6), so a platform lane cannot be absent without a failing job. The inventory missed the marker because workflow files are outside its scan roots.

Upstream keeps one list of packages whose tests never run on Windows, so a Windows defect in them is found by a user. The toolchain specification changes this (section 3, the row for vitest.config.ts:24-64): a file that cannot run on an operating system carries a build constraint next to the code, the required harness job runs on Linux, Windows and macOS (DH-ADR-TOOLCHAIN-12), and a listed scenario that does not run fails the job (DH-ADR-TOOLCHAIN-6). The areas concerned state their Windows behaviour themselves (PowerShell executors, the Windows sandbox backend, a Windows local end for SSH, hook scripts in PowerShell).

The Go design answers each open question of the note. A tool call's budget counts execution time only and pauses while a nested call waits for approval (DH-D-TOOLS-3, test DH-T-TOOLS-8). A workflow run has a wall-time budget counted by the host, which keeps running while a nested call waits for a person and says so as its tradeoff, plus a memory and a process-count limit carried out by the tree owner and reported as enforced, partial or unavailable (DH-ADR-PTC-5). No processor meter is added, which the same decision states.

Upstream switched off its live test of the model-backed search provider because an answer can arrive with no structured sources. The Go design defines that case: DH-D-CONNECT-11 returns such an answer as a query result with zero sources and the flag unsourced, its text labelled "answer without sources" so the model is told not to cite it, never inventing a source, and logs a warning after three in a row (test DH-T-CONNECT-24). Its real-vendor scenario DH-E-CONNECT-8 expects both kinds of answer and asserts each is handled, instead of assuming sources, so the live check need not be switched off. The selection and no-fallback rules are those of DH-ADR-CONNECT-8. Re-examined by debt reviewer K1; nothing has run. The fact that the endpoint may send no source remains, and is reported, not hidden.

Upstream lets the owner omit the lifetime, and such a share never expires. In the Go design the end time is a required field with a default of one hour and a configured ceiling, it is enforced by the binding's clock check at every decision and by a timer, and a host restart ends every share.

Upstream's lowest tier still lets a viewer prompt the session and stop its turn, so an owner who wants a passive viewer must rely on the viewer's restraint. The Go design has one role with four read actions; no route that sends input is in it, and a sweep of the route table proves the refusal.
The vendor account protocol issues tokens with no expiry or refresh and accepts a loopback callback address only.
justification: Third-party fact: redirect addresses and token lifetime are decided by the vendor service, not by the client. The design adds what it can: sign-out removes the local grant first and then revokes, a pending revocation is not kept on disk because that would keep the old token, and the user is told when issuer revocation failed (DH-ADR-HUMAN-10, DH-ADR-HUMAN-11).

reason: A request names its route and the authoriser reads that route's own endpoint and credential reference from configuration, so any number of key-authenticated vendor routes can exist; there is no single connection per kind.
The kind of a conversation's route is read from configuration and from the credential reference name in the logged request header, so it does not depend on which component is loaded at that moment.
A stored key is reported as configured by presence alone; a wrong key is found out when the provider rejects it or when the user runs the route check.
justification: Deliberate boundary: nothing leaves the machine unasked (owner decision DH-ADR-9, DH-ADR-HUMAN-11), so no background validity check is made. The user-started check that the interaction spec lists as a request to the model area already exists there: the on-demand route check of DH-D-LLM-4 sends one small real request and reports the classified result.

reason: ACP session/new accepts additionalDirectories: each becomes a session write root registered through the sandbox policy resolver in the agent's scope, advertised only when that service is mounted, and rolled back with the agent if any directory is invalid.

An ACP prompt accepts text, resource links and raster images (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF) only, and images only when an attachment store is mounted and the model route accepts them; audio and embedded resources are refused.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-SDK-9 has 'Scope boundary of this record (unit acp.acp.2): an ACP prompt carries text, resource links and raster images only, because those are the whole model-input vocabulary of the harness; audio, embedded resources of other types and other content blocks are refused'. Image support is advertised only when the store and the route exist (truthful capabilities).

reason: An MCP server that an ACP client supplies is used for its tools and for reading resources on demand. Its prompt templates cannot be used from an ACP session, and resource subscriptions are not followed.
justification: Register entry U-K2-14, now a recorded boundary. The missing consumer is built in the MCP area (U-K1-7): DH-ADR-CONNECT-4 registers each server prompt as a human command that a person runs and the model can never invoke, and records 'subscriptions are not followed' as scope. Over ACP that command has no way in, because DH-ADR-SDK-9 keeps ACP automation-only and offers no commands. So the ACP carrier's residue is stated by those two records; sdk-acp-typert.md does not say it in its own words, which one sentence in its section on what ACP cannot express would fix.

reason: Through ACP a client cannot replay a transcript (session/load), delete or fork a session, or use modes, commands, plans, terminals, client file operations or elicitation.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-SDK-9 lists these as not offered and DH-ADR-WIRE-7 keeps ACP automation-only, because presentation belongs to the web UI. A program that needs the transcript reads session history on the SDK protocol. Not offering session/load is a recommended default that the owner has not confirmed (sdk-acp-typert.md section 10).

reason: An unclassified failure is answered as one Problem with the code web/internal and a request id that names the log entry holding the full error chain; classified errors keep their own code from the one error table. In-process callers are ordinary Go calls and keep the wrapped error.

There is no generic uplink to give credits to. Everything a browser sends is an ordinary request with a body limit, except the terminal socket, whose protocol bounds unacknowledged bytes in both directions by acknowledgements (area A09's Attach, framed here).

SRC mode is a weaker validation path for running the host from TypeScript source, where the compiler plugin does not run. Go has no source-versus-built difference: a form is decoded strictly into a Go struct in every build.

The need for a generated codec per client-supplied field comes from TypeScript types being erased at run time and from host and client being separate builds. Go types exist at run time and there is no client contribution to mount.

Upstream leaves resume to each domain. The Go hub owns it: a stream source declares one of three recovery classes (journal resumed by cursor, state restarted from a baseline, notice that may be lost), so a feature cannot forget to define what happens after a reconnect.

Activation is a field of every route declaration (None, LiveOnly, MayResume), not a property of the lookup key, so two routes that address the same session can differ and a test lists which routes may wake a session.

No host event payload is forwarded to a browser. A change becomes a fragment rendered for the principal that reads it, so there is nothing unprojected to redact; what must survive a reconnect is a state baseline, and the notice class is declared lossy.

The event stream has a heartbeat interval and a separate write deadline, and the terminal socket a ping interval and a separate dead-after deadline, so a deployment that stalls longer than the cadence raises the deadline alone.

The per-frame compression decision works around the ws library ignoring its threshold option. There is no multiplexed socket, the event stream is never compressed and the terminal socket is uncompressed by default, so the workaround has no subject.

Behind a reverse proxy that buffers, a browser tab that vanished is noticed only when the proxy closes the connection or when the event stream is rotated at MaxAge (30 minutes by default); until then the ghost holds one goroutine and one stream slot.
justification: Server-sent events are one-way by definition (WHATWG HTML, server-sent events), and a buffering reverse proxy accepts the bytes on the browser's behalf, so a successful write proves only that the proxy took it. The design bounds the cost: MaxAge is configurable and the per-peer cap parks the oldest stream first. Upstream's compression half does not arise.

reason: The order of a job's standard output and standard error relative to each other is approximate: two chunks read in the same round cannot be put back in the order the program wrote them.
justification: Standard output and standard error are two operating-system pipes with no shared clock or sequence number; only the program can merge them by writing both to one pipe. The page labels each chunk with its channel and says that order across channels is approximate, which removes upstream's blind joining of chunks.

reason: A background job and its output buffer end when the host process stops; after a restart the job list starts empty and a request for an old job answers not-found with a plain message.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the records' own words: DH-ADR-JOBS-1 says 'Jobs do not survive the host', and DH-ADR-EXEC-2 says jobs and terminals end with the host because the host holds every process tree it starts; a job that outlived its host would be a process nobody owns. What survives is what the jobs area writes to the session log.

reason: The job routes carry the session in the URL path and declare it as their resource, so access is decided before the registry is read, and the job id must belong to the set that session can see.

A decision reads the principal, the action, the resource and the time, never request arguments, and the host renders a control by calling the same Allows function that guards its route. A page can therefore not show as allowed what the check refuses.

A route cannot register unless every path parameter is bound to a resource kind or declared opaque, a form field typed as a resource id must carry an access tag, and a handler can obtain a session or workspace id only through an accessor for a declared parameter.
Resources are never found by matching field names. They come from the URL pattern's bound parameters and from Go field types, so adding a field with a familiar name adds no resource and removes none.

There is one kind of route. Downloads, uploads, streams and the terminal socket use the same declaration with an access rule as pages and form actions, so no route sits outside the check and none needs a blanket refusal.
Only the owner can answer an approval or a question; a non-owner who was given access to a session can watch it but cannot answer for it.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the records' own words: DH-ADR-API-5 ships no principal kind other than the owner except the viewer of a live share, 'whose role holds read actions only, because the owner decided that viewers only watch'; owner decision DH-ADR-37 says 'viewers only watch'. DH-ADR-SECURITY-5 allows one answerer per agent. An approval widens what the model may do, so answering stays the owner's.

reason: No event payload reaches a browser. A session row is rendered for the principal that sees it, through the list filter, and a link to a parent session is rendered only when that principal may see the parent.

There is no ready frame and no host-facts value: the stream sends rendered fragments only, and the harness home is not part of any of them. Residual and stated: the content of a shared session still contains the owner's absolute paths.

A grant or revocation calls Invalidate, which raises access.Changed. The hub then re-checks every open stream of that principal: a stream on a session that is no longer allowed ends, and state baselines are re-sent without the revoked rows.

The capability set is fixed by value imports because the client is a separate TypeScript build that must import generated artifacts. The Go UI has no client build: a route exists when its component is loaded.
The explicit /remote import and mount per capability is a consequence of the generated client projection and the split TypeScript faces. A Go component registers its own routes at run time.

What needs reliable recovery is no longer left to each owner: a stream source must declare its class, state sources send a complete baseline on every connection including all pending interactions, and the notice class is reserved for messages whose loss is harmless.

The work slice exists because Node runs all host work on one thread and must yield by hand. A Go list request runs on its own goroutine, is preempted by the scheduler, is cancelled through its request context, and reads one keyset page of stored rows.

The upload route stores through area A07's attachment store, whose image admission checks decoded dimensions and pixel count within fixed limits before anything is kept (areas/storage.md, untrusted image admission); the byte cap is only the first check.

A stream that fails is retried by the stream script with a bounded, growing delay for as long as the tab is open, and the page shows a host-not-reachable state meanwhile; on return the host resumes from the cursor or sends reset.
An attachment upload is one streamed request under the attachment size limit; if it fails part-way the browser sends the whole file again.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UICORE-8 uploads a file as one streamed request and states 'No resumable' upload in its tradeoff; DH-ADR-API-8 keeps attachment bytes plain, bounded HTTP. A resumable protocol would add partial state on the host that must be cleaned up, to save a retry of a bounded file; the request id still prevents a duplicate attachment.

reason: The host assigns a fork's title inside the fork command, after normalising it and against the titles the store holds, and forks of one source run one at a time, so two concurrent forks cannot pick the same increment.

The completion route is declared with Activation None: it reads the session's recorded directory and searches through the filesystem seam without creating an agent, for file references as well as for skills.

There is no display memory in the browser. Prompt acceptance is a committed inbox event, the list summary marks the session as not blank at that event, and a reloaded page is rendered from the same durable facts.

Every tab renders the session list from host state and receives the same shell replacement on the stream, so two tabs cannot disagree about whether a session is blank for longer than one event delivery.

The bound of 64 references exists for a batched describe call from the browser. The settings page is rendered by the host, which reads credential presence directly, so there is no batch call and no bound to configure.

A terminal survives a page reload but not a host stop or the deletion of its session, and no shell is started again automatically. (Removed: exited terminals no longer count against the terminal limit.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-API-7 makes a person's terminal a child process owned by a session, and DH-ADR-EXEC-2 states it in its own words: 'Jobs and terminals still end with the host, because the owners are held by the host process on purpose; a restart keeps jobs story would need a supervisor process and is not designed.' Keeping a shell alive across a host stop would need a separate daemon that owns it, and replaying a shell cannot restore its state. The roster says that the previous host's terminals ended.

reason: Whether a terminal can be opened is known only by opening one: finding the shell program does not prove that the operating system will allocate a pseudo-terminal.
justification: Pseudo-terminal allocation depends on the operating system's state at that moment (the device limit on Unix, the console host on Windows) and neither system offers a probe that reserves one. The design removes the consequence: a terminal is published only after its backend is set up, so a failed creation is a typed error on the form and leaves nothing behind.

reason: An unattended terminal is closed automatically only after it was positively seen idle; a terminal whose activity cannot be observed, or that is busy, is kept until someone closes it, and no maximum run time is imposed.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-API-7 reclaims only on confirmed idleness and states the tradeoff ('a shell whose activity cannot be observed is never reclaimed automatically'), because treating unknown as idle would kill a person's running work. The design narrows upstream's limit: idleness is read from the terminal's foreground process group, not from the shell's prompt.

reason: Only one browser window at a time can type into and resize a terminal, and a window that attaches later gets the current screen and a bounded scrollback, not everything that was ever printed.
justification: A pseudo-terminal has exactly one window size (one TIOCSWINSZ value on Unix, one ConPTY size on Windows), so two windows of different sizes cannot both set it. The scrollback bound is the per-terminal memory limit and is configurable through the execution area's screen settings.

reason: After a reconnect the workspace list is sent whole again; there is no cursor and no replay of the individual changes that were missed.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-WIRE-3 and DH-ADR-API-4 give every small piece of machine state a baseline that is replaced whole, and keep cursors for the session journal only. A value of a few kilobytes cannot be applied out of order and needs no durable change log; the user sees the current list either way.

reason: Deletion markers protect a client model from delayed data. There is no client model: each connection receives whole regions rendered from the registry in one order, so a removed workspace cannot be revived by a late frame.

When the filesystem provider of the session's world cannot watch, wsfiles polls Stat for each watched interest at PollInterval. The number of interests per tab is capped, so the polling cost is bounded, and an SSH world gets automatic refresh.
When a watch ends or fails for good, the hub replaces the region with a marker that says it is no longer live, and the polling fallback is tried first, so a view never keeps old metadata silently.

Local watching goes through the harness watch service, whose requirement covers a parent directory that is deleted and recreated; this is the same resolution the filesystem area records for the provider.
The file browser lists, searches and watches only inside the session's workspace, while a file named by its path is read wherever the filesystem backend allows.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-API-8 states exactly this split (a listing or a watch explores, a named read does not) so that one read policy, owned by the filesystem seam, decides and the UI layer adds no second, different check.

reason: A text page reports the total number of lines when the file is within the whole-file cap, counted in one pass and remembered per file version; above the cap it says that the total is unknown.
A line longer than the page byte cap is cut at a UTF-8 boundary into continuation segments, so every window makes progress and a file with one very long line can be read to its end.

Metadata is taken from the opened file, and the version is compared again after the read; a difference is reported as changed-during-read with the newer version, so a mismatch is stated instead of silent.

An invalidation is a state slot per region in the hub: a newer one replaces a waiting one, and the number of regions per tab is capped, so a tab that reads nothing holds a bounded amount of memory and is closed at the write deadline.

Register entry U-K2-1, resolved in the convergence round. The filesystem seam's ReadDir now takes a limit and reports truncation (filesystem.md section 6.2): the local provider reads the directory in batches and stops, a remote provider passes the limit to its helper. The files route asks for its entry cap plus one and never more, and draws the sorted partial listing with 'more entries not shown' (DH-D-API-9). Tests DH-T-FS-8 and DH-T-API-24 check with a counting fake provider that no more than the cap plus one entries are requested. The one stat per child was already gone.

Search uses area A08's search helper, which walks the provider of the session's world in Go and needs no packaged binary, so it works on an SSH world. A search that stops at the file cap still reports that it is incomplete.
Every citing event gets a reference row in its append transaction and a draft lists its references, and a maintenance duty deletes objects that neither names once they are older than a grace period.

The two cases where a machine-local store hurts are covered: a remote execution world reads an attachment by identifier through the host, and a session export carries its objects by digest. Two machines sharing one live store is excluded because the home must be on a local filesystem.

The model still receives the first frame, but an animated source now keeps its original bytes as a linked file object, so the transcript can show the animation and nothing the user attached is discarded.

Output bytes no longer depend on an installed native library build: the encoders are Go code pinned by go.mod and the toolchain, and a transform version is part of every cache identity so an upgrade re-addresses variants without invalidating stored objects.

Generic files get a per-file size limit and a per-message count limit enforced while streaming, which removes the unbounded case. Audio and video remain generic files by decision and are listed as a limitation.
Attachments are collected by a reference-aware maintenance duty: an object no session event or draft cites is deleted after the grace period.

A draft record per session in the machine-state store holds the unsent text and lists its staged uploads, which the collector treats as references, so a draft and its files survive a reload or restart; the composer area writes the record.

Exists only because profile packages are resolved through Node's internal ESM and CommonJS resolvers and a native builtin-access addon. Go components are linked at build time and named through the build catalogue.
Exists only because Node caches the real path of every resolved package link, so a moved npm package cannot be remapped without a restart. The Go host maps no package directories.
Describes how linked npm package directories take part in Node's ancestor node_modules lookup. There is no node_modules lookup in a Go binary.
Exists only because a source launch uses an ESM-only Node loader hook while CommonJS requests need built files. Go has one build and no module formats.

The cause is a replay mode that swaps the config file by its basename. The Go launcher has no config-file argument and no swap: a replay run names its replay configuration as an explicit overlay layer, which takes the same path through composition as any other overlay.

Environment files are read once at launch, from the directory the harness was started in and from the harness home; parent directories are not searched and a workspace chosen later contributes nothing.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-BOOT-4 freezes launch facts before the component tree exists, so that a configuration dump shows what actually runs and a directory the model can write cannot change host configuration in the middle of a session. Per-workspace variables for commands belong to the child environment the execution area builds.

reason: The cause is that an id-targeted patch replaces the whole config. The Go layer model has a merge operation that deep-merges into config, so an override states only the fields it changes and keeps receiving the bundle's other fields.

The cause is a split at the first word the launcher does not recognise. The Go grammar splits at the profile name: launcher options come before it and every later word belongs to the app, so a launcher option written after an app option is reported as an unknown app option instead of being silently reassigned, and the launcher no longer consumes a double dash.

The cause is that a service's provider is not declared anywhere static.
