Each catalogue item declares the services its component may provide, so the static check reports, before anything starts and in the preview commands, an enabled entry that injects a service no entry in the composition provides.

The cause is whole-config replacement, which drops the expressions of fields the user did not mean to change. A merge operation leaves untouched fields and their expressions to the lower layer, and an edit that targets a computed field is refused unless the operation says to overwrite it.
A setting changed at run time is written only to the profile layer; the home layer and command-line overlays are read for precedence and never written by the harness.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-LOADER-4 requires exactly one writable layer and DH-ADR-BOOT-2 says which. The cost is bounded: an edit that a higher layer shadows is refused with that layer's name and file, and the other layers are plain files whose hand edits the same reload picks up.

reason: The cause is that the editor stores a complete config override, which pins every field at its current raw value. config.Service writes a merge operation holding only the edited fields, so later bundle changes to the other fields still arrive.

The cause is that only rows of the root include with a unique patch id can be addressed. In Go every bundle entry must carry an explicit id (a build test checks it) and an operation addresses an entry by its path in the composed tree, so entries inside groups are editable at any depth. A preset that runs a tree of its own is edited through that tree's layers, which area A27 owns.

Module replacement through Node loader internals and the loader.exit hook for framework changes exist only because Node can swap modules in a running process. The Go host never replaces code; a new binary is a restart.
A hard link from pnpm's store keeping an older modification time defeats upstream's time-based module comparison. There is no pnpm store and no time-based comparison in Go.

The cause is that a dependency-only manifest change does not trigger recomposition, so an install made outside the manager is not seen. In Go a plugin is an entry in the profile layer: adding it by hand is a layer edit that the same reload applies, and replaced plugin files take effect when that entry is restarted.
TSX loaders and application-created Worker threads are Node runtime features outside upstream's package-cache refresh. Neither exists in Go.
Concerns CommonJS request resolution and synchronous Node resolve hooks. There is no CommonJS in a Go binary.
Future work on keeping Node's package-configuration invalidation across disposal of the hot-reload plugin. The Go host has no package-configuration cache.
Concerns assigning replaced JavaScript plugin callbacks to instances that share a runtime. No code is replaced in process in Go.

The cause is an operating-system notification stream that starts after the watcher reports readiness, so an early write is missed. Layer files are watched by a poll that compares content against the text read at boot, so a write at any moment after that read is seen at the next poll.
Concerns detecting changes to package.json files and the browser client's separate module graph. The Go host reads no package manifests and has no client module graph.
Describes the difference between static and dynamic JavaScript imports, Worker threads and the TSX loader during module replacement. None exists in a Go binary.
Describes how symbolic links under a profile's node_modules widen the set of JavaScript files compared for replacement. There is no node_modules tree and no file comparison.

The comparison records are the per-instance table of loaded JavaScript module files. The Go reload compares the content of layer files only, and that state belongs to the loader's layer source, which a reconfiguration of the reload component does not reset.

Describes a replaced JavaScript module that fails to import after the old one was evicted from Node's cache. No module is replaced in Go. The plugin-process analogue (a restarted plugin that fails stays failed and is reported) is owned by area A22, and a configuration edit with a static error never stops the previous instance.

The compatibility checks compare npm version ranges (engines.dsh and peer ranges) of packages changed outside the manager. First-party components carry the binary's version, and a plugin process is checked by its protocol version at every start, which area A22 owns.
Concerns the packed loader of the in-browser WebWorker preview runtime, which is JavaScript-only and dropped by DH-ADR-17.

The limit comes from comparing file modification times of loaded JavaScript modules against a marker file. The Go layer watch compares file content, so timestamp granularity and clock skew on network filesystems do not matter.

The pending group is pnpm's list of dependency build scripts awaiting approval. No package manager runs in Go, so there are no build scripts to approve; capability grants for a plugin are selected one by one.

The cause is that a start-up-only profile cannot unload modules it loaded, so their package cannot be removed while it runs. In Go a management change always reconciles the running tree whether or not file watching is on. Removal unloads the entry's fiber and deletes the entry; the operator's directory is never changed, and the approved copy and the plugin's state go only with an explicit purge (test DH-T-BOOT-20). A running plugin can therefore be removed in every profile.

The running plugin manager refuses to disable or remove protected entries (required entries and its own components), manages only the profile it runs in, and does not edit an agent preset's composition. The model's own tool changes nothing in a profile at all: it can only attach a plugin to its session.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-BOOT-10 says 'Protected entries are refused', so the management surface cannot remove itself, and that the model-facing tool 'changes nothing in the profile'; owner decision DH-ADR-30 limits that tool to list, inspect, attach and detach. The clause 'manages only the profile it runs in' is not in a record's own words: boot.md section 6 says another profile is managed from the command line, which composes it without a running host. A sentence in DH-ADR-BOOT-10 would close that.

reason: The cause is that an operation spans a package-manager run that writes many files and cannot be undone. A Go management operation downloads nothing and writes one file atomically. An add first lets the extension area make one approved copy of the plugin's bytes in the harness home (DH-ADR-EXT-3); if the write of the entry then fails, the copy is unreferenced, nothing runs, and retention removes it. The only split outcome is saved but not applied, which the result reports as two separate facts.
Browser synchronisation failures belong to upstream's client plugin runtime, which loads plugin code into the page. The Go UI is rendered by the host and has no client plugin runtime.
Dropped by DH-ADR-18 (no desktop application). The limit concerns package operations owned by the Electron desktop shell.

The stale approval is a key in pnpm-workspace.yaml for a git-hosted npm package. That file does not exist in Go; a plugin's grants live in its own entry, are deleted with it, and are void when its manifest digest changes.
The failure is pnpm verifying lockfile tarball URLs against its default npm registry. There is no lockfile and no registry.

Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (plugins come from local directories; no download, discovery or auto-update). The limit concerns how an npm registry update saves version specs and where a reinstalled bundle lands in the bundle order; there are no registry updates, and a profile's bundle order is fixed in the binary (DH-ADR-BOOT-1).

The cause is an update made of two separate profile operations. The Go manager has no update operation: every management operation is one write of the profile layer under one lock, followed by reconciliation, so no other operation can run inside it. The one copy an add needs (the extension area's approved copy, DH-ADR-EXT-3) is made before that write and is merely unreferenced if the write fails. A replaced plugin takes effect when it is added again, because a grant binds to the approved bytes and a different digest is a different plugin.

Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (no plugin download). The limit concerns reachability checks and reinstall behaviour for npm bundles fetched from Git through pnpm; the Go harness fetches and installs nothing from Git.

Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (no plugin download). The limit concerns console prompts and timeouts of the Git transport probe that precedes a pnpm install of a fetched plugin; the Go manager fetches nothing and starts no Git process.
Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (no auto-update). The limit concerns pnpm build-script approval during an npm version update; there are no plugin updates, and no build scripts run.

The cause is that the host itself loads a package's JavaScript, so a replaced package needs a new process. A plugin's code runs in its own process, from an approved copy in the harness home (DH-ADR-EXT-3). A changed directory takes effect when the owner adds it again, which approves the new bytes and runs them as that one entry, in any profile; the host is never restarted for it.
The limit is about icon references in a Git-hosted market index. No index reader is built, so no index icon is ever resolved.
The limit is the fixed list of README file names asked of GitHub and GitLab file APIs. The harness calls neither API for plugins.
The limit is anonymous access to GitHub and GitLab APIs with a clone fallback for private repositories. No repository is read for plugin listings.
The limit is that pages of a cached index document can change between reads. There is no index document and nothing to page.
The limit is about which installed copies a market index can update. There is no market and no update operation; an operator replaces a plugin directory and restarts its entry.
Unsigned index content cannot mislead a harness that reads no index. Signed index content is recorded in DH-ADR-BOOT-11 as a requirement for a later registry design.

The lost update is in the list of index sources, which does not exist in Go. The general cause (two writers replacing a whole list) is removed for configuration by the revision check and the lock of config.Service, and is recorded for a later registry's source list.
The limit is the index reader's refusal of HTTP redirects. No index is fetched; the refusal is recorded as a rule a later registry keeps.

The memory and event-loop cost comes from downloading and indexing a whole market document in the host. No document is downloaded; server-side queries are recorded as a requirement for a later registry.
The limit is about which branch a market entry's README is read from. No market entry pages exist; a local plugin's description comes from its own directory.
The limit is that public npm file hosts do not serve packages of private registries. Nothing is read from npm file hosts or registries.
The limit is a Git server setting needed to fetch a pinned commit for a market entry. The harness fetches nothing from Git.

Upstream's service stores no browser state and leaves session isolation to every provider. The Go browser service owns the table from session to browser, opens one browser per session, runs one call at a time per session, bounds the number of browsers and closes each with its session, so isolation is written once and a provider cannot forget it.
The model cannot switch the browser backend; configuration selects the one provider.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-MEDIA-1 (no tool argument can select a provider, an endpoint or a mode): otherwise the model, or text injected into a page, could select attach mode and with it the user's own logged-in browser.

reason: A custom profile in Go extends a built-in profile and has only its own layer, so it cannot omit the bundle that mounts the ACP server (boot.md, DH-ADR-BOOT-1). The carrier entry wire.acp is on the required-entry list, so a carrier that fails to load stops start-up with a report instead of leaving a client waiting.

No third-party code runs inside the host: plugins are separate processes whose standard output is their own protocol pipe. In the host, standard output is claimed once by area A20's stdio component, logging and the start-up report go to standard error, and a composition test of A20 forces every logger on and checks that every line is a frame.
The acp profile reads its configuration once: an edit to a configuration layer takes effect at the next start, not while a client is connected.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-BUNDLE-1 says in its title that only web follows configuration edits and in its tradeoff that 'Stdio and one-shot profiles need a restart to see a configuration change'. A reload that restarts a spine entry would unload the ACP server and its agents, and the restarted server would have to claim standard input and output a second time. The acp profile is deliverable DH-D-BUNDLE-8 since the split of the fix pass.

reason: A layer operation may merge into an entry's config, so an override changes one field and keeps the rest. The shipped mode layers and the user's profile layer no longer restate whole settings blocks.

The rule that a per-surface default must live whole in the surface bundle followed from whole-config replacement. With merge, a mode layer states only the field that differs (for example headless.yml merges the secret sources) and the shared row stays in core or base.

Upstream's bullet described a Windows-only difference: other platforms granted the real temporary areas, Windows granted a private per-session directory, and read-only granted nothing. DH-ADR-SANDBOX-4 gives every confined start on every platform the session's own scratch directory as a write root and as TMPDIR, TMP and TEMP, also under read-only, and lists the actual paths to the model. The private directory is now the stated contract on all platforms and not a Windows exception.

The conflicting pair no longer exists: area A08 makes the fence part of the one file operation service instead of a second provider that replaces the first. In general, two enabled entries that provide one service are found by the static check from the catalogue's declared provides before anything starts, and reported for that entry instead of failing the profile at load.
A headless run answers one task and exits; there is no interactive follow-up in the same process. A later run continues the conversation with the session option.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-BUNDLE-9 has 'Scope boundary of this record (units bundle.headless.1, bundle.headless.9): dsh headless runs one task, or resumes one session for one more task, and exits; it is not a daemon or a queue, because unattended long-lived work is the web host's job and a one-shot run must end so that its exit status means something'.

reason: The capped projection is not built. Area A24 specifies the JSON mode as every committed session event of the run in area A05's export line format followed by one result line, with no string cut and no event omitted, so the stream is the log.

Area A13 appends a job's settlement before its owner's final flush, the runner of area A24 waits for the agent and its descendants to be idle and flushed, and boot unloads the tree leaves first inside a bound. A job still running at exit is stopped and its settlement is recorded with the cause, so the interval is closed in the log.

There is no separate start-up row that a composition could disable: the headless layer mounts one runner, which parses its own words, and it restates no policy row. A composition that changes the sandbox policy entry merges fields and does not have to re-wire start-up values.

Area A10 changes the upstream rule that only file tools honour extra roots on Windows: extra roots apply to spawned processes as well, so a run with an added directory no longer fails at the first tool call. This document also asks area A24 to check each added directory against the resolved policy before the first model request.

The limit exists because the upstream bundle is an npm package that another embedder could mount without the launcher that provides the exit request. The Go harness is one binary with one way to start a profile, and the exit request is a launch service that always exists.

Register entry U-K2-4, resolved in the convergence round. app-cli.md (the dsh headless row of the command table and the output rules of section 6.2, under DH-ADR-CLI-3) has a headless run write one progress line to the diagnostic stream when the run starts and one at each step start, before any token, naming the step and the model route and holding no model output. Test DH-T-CLI-12 checks that the line precedes the first token of every step. A recommended default the owner has not confirmed.

Register entry U-K2-4, resolved in the convergence round. dsh headless gains the option --reasoning auto|show|hide (app-cli.md, under DH-ADR-CLI-3). The default, auto, writes reasoning to the diagnostic stream only when that stream is a terminal, so a log collector that keeps standard error no longer keeps model output unless the operator asks with show. Test DH-T-CLI-12 checks all three values against a buffer and a pseudo-terminal. A recommended default the owner has not confirmed.
Standard output of a headless run carries only the final answer; intermediate tool output appears only with the JSON option, which prints the complete event log.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the fix pass: DH-ADR-CLI-3 has 'Scope boundary of this record (unit bundle.headless.8): the result stream carries only the result, so dsh headless without --json prints the final answer and nothing else there'.

reason: A headless run refuses to continue a session that was recorded in another working directory, a subagent's session, or a session another process currently holds. (Removed: a session recorded under a preset is no longer refused.)
justification: Deliberate, and all three clauses are now stated in the records' own words: DH-ADR-BUNDLE-9 says 'A resume is refused for a session created in another working directory (its file tools would act on a different tree than the operator named) and for a subagent's session (it belongs to its root); a session held by another process is refused by DH-ADR-12'. DH-ADR-BUNDLE-3 removes the preset clause by composing every agent through a preset.

reason: The sdk profile starts no web server, so file cards and opening a file are the embedding program's job. Narrowed: a web host on the same home lists and shows the sessions an SDK host wrote.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-BUNDLE-1 has 'Scope boundary of this record (unit bundle.sdk-app.1): the stdio profiles (sdk, sdk-minimal, acp) mount no web listener, because the program that started the process owns it and talks over its pipes; a person who wants to watch the same sessions in a browser runs dsh web on the same home' (DH-ADR-12).

reason: Register entry U-K2-5, resolved in the convergence round. The SDK protocol carries an optional timeZone (an IANA zone name) on initialize, with an override on session/create (sdk-acp-typert.md section 6.2). The host validates the name and refuses an unknown one; the clock context uses it as the user's zone, says 'unavailable' only when none was given, and never presents the host process's zone as the user's. The Go and Python clients expose it as an option. Test DH-T-SDK-25. A session driven over ACP keeps the limit, because that protocol has no such field; the specification says so.
A question from the model needs someone to answer it: when the SDK client registered no answerer, the question tool call is settled as unavailable with the reason.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-SECURITY-5 fails closed when nobody answers, and DH-ADR-HUMAN-2 has answerers register per channel with nothing transferring automatically. Whether the question tool should be hidden from the model when no answerer is bound is an open request to the human-interaction area (section 10 of bundle-preset.md).

reason: A schedule fires only while some host process is running on the harness home; occurrences missed while none ran are reported, not replayed.
justification: Deliberate: the product has no background service. DH-ADR-JOBS-7 has a due occurrence claimed in the database and delivered by a process that can write the target, and DH-ADR-JOBS-6 fixes latest-only catch-up. A schedule made in an SDK session is stored in the shared home, so any later host on that home delivers the next occurrence.

reason: A custom profile in Go extends a built-in profile and cannot omit the bundle that mounts the SDK server, and the carrier entry wire.sdk is a required entry, so a carrier that fails to load stops start-up with a report instead of leaving the client's initialization without a peer.

No third-party code runs inside the host, so an inserted plugin cannot write to the host's standard output: a plugin is a separate process with its own pipes. Standard output is claimed once by area A20's stdio component and all logging goes to standard error.

Saved plugin and configuration changes belong to one profile of one harness home, so two embedding programs that use the same home and profile share them. (Upstream's other half, a Python launcher needing Node and pnpm, cannot arise.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-BOOT-2 makes the profile layer the one writable layer, which is shared state by definition. An embedding that wants its own composition names its own profile (one small file that extends sdk) or its own home, and per-launch overlays change nothing on disk (DH-ADR-BUNDLE-1).

reason: The sdk profile reads its configuration once: an edit to a configuration layer takes effect at the next start.
justification: Deliberate, and the same boundary as unit bundle.acp-app.3: DH-ADR-BUNDLE-1 says only web follows configuration edits and 'Stdio and one-shot profiles need a restart to see a configuration change', because a reload would unload the SDK server and its agents and the restarted server could not claim standard input and output a second time.

reason: The minimal profile leaves out the product services (settings, managed credentials, policy presets, telemetry, web tools, the full tool roster) on purpose.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-BUNDLE-2 makes the minimal profile a subset of the full one, so that an embedding or evaluation run gets an explicit kernel and the profile proves the spine runs without product services. Because it is a subset and not a copy, adding one service is one insert in the profile layer. The sdk-minimal profile is deliverable DH-D-BUNDLE-8 since the split of the fix pass.

reason: Reading an image needs a model that accepts image input; with a text-only model the image tool returns an error.
justification: Whether a model accepts images is a property of the third-party model the operator selected, not of the harness. Upstream's fixed storage directory is gone (images go through the attachment store). Whether the tool is hidden when the route takes no images belongs to the filesystem and model areas.

reason: The command registry is part of the core bundle and the minimal preset mounts the compact command, and area A20's SDK protocol runs a recognised command through its query method. An SDK client of the minimal profile can therefore run the compact command; compaction settings are still changed in a layer.

A user layer can only name compiled-in components and plugin processes. Neither can write ordinary text to the host's standard output: host logging goes to standard error, standard output is claimed once by the stdio component, and a plugin process has its own pipes.

The limit exists because upstream's frontend is a JavaScript bundle that must be built before the server can serve it. The Go user interface is rendered by the host from templates and assets embedded in the binary, so there is no separate build to forget.
TLS is something the operator turns on by naming a certificate and key; the harness obtains and renews no certificate. (Removed: a renewed certificate file is picked up without a restart.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-HOST-2 requires TLS or an explicit flag for a network listener and now states in its tradeoff that the harness obtains and renews no certificate and that the operator supplies the pair, because issuing one needs a name, a challenge path and a trust decision that belong to whoever runs the machine. Obtaining one would also add outbound requests and a renewal duty to a local tool (DH-ADR-9).

reason: Area A18 refuses a non-loopback bind at start-up unless TLS is configured or the operator sets an explicit insecure-remote flag, which warns at every start. The web layer leaves the bind on loopback and the flag off, so the external leg is never plain HTTP by default.
The host knows only that it asked the operating system to open a browser, not that a browser window appeared or that it was later closed; the printed URL is the manual fallback.
justification: The operating systems' launchers (xdg-open, open, the Windows shell) return before the browser shows anything and report nothing afterwards; no portable call gives the outcome. The Go host does see a launch token being exchanged, which shows that some browser signed in.

reason: When the harness is started in an SSH session it prints the URL and opens no browser; the user's SSH client or editor must forward and open the address.
justification: A browser started on the remote machine cannot appear on the user's screen; only the forwarding client on the user's machine can open the local address. This is a fact of remote sessions, not a missing feature.

reason: The BROWSER override that chooses the program for the automatic hand-off is taken only from the inherited process environment, never from an environment file found in a directory.
justification: Deliberate security rule: DH-ADR-BOOT-4 forbids a discovered file from setting a launch-only name, among them the names of programs the host starts, so that a file in a project directory cannot choose a program for the host to run.

reason: The web listener cannot be bound to all network interfaces: a wildcard address is refused at start-up and the operator must name one concrete address.
justification: Deliberate security rule: DH-ADR-API-6 lists a wildcard bind among the refused start-ups, because whoever reaches the listener with a launch URL is the owner and can run commands, so binding every interface must never happen by default or by accident.

reason: The lookup trusts a TypeScript type argument because TypeScript erases types at run time. A Go component's config is a struct decoded strictly from its own entry, and no component reads another package's config by name from the browser.

The 300 MiB buffer exists because images travel as base64 inside JSON call envelopes. The Go UI has no such envelope: a form body is bounded by A19's small form limit and decoded strictly, and files and images go through the streamed multipart upload route, which is never buffered whole. This area's upload client sends one file per request from a File object.

Upstream only documents that a plain-HTTP network listener exposes the cookie. The Go listener refuses a non-loopback bind without TLS unless the operator sets an explicit insecure flag, and marks the cookie Secure whenever it speaks TLS; area A18 implements it under the foundation decision cited.

API peers are created by the /connect exchange for scripted callers of the browser RPC gateway. The Go design has no gateway and no such exchange: a program uses the SDK protocol or ACP on stdio, so no lightweight peer record can linger. A browser peer exists per signed cookie and ends on sign-out or expiry.

Upstream leaves revocation to each credential provider and its default provider shares one peer among browsers. In the Go design there is one credential scheme whose cookie carries a browser id, so one browser can be signed out and all can be revoked; the stream client of this area shows the signed-out state and stops sending.

An upload is one streamed request per file; a failed or cancelled transfer starts again from the first byte. Narrowed: files are sent one at a time, so only the failed file is repeated, and files already stored stay staged across a reload and a host restart.
justification: Deliberate, and the same boundary as unit api.session-controller.4: DH-ADR-UICORE-8 uploads a file when it is picked as one streamed request, and DH-ADR-API-8 keeps attachment bytes plain, bounded HTTP. Resumable offsets would need partial objects in a store that verifies a digest over the whole object.

reason: The limit comes from accepting a ReadableStream, which is consumed once. The Go upload client accepts only File objects from an input, a drop or a paste; a File can be read again, so a retry re-sends the same object without the caller creating anything.

A stream has no length, so its progress has no total. Every upload in the Go UI is a File with a known size, sent by a request whose upload progress events carry loaded and total, so each row shows a real fraction.

The Worker is emitted from a function string because the upstream bundler (tsdown) has no separate Worker entry for it. The Go UI has no bundler and no upload Worker: the upload module is an ordinary ES module file embedded in the binary.

The limit describes what re-executing a React plugin bundle does to component state. No bundle is re-executed in the Go UI. The related user-visible concern, that a region refresh must not undo what the user did, is answered separately by the keep and focus rules of the first-party script and by hx-preserve.

Upstream tears the old plugin instance down before the replacement is known to work. In the Go design a region refresh is a request: if it fails, nothing is swapped, the old HTML stays on the page, and a notice offers a reload. On the host a component that fails to load leaves its siblings running and is listed.

Upstream's update stream runs on plugins that can themselves be replaced, so a failed replacement of the carrier ends updates until reload. The Go stream client is a static file that is never replaced in a running page, it retries without end, and before each new stream it asks the state route, which also reports a release change.

Upstream registries capture translated text at registration, so it keeps the old language. In the Go design a registration (a command label, a region title, an island fallback) stores a message key, and the text is looked up in the request's language each time a response is rendered. A test rejects literal text in templates.

Upstream leaves plural rules and bidirectional layout to each language pack. The Go catalogue selects the plural form of a message from the first integer argument with the plural rules of golang.org/x/text, and the shell sets the dir attribute from the language, so a pack supplies data only. Right-to-left styling itself is area C2's use of logical CSS properties.

Revisions from file modification time and size exist because plugin bundles are files rebuilt on disk by the npm build and re-served. Go assets are embedded in the binary and addressed by the SHA-256 of their content; nothing is rebuilt under a running host.

The flat module graph is a property of the browser-side CommonJS module table for plugin bundles. The Go UI has no module graph of its own: the first-party script and each island are plain ES modules that the browser links.

Upstream learns of a new host release only from one stream that can fail for good. In the Go design the release identity is in the state region that every stream connect sends as a baseline, and in the answer of GET /ui/state, which the script requests before every reconnect; the stream client never gives up.

The missing commit is a consequence of launching the host from TypeScript source without a build step. A Go binary always carries its version and source revision in its build information, which is where the release identity is read from.

The limit is about replacing the module bootstrap and package code inside a running page, which exists only because plugin code is loaded at run time. The Go design replaces no code in a page: code changes with the binary, and a page then shows a reload prompt.

The retained response bodies belong to the bundle server and its one-generation tolerance for hot replacement. Go assets are served from the embedded file system with no per-request body cache and no generations.
Source maps of rebuilt plugin bundles are an artefact of the upstream JavaScript build. The first-party script is shipped as written, unminified and without a source map.

The unobserved edit is to an npm package manifest and to Node's package configuration cache. No package manifest describes UI contributions in Go: a component registers its regions, islands and commands in code when it loads.

The cause is the desktop forwarder that rewrites cache headers to no-store. There is no desktop application and no forwarder; asset URLs carry a content hash, so the browser may cache them for as long as it likes.

The one-shot environment sample exists to attach processor, memory and operating-system build facts to every event. The Go design attaches none of them, so nothing is sampled and nothing can time out; the resource is the service name and version, operating-system family, architecture and an anonymous installation id.
The fixed PowerShell queries gather the machine facts of the previous unit. With no machine sampling there is no query for a managed Windows machine to block.

Upstream's switch stops collection but queued records are still exported. In the Go design a sender works only while it holds a permit from area A18's sharing gate, and the permit's context ends the moment the setting is turned off or the off-switch is set, so queued records are dropped, not flushed.

Usage events wait in memory only and no warehouse acknowledges them, so events are lost on overflow, on a failed send and when the host exits; the loss is counted and shown. (Removed: there is no browser-side sender whose failures are discarded.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-HOST-7 keeps every reporting channel memory-only and has it report each batch's outcome, because a durable outbox would keep usage data on disk and would have to be purged whenever consent is withdrawn. DH-ADR-UICORE-9 records usage on the host from a closed catalogue and sends nothing until the user opts in.

reason: The limit is about a native desktop launcher that must wait for the host before it can report its own start. There is no native launcher: the host is the only process, and a start that fails is recorded by the local fatal diagnostic, not by analytics.

Upstream keeps a record in the page for every address ever read. In the Go design the browser holds no records: a held address is an interest in the host's tab record, which is capped per tab, removed when the region is closed and dropped a short time after the tab's last stream ends.

Upstream relies on each provider to honour its abort signal. Sources are now compiled-in Go components, not third-party browser code, and a conformance test runs every state source behind a live region under a leak check that fails if work continues after stop, so the convention is enforced.

The limit describes a same-origin iframe used as a script environment for client plugin code, which exists only because plugins run in the page. The Go design runs no plugin code in the browser; its frames are for vendored island code and carry their own Content-Security-Policy.

Isolation requests, capability matching and plugin placement are deferred features of an environment registry for client plugin code. With no JavaScript plugin runtime in the browser there is nothing to place or isolate; untrusted code runs in plugin processes on the host.

Some key combinations cannot be used as shortcuts because the browser keeps them for itself, so web defaults use longer chords and a few commands have no default key; every command still has a visible control.
justification: A web page never receives a chord the browser reserves (new tab, close tab, settings and others, different per browser and operating system). Upstream's desktop application intercepted keys natively; DH-ADR-18 removed it. DH-ADR-UICORE-6 states that the browser's own keys stay with the browser.

reason: Upstream persists view state as JSON in localStorage, so it differs per browser profile. Preferences that shape rendering are now stored by the host per principal and rendered into the first response, so every tab and browser of that principal agrees; only shortcut overrides stay on the device, by decision.
The bullet is about how the store library is fed to the Vite build and when Immer freezes snapshots. Neither Vite nor the store engine exists in the Go design.
A notice from the vendor account is shown as plain text with two actions (dismiss, open the account section), and a failed poll keeps the cards already shown.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-UISET-7 has 'Scope boundary of this record: a vendor account notice is shown as plain text with two actions (dismiss, and open the account section), and a failed poll keeps the cards already shown, because rendering the vendor's markup or links would mean trusting a third party's content inside an owner's page'. Notices are off by default.

reason: The web view shows a preset but cannot create or edit one. (Removed: an override no longer replaces a preset's whole child list, and the viewer shows which layer supplied each child.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UIWORK-8 states that a preset is chosen for a blank session and inspected, not edited, in this view. Authoring a preset is editing composition, which has one owner and one validation path (configuration layers and the settings forms); a second editor would be a second way to write layers.

reason: Register entry U-K2-6, resolved in the convergence round. The team view gains a read-only message timeline (DH-D-UIWORK-5): what the agents of one tree told each other, across sessions, each with sender, recipient and a link to the message. It is drawn from a new bounded query, Query.TreeMessages in session-views.md (DH-D-VIEW-5), which returns the messages of source agent-message of one tree within the caller's visibility. Tests DH-T-UIWORK-24 and DH-T-VIEW-25. A recommended default the owner has not confirmed.

From the team view a person can interrupt a running member, dismiss a settled one and manage tasks, but cannot start or rename a member, and a member's write scope in a shared checkout is a label marked 'advisory, not enforced'.
justification: Register entry U-K2-6, recorded as scope in the convergence round (a recommended default the owner has not confirmed). DH-ADR-UIWORK-5 and DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-11 state that starting and renaming stay the model's: a start needs a creator agent and its delegation bounds, and a member's name is the ledger's key for messages. Write scopes stay advisory in a shared checkout; a member that must not touch its siblings' files is started with isolation: worktree (DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-12, the owner's resolution of U-K1-3 in DH-ADR-40).

reason: Upstream's shared card leaves scope, identity checks and saved grants to each caller, and application consent reuses it with its own always-allow. In the Go design approval outcomes are the interaction area's closed set, a grant is host state that is logged, listed and revocable and never outlives the session, and the consent kind uses the same card with no grant choice.
The viewer is a host-rendered modal dialog that offers a fit view and an actual-size view that scrolls, plus a download link to the stored original, so zoom and download both exist.

The viewer is a native dialog element opened modally by the first-party script, and a modal dialog makes the rest of the page inert, so Tab cannot reach the page behind it; a real-browser scenario asserts that focus cannot leave the dialog.

Presentation is no longer a set of slot occupants that another package must replace. The product's name and mark are one configuration value (brand.Config) read by every view through brand.Identity, so a deployment changes its identity by configuration.
The canvas whale decoration is not built: it is vendor brand artwork and not a function of the product, so there is no rendering that needs a Canvas 2D context.

The page title is no longer a build-time variable separate from the brand. The shell's title, the navigation header, the about page and the web manifest all read the same run-time value, brand.Identity.

The cause is a persistent script-held anchor that keeps restoring the scroll position during a touch gesture. The Go UI holds no anchor: an older page is one fragment inserted above the viewport and the browser's own scroll anchoring keeps the reading line, so nothing constrains a gesture afterwards.

The running indicator is a vector shape animated by a style sheet rule from the design system, not a 28 by 28 raster animation, so it stays sharp at any font size or pixel ratio and its animation restarts with the element.

Tool additions and removals no longer share the generic context presentation of a developer message: the reading plan gives a tool change its own row kind, and the row lists what was added and removed in full.

There are no local echoes whose order is a prediction. A message is shown only after the host admitted it, and waiting messages are drawn from the host's inbox projection in queue order, the same in every tab.

Paging by window is kept on purpose, but the fallback this bullet describes cannot occur: the turn rail is always rendered by the host from area A06's turn outline, which covers every started turn whether or not its page is loaded, and a jump requests a window around the target turn.

A preview card is a fragment the host builds from the turn outline, so a loaded and an unloaded turn give the same card and an open turn shows its latest committed assistant text. The card stays small by design; that is not a limit of data.

A command's result is not a client notice that needs a live composer to land in: area A17 logs command/run and command/done, and the result is drawn from the log by the stream in every tab, also after the session view was closed and reopened.

The page has no phase vocabulary of its own. It renders area A15's account view, whose closed status set separates states upstream folds into five phases, for example needs re-authorisation from never connected and waiting for credentials from failed.
Account views are derived from configuration and saved grants, not from a live registrant, so an entry that failed to load still shows its account with the failure and a sign-out action.
Opening a page reads host state and starts nothing. A check or probe is an explicit button that calls the fleet once; a test counts the fleet's calls while the section is opened.
There is no account registry to load. The account list is a method of the MCP fleet, and the section shows accounts only when that list is not empty.

No script opens a tab after an answer arrives. Starting an authorization answers a fragment that holds an ordinary link to the authorization address; a click on a link is a user gesture, which no pop-up blocker stops, and the link stays in the page while the attempt is pending.

Dropped by DH-ADR-18 (no desktop application). The limit is that Electron's native menu is not used inside the desktop window; in a browser tab the page menu of DH-ADR-UIKIT-5 is the only programmable menu, and the browser's own menu stays on elements with no target.

The gap came from two kinds of contribution, plain data and React components, of which only the first could be listed. The Go registry has one kind: an item is data plus a request to a route, so every action is in every resolution.
An open context menu belongs to one browser tab and is gone when the tab closes; it is not written to the session log.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-UIKIT-5 has 'Scope boundary of this record: an open menu is view state of one browser tab, gone when the tab closes, and is never written to the session log or any store, because a menu changes nothing by being open and what an item does is recorded by the route it calls'.

reason: The limit is about upstream's registry of view targets in the browser, where a session renders nothing unless a target such as chat is registered and selected. A server-rendered page has no target registry: the transcript is one compiled view at one URL and the Trajectory view is another page. It exists only because of the React client plugin runtime.

Upstream's conversation content takes its session from where it is rendered, so a second conversation cannot be addressed independently. In the Go design every transcript page, body and region route names the session in its URL path, so any panel can show any session the principal may read.
The Continue action is offered after a fixed list of six failure codes that does not follow the provider's configurable retry settings, and continuing after a closed stream may fail again.
justification: Deliberate: a manual action a person relies on must not appear or disappear when an operator tunes automatic retry, and the page says that continuing may fail again. DH-ADR-API-3 states it since the convergence round, as a recommended default: the list is fixed, independent of a provider's retry settings, and a new code joins it by a change to the specification, not by configuration. DH-D-API-5 builds it.

reason: The limit describes one rule of upstream's composer style sheet (a backdrop blur under a transformed layer) that was checked only in Chromium. That style sheet belongs to the React composer and is not carried; the Go page specifies no backdrop blur, and visual rules are the design-system area's, tested per supported browser.

Upstream keeps draft attachments as browser objects, so a reload discards them. In the Go design a file is stored on the host when it is added and the draft, a host record, holds the reference (area C3, areas/ui-chat.md, composer.Drafts), so a reload, a session switch and another tab all show the same staged files. This area's page gives the composer one place and never replaces it from the stream.

Upstream lets every mounted attachment view handle a document-level drop, so one drop reaches two composers. The session page declares exactly one composer place per shown session, and area C3's composer rule sends a drop outside a composer to the page's one main composer and to no other.

Upstream replays the whole loaded window whenever one definition fails during an incremental update. The host renderer contains a failing or panicking node definition or card: that one node is drawn as a could-not-render fragment with the event type and sequence number, nothing else is redrawn, and the stream is not closed.

The limit exists because the desktop application serves pages from a dsh-app scheme that has no file route. There is no desktop application, so every page is HTTP and local images use area A19's session file routes on all pages.

The resolver adds the case upstream deferred: a token that is a suffix of exactly one recorded path, starting on a path-segment boundary, links. The candidate set is the turn's recorded files, so the match is cheap and still never guesses from the text; an ambiguous token stays inert.

The mention resolver takes its candidates from the workspace/changes event, which in area A08's design lists files a shell command created (labelled other) inside and outside a repository, so such a file links without present. A delivery card still needs present, because a deliverable is by definition a declaration.

Area A08's present records a digest and keeps a bounded copy in the blob store. The card says changed since presented or source missing and its download route serves the kept copy, so reopening or moving a session no longer depends on the source file.

Native opening is not part of this view: there is no desktop application. The actions that always exist are the browser's own, preview and download; opening a directory in a host application is area A18's optional openpath component and the card does not depend on it.

In a file comparison each hunk is coloured on its own, so a line inside a comment or string that starts above the hunk can be coloured wrongly, and unknown file types stay plain. (Removed: the 5,000-line drawing cap.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UIWORK-7 draws deliverables from logged facts and stored hunks and says 'Colour is computed per hunk, so a line inside a long comment or string that starts above the hunk can be coloured wrongly'; only bounded hunks are stored with the event. Colouring with full context would need the whole old and new file again. The effect is cosmetic and limited to multi-line constructs.

reason: The review route renders only the bounded hunks area A08 stored for the event, never a file's complete text, and a file outside compareScope or above the bound is listed without content. The route declares the session as its resource and checks that the event belongs to it.

A changed file outside the workspace is found only by the absolute path recorded at the time; after it is moved, opening the current file reports that the source is missing. Narrowed: the comparison and a presented file's kept copy no longer depend on that path.
justification: An absolute path names a place, not a file: operating systems give no portable identity that follows a file when it or its folder is moved, and a path outside the workspace has no root to be made relative to. The card states the condition instead of failing silently (DH-ADR-UIWORK-7).

reason: The directory picker lists directories and creates one; it has no search, no multi-select, no rename and no delete. A prefix filter of the listed level is kept.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the records' own words since the fix pass: DH-ADR-UISIDE-8 has 'Scope boundary of this record: the directory picker has a prefix filter and New folder, and no search, multi-select, rename or delete', and DH-ADR-HOST-8 has the same boundary for the host's browser. The dialog's job is to return one directory path; rename or delete would let a web page change the host's filesystem outside the tool pipeline, and search would walk the whole machine.

reason: Upstream always sends hidden entries and hides them in the browser (packages/client/ui-directory-picker-browse/README.md:79). The Go picker passes the show-hidden choice as a query parameter and the host leaves hidden entries out of the fragment it renders, using the host's own hidden rule, which on Windows includes the hidden file attribute.

An open operating-system chooser cannot be closed from the browser because the wire has no per-request abort (packages/client/ui-directory-picker-native/README.md:80). No chooser is opened on the host: the picker is a dialog in the page, closed by the page, and each of its requests ends with the request context.

The native surface works only for local carriers, and remote or in-process deployments must be composed with the browse surface (packages/client/ui-directory-picker-native/README.md:81). There is one surface, rendered by the host, which works the same from a local browser, a forwarded port and another machine, so no composition choice exists.

On Linux without zenity or kdialog the host silently selects the browse surface even on the desktop (packages/client/ui-directory-picker-native/README.md:82). No helper program is looked for and nothing is selected at boot: the server-rendered picker is the only surface on every platform.

Cascading squeeze, snap and priority matter when several dividers share one axis. The Go dock has at most two panes and one divider, sized by a CSS grid in which each pane has its own minimum and the ratio is clamped between 0.2 and 0.8, so there is no neighbour to cascade into.

Upstream's dock depends on pointer drags that were never tuned for touch. In the Go dock every action (open, close, move, split, merge, focus) has a button, a menu item and a key, and only the divider is dragged; it also moves from the keyboard. The real-browser scenario includes a pass with touch emulation; a real touch device is not covered and that is stated.

The divider is a focusable element with the separator role, its orientation and its three value attributes, moved by arrow keys, Home and End. Split, move and close are commands with keys and menu items. Float does not exist. A lint over the rendered markup checks the roles.

Hashed class names came from CSS Modules. Kit stylesheets are plain CSS: the k- class prefix, the data and ARIA attributes each partial renders, and its component properties are the published contract, pinned by golden files and shown in the gallery.

Only the left sidebar offers pin controls and the choice lives in memory, so a plugin reload restores every entry (packages/client/ui-entry-customization/README.md:68). The navigation column and the side panel's start page each store their hidden entries as a host preference per principal, rendered into the first response, so the choice survives a reload, a restart and a second browser.

Dropped by DH-ADR-2 (not a compatible port): the bullet says that pin values an older upstream client wrote to browser storage are neither read nor written. The Go UI reads no upstream browser storage and has no earlier format of its own.

Create your plugin does not check that the Creator preset exists, so the action can fail after the click (packages/client/ui-entry-customization/README.md:70). The host renders the menu, so it asks the preset registry first and draws the row only when the preset exists and a workspace can be resolved; a failure of the create route afterwards is an ordinary error answer in the notice area.
Entries in the navigation column and the start page can be hidden but not reordered; they appear in the order the product declares.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-UISIDE-9 has 'Scope boundary of this record: entries in the navigation column and the start page can be hidden but not reordered, and appear in the order the product declares, because a second stored order for a handful of links would have to be reconciled whenever a component that contributes an entry loads or unloads'.

reason: The side panel and its More menu exist only on a session page; the navigation column's menu is available everywhere.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UISIDE-3 makes the side panel a host-stored list of tabs that belongs to a session and says 'The panel still needs a session', and DH-ADR-API-8 addresses every file and terminal route through a session for access control. Without a session there is nothing the panel is allowed to show.

reason: The More menus do not list plugins; they hold one link that opens the plugins page.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UISIDE-9 says what each More menu holds (the hidden entries, 'Browse plugins' and 'Create your plugin'); DH-ADR-13 gives the product no plugin discovery, and DH-ADR-UISET-5 shows what is installed, what it asked for and what it was granted in one place, the plugins page. A second list in a menu would add nothing a person can act on there.

reason: The UI offers Download but not Save as, and copying an image needs the browser's clipboard permission. (Removed: the copy no longer depends on the browser decoding the image, because the host serves a PNG.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UICHAT-9 drops save-as with the desktop application that offered it (DH-ADR-18). A web page cannot choose where a download is saved or grant itself clipboard access; the browser's own setting can ask for a location.

reason: Dropped by DH-ADR-18 (no desktop application). The start-up deadline for native downloads and the credential-free clipboard reader describe the Electron download adapter; a download is an ordinary response the browser handles (DH-ADR-UICHAT-9).
After a download the page cannot offer to show the saved file in its folder, because it is never told where the file went.
justification: No browser reports a download's destination to the page that started it; the browser's own downloads list has the reveal action. For a file that already exists in the workspace the host path is known and its open-in-folder action belongs to the area that opens host files.

reason: Dragging a file out of the page into another application works only in Chromium-family browsers; elsewhere the user downloads the file. (Removed: application-local tokens and the unreadable cross-origin image case.)
justification: The web platform has no cross-browser way to hand an original file to another application during a drag; only Chromium implements the DownloadURL drag type. The native path existed only in the desktop application removed by DH-ADR-18 (DH-ADR-UICHAT-9). The scenario records the browsers where drag-out is unsupported.

reason: The cause is a Blob URL owned by the page that is revoked when the transfer ends. The drag now names a durable host URL that stays valid for as long as the object is stored, so a receiver that reads late finds it. Delivery to another application is asserted in a real-browser scenario or recorded as unsupported for that browser.
A session's goal survives a switch to a preset that has no goal tools, and the goal strip can still edit, pause, resume or clear it; the strip now says when the current preset offers no goal tools.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-JOBS-9 has 'Scope boundary of this record: a goal belongs to the session, not to the agent preset that offered the goal tools, so it survives a preset switch and the host's goal service still drives, pauses and clears it; this is a product choice because the goal is state in the session's own log, and a preset only decides which tools the model sees'.

reason: Upstream's strip cannot raise the round limit, so resuming a goal blocked by its limit fails. The goal form edits the round limit through the same checked service operation the model's tool uses, and a goal blocked by round-limit shows that form. This relies on the goal service's edit operation accepting the limit, listed as a request to area A13.

Session-scope registration exists: a completion source registered through one agent's scope context is listed only for that session and is removed with the agent, which is the ordinary cordis scope rule; a local test asserts both.

The split between where a slot's type merge lives and who owns the slot exists because of the import direction between two TypeScript packages and the client slot map. The Go design has no client slots; the menu is a fragment that the composer's own component renders.

Area A19's job output route delivers chunks labelled by channel, and the output panel view gives standard error its own class, so the two channels are told apart. Order across channels stays approximate, which area A19 records on its own unit.

Pane widths and the collapsed navigation are a host preference per principal, written into the generated stylesheet, so a reload and another tab draw the same widths with no flash. Whether the side panel is open is in the URL. A width stays one value per person, not per session, on purpose.

The centre column is minmax(400px, 1fr) in the grid. When the frame cannot hold a 400 px centre beside the side panel, the panel covers the centre instead of squeezing it, and below 768 px the navigation is a page of its own, not a drawer over a column that reserves nothing.

The risk was two separately animated things, the frame's track and the occupant's slide, owned by two packages. In the Go frame only the grid track has a transition; the panel inside it has none, so they cannot move on different curves, and reduced motion removes the one transition.
When a side pane opens or is resized the transcript reflows, and in a browser without scroll anchoring the line the reader was on can move out of view.
justification: Reclassed from platform limit in the re-sweep: a script could keep the reading position, so the limit follows from a design choice, not from the browser alone. DH-ADR-UICHAT-8 makes the choice in its own words: 'this area adds no reading script', and its tradeoff says 'Where a browser lacks scroll anchoring an inserted page may shift the view'. The server-rendered transcript leaves CSS scroll anchoring enabled, so engines that have it keep the line.

reason: The form is rendered by the host with area A17's limits as field attributes, for a message note and for a session remark alike, and an oversized value is answered with a 422 that marks the field and keeps the form open, so the user learns the limit while writing and a remark is bounded.
A rating is a committed log event, and the event stream's fragment for that event redraws the message's rating control out of band in every tab that shows the session, without a reconnect.

The rating control is a partial keyed by message id, not a part of the chat view. The conversation places it in each turn's footer, and the trajectory page (ui-work.md DH-D-UIWORK-1) places it on every assistant-message record; each bar of the timing overview links to its record. DH-T-UIWORK-1 checks the control on the trajectory record.

A model can be chosen before the first message: the picker works on a blank session, and session creation accepts an initial selection, which the agent contract already carries in its create options. Subagent sessions deliberately get no picker of their own; that is a rule of the delegation area, not a missing feature here.

Selection by ids is kept as correct. The unselectable failure row that lasts until reload is removed: area A04 serves the last good listing and then the embedded catalogue, the picker fragment reloads when the model set changes, and a failed provider is a row with a retry that requests the fragment again.

The picker still offers only advertised effort levels, because a free value would fail at the provider. The cause of a missing Effort row is removed: effort levels are catalogue data that an operator can correct per model in the route's overlay, so a model whose adapter reports nothing can still be given its levels.
The composer control and the /model command open the same picker view, so a badge appears on every row in both, and the control's accessible name is rendered by the host with the badge text in it.

An application added to the host catalog stays invisible until both client dictionaries gain a matching label (packages/client/ui-open-in-app/README.md:96). The host renders the menu: a built-in entry takes its label from the message catalogue, and an operator-defined entry from a config layer shows the name the operator gave it, which is data and is shown as written. No entry is hidden for lack of a translation.

Application availability is read once per page, so a newly installed application appears only after a reload and a host restart (packages/client/ui-open-in-app/README.md:97). The menu is rendered from the host's catalog each time it is opened, and the host resolves launchers again on demand after a refresh interval, so neither a reload nor a restart is needed.

File associations are cached per file type for the page, so one file's answer is shown for another (packages/client/ui-open-in-app/README.md:98). The Go design never hands a file to an application on the host, so it asks for no file association and caches none. A file is previewed in the side panel, popped out, downloaded or its path copied.

A file type's first open-with menu waits up to 300 ms for the host's association answer (packages/client/ui-open-in-app/README.md:99). There is no association query: file menus hold only actions the host can render at once (open in side panel, open in new window, download, copy path).

Opening another file menu cancels the previous menu's unanswered association query (packages/client/ui-open-in-app/README.md:100). With no association queries there is no background refresh to cancel.

The reveal action has one label for every platform because the client does not know which file manager the host runs (packages/client/ui-open-in-app/README.md:101). The reveal action is not built: the host opens workspace directories in catalog applications only and never reveals a file, so no label is needed.

Delivery cards keep their own way of opening declared files instead of the shared file controls (packages/client/ui-open-in-app/README.md:102). In the Go design there is one way to show a file from anywhere: a link built by side.Surface.Href that opens the preview kind, so a delivered file and a file in the tree open the same way and no second opener exists.
The default preset is a live field of the permission presets config, not a browser contribution, so the settings page, a layer file and any other configuration surface edit the same value.
Automatic review can be chosen for the current session only, never as the default for new sessions, and it is offered only when the experimental review layer is loaded, behind a confirmation.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the records' own words: DH-ADR-HUMAN-6 has 'Scope boundaries of this record: ... the reserved auto preset of the experimental review layer can never be the default for new sessions, because a default must work in a composition that does not mount that layer', and DH-ADR-UISET-8 says 'auto appears only if the experimental review layer registers it'.

reason: Labels and descriptions of the shipped presets are message-catalogue keys resolved in the request's language, so they cannot disagree. Text an operator wrote for a preset of their own is data and is shown verbatim, by the rule that data is never translated.

Upstream's plan mode is guidance only. Area A13 makes it enforced read-only by default (its decision DH-ADR-JOBS-11: a deny-only guard and a read-only sandbox ceiling), and this area's plan control states whether the mode is enforced or guidance, so a person is never told more than is true.

Upstream's chip sits in the default composer, which a pending review replaces. In the Go design the interaction region, the docks and the composer are separate regions, so the plan control stays visible and usable while a plan review or any other interaction is pending.
Upstream shows no control while plan mode is off. The plan control is shown whenever the plan component is loaded: off enters plan mode through the controller with origin ui, on leaves it.
Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (no plugin download; the plugins page manages local directories, DH-ADR-UISET-5). The limit is a ping race between two npm registries.

There is no installation run and no host log file to point at. Adding a plugin is one inspection and one layer write, and a refusal renders the inspection's problem list in the page, also for a browser on another machine.

No request is tracked in the page. An operation is a short synchronous call whose result is host state: after a reload the list shows whether the entry exists and its status, and the inventory keeps a history of recent phase changes.
The bundle concept is gone. The page lists every composed entry from the inventory and every plugin process from the plugin host, so nothing that runs is left off the page.
A row shows the status with its reason: the failing stage and message of a plugin, or the entry's current diagnostic from the inventory, not only a phase.
The limit is that one pnpm command runs at a time. No package manager runs in the Go harness; an add is one write of the profile layer, serialised by the layer lock for a few milliseconds.

Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (no download or auto-update). A version picker would list npm registry versions; a Go plugin is a local directory with one manifest version, and replacing the directory and approving it again is the only way to change versions (DH-ADR-UISET-5).
Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (nothing is downloaded, so there is no registry to choose). The limit is where the chosen npm registry is remembered.
The limit is that reading the registry configuration runs pnpm and fails on a machine without it. No view or operation of the Go plugins page runs a package manager.

The limit is about which installed copies the Discover tab can update. There is no market and no update operation; the page shows a banner when a directory changed after approval, and approving the new content is the update.

No market detail document is fetched or rendered. A plugin's page shows its manifest and inspection report as escaped text; if a plugin's own README is ever shown it passes area C4's sanitising renderer, which omits raw HTML by rule.

The page requests no remote icon. The content security policy allows images from the host's own origin only, and a plugin is shown with a glyph and its name, so no image host learns the user's address.

The managed transfer (an application token plus a Chromium-only DownloadURL, with native delivery left to the desktop application) is not built. Every image shown is served by the host from its own origin, so a download action and the lightbox's link to the original work in every browser; dragging an image out is whatever the browser does natively.

The patch rewrites one rule of the TextMate Go grammar shipped by the @shikijs/langs npm package when it loads in the browser. The Go design does not use that package: highlighting runs on the host with chroma's own lexers, each rule under a time limit (DH-LIB-SHIKI).

The patch rewrites the match rule of the TextMate Perl grammar from the same npm dependency. The Go design has no TextMate grammars. Whether chroma's Perl lexer mis-colours the same patterns is not known and would be an ordinary defect of DH-LIB-SHIKI, not this patch.
The fish logo is upstream's brand mark and is not carried in any form, so there is no approximation to replace. The Go product draws its own neutral mark as a sprite symbol.

The gap is two atoms with no entry in an external design system. In the Go design the kit is the design source: every partial has registered examples, golden files and a gallery page, and there is no second source it could drift from.

An icon needed a sprite that one plugin put into the main document. The sprite is now an embedded file referenced by address, so any same-origin document, including a framed island, draws icons, and no component has to be loaded first.
The status mark has five states (done, warning, ongoing, error, idle) and no 'active' state.
justification: Reclassed from not applicable in the re-sweep (the Go design builds the same five-state mark), and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-UIKIT-1 has 'Scope boundary of this record: the status mark has exactly five states (done, warning, ongoing, error, idle) and no active state, and a sixth state is added only when a consumer needs one, because each variant is a typed constant that every view, its stylesheet and its accessible name must handle'.

reason: The atoms could not reach the locale, so every feature passed complete labels. A Go template can call the catalogue through area C1's helper in the request's language: the kit keeps its standard labels in its own namespace, and a parameter is typed as a message key or as data, so a feature passes a key, not a translated string.

The frame that shows a command's output replays only line-level control (colours, carriage return, backspace, erase in line, tabs); output from a program that addresses the cursor or switches screens is shown with those sequences stripped.
justification: Deliberate: command output is an unbounded stream of lines, while cursor addressing needs a fixed grid with bounded history; an interactive program belongs in the terminal island, which is a real emulator. DH-ADR-UIKIT-3 states it since the convergence round ('the frame that shows a command's output is not a terminal emulator'), and requirement R2 of DH-LIB-ANSER carries the detail.

reason: A comparison of two texts is bounded: beyond the bound the view shows a coarse whole replacement, flagged as such, instead of a line-by-line alignment.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-DIFF-1 keeps one diff package on the host, bounded by input size, because an unbounded diff of model-controlled text is a denial of service. The bound is now a rule of the two texts alone, computed once on the host, so the same edit always renders the same way and the browser allocates nothing.

reason: Only a fixed list of well-known sites gets its own icon next to a link; every other link keeps the generic globe.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the records' own words since the fix pass: DH-ADR-UIKIT-6 has 'Scope boundary of this record: site marks are a fixed list of known sites shipped in a sprite; a site not on the list gets a generic mark, because fetching a site's own icon would tell that site what the reader is looking at', and DH-ADR-9 has the same sentence. The list is data in the binary and grows by one symbol and one table row.

reason: While a reply is still streaming, a reference-style link or a footnote whose definition arrives later is shown as literal text; it is drawn correctly once the reply is complete.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-REACT-2 sends streaming text as block-level deltas and freezes finished blocks, and says in its tradeoff 'A reference-style link whose definition arrives after its block froze stays literal until the message settles'. Resolving a late definition would mean re-rendering frozen blocks on every chunk.

reason: The host appends the lines of an open fence uncoloured and colours the block once, when it closes; a block above a size limit stays plain (DH-LIB-SHIKI requirements R3 and R4). The page therefore never holds token elements for an unbounded fence, and nothing is tokenized in the browser.

The limit came from one copy handler per React Markdown root. Formulas are host-rendered MathML that keeps its TeX source as an annotation (DH-LIB-KATEX requirement R4), and one copy handler wraps the whole transcript, so a selection that spans messages copies TeX. Header controls of a code frame are excluded from selection by CSS. The handler's placement is requested from area C4.

The cost named here is re-tokenizing a streaming diff on every chunk. On the host an open fence is not coloured until it closes, so a diff fence is tokenized once. Colouring each file's sides by the language its header names, and leaving the body plain for an unknown path, are kept as behaviour.

A very long source line is shown without syntax colours, and a comment or string that opens on it can mis-colour the lines after it. (Removed: highlighting runs on the host and cannot freeze the page.)
justification: Reclassed from platform limit in the re-sweep (audit Q3-3), and stated as a choice in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-UICONV-4 has 'Scope boundary of this record, code highlighting: a source line longer than the cut-off of DH-LIB-SHIKI-R3, and a block above its size limit, is shown as one plain run ... This is kept on purpose, not forced by a platform: highlighting runs on the host for every viewer, so its cost must be bounded per render, and the chosen tokeniser (chroma) backtracks and needs its per-rule time limit', with DH-ADR-15 ruling out a native engine. The loss is cosmetic.

reason: The debt is two version-keyed patches whose rule vanishes silently on an upgrade. In Go the rule that a bare URL ends before non-ASCII punctuation is a configured pattern of the Markdown library with its own test (DH-LIB-MICROMARK requirement R5, DH-T-MICROMARK-3); no file is patched. The behaviour itself is kept on purpose.

A completion source that errs or times out is shown as a named group that could not load, with a retry, and the other groups are still listed. A session mention the caller may not read is refused at admission with the chip marked and the draft kept, so that failure no longer arrives after acceptance and ends a turn.

The bullet describes a client plugin that cannot work when its host provider is not mounted, because upstream's client is a separate program. In the Go design every candidate comes from the host by construction and the browser has no file access; a composition without the file source simply has no file group.

A file mention in a sent message does not follow a later rename or deletion of the file: it shows what was true when the message was accepted. (Removed: the answer no longer depends on the page load; every tab and every reload draws the same thing.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UICHAT-2 fixes what a sent mention shows at admission and says 'A sent mention does not follow a later rename', so that a rendered fragment is a function of the session log alone and a replay draws what the live stream drew. The chip opens the file preview, which shows a missing file as missing.

reason: The session completion source asks area A14's session reference service, which finds sessions by body text through the session search index and not only by id, directory and title.
There is no client roster to wait for. A page is one complete HTTP response, readable before any script runs (requirement DH-LIB-REACT-R1), and a slow region can be a fragment fetched after the page.

Document scopes, Shadow DOM placement and style retention per module are properties of the React renderer that installs plugin stylesheets at run time. The Go UI has no such renderer: stylesheets are static files, and a framed island links the same token stylesheet from its own document.

Suspense and per-entry lazy loading are features of React slot rendering over a client plugin roster. Neither exists in the Go design; an island's module is loaded when its element first appears, by area C1's script.

A delivery row in area A13's table carries a state (enqueued, ran, discarded, skipped, failed), the turn that claimed it and the prompt that was sent. The records view draws each state distinctly and links ran to its turn, whose ending the transcript shows. Rows of a deleted schedule are still deleted with it, by the user's own action.

History stays bounded by days and records on purpose (anything that grows with history is bounded) and the page says so. The byte gap is closed: a prompt is at most maxPromptBytes, so a records page is bounded by RecordsPage times that value, and each record is drawn as a preview whose full prompt is fetched when opened.

A delivery row names its message id and turn, so the record links to a window around that turn in the conversation instead of the session's tail. Deleting a schedule removes its still-queued message when this process holds the session, and the answer says whether it was retracted.

The bullet asks the host to enforce access. Area A13 does: the model may schedule only for its own session, only in a turn a person started, within caps. This view adds what a person needs to check it: each row shows whether a person or the model wrote it and from which session, and every schedule route is owner-only.
