A credential that follows no published format is shown as written, and values after names such as password= are not masked. Narrowed: any value the host's own secret store released is masked whatever its shape.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UICHAT-7 masks on the host at render time by recognised format and by store-released value, and says 'A credential in no published format, and not held by the store, is drawn as written'. Masking by name would hide ordinary values that use the same names and would train users to ignore the masks; a string with no known format cannot be told from ordinary text.

reason: The cause is that masking is attached to one renderer. Masking is now a pure host function that every view printing user-written text calls: bubbles, queued rows, rail previews, titles and excerpts. The editable draft is deliberately shown as typed, and the host warns before sending when the draft appears to contain a credential.
The sent-text view passes a mention's label through the same masking function before it draws the chip, so a credential inside a file mention is masked in the chip; a local test asserts it.

Register entry U-K2-7, resolved in the convergence round. DH-ADR-UISIDE-9 now defines 'room' against the transcript's minimum readable width (the design-system token --frame-centre-min, 400 px) and not its default width, so the session panel docks on laptop widths by narrowing the transcript and is an overlay only below that. DH-D-UIKIT-5 owns the token and the proof: test DH-T-UIKIT-12 fails a dock rule that names the default width, and scenario DH-E-UIKIT-3 expects a docked panel at 1,600 and 1,100 px and an overlay at 900 px. A recommended default the owner has not confirmed. One stale sentence remains: the tradeoff of DH-ADR-UISIDE-9 still says the panel is an overlay on laptop widths.

The client has no per-session fact for the local machine, an SSH host or the sandbox mode, so the Environment section names only the working folder (packages/client/ui-session-panel/README.md:121). The host renders the section and knows all three: it adds rows for the execution world and the sandbox mode beside the working folder.
The sections of the session panel cannot be hidden or reordered by the user; every section with something to show is drawn, in the product's order.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words: DH-ADR-UISIDE-9 says 'Sections cannot be hidden or reordered'; it makes the panel's sections regions and spends the hidden-entry preference on the navigation column and the start page, where the lists are longer. The panel holds a few sections, each of which draws nothing when empty.

reason: The toggle in the trajectory view cannot select the chat view, because the conversation package exposes no view selection to plugins (packages/client/ui-session-panel/README.md:123). Views are URLs in the Go UI, so on a view that does not show the panel the toggle is an ordinary link to the session's chat view, where the panel is.

A session shown in the main body and in an embedded conversation shows its overlay in both, because every chat view occurrence renders the aside (packages/client/ui-session-panel/README.md:124). The panel is one element with one id on the session page's main view; a conversation embedded in a side tab does not declare the panel region.

Concurrent explicit marks have last-processed semantics with no revision comparison, so a delayed read action can clear a newer manual unread mark (packages/client/ui-session-status/README.md:95). Each record has a revision; the mark form carries the revision it was rendered at, and a stale one is refused with the row re-rendered. Automatic acknowledgement still never clears a manual mark.

Separate host processes do not synchronize reading state (packages/client/ui-session-status/README.md:96). Records live in a table of the shared harness home, and a process sees another process's write at the next revision refresh, so every dsh process on one home shows the same reminders. Machines with separate homes still do not synchronize, which is the scope of a home.

A host restart or plugin reload resets all reading state, forgets failed outcomes, and can leave reading commands disabled until a page reload (packages/client/ui-session-status/README.md:97). The read position and the manual mark are stored, and the last completed turn and its outcome come from the list summary folded from the log, so nothing is lost on restart. There is no client reading stream that can end in a terminal error: a mark is an ordinary form post.

Only web profiles run the reading service, so a turn finished under another profile leaves no completion (packages/client/ui-session-status/README.md:98). Completion is no longer observed by a web-only service: it is a field of the list summary that every profile folds from the log, so a turn that ended under a command-line run shows as unread when the web UI next lists the session.

A terminal stream or protocol failure disables reading commands until the page reloads (packages/client/ui-session-status/README.md:99). The page holds no reading stream of its own: marks are requests and reminders arrive as replacements of list regions on the tab's one event stream, which reconnects by itself. A failed request leaves the previous mark and shows the error; the next request works.

Records of sessions unloaded from memory remain until the service stops, because no session deletion lifecycle exists (packages/client/ui-session-status/README.md:100). Sessions can be deleted in the Go design, and the reading component deletes a session's records when it is. Nothing is held per unloaded session in memory. Archived sessions still read as read and offer no mark, which is kept as a rule.

Acknowledgement can run while a settings or auxiliary panel covers the conversation, because main-view retention does not distinguish them (packages/client/ui-session-status/README.md:101). Acknowledgement is sent by the end-of-turn element itself when the browser draws it in a visible page. Settings and other panels are separate pages, so while one is shown the conversation's elements are not in the document and nothing is acknowledged.

The unread marker tells one person whether something finished that they have not looked at; there are no message counts and nobody sees what another person has read. (New: a non-owner gets reminders of their own.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UISIDE-2 defines reading state as a stored position per person, kept 'keyed by principal and session', so each person's marker is their own and no other person's reading is stored or shown. Showing one person what another has read is a different feature with its own privacy question, and no outcome asks for it.

reason: Pending interactions are process-local projections in the browser, so the owning remote must replay an outstanding request after a reconnect (packages/client/ui-session/README.md:48). The browser keeps no projection: the pending interaction of each session is read from the host's interaction registry when a row is rendered, and the interaction state of the event stream is complete on every connect.
Profile and balance are read from the vendor's web endpoints when the account panel is opened; each card can fail on its own, and usage and top-up are links to the vendor's site.
justification: The vendor offers no other interface for these facts, and what the endpoints return is the vendor's to decide. DH-ADR-HUMAN-11 and DH-ADR-UISET-7 bound the cost: nothing is fetched until the person opens the panel, no token rides on the links, and a failed query never shows a manufactured zero.

reason: The limit describes the completion marker of the desktop introduction. That introduction is not built, and first run in Go stores no completion: area A25's setup page computes whether a model is usable each time.
The illustration sets belong to the desktop introduction, which is dropped with the desktop application, so there is no artwork to keep in step with language and theme.

Signing in to the vendor account from the web UI works only when the UI is opened at a loopback address; behind another host name or a reverse proxy the panel explains this, offers no start control, and the deployment uses an API key instead.
justification: The vendor's authorization service accepts only loopback callback origins; that list is the vendor's and cannot be changed from this side. The Go design replaces upstream's generic retry state with an explanation (DH-ADR-UISET-7).

reason: The limit is a conflict between an embedded vendor page and the desktop caption menu. Neither exists: vendor pages open as ordinary links in a new tab.

The card is generated from the config type, so every field its owner marks live appears without a UI change. The composed agents list is not live and is shown as file-only with the layer file's path, instead of being absent.
How the settings page behaves under a phone's on-screen keyboard is not validated: a phone may work, and is not tested.
justification: Register entry U-K2-10, recorded as scope in the convergence round. DH-ADR-UIKIT-3 now states a device floor as a recommended default the owner has not confirmed: desktop browsers are the supported target, narrow layouts are for narrow desktop windows, and behaviour under an on-screen keyboard is outside the guarantee. Owner decision DH-ADR-39 names the supported browsers. The risk is lower than upstream's because settings is an ordinary scrolling page.

reason: A row is still contributed by the component that owns the preference, by design, but a preference no longer disappears when no row was written for it: every live field has a generated card, shown under Advanced when nobody placed it.
The limit is about a badge in the desktop window's caption on Windows. There is no desktop window, caption or desktop update badge; the update notice is a region of area A25's product status.

The written card covers the common fields and a generated fold below it lists every other live field of the route's config type, so timeouts and advanced fields are editable without a hand-written editor.

Removal still deletes a key only when the row can show nobody else uses it, but a retained key is no longer invisible: the credentials list shows every reference with its source and the entries that name it, so an unused stored key can be seen and deleted there.
The custom-endpoint form writes a keyed route on any of the four protocols area A04 drives, the Anthropic Messages protocol among them, so an endpoint of any vendor can be declared from the page.

Register entry U-K2-11, resolved in the convergence round. DH-ADR-LLM-6 gives every vendor entry of the embedded catalogue a display name and optional search aliases, and test DH-T-LLM-9 fails when an entry has none. The provider picker shows the name with the route identifier as secondary text and filters on the name, the identifier and the aliases (DH-D-UISET-4, test DH-T-UISET-11). The picker was already one host-filtered search with the custom endpoint pinned.

Discovery is a method of the adapter seam, and all four protocols of the first plan can list models, so the page asks whichever adapter serves the route and needs no per-protocol code. A later sign-in component answers through the same method.
The list is the runtime's route list, so every registered route has a row. A route that no config entry of the page can edit is shown read-only and names the component that provides it.

The row is generated from the senders registered with area A18's gate. A profile that does not compose the upload component has no such sender, cannot send, and correctly has no row; nothing is shown as present but unavailable.

The card is generated from the composed entry's own config type, so a PowerShell host shows the fields of the PowerShell type, including the ones bash does not have, instead of the same two fields on both.
The page keeps no copy of the route catalogue. The options are read from the model runtime when the card is rendered, and the region is replaced when the runtime announces a change of models.

The menu shows what automatic selection resolves to now, from area A15's availability check for the route, including a provider chosen by an environment expression and the ambiguous case, which is shown as a warning before a tool call fails.

Each provider's availability carries a reason code, such as a missing credential or no signed-in account, and the page shows it beside the billing choice; the host can read the account and key state that the upstream page could not.

Configuration is shared by every admitted browser on purpose. A choice that should differ per browser now has a home of its own: shortcut overrides stay on the device, a layout preference may be declared per platform class, and area A25 has a fragment for what is specific to one browser.

The draft was invalidated because the dialog re-rendered from a store when the command catalogue changed. In the Go design the held chord lives in the kit island; a composition change refreshes area C1's key table but not the open dialog, and the chord is checked against the current table when it is saved.

A shortcut is bound to a physical key position and shown with its US-layout key name, browser-reserved combinations cannot be bound, and only components that are loaded contribute rows to the shortcut table.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UICORE-6 registers shortcuts as host commands, declares defaults 'with physical key codes', and says in its title that 'the browser's own keys stay with the browser'; with no desktop application (DH-ADR-18) there is no other window. Rows from loaded components only is how owned lifetimes are meant to work.

reason: Many sites refuse iframe embedding or need capabilities the sandbox withholds, and disabling the sandbox lets the framed page navigate the application (packages/client/ui-sidebar-browser/README.md:104). The browser tab kind is not built, so no foreign page is framed and there is no sandbox to disable. Links open in the user's own browser.

On the web a popup that escapes the sandbox keeps its opener and can navigate the top-level application (packages/client/ui-sidebar-browser/README.md:105). No page is framed, and every link the UI writes carries a fixed noopener relation, so a page opened from the product has no handle on it.

A later iframe load shows that navigation happened but not the new cross-origin address, so Back and Forward become unavailable (packages/client/ui-sidebar-browser/README.md:106). The limit belongs to framing a foreign page; with the tab kind not built, history is the user's own browser's.

Browsers conceal many iframe failures, so the load-failure notice is best effort (packages/client/ui-sidebar-browser/README.md:107). No foreign page is loaded inside the product, so there is no failure to detect; the user's browser reports its own.

A browser tab's saved title and address survive reloads but page memory, forms and history do not, and saved addresses can hold sensitive query values (packages/client/ui-sidebar-browser/README.md:108). No browser tab state exists and no visited address is stored by the harness.

Local files are rejected by the browser tab and remain owned by document preview (packages/client/ui-sidebar-browser/README.md:109). With no browser tab there is nothing to reject: the side panel's registry has no kind that claims a web address, and a file address is claimed by the preview kind.

The desktop shares storage partitions by workspace directory, loses cookies on restart and denies guest permissions, and its host-address filter is not a private-network firewall (packages/client/ui-sidebar-browser/README.md:110). There is no desktop application and no guest browser, so there are no partitions, leases or filters to maintain.

The preview panel shows files but does not edit them and has no search of its own; a file of unknown type is shown as plain text. (Gain: host-rendered text is ordinary page content, so the browser's own find works on it.)
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the fix pass: DH-ADR-UISIDE-5 has 'Scope boundary of this record: a preview never edits; changing a file is the agent's tools' job or the person's own editor's'. Writing a file is the agent's work through the guarded tool pipeline, or the person's own editor and terminal; an editor in the page would be a second, unguarded way to change the workspace.

reason: How faithfully an office document is previewed, and whether missing fonts are reported (they are not for binary doc and ppt files), depends on the LibreOffice the operator installed; the preview opens no native Office application and downloads no engine.
justification: Conversion fidelity and font diagnostics are properties of LibreOffice, a third-party program, and of its version, which the preview reports but cannot improve. That LibreOffice is operator-installed, never bundled or downloaded, is owner decision DH-ADR-20.

reason: Deep source lines require loading every preceding page, and PDF, HTML and images need the complete file inside the host cap (packages/client/ui-sidebar-documentpreview/README.md:148). The text route takes a line parameter, so a preview opens a window around any line without the lines before it. Images and PDFs are fetched from the byte route, which supports ranges, so the PDF island need not hold the file whole. An HTML file is still filtered as one bounded document.
A PDF page is drawn into a bitmap of at most 16,777,216 pixels, so a very large page, or a high zoom on a dense display, looks softer than the display could show.
justification: Reclassed from platform limit in the re-sweep, and stated as a choice in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-UISIDE-5 has 'Scope boundary of this record, PDF sharpness: each page bitmap is capped at 16,777,216 pixels; ... the cap is kept on purpose, not forced by the browser, because one such bitmap is already 64 MiB of memory in the tab and the cost grows with the square of the zoom, and drawing large pages in tiles would add a second drawing path ... for a side-panel preview whose full-quality route is Download'.

reason: An HTML preview can return to the top when it is reloaded, because the page cannot read or set the scroll position inside the sandboxed frame that shows it. (Removed: host-rendered previews, images and the PDF page and zoom keep their position.)
justification: The browser hides the inside of a frame without same-origin access from the page that embeds it, and that isolation is what keeps a previewed file from reaching the application (DH-ADR-UISIDE-5). Weakening it to restore a scroll offset would trade a security control for a convenience.

reason: A scripted HTML preview gets only the script and stylesheet files it references directly, packed by the host; the previewed page cannot read other workspace files.
justification: Deliberate security boundary, stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-UISIDE-5 has 'Scope boundary of this record: a scripted HTML preview gets only the script and stylesheet files the page references directly, packed by the host, and has no bridge to the workspace, so the previewed page cannot read or list any other file, because a script in a previewed file is untrusted content and the sandboxed frame is the control' (DH-ADR-DOMPURIFY-2).

reason: Every scroll event writes its offset to a client store, and memoized line blocks keep React from re-rendering (packages/client/ui-sidebar-documentpreview/README.md:152). The limit exists only because of the React store and its render cycle. The Go UI has no client store: the first-party script keeps scroll positions in the per-tab store without rendering anything.

A failed PDF chunk load needs a page reload because React caches a rejected lazy import (packages/client/ui-sidebar-documentpreview/README.md:153). The PDF viewer is an island whose module the first-party script imports when the element appears and imports again the next time it appears after a failure; until then the element shows its fallback, a download link.
The files view lists and opens files and searches names and paths; it has no search inside file contents, no artifact filter, no drag-and-drop and no rename.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UISIDE-6 draws a read-only tree, for the reason given for the preview: a rename or a drop from a web page would change the workspace outside the tool pipeline. Content search is a tool the agent has; a person uses their editor or the terminal. Since the convergence round the tradeoff of DH-ADR-UISIDE-6 records the whole list as scope (a recommended default the owner has not confirmed).

reason: A hidden current file is left out of the tree while hidden entries are off, so its row cannot be marked or scrolled to (packages/client/ui-sidebar-files/README.md:114). The host renders the tree and always includes the current file's row and its ancestors, marked as hidden entries, whatever the toggle says.

On Windows the tree hides only dot-names while the host search also hides entries with the hidden attribute, so an entry can be drawn but not found (packages/client/ui-sidebar-files/README.md:115). One rule is applied on the host for both: a dot prefix or the Windows hidden attribute. It depends on the listing carrying a hidden flag per entry, which this area asks of the workspace-file routes.

A query containing a slash highlights nothing, because each name is highlighted on its own (packages/client/ui-sidebar-files/README.md:116). The host renders search results as relative paths and highlights the match on the path it matched, so a query that spans a separator is marked.

An exclusion rule may not contain glob characters, so a literal path such as a directory named with square brackets cannot be excluded (packages/client/ui-sidebar-files/README.md:117). A rule is defined as a literal name or a literal relative path and is never interpreted as a pattern, so any character is allowed. It depends on the search route taking literal exclusions, which this area asks of the workspace-file routes.

Search preferences are read from browser storage once per tab and written back whole, so one tab overwrites another's changes (packages/client/ui-sidebar-files/README.md:118). The preferences are host state per principal and workspace root, changed by a request and rendered into every response, so tabs and browsers cannot diverge.
The files tree starts at the session's workspace root and cannot go above it.
justification: Deliberate, and the same boundary as unit api.workspace-files.3: DH-ADR-API-8 keeps listing, search and watching inside the workspace so that a session's file view is scoped to its project. A single named file outside the root can still be previewed when the session's filesystem backend allows the read.

reason: The layout is saved in the browser's localStorage and does not synchronize between devices (packages/client/ui-sidebar-right/README.md:151). The side tabs of a session and their placement are stored by the host per principal, so every browser and device of that person shows the same tabs; pane sizes are a preference per platform class.
The page with no session selected shows nothing in the side panel.
justification: Deliberate, and the same boundary as unit client.ui-entry-customization.5: DH-ADR-UISIDE-3 keeps the side panel's tabs per session, and files, previews and terminals are reached through a session because their routes are access-controlled per session. Without a session there is no directory and no access rule to draw under.

reason: The content tree uses a fixed stacking layer and floating panels reorder inside it without rising above menus (packages/client/ui-sidebar-right/README.md:153). There are no floating panels and no hand-numbered layers: the side panel is a column of the page, and menus, dialogs and the session panel overlay use the browser's top layer.

A session that leaves the catalog does not retire its retained view; tab lifetimes and plugin teardown own the release (packages/client/ui-sidebar-right/README.md:154). Nothing is retained in the browser per session. The host's side record of a session is deleted when the session is deleted, and its fragments then answer not found.
A change to the side panel's layout cannot be undone with an undo command. Upstream's hidden undo machinery is gone as well: no operation sequence is recorded.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UISIDE-3 states that there is no dock engine and no operation log, and its tradeoff says 'no undo'. The layout is a short list of tabs in at most two panes; a closed preview is reopened from the tree or its link, and a terminal's tab cannot be lost because it is the host's roster.

reason: A tab's title is captured when the tab opens and does not follow later changes (packages/client/ui-sidebar-right/README.md:156). A kind's Title function is called on every render with the request's language, so a renamed terminal, a moved file or a language change shows at the next response.

There is no back and forward over visited content; stepping back replays layout operations (packages/client/ui-sidebar-right/README.md:157). The selected side tab of each pane is part of the session page's URL and a selection pushes a history entry, so the browser's Back and Forward step through the content the person visited.

Starting a terminal can fail because the shell program is missing or the operating system gives no pseudo-terminal; the tab shows the error with a retry and does not start a different shell on its own.
justification: Whether a shell exists and whether a pseudo-terminal can be allocated are facts of the machine at that moment (see unit api.terminal-controller.2). Falling back silently would run the person's commands in a program they did not choose; the shell menu lets them choose another one explicitly (DH-ADR-UISIDE-7).

reason: Completion menus and inline suggestions in a terminal are whatever the user's shell provides; the web UI adds none of its own.
justification: Completion is a feature of the shell program and its configuration. A terminal's contract is that keys reach the program unmodified; a completion engine in the page would have to guess the shell's state and would compete with the shell's own.

reason: Register entry U-K2-8, resolved in the convergence round. The snapshot a terminal attachment receives gains a bounded palette section (execution.md section 6.2, DH-D-EXEC-7): the indexed, foreground, background and cursor colours a program set through escape sequences and has not reset, recorded by the host from the byte stream itself, so it does not depend on what the emulator exposes. The terminal island applies the section before it draws (DH-D-UISIDE-7), so a shell theme survives a tab switch and a reload. Tests DH-T-EXEC-12 and DH-T-UISIDE-16; scenario DH-E-UISIDE-3.

A person's terminal has bounded history, its output is not sent to the agent, a tab has no split panes of its own, and its process is not restored after a host restart. Two terminals can be shown side by side in the side panel's two panes.
justification: Deliberate, and stated for the parts a person meets: DH-ADR-API-7 says a person's terminal 'produces no session event' (so nothing reaches the model), and DH-ADR-EXEC-2 says terminals end with the host. Bounded history is the per-terminal memory limit of the execution area; the absence of split panes inside one tab is not in a record, but two terminals can stand side by side in the panel's two panes (DH-ADR-UISIDE-3).

reason: A failed terminal chunk load needs a page reload because React caches a rejected lazy import (packages/client/ui-sidebar-terminal/README.md:82). The terminal is an island: its module is imported when the element appears and again the next time it appears after a failure, and the element shows fallback text meanwhile.

The bullet records that session state dots are drawn by the ui-workspace plugin because the sidebar shell has no notification sources (packages/client/ui-sidebar/README.md:134). It describes which React plugin owns a piece of rendering in the client's slot composition. The Go host renders the whole row, status mark included, in one view from host state, so the division does not exist.

The bullet records that grouping, ordering, search and row state belong to the ui-workspace plugin and not to the sidebar shell (packages/client/ui-sidebar/README.md:135). It is a statement about package boundaries of the client plugin composition, not a limit a user feels. In the Go design one component renders the navigation column.

Copying the local-build version works only with the mouse, because keyboard activation of the brand starts a session (packages/client/ui-sidebar/README.md:136). The version badge is rendered as its own button beside the brand link, so it is reachable by Tab and activated by Enter or Space, and the brand link keeps its own action.

Only wheel and trackpad gestures cross the boundary between the navigation and the session list in one gesture, and the split runs in JavaScript on the main thread without smooth scrolling (packages/client/ui-sidebar/README.md:137). The Go column has one scroller with a sticky toolbar instead of a list scroller nested in a viewport, so every input device scrolls it natively and no script splits a gesture.
A card is found by the tool name in the logged call, and history pages are aligned to turns, so a result is always drawn with its call. The skill card is registered globally and needs no live agent.
A skill reference in a message is plain text: a name typed by hand is the same reference as one picked from the menu, and the host judges the text that was sent.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-UICHAT-2 makes a chip's identity its canonical mention text and says 'A typed or pasted token becomes a chip only when the host next renders the draft'; DH-ADR-UISET-9 says 'A reference stays text, by A14's rule' and draws a skill call from the log alone. A model request must be rebuilt from the log as it was sent, so a chip must not become a second truth beside the text.

reason: There is no prewarmed browser cache to race. The menu is a host fragment computed from the skill registry for each request, so the first keystroke already lists the skills.

Nothing is cached in the page. Area A14's filesystem provider watches the skill directories and announces a change, and the skills region of an open session is replaced then; the next menu request reads the registry anyway.
Highlighting no longer depends on a browser-side lexicon that can be emptied. Area C3's host computes the spans of a draft from the current registry whenever the draft is saved or rendered.

The linear scan is in the TypeScript ledger that answers whether an entry is live. The Go registry keeps contributions in a map by region and removes each through its own effect cleanup, so liveness is never searched for.
The phantom type member exists to make TypeScript compare generic method signatures strictly. Go has no counterpart; region ownership is checked at load by the registry.

The tree draws the latest run of each member with the stop reason area A12 records (completed, aborted, error, max-tokens, refusal, start-failed, interrupted) and its run id, so a failure no longer looks like an idle child. An owner can interrupt any running member from the tree, not only through a continuable child's composer.

There is no per-level client cache to prepare. The breadcrumb menu is the same host-rendered tree fragment, fetched when opened by pointer or keyboard alike, read from the ledger in one bounded request.

Discovery is not a sequence of client reads that one rejection can cut short. The tree is one read on the host; a failed read is an error panel with a retry, and after a reconnect the region is re-sent whole as a state baseline.

The section is drawn from the whole tree of the root, so a member with children shows them without anyone having opened its conversation first. The page size bounds the read, and deeper levels are part of the same nested list.

The cause was that display labels can repeat. The Go ledger holds a short name unique among one creator's children, and the path of names is unique in the tree. The at-sign source inserts that path, which is what the model's send_message accepts, so the reference identifies one member; it grants no authority by itself.

A theme is registered by a compiled-in component and validated: every token it names must exist, every value must parse as a colour, and an icon replacement must be a well-formed symbol. It is an overlay on the complete built-in values, so it cannot be incomplete; a test checks that every alias has a light and a dark value.

The statement is a governance rule, not a defect: the token file is the only place a colour is defined. The Go design keeps it and enforces it with the stylesheet check, which rejects a literal colour or a static step outside the tokens layer, so a new colour is always a reviewed token with both scheme values.

File-type, site, artwork and brand symbols were inline SVG in components and so could not be replaced. In the Go design every icon family is a symbol in an embedded sprite file, and a registered theme may replace any symbol by id.

Upstream produces one level of nested calls because run_code is excluded from its own bindings. There is no run_code in the Go design; a script calls tools through the tool command line and each nested call is logged with its parent, so the card frame draws children under their parent to whatever depth the tool pipeline's bound allows.

Dropped by DH-ADR-2 and DH-ADR-11: the store reads no upstream session format, and the deferred importer converts only upstream's current format, so nested calls recorded by older upstream builds without presentation metadata are never drawn.

Upstream keeps the first-party tool views in the one client package. In the Go design the component that owns a tool registers its card by tool name in the card registry; only the frame and the six closed kinds live in the conversation area.

Upstream's tool views get no link callback, so their links ignore the link-opening setting. Every link in rendered content and in a card is written by one helper of the render package with fixed attributes, and with no embedded browser pane (DH-ADR-18) there is one behaviour for an external link everywhere: a new browser tab.

Upstream's tool copy lives in another package's dictionary. A card registered by a tool's owner uses message keys of the owner's own catalogue namespace, and the frame's own text is in this area's namespace, each with English and Chinese complete.

A tool-change record opens to one line per added and per removed tool, each with its schema as of that request, instead of a comma-separated list; a message with tool changes and other content shows both parts. The detail is a fetched fragment, so the length of the list costs nothing in the row.

An in-flight record shows its recorded start time and the elapsed time since it, labelled as elapsed and never as a duration, and the overview keeps a start tick. Selection is no longer local: the selected record, turn and filter are in the URL, and every record has a link that opens a window around it.
A half-typed answer to a question is kept in the browser tab where it was typed; another browser or device sees the question, which is host state, but not the unsent answer.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the records' own words: DH-ADR-UICONV-7 says 'Unsent question answers are fields marked data-draft, kept by C1's per-tab store, so another browser sees the question and not the draft', and DH-ADR-REACT-1 lists unsent question answers in the small per-tab store. Saving each keystroke on the host would cost a request per pause in typing and need a merge rule for two people answering one question.

reason: Upstream shows one request in the composer seat and reveals the next only when it resolves. The interaction region lists every pending approval and question of the shown session in ask order, each with its own form.

Upstream shows a pending question only in its own session's composer. The interaction stream event carries the pending items of every session the principal may answer, so the region also names other sessions with something waiting and links to them, and the attention stream raises a notification when no tab shows the session.
In area A11's design the workflow service is the only way to create a run and it writes the run record itself, whoever called it, so there is no run without a record for the node to draw.

The log now carries the missing fact. On resume the lease holder appends member endings with outcome unknown and a run end with stop reason interrupted, and a background run is a job that settles with host-exit. The node draws those and never shows a lost run as running.

A member row links to the child's stored session at any time. A session page needs no live agent in the Go design (area A19 reads it through the store), so a finished member opens read-only; a deleted child shows as missing.

The run detail shows what the run record holds: interpreter, limits, sandbox facts, the script from the hosting call's logged arguments, each member's outcome and usage, stop reason, cause, exit status and cleanup, with live narration. The control is the one that fits: cancel the turn for a foreground run, kill the job for a background one. Static topology does not exist because the host never parses a script.
Searching the content of sessions matches literal words and phrases; a misspelt query finds nothing. (Removed: a result now opens the session at the matching event.)
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-VIEW-5 has 'Scope boundary of this record: session search matches exact tokens, prefixes and literal substrings, and does not tolerate typing errors; this is a product choice because stock FTS5 has no fuzzy matching, a spelling index would add a second index and a custom extension, and exact matches give results a person can predict'.

reason: Sessions can be archived but never deleted, and deleting a workspace registration does not delete its sessions (packages/client/ui-workspace/README.md:292). The Go store can delete a session and the remote surface has an owner-only delete route; the row menu offers Delete behind a confirmation that names what is removed. Removing a workspace still leaves its sessions unless the person asks for the cascade.

A waiting row inside a collapsed group lights no indicator on the group header (packages/client/ui-workspace/README.md:293). The host renders the group header and knows the status of every session in it, so a collapsed group shows a count of sessions that wait for the person, and the header region is replaced when that count changes.

Register entry U-K2-9, resolved in the convergence round. The session list and the search results are marked for the design-system area's navigable-list island (k-list, in the widget table of ui-kit.md under DH-ADR-UIKIT-3): one row is in the Tab order, Up and Down move, Home and End jump, Right and Left open and close a workspace group. Without script every row is still a native link reached by Tab (DH-D-UISIDE-1). Test DH-T-UISIDE-1 checks the marking, and scenario DH-E-UISIDE-1 walks the list with the keyboard alone.

Under the native composition a remote or in-process browser cannot open a folder dialog, so adding a workspace depends on which picker package was composed (packages/client/ui-workspace/README.md:295). There is one picker, rendered by the host, so adding a workspace works from any browser and does not depend on composition.

Upstream reports an optional plugin's boot failure only in the browser console. In the Go design a component that fails to load is a failed fiber on the host; the shell contributes a notice for the owner that names the count and links to the inventory, and the page itself renders without that component's regions.

The Go command waits for the agent to become idle by default and then runs the compaction as a maintenance task; a caller may ask for an immediate compact/busy error instead. The wait is cancellable and queued prompts keep their order.

The command registry is host-side with one parser, so arguments no longer vary by adapter: /compact takes an optional focus text, which is logged in compaction/request, and keep=N to keep the last N turns verbatim. Arbitrary ranges stay the programmatic Engine.Region call.

Commands are a host service, not a client adapter, so the HTML UI, the SDK protocol, ACP and the command line reach the same /compact, and Engine.Now is a plain service call. It depends on areas A17, A20 and A24 exposing command invocation.
The compaction trigger rests on an estimated token count, not an exact one.
justification: Deliberate boundary inherited from DH-ADR-LLM-9 (the meter is a deterministic fold with no model call). DH-ADR-CONTEXT-4 bounds the effect: the threshold keeps headroom below the window, and provider-confirmed overflow recovery is the backstop.

reason: The summariser has an ordered route list (configured, answering route, latest header, the session's selected route). On a permanent failure of a candidate the engine moves to the next one only if it is the route the user selected for this session, and records the reason in compaction/request, so revoked credentials on the old model no longer block compaction.

A span whose estimate exceeds the summarising route's window is cut at balanced edges and summarised left to right, each call receiving the previous partial summary; nothing commits until the last call succeeds.

Classification stays with area A04 as a closed repairable failure code checked by a driver conformance table. This area adds a second signal so that changed provider wording does not disable recovery: a rejected request while the calibrated estimate is at least 95% of the window is treated once per step as a suspected overflow, logged with that trigger and bounded by maxOverflowRetries.
A system prompt plus tool list that alone approaches the context window cannot be shrunk by compaction.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-4 (the system prompt node is never in a span): compaction acts on history, and the envelope is fixed by composition. The engine reports compact/envelope-too-large with both sizes. The single-oversized-unit half of the upstream bullet is removed by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-5.

reason: Engine.Region runs inside the caller's open turn or, on an idle agent, as a maintenance task; the owner recorded on compaction/start is the turn number or none, so a fully closed session can be compacted by range.

The surface is still left as it was on failure, which is the intended fail-safe, but failure is no longer only a warning: each failed call is a compaction/attempt event and a UI notice, the summariser uses the lowest reasoning effort so hidden reasoning cannot consume the output cap, and after maxConsecutiveFailures on one route the engine stops paying for a failing call at every step.

One price basis is chosen when the reduction is planned (the destination route for a model switch, the committed route otherwise) and is used both to select the span and to check that the summary is smaller, so a useful summary is not rejected by a second price.
An offloaded image stays offloaded when a budget grows or history shrinks.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-6 (an offloaded image is never restored automatically): automatic restore would make the model-visible image set depend on unlogged request preparation. The placeholder names a read-only path, and reading it creates a new logged occurrence.

reason: Where the route's catalogue entry declares an image budget, the offload is planned at the proposed step before the request is sent, so no attempt fails; the provider's rejection remains the signal only for a route with an undeclared budget. It depends on area A04 publishing the budget.
A route with a small image budget, used briefly, offloads images for the rest of the session.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by the tradeoff of DH-ADR-CONTEXT-6 (a brief small-budget route offloads for good): an omission, once logged, holds for every later request. The image bytes are kept and can be read again.

reason: Prune budgets are character counts, not token counts.
justification: Deliberate boundary: a character budget makes pruning a pure, idempotent function, which a token estimate that moves with calibration would not guarantee. DH-ADR-CONTEXT-6 now states it in its tradeoff (prune budgets are counted in characters, not tokens, by this decision).

reason: Pruning keeps the head and the tail of a tool result without judging which middle lines matter.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by the tradeoff of DH-ADR-CONTEXT-6 (pruning is syntactic): a reduction without a model call cannot rank lines. The marker states how much was removed and where the full text is, and the original stays in the log.

reason: A prune cut can still split a grapheme cluster in rare cases.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-6: a cut snaps to a line boundary where one lies inside the budget and is otherwise never placed before a combining mark, a variation selector or a joiner. Full Unicode segmentation is not a platform limit, only a module the design chose not to add for a cosmetic gain; the original text is in the log.

reason: There is no model-facing compaction tool; people compact through the command and pressure triggers it automatically.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-4 (there is no model-facing compaction tool): a model that could compact at will could discard history the user relies on. DH-ADR-CONTEXT-10 gives the model read-only recall of compacted spans later.

reason: Tool results are bounded before they enter history and prunable afterwards, and a single non-tool unit that is still too large for the summariser is summarised from a pruned view of its text and replaced by that summary, with the original in the log.
A system prompt plus tool list that alone approaches the window is reported, not compacted.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-4, the same as unit compaction-basic.5; deferred tool disclosure in the tools area is the mechanism that shrinks a tool list.

reason: Upstream lets concurrent sessions and separate processes operate one desktop and tells callers to coordinate. The Go computer-use service takes a desktop lease for the length of a session's turn, held as a kernel file lock in the user's runtime directory, so a second session and a second dsh process of the same user get computer/busy instead of interleaving input. The user and programs that are not dsh still share the desktop, which the bullet did not cover.
The model cannot switch the computer-use driver; configuration selects the one provider.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-MEDIA-1: which software controls the user's desktop is an operator decision and never a tool argument (see also owner decision DH-ADR-19).

reason: The wait-for-user deadline and the standard-output limit become fields with the upstream values as defaults, and a registration may set its own.
commandTimeout is the default for every registration and each registration may override it.
An authorisation host pattern is exact by default and matches subdomains only when written with a leading wildcard label.
A registration may add an error code to a failure; the service accepts it only if it matches a short closed character set, so no credential text can travel in it.
The cost exists because npm loads a package at boot whether or not anything uses it; a compiled-in Go component with no registration holds no process, file or prompt text.
The model is told a vendor CLI's absolute path but nothing enforces it; a command that names the CLI by bare name runs whatever PATH resolves.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONNECT-10 (the harness changes no command environment): a private PATH would hide the user's own installation. A hint with the registered path follows a shell result that failed to find the bare name (DH-D-CONNECT-9).

reason: The runtime-context text is rendered for each shell dialect that the agent's tools provide, read from the shell registry, not from the host platform.
Account views are computed from configuration and saved grants, so a grant whose connector is turned off is still listed and can be signed out.
The mcp component is in the base bundle of every profile, so a connector activates in headless and SDK compositions and uses a saved grant there; sign-in is also offered from the command line.

The callback is a fixed path under the host's configured public address, so a browser on another machine can finish authorisation when the operator serves the host over HTTPS there; loopback stays the default.
There is no desktop application with a per-launch port (DH-ADR-18), and a new dynamic client registration replaces the stored record instead of accumulating beside it.
The resource tools and their server-name text list only servers that are connected and advertise resources, so an unconnected Linear is not named.
A connector preset can be instantiated more than once under different names, each with its own credential record and tool namespace, so two workspaces can be linked side by side.
A paid Linear workspace can require an administrator to approve the application before a user can grant access.
justification: Third-party fact: it is a policy of the Linear service, documented by Linear, that no client design removes. The account view shows the service's refusal so the user knows to ask an administrator and connect again (DH-D-CONNECT-4).

reason: Sign-out asks the authorisation server to revoke the grant where its metadata offers a revocation endpoint, reports whether that was accepted, and deletes the local grant either way; a grant of a disabled connector stays listed for sign-out.
Account views are computed from configuration and saved grants, so a grant whose connector is turned off is still listed and can be signed out.
The mcp component is in the base bundle of every profile, so the connector activates outside the web composition and uses a saved grant there.
The callback is a fixed path under the host's configured public address, so a browser on another machine can finish authorisation when the host is served over HTTPS there.
There is no desktop application with a per-launch port (DH-ADR-18), and a new dynamic client registration replaces the stored record.
The resource tools and their server-name text list only servers that are connected and advertise resources, so an unconnected Notion is not named.
A connector preset can be instantiated more than once under different names, each with its own credential record and tool namespace.
Sign-out asks the authorisation server to revoke the grant where it offers a revocation endpoint and reports the result; the local grant is deleted either way, also for a disabled connector.

Loading never needs the network: a skill set is installed by an explicit operator command or given as a local directory, and a set that is not installed is reported with the command to run instead of a failed state.
The skill-set component registers a retention step that removes digests no registered set names and staging directories whose writer is gone.

A manifest of paths, sizes and digests is written with the files and checked at load, and a verify command recomputes it; a changed or missing file makes the set not installed instead of silently listed.
The archive reader keeps the executable bit of a regular file and nothing else of its mode, so a vendor script stays runnable.

It describes the node-tar library failing to load in the experimental browser-worker preview of the JavaScript host. That preview runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-17, and the Go host reads archives with the standard library.
A change of directory that begins and ends inside one shell command triggers no discovery of nested instruction files.
justification: Fact of shells: what a command does inside the shell process is seen by no observer outside it. The lasting case that the review tracked as U-K1-10 is removed by the design: a persistent shell's end line carries its working directory (DH-ADR-EXEC-6), the tool result has a cwd field, and a changed cwd is a trigger in DH-ADR-CONTEXT-2 (DH-D-CONTEXT-2, test DH-T-CONTEXT-6). A shell call's working-directory argument also counts as a touch.

reason: Loaded instruction files are watched through the shared watch service, and a notice marks the file for reconciliation at the next proposed step. Where watching is unavailable (polling mode, a remote workspace) loaded files are checked by metadata at each proposed step.
Lower-case file names, rule directories and @path imports are not interpreted in instruction files.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-2 (no @path imports, no rule directories): an import would let a repository file pull arbitrary paths into the prompt. Other file names are available through the candidates configuration field.

reason: De-duplication is by content digest across the whole rendered chain, and the state is a registered fold holding one digest per path; a file is hashed again only when its size, time or identity changed, so the cached-metadata special cases are gone. A copy that has drifted is different content and renders, which is correct.

Failure is contained per file: an unreadable candidate keeps its own last-good digest and gets a diagnostic, while the other files of its group reconcile normally, so one unreadable root no longer postpones a notice for another.

A file dropped by the budget stays tracked as omitted with its digest and is evaluated again at every reconciliation; when room appears it is added as an additional-instructions message without rebuilding the baseline.

A project-chain candidate is resolved through the filesystem seam's rooted handle; if the target lies outside the project root it is refused, never read, and reported. Only the user's own global files may link elsewhere.
Instruction text is bounded and truncated, never summarised by a model.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-2 (no summarising of instruction text): summarising would add a model call to every session start and make the guidance differ from the file the user wrote.

reason: Each chain is guaranteed maxBytes and the bytes one chain leaves unused are lent to the other, so a large user-global file is no longer truncated while the project chain is nearly empty; neither chain can push the other below its floor.

Candidates are listed through the filesystem seam of the session's workspace, the same seam the read tool uses, so local, sandboxed and remote workspaces each see their own namespace; the separate host-local provider is merged away.
The file-mention index is bounded and omits excluded or unreadable directories.
justification: Deliberate boundary required by outcome DH-O-14 (anything that grows is bounded) and narrowed by DH-D-CONTEXT-4: ignore files shrink the index, a query with a slash lists the live directory whatever the bound, and the result carries a truncated flag. DH-ADR-CONTEXT-9 now states it (the file-mention index is bounded by this decision and says when it is incomplete).

reason: The harness's own file mutations update the index from the fs.Observed notice of area A08, so a query right after a write sees it; changes made outside the harness are picked up by the background rebuild.
Discovery applies the workspace's ignore files through area A08's rule evaluator (respectIgnoreFiles, default true) in addition to the configured directory names.
The service no longer has a namespace of its own: the one implementation reads through the workspace's filesystem seam, so a candidate is by construction a path the read tool can open.
A mentioned file is text; its content enters the conversation only when the model reads it.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-9 (a file mention stays text): content then arrives as a logged tool result under the read tool's bounds. A user who wants content attached uses attachments.

reason: A release that changes system-prompt text rewrites the first system message on routes that cannot take an in-history prompt update.
justification: Fact of model provider interfaces: the system prompt is the head of every request, so changing it changes the prefix a provider caches, and only some protocols accept a prompt update inside history. The package itself is not built (DH-ADR-CONTEXT-3); the rewrite is a logged new request series, and no per-process value may enter the prompt (DH-ADR-CONTEXT-1).

reason: No Go session has a per-process value in its system prompt, and the Go store reads no upstream session, so there is no earlier format whose values could persist for a session's lifetime.
The two sections are not built, so no binary can differ from another in having them; several hosts on one home assemble the same prompt sections.
The two sections and their runtime-context lines are not built, so no persona can keep guidance that points at values its requests never carry.
The sections are not built, so a resumed session has nothing of this kind added to its prompt.
No projection that recognises earlier prompt wording is built, because no Go session holds an earlier wording and upstream sessions are not read by the store.
Candidates accepts a mode: title, the default, or text, which uses the session search of area A06 over message bodies. Body search is scheduled at P2 inside the same deliverable.

In the Go store a title is a list column committed with its events (area A06), so every stored session has a label without folding a log, and no session lacks one for having been written before a cache existed.
Candidates and Prepare take the admitted caller's principal and apply the access filter, so a non-owner sees and captures only sessions it may read; the service is still not a model-facing tool.
Only the text of user and assistant messages crosses from one session into another.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-9 (tradeoff: images and tool results do not cross sessions): tool output from another session is the least trustworthy content to import.

reason: A session reference is a snapshot, not a live link.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-9 (a reference is a pointer or a snapshot, never a live link): the snapshot in the target's log keeps its replay independent of the source session.

reason: A truncated capture is saved as plain text, each message under a header carrying a per-capture boundary token and with its own line breaks kept, so a literal phrase is searchable except across an original line break; reference-aware retention in area A07 keeps the file while a session event cites it.

Clock state is a registered fold of fixed size: the last reading, the last model-visible message time and the current turn's zones up to maxZonesPerTurn, after which the turn counts as mixed. A proposed step always concerns the driver's current turn, so the full-prefix scan fallback does not exist.
The time-zone reading guides interpretation; it never fills another tool's zone argument.
justification: Deliberate boundary: a tool that needs a zone must receive it explicitly so that the logged arguments say what was scheduled. Stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-11 (no tool takes a hidden zone argument; recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: A turn holding prompts from different time zones tells the model to ask instead of guessing.
justification: Deliberate boundary: guessing which zone owns an unqualified time is the error this context exists to prevent. Stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-11 (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: A zone the user set in settings, or one an SDK client sends with the message, is authority when no browser zone is present; only the process zone remains a display fallback under the ask policy.
Clock readings show whole seconds.
justification: Deliberate boundary: sub-second digits cost tokens in every reading and no tool consumes them; event times in the log keep full precision. Stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-11 (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: Clock readings accumulate in history between compactions.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by the tradeoff of DH-ADR-CONTEXT-1 (context costs history tokens until compaction): history is append-only so that the provider's prefix cache stays valid. The cost is bounded by the ten-minute default interval and by mounting the contributor only where it is used.

reason: The terminal location is read on the first step of a turn only.
justification: Deliberate boundary: a reading costs a process start and a pane rarely moves inside a turn. Stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-11 (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: Only the agent's own pane location is reported; the text of sibling panes is never read.
justification: Deliberate boundary and a guarantee: sibling panes may hold secrets, which outcome DH-O-7 keeps out of the log. Stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-11 (the host's own pane only; recommended default, not confirmed by the owner) and pinned by a test.

reason: The pane layout tree is reported, not pixel sizes.
justification: Deliberate boundary: sizes change on every resize and would defeat the rule that an unchanged location adds no message. Stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-11 (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: The command asks tmux for fields joined by the ASCII unit separator, and the contributor rejects that character inside a field, so a window name cannot mis-split a reading.
Detection of a tmux pane relies on the POSIX controlling terminal; on Windows the contributor does nothing.
justification: Third-party and operating-system fact: tmux does not run natively on Windows, and matching the controlling terminal is the only way to exclude a terminal that merely inherited tmux's environment variables. The contributor is off by default (DH-ADR-CONTEXT-3 keeps it at low priority).

reason: The default is no longer one per process: the driver finds the default-model service through the agent's scope, so a preset composition can mount its own instance.
Saving no longer depends on an optional editor: Save writes to the loader's one writable layer, which every profile has, and a failed write is returned as an error instead of being a silent no-op.

The batch contract lets a tool classify a call as parallel with read or write resource keys, and the scheduler treats a key conflict as a barrier, so safety that depends on a sibling call no longer forces exclusive. The executor is area A03's; the spec says to reopen this row if A03 keeps a unary classifier.

Teardown flushes the session within a bound before the write lease is released, and the driver component injects the store so the tree keeps it alive until the driver's cleanup returns; a flush failure is returned with the last durable seq.

A closed step with an unanswered call cannot be written: the missing results and step/end are one atomic batch on the step's single close path. No older inconsistent logs exist because the Go store reads no upstream session.

Every configured agent has a required start field (fresh, resume-or-create or resume) with no default, so a new session at every start is a written choice and resume-or-create derives a stable id from the label.
A configured agent may name a preset, which gives it its own persona, prompt sections and tool set through the same scoped composition a programmatic creator uses.
The driver has a built-in budget: steps per turn (default 500), attempts per step (default 8) and an optional time limit; a step limit ends the turn between steps with reason budget.
There is no PTC runtime for a preset to wait for: the owner decision replaces the guest runtime with an external command line, so the pending-selection state cannot occur.

Identity is a serialisable agent reference (session id plus incarnation) that each boundary carries and resolves on arrival; a child process gets it through the call token, so crossing a boundary has one stated mechanism.

The context carries a reference and not the live object; Registry.Resolve fails for a disposed or replaced agent, and the context itself is cancelled when the agent leaves, so stale identity cannot be used as a live agent.
WaitIdle and Dispose called from inside that agent's own Created dispatch return an error at once, so the documented deadlock becomes an immediate, testable failure.
Cancel takes a required inbox choice (Keep or Discard) and a scope (Turn or Step); a step-scope cancel closes the step with paired results and lets the turn continue when steering is pending.

The driver never merges messages, and the design requires a message source with a kind and a list of producers, so a producer that merges contributions names all of them. The message type is area A04's and is listed as a dependency.

The silent trap is removed: a scope's context reaches no service, so calling a service through it fails with ErrNotInjected; a scoped event cannot be dispatched without a key; every service that accepts registrations declares Layered or Shared, and mounting a component that writes to a Shared one under a scope is reported. A Shared service stays shared, as its declared and catalogued contract.

Scope contexts cannot nest because every scope fiber hangs under the scope component, so hierarchy has one representation: the key's ordered list of enclosing scopes. That list may name several unrelated scopes, which gives the multi-membership upstream lacks, with the creator's order deciding shadowing.

The scope fiber's parent is a component that injects nothing, so a holder of the scope context reaches only the services its own component declares, never the creator's. Third-party code runs in plugin processes and never holds a context.

Fork names its source by id and reads the prefix from storage, so the source need not be live. A step cannot be closed while one of its tool calls has no result, so a Go log contains no closed step with a missing result for fork to repair.

There is no log-wide format version and no migration chain: each event type carries its own payload version with converters applied on read, the store reads only its own layout, and upstream files go through the separate deferred importer.

The turn/end payload has the reason kinds refusal and budget (the Go name for ACP's max_turn_requests) from payload version 1, and an unknown kind read from a newer log is preserved, so a producer needs no vocabulary or format change. Area A02's turn budget emits budget; refusal still needs a producer in areas A04 and A02, listed as an open question.

A fork records its source session and cut position in its own header fields, separate from a subagent's creator, so the tree of branches is a query over headers. Building the view belongs to area A06; the data that makes it possible is recorded here.

Persona prefix and suffix are live fields of the prompt component's config struct, so the generic settings form and the one writable config layer edit prompt text at run time and the next step uses it; no separate prompt-editing API is needed.
The Go interpolation syntax has an inline escape: four opening braces render two literal braces, and a section can still be marked literal as a whole.

Every compiled-in tool name is known to the binary, so config load rejects a toolOrder name that is neither compiled in nor under a declared dynamic prefix, with file and line; a known but hidden name is skipped at assembly instead of failing every turn.
A tool body that runs inside the host and ignores cancellation cannot be stopped by the host.
justification: Go runtime fact: no API stops a goroutine from outside, and running every first-party tool in its own process would cost a process start per call. DH-ADR-TOOLS-5 bounds the wait, settles the call as outcome unknown and lists the body as detached; third-party tool code runs out of process under DH-ADR-4.

reason: A script selects images with the attach flag on a nested call; the host appends that result's image blocks to the outer result by attachment reference, which works for any image-producing tool and needs no special Image value.
The script never reads the image file: the host attaches the stored image itself, so no mapping from host attachments to program-readable paths exists and the SSH filesystem case cannot arise.
The JavaScript guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so there is no retained Node process whose variables a reset would clear: a script keeps no program state between calls.
The harness imposes no script language, and reach (direct, script or both) is declared per tool, so one agent can have tools that are callable only directly and tools callable only from scripts.

Each nested result is bounded by maxNestedValueBytes before it is returned to the script and its shaped content is logged as a tool/subresult event, so intermediate results are both bounded and present in the session log.
The limit describes the evaluation modes of the Node vm guest runtime, which is dropped by DH-ADR-8; a script keeps state only in files it writes.

The parallel classifier stays on the declaration and operator config can force named tools exclusive; nothing can force a tool parallel, the same one-way rule as guards, so policy outside the tool's owner can tighten scheduling.
A policy listener cannot rewrite the arguments of a tool call.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-TOOLS-3: logged arguments are never rewritten, so that the log, the audit trail, the UI and the execution agree (outcome DH-O-6).

reason: In the tools contract a declaration's output type may be any JSON root and the shared schema package has no root restriction; whether subagent and workflow consumers keep an object-root guard is an open question for areas A11 and A12.
The declared timeout is enforced by the execute stage of the pipeline itself; no separate wrapper has to be mounted for a deadline to apply.
A sign-in prompt is an interaction registry item addressed to the peer that started the attempt, so a browser reload receives the pending prompt again; only a host restart still abandons an attempt.
A flow may declare a Revoke operation; sign-out deletes the local record, closes its leases and then calls the issuer with bounded retries.
The authorisation service joins stored records with registered flows and lists each record as claimed or orphan, so the caller no longer has to recognise a record left by a removed component.
Describe returns a revision and Set takes the revision the caller saw, so a second writer of the same reference is refused instead of silently winning.

The keychain provider upstream deferred is built: stored values are encrypted under a key in the operating-system keychain and the secret directory is masked from confined commands where the sandbox backend can; the residual, an unconfined process of the same user asking the keychain, is stated in the security model.
The launch environment is a snapshot taken at start, so a variable exported later in the launching shell is not seen.
justification: Operating-system fact: a running process cannot observe a later change to its parent shell's environment on any system. The layers that can change, the two .env files and stored values, are watched and apply without a restart (DH-D-HUMAN-7).

reason: A store write is a temporary file, a sync, a rename and a directory sync under a cross-process lock, so an acknowledged write survives a crash and an interrupted one leaves the old file whole.
The store has a References operation that returns every reference named by configuration or stored; the process starter needs it to scrub child environments and the settings form uses it.
A credential reference is an environment-variable-shaped name in one flat namespace.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-HUMAN-9 in its own words (Scope boundary of this record: a credential reference is an environment-shaped name in one flat namespace, never a path or a structured key; a credential with structure, such as a sign-in grant, is a record under owner and id), because one namespace lets the same name be set in the launch environment, a .env file or the store.

reason: No notification can be raised for a variable changed in the launching shell, so a page that shows an environment-sourced credential learns of a change only after a restart.
justification: Operating-system fact, the same as unit credentials-local.3. Changes to stored values and to the .env files do raise a change notice, including for another process on the same home (DH-D-HUMAN-7).

reason: The authorisation service, which holds the flow registry, reports for each record whether a registered flow claims it, so an orphan is identified by the service and can be deleted from the settings page.

The guidance section is rendered only when the carrier declares that it shows file links, and its card sentences only when it shows cards and present is visible, so the text never promises a rendering the host lacks.
No desktop application opens the file. The host opens it once and checks and streams from that one handle, so there is no gap between the check and the open.
A declaration stores a digest and a bounded copy. The card says when the source changed or is missing and can open the copy, within the stated size bound.
The delivered copy is a blob referenced by the event, which is the persistent delivery version upstream deferred. Whether an export bundles blobs is the export owner's decision.
The workspace/changes event carries the whole summary and references a blob holding the hunks, so cards and comparisons are served from the log after a host restart.
A coarse comparison above hunkMaxBytes carries line counts only, so a degraded result no longer holds every line of both sides.
Stored paths use forward slashes on every platform and are converted to the host form only at the boundary.

Git is run with core.splitIndex and the LFS filters switched off for the call. A real-Git scenario checks that the user's Git directory is unchanged, and a repository class where it is not uses the manifest instead.
A Git failure no longer abandons the turn. The recorder falls back to manifest and captures and records the coverage used and the reason in the event.
Temporary space is bounded: untracked files above maxFileBytes are excluded from the snapshot, and above snapshotMaxBytes in total the turn uses the manifest.

Each listed file is labelled tool, when a file tool changed it, or other, when it changed during the turn by something else, and the card shows the label. The summary no longer claims the turn made a change it cannot attribute.
Without a repository a manifest of the working directory is taken at turn start and end, so shell edits are listed as added, modified or deleted. A comparison exists where a before side exists.
Changes to ignored files and to files outside the working directory are listed only when a file tool made them.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-FS-11 item (e): walking ignored trees every turn costs more than it tells, and files outside the write roots cannot be enumerated. The event's coverage field and the card say so (DH-D-FS-9).

reason: The recorder evaluates ignore rules in process and skips the capture for a path the turn's snapshot already covers, so a covered file is not copied a second time.
Only bounded hunks are stored and rendered, never a file's complete text. A compareScope setting lists files outside the workspace without content, and the route declares the resources it reads.

Upstream never searches for a system LibreOffice because the engine is an npm package it ships. The Go provider discovers an operator-installed LibreOffice (configured path, standard install locations, then PATH), probes its version and reports path and version in every result and in the status. It still downloads nothing, by owner decision DH-ADR-20. Fidelity belongs to the installed LibreOffice and is reported, not owned.

Upstream's deadline starts only when conversion begins, so time in the queue is unbounded. The Go service has two bounds: queueWait ends a wait as office/busy, timeout ends a run as office/timeout, and the tool pipeline's deadline covers their sum.

Upstream locates only the kit installation it resolves next to itself. The Go provider searches the configured path, a fixed list of standard install locations per operating system and PATH, and runs discovery again at most every reprobeInterval so that installing LibreOffice needs no restart. It still installs nothing, by DH-ADR-20.

Upstream stores converted and recalculated files in a private output directory and makes the caller copy them. The Go tools write the result to the path the model names through the filesystem operation service, under the same policy as any write; the private output store, its retention and its per-session release are not built. Rendered images are stored as attachments.

The bullet describes mapping an engine path out of an Electron application archive (the .asar to .asar.unpacked rewrite) for an npm package. It exists only because of the Node package and the Electron desktop build; the Go harness has neither, and its engine is a program found on disk and probed before use.

Upstream's filesystem service creates no binary files, so the model must copy a temporary file with the shell and a deployment without a shell cannot deliver a conversion. In Go office_convert and office_recalculate take a required output path and write it through the filesystem operation service; no temporary file, no shell copy and no retention deadline exist.

Upstream refuses conversion on a remote workspace because a remote shell cannot read the host's output store. In Go the input is read through the session's filesystem provider into a host scratch copy and the result is written back through the same provider, so a remote workspace converts like a local one; the engine always runs on the host.

Upstream's office_render writes no image file. The Go tool takes an optional save_dir and then also writes each PNG as a file through the filesystem operation service, with the same guard as a conversion output.

Upstream's web client shows only the text blocks of a render result. In Go the result carries each page as an image block by attachment reference and the tool's view carries them, and the host renders tool results as HTML from that logged result; the card that shows image blocks is requested from the tool-card UI areas in the deliverable's dependencies.

Upstream runs the native LibreOffice engine inside the host process, outside the sandbox. In Go the engine is one child process per job, started by the one process starter under a policy that allows writes only to the job's scratch directory and the slot's profile and denies the network where the backend can; with no working sandbox it does not run unless the operator opts out.

Upstream loses activation on resume or fork in PTC mode because that mode's request header records only run_code.
