In Go activation is a fold over the session log (a successful load of a configured Office skill), independent of how tools are presented, and there is no PTC presentation mode (DH-ADR-8); a resumed or forked session has the tools from its first step.

Upstream keeps activation marks in plugin memory, so a hot reload or a disable and re-enable clears them. In Go nothing is kept in memory: the tools component reads the fold office.active from the log each time a step resolves its tools, so reloading the component changes nothing. Code is never hot reloaded.

Upstream fixes a step's tool set before the content of a user-invoked skill is injected, so the tools appear one step late. In Go the user's skill invocation is a logged record committed before the step resolves its tools, and the fold is advanced inside the append, so the very next model request declares the tools. This depends on area A14 logging the skill load before the step view is resolved, stated as a dependency of the deliverable.
Rendering, fonts and pagination follow LibreOffice and can differ from Microsoft Office, and between two machines with different installs.
justification: Third-party fact: no design in the harness makes one layout engine reproduce another, and owner decision DH-ADR-20 fixes an operator-installed LibreOffice as the engine. Every result names the engine version and missing fonts are reported (DH-ADR-MEDIA-2).

reason: The model is not told when its block creates no card. In Go there is no block: an offer is a tool call, and every tool call returns a result to the model (allowed, denied or an error), so a failed offer is always visible to it.

The host scans blocks line by line while the browser's Markdown parser hides them, and the two disagree in block quotes, nested lists, HTML and math. Go reads no action-card block and hides none, so there are not two readers to disagree; such a block is shown as an ordinary code block.
The limit is about sessions recorded with a removed upstream tool. The Go store reads no upstream session (DH-ADR-2), and Go has no card records at all, so no old record can be skipped.

An invalid card still replaces an earlier unstarted card. Go has no replacement rule: a call with unknown or invalid arguments is refused by the pipeline's schema check and leaves every other pending approval untouched.

Cards exist only in the main conversation because only a live root can act on one. A tool call needs no live-root rule of its own: whether a subagent may propose set_enabled follows from its preset's tools, and who may answer the approval is area A17's rule.
Only one card per turn is offered and a later card replaces an earlier one. Each proposed tool call is its own approval, so a second offer does not replace the first.

Refusal reasons are free strings that each browser body must know. The outcome of an offered action in Go is the pipeline's closed decision set plus errors from the one domain/reason table of design.md section 4.8.

Each kind validates the same details with a host schema and a separate browser schema that must change together. Go has no browser schema: the arguments of the tool call are one Go struct validated once by the pipeline.
Dictation takes one complete recording and returns text; there is no audio file upload, no stored history of transcripts and no streaming. (Removed: the recording is sent as plain audio, not base64.)
justification: Deliberate, and every clause is now stated in the record's own words: DH-ADR-XCUA-5 says 'There is no automatic send, no always-on microphone and no streaming' and has 'Scope boundary of this record: dictation takes one complete recording and returns text, with no audio file upload and no stored history of transcripts, because a history would keep speech the user never chose to send, and an uploaded file is an attachment, not dictation'.

reason: Automatic review is a default-off optional component: no default profile, general setting or new-session default selects it; the user enables it and then chooses it for one session.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-4 keeps auto review as an optional policy listener, and DH-ADR-HUMAN-6 says 'the reserved auto preset of the experimental review layer can never be the default for new sessions'. The reviewer is a fallible model that lets calls run with full access, so making it reachable without an explicit choice would widen every installation.

reason: The mods bridge that could submit text with user authority is not built. In the Go design hook context carries source kind hook and a webhook prompt source kind webhook, and neither counts as instruction for the reviewer; only a carrier writes a user source. A test asserts that hook and webhook text never authorises a medium-risk action.

Under automatic review commands run with full access and no file sandbox, and what a script does directly is judged from its visible text only. Narrowed: the script's tool calls, made through the tool command line, are each reviewed.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-4 says 'an allowed call runs with full access, and what a script does beyond its visible text is not reviewed'; owner decision DH-ADR-8 makes a script an ordinary process whose direct effects are not tool calls, a tradeoff that decision names. No per-effect review point exists.

reason: The reviewing model can misjudge a call, and there are no tool exemptions, no configurable review policy and no second attempt at a verdict. Two deterministic layers remain around it: deny-only guards still run after an allow, and under the ask policy a denial reaches a person.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-4 ports 'a fixed policy' and says 'The reviewer is a fallible model, not a boundary'; exemptions or a configurable policy would lower the ceiling. The limit is stated to the user when the preset is selected.

reason: A child agent run by another vendor's product (Claude Code, Codex, an OAR runtime) keeps that product's own permission system once the delegation call was allowed; automatic review does not reach inside it.
justification: Reclassed from platform limit in the re-sweep: some of these products offer a channel for permission prompts (the audit names one for Claude Code), so routing them to the reviewer is a design choice not taken, not an impossibility. The records state the choice: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-4 says 'Foreign agents started by delegation keep their own permission systems', and DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7 runs external products in an operator-fixed mode and asks a person only where the product's protocol has an answer channel. The delegation call itself is reviewed.

reason: The Go session contract has no synchronous snapshot reader. The reviewer request is an auxiliary request built by a registered pure builder from one committed event (autoreview/requested) and the log at that position, so the request is a function of the log and can be rebuilt and compared in a test.

The badge is usable only by presets that load skills. No badge skill is shipped; a user's own skill file follows the ordinary rule that a preset must mount the skill tool, which area A14 states for every skill.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XMISC-7 (the badge skill is not shipped). The limit is about a preview image of that bundle package, shown by upstream's plugin page, that has no dark variant.
Browser use drives Chromium-family browsers only; Firefox and WebKit cannot be selected.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words: DH-ADR-XCUA-2 ships one browser provider, chromedp speaking the Chrome DevTools Protocol to an installed Chrome, and its tradeoff says 'Chromium family only'; DH-ADR-XCUA-3 admits the two Node servers only as optional recipes configured for Chromium. The browser seam admits another provider later without changing the model's tools.

reason: A browser or its server is opened on the first browser tool call by A16's service, not inside agent creation, so a start-up failure is a browser/unavailable tool result and never rejects session creation or resume. A lost server is restarted under the MCP fleet's budget and the next call opens a fresh browser.
When the harness attaches to a browser the user already runs, the user and other programs can still change the same pages; the harness's reservation only keeps its own sessions apart.
justification: An attached browser is the user's own program and its debugging interface accepts any client; nothing the harness holds can lock the user out of their browser. The design narrows the exposure: launching a private browser is the default, attach needs an approval (DH-ADR-MEDIA-5), and the optional Node recipes do not offer attach.

reason: The adapter registers its MCP entry with expose none, so no mcp__ tool name, resource tool or server instruction of the browser server reaches any model request, and no inherited server name can appear.
Cancelling a browser action cannot undo a navigation or a click the browser already received.
justification: A real browser has no undo for delivered input; this is true of every provider. The result says that the outcome is unknown and tells the model to look before retrying; nothing is replayed.

reason: The model no longer sees the server's schemas. A16 owns one fixed browser catalogue and the recipe maps it to server tools; a server whose tool list no longer matches the recipe is reported unavailable instead of changing what the model is shown.

The recipe always passes the flag that disables usage statistics and no configuration can turn it on. The server's other features, such as performance tools, are unreachable because the model sees only A16's catalogue and the connection is unexposed.
Browser use through the optional Playwright recipe drives Chromium-family browsers only.
justification: Deliberate, and the same boundary as unit browser-use-chrome-devtools-mcp.1: DH-ADR-XCUA-2 says 'Chromium family only', and DH-ADR-XCUA-3 admits the Node servers as optional recipes in launch mode only.

reason: A browser or its server is opened on the first browser tool call by A16's service, not inside agent creation, so a start-up failure is a browser/unavailable tool result and never rejects session creation or resume. A lost server is restarted under the MCP fleet's budget and the next call opens a fresh browser.
An attached browser can still be changed by its user and by other programs; the reservation keeps only harness sessions apart.
justification: The same fact as unit browser-use-chrome-devtools-mcp.3: an attached browser is the user's own. Launching a private browser is the default, attach needs an approval (DH-ADR-MEDIA-5), and the optional Node recipes do not offer attach at all.

reason: The adapter registers its MCP entry with expose none, so no mcp__ tool name, resource tool or server instruction of the browser server reaches any model request, and no inherited server name can appear.
Cancelling a browser action cannot undo a navigation or a click the browser already received.
justification: The same fact as unit browser-use-chrome-devtools-mcp.5: a real browser has no undo for delivered input. The result reports an unknown outcome and nothing is replayed.

reason: The model no longer sees the server's schemas. A16 owns one fixed browser catalogue and the recipe maps it to server tools; a server whose tool list no longer matches the recipe is reported unavailable instead of changing what the model is shown.

Because the tool catalogue is fixed, nothing has to be discovered at agent creation: A16's service opens a browser lazily on a session's first browser call. Enabling a provider therefore serves sessions that already exist, and a busy attachment is tried again on the next call instead of being skipped for the life of the activation.
Exclusive use of an attached browser holds inside one host process only; another harness process, another program or the user can act in the same browser.
justification: An attached browser is owned by its user, and a reservation shared between processes would still not stop the user or another program from acting in it. The design relies on launching a private browser by default and an approval before the first use of an attached one (DH-ADR-MEDIA-5).

reason: Cancelling or losing the connection cannot undo browser actions already delivered. (Removed for a launched browser: an operation that ignores cancellation can no longer delay cleanup without limit, because the browser's process tree is stopped by a bounded ladder.)
justification: Undoing delivered input is impossible for any provider. The result reports an unknown outcome and nothing is replayed.

reason: A failed close no longer stays failed: the launch package's stop is safe to call again, the stop ladder is retried on unload, and a sweep at the next start removes profile directories of dead run directories. Browser state is deliberately not restored from the log; a resumed session gets a fresh browser and its first result says earlier pages and logins are gone.

The limit is about npm peer dependencies: a second installed copy of a JavaScript scope package whose tags the host cannot read. Go components are compiled into one binary and share one copy of every package.

The bullet describes the Stagehand provider, which the Go design does not build: owner decision DH-ADR-24 drops the Stagehand browser layer and DH-ADR-XCUA-2 drops the provider whole. The Chromium-only boundary of the provider that is built is carried under unit browser-use-chrome-devtools-mcp.1.

A resumed or forked session gets its recorded conversation back, but not the browser: pages, cookies and logins from before are gone. The Stagehand provider this bullet was written for is dropped (DH-ADR-24); the limit is kept here because it holds for the provider that replaces it.
justification: A live browser process cannot be rebuilt from a log. The browser service records browser state events, so the first browser result after a resume says that earlier pages and logins are gone.

reason: There is no second model: the Stagehand layer and its fixed vendor catalogue are dropped, and every model request caused by browser use is a request of the session's own agent through the harness's LLM runtime.

The cause is native inference with no abort signal and an SDK close that waits for it. With no inference inside the provider, a cancelled call abandons one protocol command and returns at once with an unknown outcome; that delivered input cannot be undone is carried by the other cancellation rows.

The bullet describes the Stagehand provider, which the Go design does not build (owner decision DH-ADR-24; DH-ADR-XCUA-2 drops the provider whole). The same fact for the providers that are built, that an attached browser can also be changed by its user, is carried under units browser-use-chrome-devtools-mcp.3 and browser-use-runtime.2.

The states described come from an SDK drain and a connection Worker, which no longer exist. Cleanup is one sequence the harness owns: close the pipe, stop the process tree, confirm the exit, remove the profile. If the exit cannot be confirmed the entry is kept and reported as uncertain, the stop is retried on unload and orphans are swept at the next start.

The deferred work was to route Stagehand's model requests through the harness, reuse its credentials, capture them and account for their usage. With the layer dropped there are no such requests: browser use causes only the session's own, logged model requests.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (the Claude Code mods bridge and its band are not built). The limit lists which drawing surfaces and input events of the mod interface the bridge serves.

Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (no mod loader exists). The limit says the bridge does not read a mod's plugin.json and hooks.json; a settings hook file is read by the hooks component when the operator lists it as a source.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (the mods bridge is not built). The limit describes how the JavaScript middleware chain treats a second call to next; a hook is a separate process that returns one answer.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (the mod event interface is not built). The limit lists mod event names the bridge registers but never raises; the lifecycle points offered are the nine hook points.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (the mods bridge is not built). The limit lists members of the $ host object the bridge does not serve, a JavaScript interface handed to code running in the host.

Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (the mod tool.call handler is not built). The limit says that handler runs after the permission decision and cannot rewrite arguments; for hooks the order is stated instead by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (no mod module is loaded into the host). The limit is that a mod's module-level variables and environment writes are shared by every session.

Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (the mods bridge is not built), and DH-ADR-4 keeps third-party code out of the host process. The limit is that a mod runs in the host with Node's globals and full authority.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (the turn.complete mod handler is not built). The limit concerns where that handler's text is shown; a hook's systemMessage is recorded and shown as a transcript notice.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (the JavaScript host interface of mods is not built). The limit lists fields of $.session.usage and $.fs.stat that the bridge reports as zero or empty.
A card whose experiment ships no browser body offers only Not now. There are no card bodies in Go; an approval prompt is rendered by the host for every tool the same way.
The turn tail shows one card per turn. No card is drawn in Go, and several approvals in one turn are listed together by the interaction region.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (the mods band is not built). The limit lists what the React band component cannot draw.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XHOOKS-3 (no band and no bridge). The limit is that the band redraws only on the bridge's redraw triggers.

The two free web translation endpoints (Google, Bing) may refuse requests or disappear, and a failed request does not fall back to another provider. Only an installation whose operator added the web provider meets this limit.
justification: The endpoints belong to other vendors and no design choice here can make them reliable. The owner decided how far they reach (DH-ADR-36): the web provider is specified but not in the shipped bundle, which translates with the user's own model; an operator may add it in a layer, where it is off by default and counts as a sender (DH-ADR-XMISC-5). A failure is one logged outcome with Retry.

reason: A translation of the model's reasoning may change the inline formatting of the prose; the original is one click away. (Removed: code blocks, math and tables are never sent to a translator, so code cannot be changed.)
justification: Machine translation of prose can move or drop inline markup whatever the provider; that is the behaviour of the translating service or model, not of the harness. DH-D-XMISC-1 excludes code from what is sent.

reason: Register entry U-K2-13, resolved in the convergence round. A session nobody drives, such as a finished subagent session, can get a new translation: the two translation event types are declared log-only, and the service writes them with the session area's AppendLogOnly (DH-D-SESSION-9), which takes a free session's lease for the one append without creating an agent or running a hook (DH-ADR-XMISC-4). Tests DH-T-XMISC-2 and DH-T-SESSION-20. A narrower case is left and is new, not upstream's: when another dsh process holds the session, the translation is refused with translate/session-held-elsewhere and the view says which process to use. core-session.md says in one place that a translation succeeds in that case too; the two documents disagree and x-recommendations-misc.md is the more specific.

Saved translations are experimental plugin records kept on a best-effort basis across format changes. In Go they are declared event types with a payload version and converters like any other persisted type (DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-6). The collapsed preview staying original is kept on purpose: translating it would send text before the reader asked.
Whether the two web translation endpoints can be reached from mainland China depends on the user's network. Only an installation whose operator added the web provider meets this limit.
justification: Reachability of a third party's endpoint from a given network is outside any design. The one egress proxy policy applies to these requests, an unreachable endpoint is one classified failure, and the shipped bundle translates with the user's own model through a route the user already reaches (DH-ADR-36).

reason: The brief shown on the creation card is written by the model and existing data travels in a separate field. There is no creation card and no brief in Go.
Creation receipts on old cards do not follow later manual changes on the Plugins page. Go stores no creation receipt.

The count of local changes is computed with Git's clean and process filters skipped, so a file that Git LFS has materialised can be counted as changed although ordinary Git calls it clean. (Removed: a Git too old to honour the override is refused.)
justification: Deliberate safety rule: a filter is a program named by the repository's configuration, and running it during a background refresh would execute repository code on every tool result. DH-ADR-XFORGE-6 runs every Git command under the session's policy and, since the convergence round, states the rule and its cost in its own text: no repository-configured program runs and nothing is fetched implicitly when the harness inspects or creates a checkout. The panel marks the count 'filters skipped'.

reason: The limit concerns scopes of the changes view (a missing last-turn scope and the Branch scope's default base). The changes view is not built; per-turn file changes are shown by the filesystem area's workspace-changes card.

Upstream reads every ref and filters in the host. The Go base-branch search passes the query to git for-each-ref as a pattern with a count, sorted by commit date, so Git filters and bounds the list and nothing reads every ref.
The limit is that a patch over the size ceiling shows no files and long lines are cut in the side-by-side view. No diff is read or drawn in the Go design; the card links to the code host's page.

Dropped by DH-ADR-XFORGE-5 (the changes view is not built) and owner decision DH-ADR-38 (the code-host UI is status only). The limit describes syntax colouring across collapsed lines in the React changes view.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XFORGE-5 (the changes view is not built) and DH-ADR-38 (status only). The limit describes placeholder heights of file sections that the React view had not drawn yet.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XFORGE-5 (the changes view is not built) and DH-ADR-38 (status only). The limit says the browser's find-in-page misses lines the React view had not drawn.
The limit concerns viewed marks kept on the code host or in one browser. Viewed marks are not built: the harness neither reads nor writes them, and nothing is kept in browser storage for them.

The limit concerns review-thread writes, the pending review and avatars loaded from the code host's image server. The harness writes nothing to a code host, shows no review threads, and loads no image from another origin.

The limit concerns the lens and annotation extension interface of the changes view. It is a client-plugin extension point with no place in a server-rendered UI, and it is not built together with the view it extends.
The limit concerns review layers (Interface, Implementation, Tests) derived from path rules and .gitattributes. Review layers are a feature of the changes view, which is not built.

The status of a pull request is refreshed only while a browser tab shows that session's panel, and nothing notifies the user when checks finish meanwhile; a session-list row shows the stored status with its age.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XFORGE-3 contacts a code host only while someone is looking and states the tradeoff: 'No notification when checks finish while no panel is open; a list row can be stale and says how old it is'. Polling with no viewer would contact the user's code host in the background and spend the user's rate limit with nobody to show the result to.

reason: The limit concerns choosing commits of a change request or branch in the changes view. Commit selection is not built, and the provider operations that listed and compared commits are removed with it.

The limit lists gaps of the Code review page (GitHub-only lists, no host or account choice, a staged binding lost on restart). The page is not built; reviewing a change request the session does not own is done on the code host.

Upstream's list reads worktree and bindings of an unloaded session from a cache that may be missing. In Go both are summary folds registered with the session-views area, whose checkpoints commit in the same transaction as their events and are caught up for any session, so no session lacks them.

A change made to working files outside the session shows in the panel only at the next trigger (a tool result, a panel fetch or a refresh, at most once per 10 seconds). Narrowed: a commit or a branch switch made outside appears promptly through a watch on the Git HEAD file.
justification: Deliberate cost choice: watching a whole working tree would cost one watch per directory of every open session's repository, for a panel that is a status summary. DH-ADR-XFORGE-9 (item a), added in the convergence round as a recommended default, records 'seen at the next trigger, not watched' as scope and says what would reopen it; DH-D-XFORGE-6 builds the triggers.

reason: Upstream leaves a branch or checkout behind after a failed or cancelled attempt. In Go a journal row is written before the first Git command and a failed attempt rolls back what that row created: the registration and directory by a non-force removal, the branch only if it still points at the pinned base commit. Generated names still come from the session id, which is a naming rule and not a defect.

Upstream's hold misses a message that arrives during a turn or other maintenance. The Go design has no hold: creation from the UI is its own operation offered only before the first turn, a message sent meanwhile is latched by the driver, and a failed attempt blocks step 1 through a PreStep listener (DH-ADR-XFORGE-8). Recovery of a worktree removed by hand is settled with the session-views area (x-forge-worktree.md section 10, item 2): DH-ADR-VIEW-8 keeps every tool-made move inside the anchor, and recovery of a missing directory goes through workdir.Access with the reason recover, which this area denies for a recorded worktree so that the card offers Restore instead of falling back silently.

Upstream keeps the agent idle in maintenance with no stop control while a message waits for a failed creation. In Go nothing waits: a failed attempt ends the maintenance task, the turn ends as blocked with the reason, and the composer stays usable.

Restoring a worktree whose directory was removed recreates it from its branch, or from the commit the branch started from; changes that were never committed are lost, and an existing or incomplete directory blocks the restore.
justification: Git holds only what was committed, so nothing can bring back files that existed only in the removed directory. The card says so before the user chooses Restore, and DH-ADR-XFORGE-7 never overwrites an existing directory.

reason: Upstream disables the option when the project is itself a linked worktree, because its Git directory lies outside the writable root, and Windows ignored extra roots. In Go the worktree component retains a grant to the common Git directory when it was inside the session's roots and otherwise asks the user for a directory session grant; the sandbox area gives every write root its own identifier on Windows (its decision DH-ADR-SANDBOX-6).
Only the first proposal of a turn appears as a card. In Go each proposal is a tool call with its own approval, so a second proposal in a turn is not lost.

The card reserves a placeholder line because the React client fetches the catalogue text after it has drawn the card. This is a client-side rendering artifact: a host-rendered fragment is written with the text it already has, and no card is drawn at all.

A card keeps showing a recorded decision that later changes on the Plugins page have made untrue. Go keeps no card status: the transcript shows a tool result as a past fact, and the current state is read from area A21's manager wherever it is displayed.

After a refused or lost browser lookup the Enable button returns only on Try again. There is no browser lookup in Go: the host validates the feature id when the call is proposed and renders the prompt itself.

A card whose plugin left the catalogue falls back to the title the model proposed. In Go a call that names an unknown feature id is an error result to the model, and nothing is shown to the user as an offer.

The statistics view is not part of the default product; the operator enables the developer-tools bundle with one switch. (Removed: there is nothing to install, the view is compiled into the one binary.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-BUNDLE-1 says 'Experimental features are optional bundles, each one disabled group', and DH-ADR-BUNDLE-10 requires every catalogue component to be mounted by a shipped layer or to be on the optional list. Promotion to the default product is a later owner decision.

reason: Start times are lost upstream because the fold runs over the browser's loaded window. The stepStats row projection folds the whole log on the host, so every step row holds its start and the page never shows 'start unknown'; DH-T-XINSPECT-7 asserts it.

Upstream's inner calls carry no turn or step, so the view merges them by root-call context. In Go a nested call made through the tool command line is logged inside the bracket of its outer tool call with session, turn and step attribution (design.md section 4.4), so the fold attributes it to the step of the outer call by position and needs no separate context or merge.

The limit describes contention for the one in-flight history page that Chat, Trajectory and Statistics share inside upstream's React client. The Go UI has no client-side session window: each page request is its own bounded host read (DH-ADR-3), so there is nothing to retry.

Upstream has no whole-session wall clock and substitutes model time plus summed tool time. The stepStats rows hold each step's start and end and tool time both as a sum and as the union of intervals, so the totals row shows active wall time as the sum of turn intervals and parallel tools are not double counted.

Upstream exempted this view from a recorded-session scenario. The Go design requires one from the start: DH-T-XINSPECT-7 replays a recorded session keylessly through the built binary and compares the statistics table with a golden file.

A ghost turn arises upstream when compaction restates a result for a turn that has left the loaded window. The Go fold sees every turn's start in the whole log and files each event under the turn and step it belongs to, so a restated result cannot open a row of its own.

The timing figures are computed from the session log, not measured by a sampler: total time is last step end minus first step start, and waiting in queues lands in a segment called rest. Improved: first-token and model time are recorded on each attempt event.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XINSPECT-4 says in its title that the statistics are 'host pages over Query and one fold', with stepStats a row projection, so there is no sampler and no second source of numbers that could disagree with the log (DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-7).

reason: The limit is about who owns and revokes browser object URLs for prompt images in a shared React image cache, and about hover previews on touch clients. The Go host serves an attachment through area A19's session.attachment route as an ordinary image address, so no object URL exists to own (DH-ADR-3).

Voice input never sends a message by itself and has no always-on microphone, wake word, live captions or spoken replies; and local recognition means the machine that runs the host, which may not be the machine with the browser.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XCUA-5 says 'There is no automatic send, no always-on microphone and no streaming' and that insertion happens only into an unchanged draft or on an explicit click; DH-ADR-XCUA-4 says 'the host runs an operator-installed recognition program as a child process', which is why local means the host's machine. No record names spoken replies; the area's limits list does. The settings page states where each provider processes audio.

reason: Computer use works only after the operator installed a driver and granted it the operating system's permissions by hand; enabling the entry does not prove that every desktop action is permitted.
justification: Deliberate: owner decision DH-ADR-19 says 'The Go project ships no native helper. Computer use works only when the operator installs an external MCP server that provides it', so installation and the system permissions are the operator's steps. The adapter reads the driver's permission status at start-up without prompting and shows it before the first call.

reason: Sessions no longer coordinate themselves: the adapter serves calls only under the desktop lease of A16's computer-use service, which one session holds for one turn across every dsh process of the user; a second session gets computer/busy.

A driver upgrade can no longer change what the model sees: the model's tools are A16's fixed catalogue, the adapter checks the driver's tool list against its recipe at start-up, and a mismatch is reported as unavailable with the missing tool named. The action abstraction the bullet says is missing is that catalogue; application approval is A17's prompt and grants panel.

The limits it points to belong to upstream's MCP client. The adapter's entry carries its own start-up and call timeouts from area A15's fleet, and the adapter consumes only text and image content, which A15 stores as attachments.
Installing software grants no desktop access and creates no graphical session: computer use needs a logged-in, unlocked desktop and permissions granted by hand.
justification: Operating systems tie desktop-control permissions to a user's explicit grant and need a graphical session to observe or send input; no program can grant them to itself. They are listed as the operator's steps, and the status view shows the driver's permission state (DH-ADR-19).

reason: Dropped by DH-ADR-19 and DH-ADR-XCUA-1 (the in-process driver provider is merged into the external one, so no driver runtime is loaded into the host). The failure arises only when the driver's runtime is loaded into a headless Node host process; the adapter calls none of the driver's cursor-overlay tools (DH-ADR-CUADRIVER-1).
The user and programs other than the harness can change the same desktop between two computer-use calls.
justification: A desktop cannot be reserved against its own user. What the design adds is a turn-length lease between harness sessions (DH-ADR-MEDIA-6: one session at a time) and the rule that every reference is checked against the latest observation.

reason: A cancelled computer-use call may already have delivered its input, and nothing on the desktop is rolled back.
justification: Synthetic input, once delivered to an application, cannot be taken back by any driver. The result says the outcome is unknown and tells the model to observe before retrying; no call is replayed.

reason: A failed native shutdown inside the host cannot occur: the driver is a child process stopped by the bounded stop ladder. The slot is held until that stop is confirmed, an unconfirmed stop is named in the status and retried on the next restart or unload, and no host restart is needed.
The model's tool schemas no longer follow a pinned third-party SDK: they are A16's fixed catalogue, and the driver's own schemas are checked by the adapter's recipe at start-up.
The collapsed summary of a reasoning block stays in the original language; translation starts only when the reader expands the block, and it may change the formatting of prose.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-XMISC-4 has 'Scope boundary of this record: translation starts only when the reader expands a reasoning block, and the collapsed summary stays in the original language, because every translation is a logged provider call that costs tokens and sends text out'. The formatting half is the machine-translation fact carried under unit client-ui-cot-translation.2.

reason: The free web translation endpoints may fail, limit requests or change their response format. (Removed: saved translations are declared event types, no longer best-effort records.)
justification: The endpoints are another vendor's and stay outside the project's control. A changed response format is caught by the strict decoder as one classified error. By owner decision DH-ADR-36 the web provider is not in the shipped bundle; where an operator adds it, DH-ADR-XMISC-5 keeps it off until chosen.

reason: The Creator's restrictions are found by walking live subagent agents and break when an intermediate agent has exited. No Creator job exists in Go, so there is no restriction to look up.
Only new plugins can be created and Restore has no version history. Nothing is created or restored in Go because the feature is not built.

Generated code runs with the Creator's permissions and package validation is not a sandbox. Go installs no generated code into the host; a model-written plugin is area A22's separate, confined process that is approved per session.
Source directories and profile copies are left behind after success, failure, cancellation and Undo. With no creation there is no directory to leave behind.
A creation run has no timeout. No creation run exists in Go.
There is no Windows helper to install separately and no helperPath: the Go project ships no native helper for any platform.
On macOS the system permissions for desktop control need the user's approval in System Settings; enabling computer use in the harness grants none.
justification: macOS ties a privacy permission to a program's identity and to the user's own approval. With DH-ADR-19 the permission belongs to the driver's application, the harness never requests it, and the status view shows whether it is present.

reason: There is neither a shared programmatic runtime nor a separate computer-use program runtime to configure independently: scripts call tools through the tool command line, and desktop operations are eight plain tools. A configuration change reloads live.
The helper's held-button operation is not built, and A16's catalogue has no press without release: a click is one call. Nothing can be left held by a program that ends early.
Input sent by computer use can fail to take effect in some applications; a successful result confirms that the input was delivered, not that it worked.
justification: Applications decide how they treat synthetic input, and some ignore it; this is a property of desktop automation and of whichever driver the operator installed. The contract is that a result reports delivery and never effect, and the model observes after acting.

reason: No helper is built from source, signed, notarised or distributed, so there is no ad-hoc signature, developer identity or release signing to manage.
There is no helper release package whose start-up, identity and exit cleanup could go unverified; the release is one pure-Go binary.
There are no saved permission rows: a grant lives in memory for one session, is listed with the name the driver reported, and ends with the session.

The application a session grant names is identified only as well as the operating system and the driver expose it: a stable identifier where the driver's listing has one, otherwise the process id, in which case the grant ends when the application exits.
justification: The harness ships no native code and does not inspect applications itself (DH-ADR-19); the identity comes from the third-party driver and from what the operating system exposes for a running program. The fallback fails closed and costs one more prompt.

reason: The planned evidence proves the computer-use contract with a replayed model on one test application; whether a real model completes real desktop tasks is not measured. (Upstream's first sentence, about program execution and retained state, no longer applies.)
justification: Deliberate scope of evidence, stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-XCUA-1 has 'Scope boundary of this record: the evidence proves the computer-use contract (the action mapping, the approval path, the results and the cleanup) with a replayed model on one test application, and does not measure whether a real model completes real desktop tasks, because task success is a property of the chosen model and of a driver and applications the project neither ships nor pins'.

reason: The helper's settings navigation, drag guide and permission refresh are not built, so nothing of the harness needs qualifying on each macOS release; which releases work is the installed driver's matter.
There is no native permission guide window; the user grants permissions to the driver by hand in the system's settings.

The harness has no platform list of its own: computer use works on the systems the installed driver supports, and the adapter and A16's catalogue are the same on all of them. Surfaces the driver cannot read arrive as its degraded or error results.
A reference to an on-screen element is valid only until the next observation of its window, and a screenshot or pointer action must name a window.
justification: An accessibility tree is a snapshot: the operating system gives no element identity that survives the next read, and an old identifier may be reused for another control. The contract therefore makes a stale reference an error and never a guess (DH-ADR-MEDIA-6).

reason: Pointer coordinates are pixels of the last screenshot of a window, and the window can move or change between the screenshot and the input. (The relative 0 to 999 mode is not offered.)
justification: On a desktop shared with its user, nothing can freeze a window between an observation and an input. The adapter scales a point by the stored image size so that the model does no arithmetic, and a changed window is reported as an error (DH-ADR-XCUA-1).

reason: A window-manager feature that shrinks background windows to thumbnails (macOS Stage Manager) can defeat observation and pointer input for a background window.
justification: Operating-system behaviour that no harness code can change, and now the installed driver's to handle (DH-ADR-19). The driver's degraded flag is passed to the model, and the adapter never forces a window to the foreground.

reason: The helper's drag operation is not built and A16's catalogue has no drag, so its window checks and timing have nothing to apply to. Tasks that need a drag are listed as unsupported in the spec's limitations.
The Go project ships no code that depends on private macOS symbols. Whether an external driver does is outside the project; the recipe records the driver version it was tested with.
The cua-mcp profile is not built, so no host lists tools that name a missing provider. In the Go harness a missing provider gives one fixed computer/unavailable sentence on every computer tool.

Dropped by DH-ADR-19 and DH-ADR-XCUA-1 (upstream's first-party computer-use packages and their profile are not ported). The limit is about a hand-listed dependency closure in that profile patch; Go components declare their injections in code that the loader checks.
Neither the Windows helper nor the served profile exists, so its limits cannot pass through an MCP server of the harness.
The harness serves no computer-use MCP server and asks for consent through its own interaction registry, never by MCP elicitation; its MCP client advertises no elicitation capability.
There is no program tool, raw cua tool or program sandbox to escalate: desktop operations are eight plain tools that pass the ordinary pipeline.
There is no cua programming interface for a model to learn from a reference tool; each of the eight tools carries its own schema in every request.
A desktop observation is bounded twice: the adapter passes node and depth limits to the driver, and the result passes the tool pipeline's result bound. No program can return an unbounded value.
The stale sandbox-escalation guidance belongs to the program tool's description, which does not exist in the Go design.
The harness serves no tool description to another harness, so no client can cut it short.

Every computer-use call in the Go harness is a tool call with a result in the session log, because it is made by the session's own model through the pipeline; there are no root calls from an outside client.
There is no npm package and no Windows helper to omit from it.
There is no Always allow for an application: a grant lasts until the session ends, and another session needs its own consent.
justification: Deliberate: owner decision DH-ADR-16 says 'Grants are logged, listed and revocable, and never outlive the session. No rules are stored across sessions', and DH-ADR-33 confirms that a grant names one application and is never copied. The Go design adds the session grant itself, which upstream's Windows provider lacked.

reason: On Windows, computer-use input may move the user's real mouse pointer, depending on the installed driver; the harness cannot prevent it or ask separately for it.
justification: How input reaches a Windows application is the behaviour of the third-party driver and of the operating system's input model (DH-ADR-19). The adapter always requests background delivery (DH-ADR-XCUA-1) but cannot enforce it; the real-desktop scenario records whether the pointer moved.

reason: The helper's drag is not built and A16's catalogue has no drag, so a drop cannot land on an overlay through the harness.
The helper is not built, and the catalogue has no operation that holds a key or button across calls: each key call is a press and a release.
There is no helper whose identity is hashed and no build output directory to lock.
There is no helper handshake and no maxClickHoldMs setting.
The model cannot find or start an application through computer use on any platform; the user opens the application.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XCUA-1 exposes the driver through an allow-list of tools and says 'Hover, drag, held keys, launching an application and foreground delivery are unavailable', and DH-ADR-MEDIA-6 approves computer use per application; a grant names a running application, and launching one is an action outside any grant.

reason: The adapter lists only applications the driver marks as running, so the model never holds an identifier for an application that would first have to be launched.
Computer use needs an unlocked, interactive desktop session, and a window that is listed can still be unavailable for capture or input.
justification: An operating-system fact: a locked or non-interactive session has no desktop to capture or send input to, and capture support is decided per window by the system. It is listed as an operator prerequisite, and the driver's error is returned as a computer-use error result.

reason: There are no stored conversation decisions to retain or delete: a grant is held in memory for one live session and ends with it, and nothing is read from an earlier session.
Which applications and inputs work, and how well that was validated, is owned by the installed driver and its vendor, not by the harness.
justification: Deliberate: owner decision DH-ADR-19 makes an external MCP server the only route to computer use, and DH-ADR-XCUA-1 says 'the project neither pins nor audits the driver'. The harness validates one driver version on one test application in its real-desktop scenario, records that version, and claims no coverage of other applications.

reason: There is one tool form for every agent, so no preset selector decides between a raw binding and a nested program tool.
There is no program state to lose: application and window identifiers come from the latest listing recorded per session, and a lost process only means the model lists again.
The user and other programs can change an application between two computer-use calls, and the mouse pointer is not put back where it was.
justification: A desktop cannot be reserved against its own user, and restoring the pointer would dismiss what a hover revealed. Between harness sessions the turn-length desktop lease gives the reservation upstream declined to build (DH-ADR-MEDIA-6).

reason: Element references are opaque strings valid until the next observation; an old string may later name a different control, so callers must use references from the latest observation, and screenshots and pointer input need a named window.
justification: The same fact as unit cua-macos.5: an accessibility tree is a snapshot and the operating system gives no lasting element identity. The contract makes a stale reference an error and never a guess (DH-ADR-MEDIA-6).

reason: Upstream keeps the whole upload, up to 512 MiB, in host memory. The Go importer streams the upload to an owner-only staging file in the harness home (or reads a path given on the command line) and opens it with archive/zip, which reads one entry at a time through random access, so memory is bounded by one conversation and one image.

A file that the chat export does not contain (every non-image file and some images) cannot be opened after import; it becomes a text note with its name and size. (Changed: no file handle points the model at an empty path.)
justification: The bytes are not in the vendor's export file, so no importer can restore them. DH-D-XINSPECT-7 builds the note form.

reason: Upstream stores every image before parsing any conversation and has no removal, so images of failed or dropped conversations stay forever. The Go importer stores a conversation's images just before its events, and area A07's retention collects any blob that no event references after its grace period (DH-D-STORAGE-9).

Upstream cannot remove a session whose workspace attachment failed. In Go each conversation is prepared invisibly, attached to the workspace and only then published; if the attachment fails the prepared session is discarded, so no session exists outside the workspace.

Upstream needs its own maxTitleBytes because the title service hides its limit. The Go importer has no such field: it normalises and pins the title through area A06's title service, whose configured limit applies.

The chat importer leaves out other branches of a conversation, content-filtered rounds, risk disclaimers, tips, page-find and partial-read records, encrypted link bodies, the pinned flag, per-token times and accumulated token usage.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-XINSPECT-7 has 'Scope boundary of this record: the chat importer keeps one branch of each conversation and leaves out the other branches, content-filtered rounds, risk disclaimers, tips, page-find and partial-read records, encrypted link bodies, the pinned flag, per-token times and accumulated token usage, because a session is a linear log and the dropped records are either never shown as reply text by the vendor's site or must not enter the model's context'.

reason: Upstream writes fixed English explanations into the log and shows the host's English message in the dialog. The Go importer records a code and its data for an excluded reply and for every failure reason, and the page text comes from the message catalogue in the reader's language (English and Chinese complete).

Upstream imports searches and opened pages as web_search and web_fetch calls that have no request-header tool record and an inferred status code. The Go importer writes them as Markdown text inside the assistant message, so no tool call that this harness never made exists in history and nothing is inferred.

fflate pushes inflated bytes, so a small declared size with highly compressed data keeps the host busy until the entry ends. Go's reader is pulled by the caller: each entry is read through a reader that fails as soon as it passes MaxEntryBytes or its declared size and checks cancellation between reads, so the limit stops the work and not only the retention (DH-LIB-FFLATE-R2).

Upstream's streaming pass walks local file headers, so a second local header with an existing name can deliver an extra conversation. archive/zip returns entries from the central directory only, duplicate names there are refused, and each selected conversation id is written at most once, so data that the directory does not list is never read.

Upstream's failure response for an archive that breaks mid-way does not list the sessions already written. A Go import is a host-tracked operation whose final result always lists the sessions it published, also when it ends in failure or cancellation; DH-T-XINSPECT-13 and -14 assert it.

Upstream has two read paths, one of which truncates an over-long entry and re-parses the directory on every call. The Go importer has one read path: the directory is parsed once when the archive is opened, and an entry longer than it declares is an error, never a truncated value (DH-LIB-FFLATE-R2).

Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (the in-browser preview runtime is not built). The carrier path without byte progress exists for pages whose host runs in a browser worker; the one Go upload path is an ordinary HTTP form.
The chat importer targets one structure of the vendor's export format (version 3 as of 2026-11-12); it refuses another version and skips record types it does not know.
justification: The format belongs to the vendor's website, is not specified for third parties and can change without notice; supporting generations nobody can test would be a claim without evidence. DH-D-XINSPECT-7 builds the version check and the per-conversation skip with a coded reason.

reason: Upstream accepts only a browser upload of a ZIP. The Go importer takes an fs.FS, so the command dsh session import-chat accepts a ZIP path or an extracted export directory on the host machine, and the web form remains for remote hosts.

Upstream does not record what it imported, so a second import duplicates every session. The Go importer writes the conversation id and its update time into the store's imported_from column and skips a conversation already present unless the caller asks for a copy; the result counts what was skipped.

Upstream needs a profile patch file to add a GitHub Enterprise or self-managed GitLab host. In Go hosts is an ordinary field of each provider's config struct, shown on the settings form derived from the type and saved to the one writable layer.
The model has no dedicated tool for the pull requests bound to its session; it reads and changes them by running gh or glab through the shell tool.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XFORGE-1 makes the forge seam read-only and states that a change to a code host is made by the model's own command in the shell tool, which is sandboxed and guarded. A host-side tool would act with the user's own sign-in outside the session's sandbox and network policy. The owner confirmed the boundary: the code-host UI is status only, with no host-side writes (DH-ADR-38).

reason: GitHub status needs the gh program installed and signed in on the host for each listed host; tokens in environment variables are not used and an unlisted host is never read. Without gh the cards say unavailable with the reason.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XFORGE-2 has providers drive the operator-installed vendor program ('No token is read, stored or passed; the CLI uses its own credential store'), and DH-ADR-XFORGE-3 contacts 'only a listed host'.

reason: The number of unresolved review threads on a pull request is counted up to a configured maximum; beyond it the card shows a lower bound marked N+.
justification: GitHub's interface offers no count of unresolved threads, so a provider must page through them, and an unbounded page loop would let one pull request exhaust the user's rate limit. The bound is configuration. (The review read upstream also mentions is not built.)

reason: Upstream reads continuation pages inside the host's polling batch, so one pull request with many threads can time out the whole batch. In Go the batch returns each pull request's first page, and continuation pages are read per pull request with their own deadline, so a slow one fails alone.
The limit concerns the merge base of a diff read from GitHub after the base branch was rewritten. The Go provider reads no diff from the code host.
A pull request whose head branch lives in a fork is not found by branch name; it appears when the session's own create command prints its address, or when the user adds it by link.
justification: Deliberate deferral: discovering it needs a lookup of the fork's parent on every push, and a branch name in a fork can collide with someone else's pull request, which the 'never guess' rule of DH-ADR-XFORGE-4 forbids. DH-ADR-XFORGE-9 (item b), added in the convergence round as a recommended default, records it as scope: a head lookup qualified by the fork's owner would reopen it.

reason: Every status poll costs at least one GitHub query, counted against the signed-in account's rate limit. (Removed: the queries for diffs, review reads and review writes, which are not built.)
justification: GitHub meters its interface per account and offers a local tool no push channel, so status is read by polling. DH-ADR-XFORGE-3 bounds the cost: polling only while a panel is shown, at upstream's cadence, backing off until the reset time on a rate-limited answer.

reason: The limit is that the provider never joins a merge queue. The Go provider never merges at all; merging is done on the code host or by the model's own command.

GitLab status needs the glab program installed and signed in for each listed host; an unlisted host is never read, and a host whose SSH remotes use another name, or a GitLab installed under a path prefix, is not recognised.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XFORGE-2 (the harness holds no forge token) and DH-ADR-XFORGE-3 (only a listed host is contacted). Recognising hosts by anything but the listed names would guess at where the user's credentials may be sent.

reason: The limit is that the GitLab provider keeps no viewed marks, so the view keeps them in the browser. Viewed marks are not built for any provider.
The limit is a rebase request sent without a head check. The Go provider sends no rebase or any other write.

The limit is a mismatch between the unresolved count, which includes overview discussions, and the thread list, which omits them. The Go design shows only the count the host reports and has no thread list, so the two cannot disagree.
The limit concerns comment authors never marked as bots and draft notes carrying the read's time. Comments and draft notes are not read or shown.
The merge-request card shows only what GitLab Community Edition reports; required approvals, code owners and merged-results pipelines of the paid tiers are not shown.
justification: Deliberate deferral: a query that names a paid-tier field is refused by a Community Edition host, so reading those fields needs a capability probe per host and a second query shape. DH-ADR-XFORGE-9 (item c), added in the convergence round as a recommended default, records it as scope: a test installation on a paid tier would reopen it.

reason: Every status poll costs one GitLab query per batch plus one request per merge request whose mergeability must be rechecked. (Removed: the requests for review reads, diff versions, draft notes and writes, which are not built.)
justification: GitLab meters its interface and rechecks mergeability only when a REST read asks for it; a local tool gets no push channel. The cost is bounded by polling only while a panel is shown (DH-ADR-XFORGE-3) and by the configured batch size and concurrency.

reason: A pull request is linked to a session only when a recognised command (one with a compiled-in rule) names it plainly; commands that use shell expansion, substitutions, multi-line scripts, aliases or a bare number without a repository do not link.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XFORGE-4 states that rules never guess and never execute, so a binding is always a fact. Misses are recovered by branch discovery after a push or on inspection, and by Add by link in the panel.

reason: Upstream hashes the registered rule set into the fold's state version, so a new or changed rule refolds every session and a start without a provider removes its bindings. In Go the fold reads only forge/binding events and never consults a rule; rules are compiled-in data used once, when a command settles.
A pull request that someone opened elsewhere for a branch appears only after the next push of that branch, the next inspection that reports the branch, or a manual add.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XFORGE-3 says 'a request is made in three cases only: a tab is showing that session's panel, the user pressed refresh, or the session pushed a branch (one lookup)', so a pull request opened elsewhere is learned of only then; DH-ADR-JOBS-12 defers event-triggered automation. The registry keeps one refresh entry that an intake component could call later.

reason: The model cannot read or change the list of pull requests bound to its session through a tool.
justification: Deliberate, and the same boundary as unit forge-bundle.2: DH-ADR-XFORGE-1 keeps the forge seam read-only and host-side, and DH-ADR-XFORGE-4 writes bindings only from settled shell calls. A host-side forge tool would act with the user's sign-in outside the session's sandbox.

reason: Register entry U-K2-12, resolved in the convergence round. The binding listener also reads the durable record the jobs area writes when a job settles, for jobs a shell tool call started, and scans the job's output with the same rules and the same byte bound (DH-D-XFORGE-5). The jobs area states what that needs: the job/settled record names the originating tool call and its command, and the output is still readable when subscribers are told (jobs-schedule-goal-plan.md, persisted data; DH-D-JOBS-2). Test DH-T-XFORGE-10 covers a settled background job and the case where the record lacks the call or the output is gone, which binds nothing.

Upstream treats a tag printed without refs/tags/ as a branch and may bind a change request of the same name. In Go the live discovery step asks Git whether refs/heads/<name> exists in the session's checkout and skips a name that is only a tag.

Upstream binds a program's shell call from the logged copy of its output, which the spill policy can shorten. In Go the observer reads the complete output when the call settles, through the spill store when the result was shortened, up to maxScanBytes, and records what it found as an event, so replay does not depend on the shortened text.

Upstream shows a parent session none of its subagents' bindings. In Go the panel lists the bindings of the session's subagent children as well, each labelled with the child, read from the children's summary folds.
Upstream writes lookup failures to the host log only. In Go a failed discovery is kept in the panel state for that branch with its failure code and shown in the section, as well as logged.
Pull-request status reaches the UI on the next poll or when the user presses refresh; a code host cannot push a change to the harness.
justification: Deliberate, and the same boundary as unit forge-session.3: DH-ADR-XFORGE-3 says a request is made in three cases only (a panel is shown, the user pressed refresh, the session pushed a branch), and DH-ADR-JOBS-12 defers event-triggered automation. A code host can deliver a webhook only to an address it can reach, which a harness on a loopback address is not.

reason: Upstream keeps the latest results in memory and loses them on restart. In Go the last snapshot of each change request is written to a derived key-value namespace when it changes, and is shown with its time until the next poll.
A hook cannot rewrite a tool call's arguments: an updatedInput field in a hook's answer is never applied, and the Go types have no place for it.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1 says 'A hook cannot allow, cannot change arguments, content or values', and outcome DH-O-6 requires that logged arguments are never rewritten. A hook that wants a different call denies with a message and the model retries. A test checks that logged arguments are byte-identical after a hook returned updatedInput.

reason: The run-level halt exists in Go: a hook answer with continue false makes the component cancel the open turn through the agent's Cancel with cause extension, inbox kept, and the hook's stopReason as the recorded reason on turn/end.
Only hooks that run a command are executed; http, mcp_tool, prompt and agent hooks are listed in the diagnostics and skipped.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1 says 'Only command handlers run' and that http, mcp_tool, prompt and agent handlers 'are listed and skipped'. An http hook would send event data off the machine without an opt-in (DH-ADR-9), and prompt and agent hooks are model calls outside the session log.

reason: Of Claude Code's 30 hook events, 21 are not offered (narrowed from 23); a configured hook for one of them is listed in the diagnostics instead of being silently ignored.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1 runs hooks 'at nine points' and maps each answer onto a closed set of decisions, so the other events are not offered; it is a compatibility adapter for a third-party contract that keeps growing and not a reimplementation of Claude Code. Each remaining event needs a seam another area owns or has no counterpart in this product.

reason: A SessionStart hook can add context but cannot start a turn, rename the session, set watch paths, reload skills or change the environment of later commands. (Fixed: its context is in the first request, plain output is accepted, the payload carries the model.)
justification: Deliberate: the remaining fields are outside the closed set of answers a hook may give under DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1.

reason: A UserPromptSubmit hook can reject a prompt or add context but cannot rename the session or hide or replace what the user typed. (Fixed: plain output is accepted and the default timeout is 30 seconds.)
justification: Deliberate: hiding or replacing the user's prompt would be a rewrite of what the person typed, which is outside the closed answers of DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1.

reason: A PreToolUse hook can deny or ask, but its allow never pre-approves a call, defer is not offered and it cannot rewrite the arguments. (Fixed: its added context is delivered with the same call's result.)
justification: Deliberate: under DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1 a hook's answer can only restrict. Letting an external program return allow would skip the policy listeners, guards and approval behind it, and a rewrite would break the rule that logged arguments stay as written (DH-O-6).

reason: A PostToolUse hook can block with feedback or add context but cannot replace a tool's output. (Fixed: the hook receives the rendered text and the structured value.)
justification: Deliberate: replacing a tool's content from an external program is outside the closed answers of DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1; the result the model sees stays the tool's own or a logged block.

reason: A SubagentStart hook's context reaches a child inside the harness only, not a child run by another vendor's product, and a SubagentStop hook only observes. (Fixed: the payload names the real provider, the creator's session and the child's last answer.)
justification: Deliberate for the stop hook: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1 lists the closed set of answers (Deny or Ask before a tool, Block after it, Reject of a prompt, KeepOpen at the stop, added context, a halt), and blocking a child's settlement is not among them, because a child's result is settled by the subagent lifecycle. For an external child there is nothing to inject into: it is another vendor's process with no inbox.

reason: The Stop point is completed: stop_hook_active is true after the first forced continuation of a turn, last_assistant_message is filled from the log, background_tasks and session_crons are filled from the job registry and schedule service when mounted, and forced continuations are capped by maxStopContinuations (default 3) on top of the driver's turn budget.

A hook's suppressOutput and terminalSequence flags are not applied, and transcript_path is empty unless the hook source opts in to an export file. (Fixed: payloads carry the turn id, preset, model and effort; systemMessage is shown; continue false halts the turn.)
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-2 has 'Scope boundary of this record, Claude Code's fields: a hook's suppressOutput and terminalSequence flags are not applied, because they address a terminal interface this product does not have, and transcript_path is empty unless the hook source sets transcript: true, because the session lives in a database (DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-3) and writing an export file on every hook run is a cost and a copy of private data that each source must opt in to'.

reason: Only command hooks run, and the options async, asyncRewake, if, once and statusMessage are not honoured. (Fixed: argument-list and shell options, concurrent matched hooks, several sources, per-session project files behind a trust digest, re-read on change.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1 excludes non-command handlers, and an asynchronous hook would answer after the decision it was asked about; the other options belong to Claude Code's own interface. DH-ADR-XHOOKS-2 covers how a source is trusted.

reason: Of Codex's 10 hook events, PermissionRequest, PreCompact and PostCompact are not offered (narrowed from five); a configured hook for one is listed in the diagnostics, not silently dropped.
justification: Deliberate: under DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1 a hook has a closed set of answers. A permission-request hook would let an external program take part in an approval, which only an owner's answerer may settle (DH-ADR-SECURITY-5), and the compaction points belong to another area's transaction.

reason: SessionStart hooks run on the ordered agent.Created event, which the agent area awaits before the first turn, so their context is in the first model request. A test asserts it.

Both controls are honoured at UserPromptSubmit: systemMessage is recorded on hook/result and shown as a transcript notice, and continue false rejects the prompt and cancels the turn with cause extension.

A Codex PreToolUse hook can block, but its allow pre-approves nothing and it cannot rewrite the arguments. (Fixed: the hook sees the call's full argument object, and its added context is delivered with the call's result.)
justification: Deliberate: a hook's answer can only restrict (DH-ADR-XHOOKS-1) and logged arguments are never rewritten (DH-O-6).

reason: The PostToolUse payload carries the full logged arguments and a structured tool_response (rendered text plus the typed value), and continue false cancels the turn with cause extension.

The Stop payload reports the real stop_hook_active and last_assistant_message, continue false halts the turn, and consecutive forced continuations are capped by maxStopContinuations, so an unconditionally blocking hook can no longer loop for ever.

Payload values come from the live session: the model actually selected and the session's permission preset name replace the static configured model and the constant default. systemMessage is shown, continue false is applied, and transcript_path is filled with an export file when the source asks for one, which removes the cause (no artifact path was reachable).

Only synchronous command hooks run, hooks written inline in Codex's config.toml are not read, and statusMessage and commandWindows are ignored. (Fixed: several sources, per-session project files behind a trust digest, concurrent matched hooks.)
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the fix pass: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-2 has 'Scope boundary of this record: a hook source is the JSON hook file both products share, at a path the operator names; hooks written inline in Codex's config.toml are not read, only synchronous command handlers run (an asynchronous hook cannot answer the decision it was asked), and Codex's statusMessage and commandWindows fields are ignored'.

reason: Upstream's inspection views need the web application. In Go the pages are served by the host to any browser, and the tree, the HTTP capture and profiling also have dsh debug commands, while the session log is reachable through dsh session show and export, so a headless host can be inspected too.

Upstream warns that enabling the bundle starts unredacted capture and a local code-execution endpoint, with no dedicated control. In Go there is no code-execution endpoint, capture masks credentials and keeps no body by default, and the bundle and the separate profiling entry are ordinary switches in the settings forms.

Upstream's Memory and Performance panels cover only the host's V8 heap and CPU. In Go the host is measured with runtime profiles and execution traces (DH-D-XINSPECT-2), and the page in the browser is an ordinary document that the browser's own developer tools profile, because no client runtime is hidden behind a synthetic context.

Dropped by DH-ADR-XINSPECT-1 (no debugging target: the DevTools hub, code evaluation and client inspection are not built). The limit describes a WebSocket relay that stops when the host's JavaScript thread is paused by the debugger.

Dropped by DH-ADR-XINSPECT-1 (no debugging target). The limit is about breakpoints in upstream's browser client runtime reached through a synthetic CDP context; the Go UI also has no client plugin runtime (DH-ADR-3).
Dropped by DH-ADR-XINSPECT-1 (no debugging target, so no Sources panel). The limit is about which JavaScript bundles the client side of the inspector catalogs for that panel.
Dropped by DH-ADR-XINSPECT-1 (code evaluation is not built). The limit is about evaluating JavaScript typed into the DevTools console inside the page, which a content security policy can block.

Dropped by DH-ADR-XINSPECT-1 (no tab is an inspection source). The limit is about giving each browser tab a stable identity as a CDP source; a tab's identity for the event stream is area A19's tab id.

Upstream replaces globalThis.fetch, so direct Undici calls and fetch references taken earlier escape capture. In Go capture is one transport wrapper registered with egress, the single factory of outbound HTTP clients, so every client is observed whenever it was built; DH-T-XINSPECT-2 asserts it. What is still not seen, child-process traffic and WebSocket frames, is stated in the specification.

Upstream tees both bodies by default and its retained-body limit does not cover buffering inside the tee. In Go bodies are not kept unless Bodies is set; then a prefix of at most MaxBodyBytes is copied into a fixed buffer as the caller reads, so there is no queue that a slow reader can grow, and the ring is also bounded by total bytes.

Dropped by DH-ADR-XINSPECT-1 (no debugging target, so no CDP state). The limit is about restarting the worker thread that holds that state; a diagnostic component is an ordinary fiber that the loader reloads like any other.

The limit exists because a relay sits between viewer and owner and must assert who the viewer is outside a body it cannot read. With no relay, the principal is fixed by the owner's host from the cookie of the admitted connection, never from request data, and there is no frame to refuse.

The registration tokens, the unversioned owner-to-worker messages and the optional actor fields all serve a gateway worker process that keeps registrations at a relay. The Go design starts no worker and registers nowhere, so none of these identities or compatibility capabilities exist.

Authority snapshots are needed because the access list, mode and expiry are held by the relay and must be copied to the owner, versioned and cleared on socket loss. In the Go design the only copy of a share is the registry in the owner's host; the access decision reads it directly and fails closed when it cannot.

The unverified support for historical releases concerns a wire protocol between independently deployed owner and relay. No such protocol exists in the Go design: the viewer's browser receives HTML from the same binary that enforces the share, so there are no two versions to keep compatible.

Three separately shipped parts (owner, viewer page, Liveshare server) had to match versions. The Go design has one part: the owner's host renders the viewer's page and no server stands between them, so a version mismatch cannot arise.

A method classified as readable but unreachable, because it names no session for the access check to bind, cannot exist in the Go route contract: every access-controlled id is a declared path parameter or the route does not register. The viewer's page has no composer, so the file picker the method feeds is not offered at all.

The late removal concerns the workspace feed a viewer's page renders. A Go viewer holds no global or workspace binding and is served no workspace or session list, so there is no feed to go stale; when a share ends the access change itself ends the viewer's streams.

The advisory claim file and per-registry snapshots exist because durable share state and relay registrations are addressed by the home directory while several hosts may serve it. A Go share is memory of the one process whose listener serves it; the only durable data are audit rows written in database transactions, and another host on the home reads them without being able to change a share.

Upstream checks authorization inside each share operation and publishes no separate observer of the invariant. In the Go design authorization is one decision made before any handler runs, from a rule every route must declare, and a test sweeps the whole route table as a viewer principal to prove that nothing outside the role is reachable.

Re-registration after a worker restart, reconnect loops stopped by relay refusals and credentials presented on restore are all behaviour of the gateway worker and its relay registration. Neither exists. A viewer's stream resumes by cursor through the ordinary event stream, and a host restart simply ends the share.

The split between admission and fork or write authority, the missing per-viewer execution levels, cancellation that cannot undo writes and the rule about which running turn a lapsed grant stops all follow from viewers who start turns. A Go viewer starts and stops nothing, so ending a share never has a turn to attribute or cancel and the owner's work is never touched.

The bullet is a release gate of the upstream build process: its assembled viewer artifact and SDK snapshots still need a final verification. The Go design has no assembled client artifact; its own acceptance is the real-browser scenarios of this specification.
