Reads that bypass the carrier reach the relay instead of the owner, and root-absolute links break under the relay's path prefix. With no carrier and no relay every request of the viewer's browser goes to the owner's host, whose pages use document-relative references.

Upstream accepts as a risk that any admitted viewer may attach files to the session. The view role does not contain the upload action, so a viewer's upload is refused before the handler runs; the owner has nothing to switch off.

The path check that a symlink swap can race, the list of tools a viewer's turn may run and the run_code program that the share does not bound all exist because a viewer starts turns. In the Go design a viewer starts no turn, so no tool ever runs on a viewer's behalf and there is no grant root to confine.
A person watching a shared session has no file preview and no terminal. (Removed: no installed-plugin method is exposed to a viewer.)
justification: Deliberate, and decided by the owner (DH-ADR-37: no relay, and viewers only watch): DH-ADR-XSHARE-3 says 'One role, four read actions' and that a viewer watches and cannot act. The file routes can read any file the session's filesystem backend allows and a terminal is command execution as the operating-system user; neither can be made safe for a second person by a role alone.

reason: The missing dialog entry for adding sessions and the reload that returns to the first source both come from a share that carries several sessions. A Go share names exactly one session and its link opens that session, so there is no second source to add or to lose on reload; another session is another share.

The one-workspace rule keeps all sources of a multi-session share inside one granted workspace root, which matters because viewer turns run file tools there. A Go share has one session and grants no file access, so no workspace constraint is needed.

Upstream exposes installed plugins' remote methods to viewers with no sandbox and no read or write classification, trusting plugin code that runs inside the host. The Go design exposes no plugin method to a viewer, and a plugin is a separate process that registers no UI route, so the trust question does not arise.

The share-wide method selection with no per-viewer levels, and selections that outlive the catalog, belong to the plugin-method picker. No picker and no stored selection exist in the Go design; and because each share has exactly one viewer, every grant is per viewer by construction.

Upstream's reference picker answers a viewer from the whole session index and so discloses the id, title and directory path of every session on the host. The view role contains neither the completion action nor the session list, the viewer's page has no composer, and a list route cannot register without applying the access filter, so a viewer learns of no session but the shared one.
The bundle page lists four supporting card rows that it cannot mark or hide. The Go bundle feature-guide has exactly one entry, so there is no supporting row.

Dropped by DH-ADR-XMISC-2 (personalized pages are not built). The bullet only points at the limitations of two other upstream packages and states no limit of its own; the units it points at have rows of their own.
There is no official plugin index, so Discover lists only sources the user adds. Go has no index reader and no Discover page at all: plugins are local directories the operator places.

Eligibility excludes missing packages and third-party registries. In Go the catalogue lists embedded optional bundles, which are in the binary and cannot be missing, and no registry exists to exclude (DH-ADR-13). Plugins the operator added are visible through plugin_manager list.

The harness never looks through a conversation in the background to find something to recommend and keeps no profile of the user; a suggestion is made only inside a turn the user started, when the model uses the skill there. (Removed: a suggestion no longer needs the exact live root agent.)
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-XMISC-3 has 'Scope boundary of this record: a suggestion is made only inside a turn the user started, when the model uses the skill there; no background call looks through a conversation for something to recommend and no profile of the user is stored', because either would send data without a user action (DH-ADR-9). The record does not promise 'only when asked': inside a user's turn the model may suggest a feature unprompted, which the reason now says.

reason: A recorded card decision does not follow later changes made on the Plugins page. Go records no card decision: the log holds the tool call and its result as history, and the skill catalogue is rebuilt from the live composition every time it is loaded.

The catalogue reports one enabled flag per bundle, so a bundle with one of its rows switched off still reads as enabled. The Go catalogue row has three states: on, off, and partly when the group is on and at least one of its entries is disabled.

The need for explicit human intent is enforced, not only stated in the prompt: a guard denies ralph unless the open turn is a human turn and the caller is not a delegated agent. Token cost is bounded by round, time and token budgets. The loop is Go code that calls the subagent runtime, so no workflow engine is mounted or isolated for it.

Upstream's tables see only the history window loaded in the browser. The Go log page asks the host for bounded pages by seq over the whole log, can jump to any seq, and applies its filters in the query, so no record is out of reach and row identity is the seq.

Upstream's log view does not show projection updates. The Go page has a 'views at this cut' panel that lists every registered fold with its state (current, behind, pending or failed) and the seq it covers, read from A06's registry Snapshot and Status.

Upstream highlights rows only when the client store publishes, and warns that raw data is unredacted. In Go a new row arrives as one fragment per committed event from the session stream, so there is no publication cadence; the page is owner-only, and secret values are never written to the session log in the first place (design.md section 6).

Upstream copies a row-reference array per publication and scans all loaded rows to filter and lay out. The Go host renders one bounded page per request (LogPageSize) with the filter applied by the query, and DH-T-XINSPECT-5 asserts that rows read per page do not grow with the log.

The limit is the keyboard selection state of a React suggestion list that refreshes asynchronously. The Go page has no client-side list state: its type and class filters are ordinary form fields that the host applies on each request (DH-ADR-3), so there is no list whose selection could be lost.

Upstream locates a record only if the chat is already displayed and the node rendered, because it searches the chat's DOM. A Go log row is a link to the transcript or trajectory address of its seq; following it opens that view and loads the history page that holds the target. The click-to-pick mask in the other direction is not built (DH-ADR-XINSPECT-4).

The bundle's in-memory index is rebuilt after every restart. In Go there is no second index: search documents are rows written in the transaction of their event in the session store, available at once in every process and after a restart (DH-D-VIEW-6). Search stays limited to what the caller's visibility admits.

Input over the byte limit fails and keeps the old title, with no policy for very long sessions. Area A06's generator, which this provider uses, reduces over-limit input by keeping the first prompt and the newest prompts that fit, so a long session still gets a title from a stated subset.
The all-prompts title provider treats every eligible user message equally, with no setting to weight or filter them; when the text is too long, the reduction favours the first and the newest prompts.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the fix pass: DH-ADR-XMISC-6 has 'Scope boundary of this record: every eligible user prompt counts equally, with no setting to weight or filter prompts; when the prompts exceed the byte limit the reduction keeps the first and the newest ones'.

reason: Keeping an adequate title is an instruction to the model, so the model may still reword it. The one deterministic part is built: a returned title equal to the current one after normalisation writes no new title event.
justification: Whether two different titles mean the same is a judgement only a model can make, and a model's output is not deterministic; no semantic check exists to build. A user who wants a fixed title pins it, which stops automatic titles.

reason: The title input budget rejects oversized input instead of shortening it, and a failure silently keeps the old title. Area A06's generator shortens over-limit input and writes one attempt event for every failure, so the kept title has a logged reason.

The provider offers one fixed skill that cannot be customised. Go ships no fixed badge skill; a badge of any wording is a SKILL.md in the user's or project's skill directory, read by area A14's filesystem provider.
The shipped badge text depends on a remote image service. Nothing the Go binary ships names that service, so the dependency is gone.

The limits describe one bundled recogniser: CPU only, a fixed platform list, fixed model sizes, six language hints, retained caches and desktop signing. The Go design ships no recogniser: the operator installs a program for their platform and hardware, lists its languages in configuration, and owns its files; there is no desktop application to sign.
Speech recognition transcribes complete recordings only; there is no streaming recognition and no speech synthesis.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XCUA-5 says 'no streaming' and limits voice to text proposed for the draft; DH-ADR-XCUA-4 recognises on the host with an operator-installed program that 'reads one WAV file and prints text'. Streaming needs partial-result revision and turn arbitration that dictation does not. No record names speech synthesis; nothing in the product speaks.

reason: Only one external agent runtime is exercised by the planned real-environment scenario; the five runtimes upstream never verified (antigravity, grok, kimi, opencode, pi) can be selected, but nobody has shown that they work through the bridge.
justification: Deliberate scope of evidence: owner decision DH-ADR-23 keeps the bridge and asks for a scenario against one real installed runtime, and DH-ADR-OAR-1 says 'Five of the seven runtimes were never verified upstream and are not verified here'. Verifying a runtime needs that vendor's program and an account. DH-ADR-XHOOKS-7 gives every registered runtime the same host-owned bridge and states which were verified with which OAR version.

reason: The harness does not install, sign in to or upgrade an external agent runtime. Narrowed: what is missing (Node, the OAR package, the native agent, a version outside the range) is reported before any task text is sent and never fails host start-up.
justification: Deliberate: owner decision DH-ADR-23 keeps a path to external runtimes; DH-ADR-OAR-1 lists Node, the OAR package and each native agent as prerequisites and says 'The harness installs none of these'; DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7 runs external products as operator-installed programs.

reason: An external agent runs under its own permission mode with no approval prompt from the harness; if it asks for an approval or for input, the run ends instead of waiting.
justification: Reclassed from platform limit in the re-sweep: the bridge does receive the native agent's request (message request in DH-ADR-OAR-1), so whether a person could answer it through OAR is unverified, not shown impossible. The records state the choice: DH-ADR-OAR-1 says 'The host answers by ending the run' and that the bridge refuses an instance that does not state its permission posture; DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7 says a person is asked only where the product's protocol has an answer channel and every instance has a time limit.

reason: The host owns the bridge child and every process below it, so cancelling while the native session opens stops the process tree at once instead of waiting for OAR, and the time limit covers start-up as well as the turn.

An external agent applies its own permission mode instead of the harness sandbox (the record says so), and it may keep transcripts of its own. (Fixed: the harness owns the bridge's process tree and ends it on cancel, time limit, a failed start and disposal.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7 runs external products as operator-installed programs in an operator-fixed mode, because a native agent needs the network and its own sign-in files, and its history belongs to the user's installation of that product. Whether an external agent can also run inside the harness sandbox is recorded as open in subagent-team.md section 10: it can only be learned by running each product.

reason: A task given to an external agent is one prompt and one answer: no follow-up, no resume, and no rollback of files the agent changed. (Narrowed: a structured answer can be requested and progress can be shown.)
justification: Reclassed from platform limit in the re-sweep: the one-shot contract is a choice, stated by DH-ADR-OAR-1 ('Keep the provider, its one-shot contract'), made because one prompt and a wait for the turn's end is the only use of OAR for which upstream holds evidence. That changes by another vendor's agent cannot be undone by the harness is a fact; a child that must not touch the user's checkout can be isolated with isolation: worktree (DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-12).

reason: There is one terminal service, provided by the execution area in every profile, so the terminal tools need no web composition and no private registry; in a headless profile they work without the roster view.

This bullet only points at the sidebar backend's list of limits. That backend is not a separate component in Go, and each of its six limits has its own row (terminal-panel.1 to .6) with its own disposition.
Once a person has typed into a terminal the agent opened, the agent cannot type into it again; it can read it and open a new one.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-8 states that control passes to the person and 'There is no hand-back'. After a person typed, the shell may hold a sudo or ssh sign-in; handing input back would give the model that authority with no approval.

reason: A command in an agent's persistent terminal runs under the policy the shell was started with and cannot ask for more access; a command that needs more is rerun with the one-shot shell tool, which can ask.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-8 says 'Commands inside cannot request escalation'; an approval covers one call (DH-ADR-16) and a persistent shell has one launch plan for its whole life, so widening a running shell would turn one approval into a standing one.

reason: Whether a program in a terminal has finished or is waiting for input is sometimes a guess: exact at the shell prompt on Linux and macOS, provable for a program waiting for input on Linux only, and otherwise reported as inferred from silence, with the reason.
justification: A terminal never says done; only the operating system can show that a foreign program is blocked reading the terminal, and macOS and Windows do not expose it. The execution area's readiness tiers state which answer is exact and which is inferred.

reason: When the model reads a person's terminal it gets the screen as it is at that moment; the read never waits for new output.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the fix pass: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-8 has 'Scope boundary of this record: a read of a person's terminal returns the screen as it is at that moment and does not wait for the program to become idle or for new output'. A waiting read would tie a tool call to the person's own work and keep reading what they type next.

reason: Agent terminals use the execution area's one shell backend with its controlled bootstrap, which runs no user start-up files, so no start-up file can fail to write outside the write roots. The cost is stated: a person who takes the terminal over gets a bare shell. This depends on area A09 confirming the default start arguments.

terminal_open starts every agent shell with history disabled (no history file for bash, history saving off for PowerShell) in every sandbox mode, so the agent's commands never join the person's history and the agent's shell never loads it. A real-environment scenario checks the history file is unchanged.

Upstream's projection holds reports in memory and the view shows seven days of them. In Go reports are derived rows (timeline_report) that the reports view pages a day at a time, so any period can be opened and nothing scans a retained list. The number of open discussions stays bounded by the MaxDiscussions setting, default 512.
Every task update writes the whole current task tree to the session log as one event, bounded by the session's event size limit and a maximum number of tasks.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words: DH-ADR-XINSPECT-5 names 'a whole tree per task update (kept on purpose)' in its tradeoff, because a state-carrying session event holds the whole new value so that the latest event alone restores the state (DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-7). The bound replaces upstream's separate 2 MiB figure.

reason: Pause and Continue on the timeline are requests: they reach the agent as a notice and take effect when the model updates its plan. Stopping a running turn is the separate Stop control, shown beside them.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-XINSPECT-5 has 'Scope boundary of this record: Pause and Continue on the timeline are requests that reach the agent as a notice and take effect when the model records them in its plan, and stopping a running turn is the loop's own cancel (DH-ADR-ARCH-3) shown as the separate Stop control, because a panel click must never abort a tool call in flight'.

reason: A ralph loop ends when the worker says the objective is complete (or a bound is hit); no independent evaluator checks the claim. The result labels the status as worker-reported and names which bound ended the run.
justification: Deliberate: an evaluator needs its own inputs, tools, checks and authority, which upstream left undefined; adding one would be a new feature. Since the convergence round the tradeoff of DH-ADR-XHOOKS-6 records it as scope (a recommended default the owner has not confirmed): ralph has no evaluator, as DH-ADR-JOBS-10 records for goals; the bound on rounds and the person reading the result are the control.

reason: A ralph run is foreground only: the tool call blocks until the run ends, with no job id, no resume after a process restart and no scheduler.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-6 allows the tool only in a human turn, makes it neither a workflow nor a goal, and says 'a run still blocks its tool call'. A background loop would outlive the turn that authorised it and spend tokens with nobody watching; background delegation is what a workflow job is for.

reason: Between rounds of a ralph loop the only memory is the workspace and one bounded report; each round's conversation is discarded.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-6 calls Start 'once per round with an output schema for the report' and 'disposes each activation before the next'. A fresh context per round is the purpose of the tool; carrying conversation across rounds would make it a goal, which the jobs area owns.

reason: One round of a ralph loop is one fresh child from one provider the operator chose; there is no fan-out inside a round and the model does not pick the provider.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-6 makes ralph one Start per round on the subagent seam, so there is no fan-out inside a round; that the provider is the operator's choice is in the area's configuration, not the record. Fan-out and routing are what workflows and the delegation tool are for.

reason: Recursion is denied structurally: a guard refuses ralph when the calling agent is a delegated agent, so a round's child cannot start a loop of its own whatever the prompt says. A test asserts it.

A failed round is retried roundRetries times (default 1) with the same handoff before the run ends, and because the loop is Go code and not a script in an engine, the failed round number and the last good report are always returned.
A run is bounded by rounds, by maxDuration and by maxTokens counted from each round's reported usage; the result names the bound that ended it.

Upstream withholds a continuation token because its cursors go stale when the corpus changes. A06's keyset cursors are properties of single documents and stay valid, so both search tools take a cursor argument and return next_cursor; a capped page no longer forces the model to guess a narrower query.

Upstream compares cwd strings, so two paths to one directory do not share authority. The Go tools use A06's visibility, which rests on workspace membership recorded against the workspace's canonical path (area A07), so a symbolic link to the workspace is the same workspace; DH-T-XINSPECT-11 asserts it.

Upstream returns complete payloads inline unless a deployment also mounts the spill policy. In Go a result bound is part of the one tool pipeline for every tool (DH-O-6), and the tools ask Query for bounded windows and snippets, so no composition can return an unbounded event.
Delegation to an external runtime is one-shot: no follow-up or resume, and the model cannot override the runtime's permission mode per call. (Narrowed: a structured answer can be requested.)
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-OAR-1 keeps 'its one-shot contract', DH-ADR-XHOOKS-7 makes the selector the shared delegation tool, and DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7 says 'The permission mode is part of the instance configuration; no tool argument reaches it', so a model cannot widen another vendor's agent.

reason: The selector is area A12's delegation tool, whose visibility is resolved per step from the registered providers, and a provider with a missing prerequisite says so in its requirements list. A call to an unavailable target fails as subagent/unavailable before any task text is sent.

Behaviour no longer varies by provider: every external provider uses the subagent area's one run lifecycle for start, cancel, cleanup and settlement. Ownership is explicit: an accepted run belongs to the root's tree fiber, so removing a tool is not expected to revoke it, and the creator can interrupt or dismiss it.

terminal_send accepts named keys (for example escape, arrow keys, ctrl-c) and terminal_read returns the emulated screen including a full-screen program's alternate screen, so a terminal interface can be driven and read. The bell and declarative auto-start remain carried by the execution area's own rows.
The run_in_background field is part of the terminal_send schema only while the job registry and the job tools are in the step view, so the model is never offered an argument that is then rejected.
Upstream's tool must reject a call that has no agent. In Go the pipeline's first stage attributes every call to an agent before a body runs, so the tool body always has one.
The model's worktree tools create, enter and leave a worktree; they do not list, merge or remove one, and enter reaches only the worktrees of the checkout the session is in.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XFORGE-8 says worktrees are 'created explicitly, before the first turn or by the tool'; DH-ADR-XFORGE-6 says 'enter_worktree accepts a target only if it lies inside the session's current write roots' and that only a person can move a session elsewhere; DH-ADR-XFORGE-7 says cleanup 'never deletes a branch'. Removal and merge destroy or rewrite work, and the model already has git through the sandboxed shell tool for them. No record says in so many words that the tools do not list or merge.

reason: The two browser translation endpoints are unofficial: their owners guarantee no availability, quota, response format or regional reachability.
justification: No design can give a guarantee the endpoint's owner does not give. The owner decided to keep the web provider specified but out of the shipped bundle (DH-ADR-36): the shipped bundle translates with the user's own model, which is the path with a supported interface; an operator may add the web provider in a layer, where no provider is preselected and the sender is off until turned on (DH-ADR-XMISC-5).

reason: Paid translation charges on every miss with best-effort record retention. In Go each model translation leaves a request event and one outcome event with usage, so every charge is in the log, and the records are declared types with versions. That no route falls back to another is kept as a rule (DH-O-8), not a defect.

Consumers own session activation, paragraph scheduling, input splitting and display fallback, and bad language tags fail only at the provider. In Go the service owns reading, splitting and scheduling because the host renders the transcript, nothing activates a session, and a tag that does not parse is refused before any request. One request per miss with no automatic retry is kept as a rule.

Every fragment lookup scans the whole session log and rebuilds an index. In Go the index is the registered fold translations, kept current as events commit and checkpointed by area A06's registry, so a lookup reads one event.

A failed or interrupted attempt is left as a request record with nothing that closes it. In Go every request gets exactly one outcome event (ok, failed, cancelled or interrupted, the last appended by the next lease holder), so an unfinished attempt cannot be mistaken for a pending one. A retry is still a new request, which is what an append-only log requires.

One malformed translation record, or a result without its request, makes every lookup in that session fail. In Go a payload is validated when it is appended, and the fold skips an event it cannot use and reports it in the fold status while other lookups keep working.

The registry is no longer limited to one bundled recogniser: any installed program fits the command provider, and a cloud provider is a component the operator enables with an endpoint and a credential reference, labelled cloud and never a fallback. That the feature adds no model tool and does not touch the agent loop is kept by design.
Installing dsh installs no recognition runtime: the binary is pure Go and contains no inference library, and nothing is downloaded when the feature is disabled or enabled.

The ingress is a second instance of the host area's listener, which supports TLS and refuses a non-loopback address without it, so the ingress can terminate TLS itself. This depends on area A18 allowing a second listener instance.

Field checks are part of the rule engine: a declarative rule's conditions read payload fields by pointer, a missing or wrongly typed field makes the condition false, and a field named in include that is absent fails the rule, so a rule cannot consume a field it did not check.

GitHub gets its 202 answer before any rule runs or any session exists, so GitHub learns nothing about the work that follows. Narrowed: a delivery record keyed by GitHub's delivery id names the sessions created or the failure.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-WIRE-12 has a webhook verify the raw body and answer 202; holding the provider's request open for rule and session work would tie an internet-facing connection to model activity (DH-ADR-XHOOKS-5).

reason: The GitHub webhook endpoint accepts JSON bodies only; a form-encoded delivery is refused with status 415.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-5 has 'Scope boundary of this record: the GitHub endpoint accepts application/json bodies only and answers a form-encoded delivery with status 415, because GitHub lets the operator choose JSON, and one content type keeps this internet-facing handler to one decoder that runs only after the signature over the raw body was verified'.

reason: The webhook runtime has no queue and replays nothing by itself: after a crash a delivery is run again only when the provider redelivers it. Narrowed: a delivery is recorded before the 202 answer, and a redelivery of an unfinished or failed record runs the rules again.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-WIRE-12 keeps the runtime fire-and-forget, and DH-ADR-XHOOKS-5 says 'There is still no queue and no completion report: the provider's redelivery is the retry'; and an automatic replay could start unattended work the operator no longer wants (DH-ADR-XHOOKS-5).

reason: A machine-state table keyed by source and delivery id records each delivery for dedupWindow (default 72 hours). A redelivery whose record is admitted or no-match runs no rule and creates no session.
Accepting a webhook reports nothing about whether the agent it started succeeded or what it produced. Narrowed: the delivery record names the session ids, so an operator can open the session.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XHOOKS-5 says 'no completion report ... the record names the session to look at'; the session a rule starts is an ordinary session that the webhook runtime no longer owns once the prompt is admitted; a completion report would need the runtime to watch sessions, which the wire decision DH-ADR-WIRE-12 avoids.

reason: A rule is configuration that the host evaluates itself, or a command run as a child process through the hook runner. The host stops that process tree with the stop ladder on unload or timeout, so no rule code can ignore cancellation.
The runtime never creates a workspace: a rule must name a workspace that is already registered, checked when the session is requested, so a failed session attempt leaves no workspace behind.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (the in-browser preview runtime is not built). The hand-kept rule tables decide which npm package files enter the browser image of that runtime.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no browser image is packed). The limit is that reachability is inferred from the textual forms of JavaScript import and require calls.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no browser image). The limit is the exclusion of vendored TypeScript sources from that image.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (the packer is not built). The limit is that the packer copies built lib/ artifacts and cannot tell that the workspace build is stale.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (the packer command has no counterpart). The limit is that the command only works from inside a complete built upstream checkout.

Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no Preview fixture is packed). The restriction to raw JSONL session inputs applies to fixtures packed into Preview overlays; the Go store also reads no upstream session format (DH-ADR-2).
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (the in-browser runtime is not built). The worker writes uncompressed session logs because it carries no Zstandard codec; the Go host stores sessions in a SQLite database.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no Preview runtime). Office conversion is refused in the Preview; on the Go host it uses an operator-installed LibreOffice (DH-ADR-20).
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no browser-hosted host). Hot module replacement replaces no modules in the worker; the Go design never reloads code in a process.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no Node emulation). Only some members of Node's internal module loader are emulated in the worker.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no Node emulation). The emulated require('stream') returns a module namespace where Node returns a constructor.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no in-memory file system). A lazily fetched file cannot be read synchronously before its archive is downloaded into the worker's file system.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no emulated file watchers). File watchers in the worker see only the mounted in-memory file system; the Go host watches the real file system.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no browser-hosted host). In the worker, confinement is a check inside the emulated file system; the Go host spawns commands under a real operating-system sandbox.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no worker bundle). The worker bundle pins a private file inside an npm package to keep an unused parser out of the browser download.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no browser worker). The worker's shell is a small interpreter with no loops, functions or job control; the Go host runs the machine's real shell in a sandbox.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no emulated shell). An emulated shell process reaches the in-memory file system only by messages, one round trip per entry.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no browser worker host). Six Node built-in modules are stubs that throw because a browser has no DNS resolver, sockets, processes or SQLite.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (the worker transport, worker host and page half are not built). The unmet coverage gate concerned those modules, so no coverage is owed for them.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no Node emulation layer). The limit is the partial re-implementation of node:assert/strict in the browser worker.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no browser worker host). A browser worker cannot bind a TLS listener; the Go host runs as a process and serves TLS itself when the operator configures it.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (the worker host is not built); there is also no desktop telemetry (DH-ADR-18). The limit is that desktop product telemetry cannot be sent from the worker.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no Preview runtime). The Preview cannot run pnpm or install plugins; the Go design installs plugins from local directories (DH-ADR-13).
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no browser image). The Pi coding agent is replaced by a stand-in in that image because its native dependencies cannot run in a worker.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no Preview runtime). Model requests are unavailable in the Preview because a stand-in refuses inference; the Go host makes model requests itself.

Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (no Preview runtime). Programs for programmatic tool calling cannot run in the worker; the Go design has no guest runtime and scripts call tools through the command line (DH-ADR-8).
A session can enter only a registered worktree inside the configured pool of the checkout it works in, and only one inside its current write roots.
justification: Deliberate, and tightened: DH-ADR-XFORGE-6 states that a worktree move never widens what a session may write, so a name chosen by the model cannot move the session, and with it the write boundary, to an arbitrary directory.

reason: Leaving a worktree keeps its branch and files, and cleanup never deletes a branch, so branches accumulate until the user deletes them. Narrowed: a failed setup is rolled back, and what a crash leaves behind is recorded in a journal row and reported.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-XFORGE-7 removes only clean, unreferenced checkouts and never a branch, because a branch holds commits, which are the user's work, and a checkout with uncommitted files must never be removed by the harness. The decision names the accumulating branches as its tradeoff.

reason: Creating a worktree fetches only the one remote branch a request names; it does not fetch other commits, initialise submodules, install dependencies or copy uncommitted files.
justification: Deliberate: an explicit pinned baseline with no implicit network use and no repository code run during creation (the rule kept under DH-ADR-XFORGE-6, where every Git command runs under the session's policy). Submodules and dependencies are steps the agent runs through the sandboxed shell. Since the convergence round DH-ADR-XFORGE-6 states it in its own text: nothing is fetched implicitly, and only the one named branch is fetched when a fetch was asked for.

reason: A new worktree is checked out with Git's filters skipped, so Git LFS files stay pointers and encrypted files stay encrypted until the user or the agent hydrates them deliberately.
justification: Deliberate safety rule, the same as unit client-ui-forge.1: a filter is a program named by the repository's configuration, and running it during creation would execute repository code and may download. Since the convergence round DH-ADR-XFORGE-6 states the rule and its cost in its own text: clean, smudge and process filters are switched off for the call, so a file kept by Git LFS stays a pointer in a new worktree.

reason: Upstream needs Node beside Git in the execution world and proceeds silently on a Git that ignores GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH. In Go there is no Node helper: Git's branch lock claims the name and the file seam writes the ignore file. A version probe refuses a Git too old for the filter overrides, and one without the lazy-fetch fix when the repository has a promisor remote.

Upstream registers no grant, so a session in workspace-write cannot commit inside its worktree, and Windows ignored such grants. In Go the component holds a write-root grant for the common Git directory while the session works in the worktree, when that directory was inside the session's roots at entry, and asks for a directory session grant otherwise; the sandbox area honours every root on Windows.

No page loads code or reports a resolution: enabling a model-written plugin is one consent item in the host's interaction registry that settles exactly once by compare-and-swap, and what runs is fixed by a digest, so there is no stale success to refuse and nothing to retry.

The limit describes a JavaScript client plugin waiting for a Remote namespace it declares in its inject list; the Go design has no client-side plugin or loader in the browser (DH-ADR-3), so there is nothing to park.

Slot admission is a property of the React client's slot registry, which exists only because the upstream client is a JavaScript plugin runtime; a Go plugin contributes no UI, and what it may contribute is carried by the manifest's capability list.

The two hand-mirrored whitelists become one capability table in the contract package; the gate, the generated protocol schema, the operator's display and the PluginProtocol inspect provider all read that one table, and a test enumerates it.

The gap between a load receipt and a later React render exists only because a browser half renders in the page after loading; a Go plugin renders nothing, and its readiness is the handshake plus the first tool listing.

No plugin needs a page to run. An attach asks one consent through the interaction registry, and where no answerer is bound (headless, ACP automation) it is refused at once as plugin/consent-unavailable instead of suspending; installed plugins hold standing grants and ask nothing.

Unattended automation uses installed plugins, whose grants an owner recorded beforehand, so no request waits for a person; an attach with nobody to ask fails closed immediately, and one with an answerer is bounded by the asking tool call's deadline and cancellation.

The timeout no longer bounds a synchronous slice of a script in the host's own thread: a plugin is an operating-system process with a start-up deadline, a per-call deadline from the pipeline, a ping deadline and a stop ladder that ends in killing the process tree.

There is one authority, the host, and one identity for what runs, the digest recorded at approval; no second party reports a revision that the registry can have moved past, so a request cannot be left suspended by a refused answer.

What a plugin asks for is declared in its manifest and read by Inspect before anything runs; the inspection report and the consent display carry every requested capability with its parameters and reason.
It is an npm packaging fact: generated JavaScript files import zod at run time, so the package manifest must declare it. Go has no package manifest of run-time imports and no generated Typert faces.

The inspection tool (harness_inspect) only reads: it cannot call a service, change configuration or run code. Upstream's other half, a query that needed a responding browser page, is gone because every provider lives in the host.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-EXT-9 makes inspection host-only, read-only and generated ('no provider method changes anything'), so that a tool which shows the composition is not a second way to change it. Changes go through settings and plugin management, each with its own approval and audit.

reason: The Entries provider reads area A18's inventory, which lists loader entries with their supplying layer and also presets, so an entry that is mounted only inside a preset is listed; a test asserts a preset-only entry appears.

Every change to a plugin's state, including one that starts or stops nothing, replaces its descriptor and dispatches plugin.StateChanged, and the page is rendered by the host from descriptors, so an open page cannot hold rows the host no longer has.

A pending attach is one consent item whose display is the full inspection report, and its descriptor exists in state waiting-grant from the moment the request is made, so there is no row that can be answered but lacks the data to operate it.
A row is rendered from the host's descriptor, which carries its labels through every state from the request onwards; there is no client-side fold that waits for a registry read.
A render failure of a loaded browser half is a React client event; the Go design loads nothing into a page, so there is no page-local crash to show or relay.
Whether a plugin is running is one fact held by the host and shown to every browser tab alike; no tab loads code of its own, so no tab can fail where another succeeded.
The consent for an attach is an item in area A17's interaction registry, which only the channel bound to the asking agent may settle and only as an owner; the frame-wide rule is not carried over.

An attach is recorded by its own durable event, plugin-host/attached, which holds the whole value including title, version and digest; the transcript notice is rendered from that event and not from the arguments of an earlier tool call that may have left the window.
The feedback service lists a session's current remarks and ratings from a projection for the UI and the SDK; no model-facing tool is added because feedback is not model context.
A feedback entry carries one category and one text and has no severity field.
justification: Deliberate boundary: no consumer in the design ranks feedback, so a severity field would be data nobody reads; it can be added under a new payload version. DH-ADR-HUMAN-13 now states it (an entry has a category and no severity). The referenced-event half of the upstream bullet is removed by DH-D-HUMAN-10.

reason: Recording feedback on a session with no live agent takes the session lease for the append, so a closed session accepts feedback; the case where another process holds the lease is the separate carried limit of message-feedback.3.
Each remark has an id and a feedback/withdrawn event removes it from the current view; history stays in the append-only log and deleting the session is the erasure operation.
The acknowledgement is returned only after the append was flushed, so an acknowledged entry survives a crash.
The acknowledgement is a server-rendered fragment of the feedback form and does not depend on the transcript having rows, so a blank session shows it too.
Command dispatch is one service call that the browser, the command line and the SDK all reach, so /feedback is available wherever a carrier exists.

The message_feedback sidecar is an earlier upstream storage format. Reading upstream formats is dropped by DH-ADR-2 and DH-ADR-11 (only upstream's current session format, through a separate import command), and the Go design never had a sidecar, so there is nothing to migrate.
Deleting a rating or withdrawing a remark removes the current item only; earlier values stay in the session log.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-1: the append-only log is the single source of truth and committed events are immutable. Erasure is deleting the session, which the session store provides (DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-10).

reason: Upstream refuses a feedback change when another process holds the session. In the Go design the home database has a request table (DH-ADR-STORE-12, the owner's resolution of register entry U-K1-5 in DH-ADR-40): a process that does not hold the session files the change, the holder applies it as its own append in the transaction that marks the request applied, and a request nobody applies expires and the user is told. The feedback service is the first user, through session.Service.AppendLogOnly (DH-ADR-SESSION-12, DH-ADR-HUMAN-13). Built by DH-D-STORE-11 and DH-D-SESSION-9; proven by DH-T-STORE-17 and the request step of scenario DH-E-STORE-1.
Every feedback event records the actor (principal, channel and peer) taken from the admitted connection, and a non-owner needs a role on the session to write feedback.

Recording feedback sends nothing; a session is uploaded only when the user turned the setting on and confirmed a preview of the redacted records for that submission, and a baseline redactor always runs.
Current feedback is a registered projection whose checkpoint commits with its events, so list, put and delete read state without scanning the session log.
The feedback component caps the number of feedback events per session as well as the size of one note and one text, and refuses further changes with a limit error.
There is no unfenced provider to mount. The base directory is only a default for relative paths, and containment comes from the per-call policy enforced by the provider.
Watch delegates to the one harness watch service, whose requirements and tests cover a parent directory that is deleted and recreated.
A version carries a SHA-256 of the content wherever the content was read, and the digest decides, so a storage layer that does not update metadata no longer defeats the stale check.
Memory is bounded by a constant instead of by file size: a text mutation refuses a file above textMaxBytes with fs/too-large.
A mutation outcome carries hunks computed under the provider's lock within the diff size bounds. No whole before or after text is returned or retained.
One text classifier in fsx is applied to the whole content on the read path and the edit path, so a file with a late NUL byte gets the same verdict from both.
Harness processes serialise on a cross-process lock keyed by file identity. Programs that take no lock are detected by a version re-check immediately before publication, with or without a guard.
Where the filesystem refuses hard links, create-if-absent reserves the name with an exclusive create and renames the staged file over the reservation.

Staging is one file beside the target that the publishing rename consumes, so there is no staging directory to remove afterwards. A file left by a failure has a recognisable prefix and is swept by age.
Observations are log-only session events folded by a registered projection, so a resumed session has them, and the digest check makes an observation of a since-changed file stale.
The operation service refuses a file tool call that carries no session before it runs, so there is no caller that may run the tool yet can never satisfy the policy.
Observation is recorded by the operation service, not by one tool, so every tool that shows file content to the model through it counts as having read the file.
An observation records whether the whole file or a part was shown, and the setting overwriteRequires: full-view demands the stronger rule. The default stays freshness by a recorded decision.
The patch applier detects, normalises, matches and restores the line-ending style itself, so no caller owns the conversion.
The parser is a line-fed state machine that reports each finished operation as input arrives. Applying works on complete text that textMaxBytes already bounds.

Mutations under workspace-write go through os.Root handles, which refuse a name that resolves outside the root, closing the check-to-write race. Mount points inside a root remain the operator's responsibility.
The fence takes its write roots only from the policy value issued by the one resolver, and a test fails if a filesystem package computes roots itself.
The provider requires the policy resolver as an injected service and does not load without it, so a composition cannot end up with file tools and no fence.
Edits and patches work on UTF-8 text and on UTF-16 text that starts with a byte-order mark; files in any other encoding are not edited as text. A plain move accepts any file.
justification: Narrowed, then kept on purpose. The re-sweep's gap (U-K1-14) is removed: DH-ADR-FS-11 item (a) now has fsx decode a UTF-16 file with a byte-order mark, edit the decoded text and write it back in the same byte order with the same mark and line endings, the version digest staying over the bytes on disk (DH-D-FS-1, DH-D-FS-6, test DH-T-FS-27). What remains is stated by the same record as its scope boundary: other encodings without a mark are not read as text, because without a mark the encoding is a guess and a literal match against a guessed decoding can edit the wrong bytes.

reason: A move that must not replace its destination, applies hunks or crosses write roots is two effects, not one atomic step.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-FS-11 item (c): the rooted handles the fence requires (os.Root) offer no rename that refuses to replace, and a rename across filesystems is never atomic. The outcome states both effects (DH-D-FS-4).

reason: Copy and recursive directory operations are not part of the file provider contract.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-FS-11: no model-facing tool needs them and the shell covers them under the process sandbox. The racy separate link check of the upstream bullet is removed by the do-not-follow option of DH-D-FS-4.

reason: Every operation takes a context.Context and the operation service applies a default deadline that acts at check points up to the start of publication.
Each operation takes the unresolved path and returns the resolved target in its outcome, so a remote provider needs one round trip per tool call.
Search walks the filesystem provider's own view from the session's working directory and returns the provider's display paths, so a returned path is readable by the read tool by construction.
There is no bundled binary: search is code inside the one harness binary, and a remote provider is searched through its view or runs the same package on its side.
The walk starts at the literal prefix of the pattern and does not enter a directory under which no match can lie.
Both tools take an offset, grep takes an output mode (lines, files or count), and the description teaches (?i) for case. Paging through a complete result no longer needs a spill store.
Over-cap sampling splits its budget across the children of each directory level in turn, not only across top-level entries.
A patch that fails part-way is not rolled back; the report lists every operation as completed, failed, unknown or not executed.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-FS-11 item (b): undoing earlier operations could overwrite an edit made from outside in the meantime.

reason: The read tool returns a bounded one-level listing for a directory instead of refusing it, which gives the model a directory listing without another tool.
The read tool reads UTF-8 text and UTF-16 text with a byte-order mark; other unmarked encodings, audio and video are not read as text.
justification: Narrowed, then kept on purpose. A UTF-16 file with a byte-order mark is now read through the same decoding (DH-ADR-FS-11 item (a), DH-D-FS-6, test DH-T-FS-27; the re-sweep's U-K1-14). The record states the rest as its scope boundary in its own words: other encodings without a mark, audio and video are not read as text, because without a mark the encoding is a guess; audio and video never reach a model by DH-ADR-LLM-1, and a non-text file is answered with the name of the tool that reads it.

reason: The file signature decides the image type and the extension is not consulted, so a valid image under a wrong extension is accepted.
read_image asks the attachment store whether the path is one of its objects and returns the existing reference, so a stored image is not admitted a second time against the source limits.

The limit exists only because upstream's React client fills a plugin slot to show the image. The Go UI has no client plugin slots; the tool's own server-rendered card shows the image from the reference in the result.
read_image accepts an attachment reference as well as a path and an optional region, so a pasted image without a path can be re-read in part.
File tools run under a context deadline applied by the operation service, so a call has a time budget even though one system call cannot be interrupted.
The single-editor tool handles UTF-8 text and UTF-16 text with a byte-order mark; other encodings are not edited as text.
justification: The same as unit fs.fs.1: DH-ADR-FS-11 item (a) names str_replace_editor among the operations that work on decoded UTF-16 text with a mark, and states unmarked encodings as its scope boundary. Note: test DH-T-FS-27 exercises read, edit and apply_patch, not this tool, which shares the decoding of fsx and is built later (DH-D-FS-8).

reason: str_replace requires exactly one match and has no replace_all argument.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-FS-11 item (d): the tool exists for the schema some models already know, so it is not extended; the edit tool offers replace_all.

reason: The tool is a front end over the operation service, which always applies the fence and asks for an intent decision, so no composition gives it unconditional mutations.

The Go UI is server-rendered HTML: the goal panel is a form (objective, round cap, a confirmation before replacing) that calls the goal service directly, so editing does not depend on a text command registry. The /goal command stays as a text shortcut.
The service's create and edit requests carry the round cap and the budgets for any human caller; the panel shows them as fields, so a person sets them without asking the model.
The goal projection and the goal.ActivationChanged notice drive a live fragment on the event stream, so the current phase, round count and arming are shown continuously and survive a reconnect.

Goal operations are service calls, not only a command: the spec asks the SDK protocol, the command line and the HTTP routes to expose get, create, edit, pause, resume and clear, so headless and automation clients control a goal without a command adapter.
The model decides when evidence is sufficient and whether a blocker is unchanged; the runtime enforces only counts and budgets.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-10, the same as unit goal.goal.3.

reason: Goal rounds run in the same session; the driver starts no fresh agent and forks nothing.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-9: independent attempts with fresh context are delegation and workflows, which the subagent and workflow areas provide.

reason: The Go port releases a fiber's effects one at a time, newest first. The driver registers its pre-step fence first and its remove-my-prompt-and-disarm effect last, so on unload the queued round prompt is removed and every goal disarmed before the fence goes; no accepted prompt can start a round unfenced.

Token and time budgets are part of the goal, and the turn budget is mapped: a round ending on it counts, and a configured run of such rounds blocks the goal with code turn-budget. Each automatic stop is a blocker code, so resource limits are attributed to the goal.

A round whose turn failed with a failure the model-provider area classes as transient is retried after back-off, at most retryFailedRounds times, then the goal is blocked with code provider-failure. A failed flush is never retried: it disarms.

The split is kept on purpose (state in component goal), and the missing policies now exist as a deliverable: component goal.rounds decides when a goal continues, retries transient failures within a bound and cancels the running turn on a host pause.
A goal may carry a token budget and a time budget beside its round cap. Both are derived from the log, and the driver records a blocker with code token-budget or time-budget when one runs out.
The caller that records a goal as complete or blocked is authoritative; no independent evaluator ships.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-10 (tradeoff: the model still judges completion; the goal.Completing interception is a place for a deterministic check, not an evaluator).

reason: A session has at most one current goal and there is no goal database; history stays in the session log.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-9 (a goal is one event-sourced objective per session): parallel objectives are separate sessions or delegated agents.

reason: No third-party code runs in the host: a plugin is a separate process that cannot append session events of a host-owned type. Inside the host the typed append handle for goal/change is private to package goal. The strict fold is kept as the last check.
Execution proves that the turn holds a direct human message on a root agent, not that the request merits a goal.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-9 in its own words (Scope boundary of this record: the goal tool proves that a person spoke in the current turn, not that the request deserves a goal; judging merit needs an understanding the runtime does not have).

reason: The runtime enforces the number of consecutive rounds before a model-reported blocker, not that the obstacle is the same one.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-10 in its own words (Scope boundary of this record: whether two reported blockers are the same obstacle is the model's judgement, and the runtime only counts rounds and enforces the round cap and budgets, because counting is exact).

reason: The tools still only change state, and the two consumers the bullet names are separate deliverables of this spec: the round driver schedules, and the command and the server-rendered goal panel show the goal to a person.

The guidance about goal rounds is contributed by the goal.rounds component, so a composition that mounts the tools without the driver does not teach the model a path that cannot occur; the human-turn operations work without the driver.

A prompt section of this area is rendered only when at least one of its tools is in the step view of the requesting agent, so hiding the tools hides the guidance. The same rule is used for the job and schedule sections.
A declaration may supply RepeatKey(args), so the tool that knows what counts as the same call defines the identity; the default stays exact canonical JSON.
The chain is a projection folded from the session log and resets on the compaction event, because after compaction the model no longer sees the earlier identical calls.
An optional blockAt count registers a deny-only guard that refuses the call at that run length; it is off by default so the reminder stays advisory unless the operator asks otherwise.
The repeat reminder counts a parent and its subagent separately.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-TOOLS-9: a repeat chain describes one model's own context, and a subagent has a different context, so the two are not one loop.

reason: A polling tool declares itself RepeatExempt, so the exemption ships with the tool instead of depending on each deployment's exclude list.
The repeatEvery setting reminds again every N identical calls after the highest threshold, so a long chain no longer goes silent.

The timeout result reaches the model after a bounded grace period whether or not the body returned, and a body that owns a process is stopped by the process stop sequence; a body that still ignores cancellation is detached and reported as outcome unknown.
Every call has a budget: the tool's own, an operator override or the configured default; opting out needs an explicit NoDeadline declaration that a golden test lists.

The limitation describes the desktop start-up component and its shared owner peer for the desktop lifetime. The desktop application is dropped by DH-ADR-18, so the component and its limit cannot arise.

The cookie payload carries a random browser id and each id gets its own peer, so one browser can be signed out and only its streams end. Unloading the authentication component still ends every peer, which is ownership working as designed.

A listener on a non-loopback address without TLS is refused at start-up unless the operator sets an explicit insecure flag, which warns at every start and in the UI. On loopback the cookie does not leave the machine. The Secure attribute still follows the listener's own protocol.

The listener owns the rule for the token parameter on every path: only GET on the root is the exchange, and a token parameter on any other request is answered 400 before routing and is never passed to a handler or written to a log.

Nothing infers where the operator sits any more. There is one directory browser, rendered in the page, which works the same for a local browser, a forwarded port and a detached terminal session, so a wrong inference cannot open a dialog on an unattended machine.
The probe for a Linux chooser program on PATH is not built, because no native chooser is started. The directory browser needs no desktop tooling.
The boot-time choice between two interactions is removed. Every client of a host gets the same browser interaction, so no per-connection capability or wire advertisement is needed.

A proxy that presents a loopback authority can no longer cause a native dialog on the host display, because no native dialog exists. The same case for open-in-app is bounded by the rule that only a workspace directory can be opened in a catalog application.
Go exposes the Windows file attributes of a directory entry, so the hidden flag is the dot prefix on every system and also FILE_ATTRIBUTE_HIDDEN on Windows, with no native probe.
The listing has a roots level above the top of a tree. On Windows it lists the drive letters that answer a bounded probe, so a person can cross drives without typing a path.

The browser accepts an optional list of roots in config and performs every listing and creation through an os.Root handle for its root. The specification states that this is a security boundary only when workspace creation honours the same roots, and asks area A07 for that.
The macOS activation problem belongs to a scripted native panel started from a background process. No native panel is started; the picker is part of the page the user is already looking at.
The dependency on Zenity or KDialog is removed with the native backend. The browser interaction, which upstream names as the fallback, is the only interaction.
The Windows child process that drives a COM dialog through a native binding is not built, so a COM refusal or dialog crash has nowhere to occur, and the binary needs no native binding.
The synthesised key press that lets a background process bring its dialog to the foreground is not needed: the harness opens no window of its own on the host.
The contract has a roots level: a listing above the top returns the configured roots, or the drives on Windows, so several roots and drive enumeration are part of the one browser interface.
Content types come from the one harness media-type table that every file-serving path reads, not from a nine-entry starter table, and an unknown extension is served as a download with nosniff.

There is no single-page application and no fallback for unmatched paths. Every page is a route its owner registers explicitly in area A19's route table, which the listener reaches as one mount, and a miss is 404.

An operator can add application entries in a config layer, each with a label and an argument template, next to the embedded catalog. A request can still never name a program; only catalog ids and operator entry ids are accepted.

Upstream finds a macOS application only in known directories. DH-ADR-HOST-9 now also runs one Spotlight query by bundle identifier (/usr/bin/mdfind) through the host starter, at resolution time only, with a deadline and bounded output, and accepts a result only if its Info.plist names the same identifier (audit finding Q3-11). Built by DH-D-HOST-9; proven by DH-T-HOST-28 (a fake starter finds an entry outside the known directories, ignores a mismatched identifier, and survives a timeout) and by scenario DH-E-HOST-10 with an editor moved out of /Applications. Remainder: an application Spotlight does not index is added by an operator entry, as the record says.
No application icons are extracted; the UI shows a category glyph and the application's name.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-HOST-9 (application icons are not extracted): extraction needs a platform helper or a native API on each system, for a decoration.

reason: Resolution runs on first use and again when the list is asked for after a configured refresh age, so a newly installed application appears without restarting the host. A missing launcher is still re-resolved on the spot.

The inventory raises a change event and keeps a bounded in-memory history of phase changes, so an entry that failed and was removed can still be shown with its reason. The history ends with the process; the log file is the durable record.

Each entry row names the layer that supplied it, read from the loader's ownership index. Mutation stays out of the inventory by decision: composition is changed through settings forms and plugin installation, which other areas own.
The presets part of a snapshot is always present and carries an explicit availability flag, so a reader can tell that no preset registry is composed from an empty roster.

Event selection is no longer free: an event is a Go type declared in a catalog whose fields may only be booleans, integers, duration buckets and strings from a closed set. There is no renderer-to-host transport because the host renders the UI, and the only identity attribute is the anonymous installation id.
The queue for analytics and telemetry records is memory-only: overflow, a failed request and process exit lose records. The loss is counted and shown.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-HOST-7: a durable outbox would store usage data on disk and would have to be purged when the user withdraws consent (owner decision DH-ADR-9 makes all of it opt-in). A consumer that needs delivery, the session upload, keeps its own progress in the session log.

reason: Every channel is bounded by record count and by uncompressed request bytes, because the exporter owns the encoder and knows each record's size. An ordinary channel defaults to one million bytes per request and cannot exceed four million.

There are no caller-selected free strings to redact: the catalog refuses an event type with a free-text field at start-up. Disclosure and consent are decided in one place, the sharing gate, whose permit the reporter needs before it creates a channel.

The certificate and key are re-read when the files change, so a renewed certificate is served to the next handshake without a restart, and a bad replacement keeps the last good pair. Issuing and renewing certificates stays with the operator, as upstream decided.

The source check and the route class are steps of the listener itself and cannot be unmounted, so an anonymous route is never reachable without the Host and origin checks. Only the credential lookup and the non-owner policy are answered by other components.

The settings a deployment tunes are config fields with defaults: header read timeout, idle timeout, header size and shutdown grace, with write deadlines set per route. Go takes the accept backlog from the operating system's limit, so there is no harness constant to expose.
Resetting or losing the anonymous identifier creates a new identity that cannot be linked to the old one.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-HUMAN-12: this is the anonymity property itself; recovery would need stable material derived from the machine or the user.

reason: The identifier is created by one insert-if-absent transaction in the shared database, so two processes that race get the same value and no run uses a private one.
Two harness homes have unrelated anonymous identifiers and cannot be correlated.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-HUMAN-12 in its own words (Scope boundary of this record: the identifier belongs to one harness home; two homes of the same person have two identifiers and nothing links them, because a link would need an account or a shared secret, which is the identity the anonymous identifier exists to avoid).

reason: The identifier is attached to a model request only when that route's Installation switch is on, and Ensure refuses to create or return it for a purpose the user did not enable, so a configured gateway receives nothing by default.
The identifier is read through the key-value store's revision check and not memoised per process, so a reset takes effect at once in every process on the home.
A command may declare a Go argument struct from which validation, the UI form, completion and the SDK schema are derived; raw text remains as one argument type among others.
A command handler must honour cancellation; one that does not is settled as aborted after a grace period and tracked as detached.
justification: Go runtime fact, the same as tools unit tool-executor-native.1: a goroutine cannot be stopped from outside. DH-ADR-HUMAN-8 bounds the wait and reports the detached handler instead of hiding it.

reason: A permission preset bundles two knobs, sandbox mode and approval policy, and does not choose the agent composition.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-HUMAN-6 (a preset bundles two knobs): which tools and prompt an agent has is the agent preset; folding it into the Permissions choice would make one control change both authority and capability.

reason: The preset table is live configuration that the settings form edits in the writable layer, so a user who wants a named combination adds an entry and selects it; custom stays the label for an unmatched pair.
The preset component accepts a configuration update in place and notifies permission.CatalogChanged, so the table can change without reloading the component.
The reserved auto preset cannot be the default for new sessions.
justification: Deliberate boundary under DH-ADR-HUMAN-6: auto is contributed by an experimental, default-off review component, and a default that names an entry which may not be loaded would leave new sessions without a valid permission state.

reason: The default preset must name an entry of the preset table, so removing that entry and changing the default happen in one configuration edit.
justification: Deliberate fail-closed rule under DH-ADR-HUMAN-6: falling back to some other preset when the named default disappears would change a security default without the operator saying so. An edit that breaks the rule is rejected with its position.

reason: There is one tool schema, so every call is tracked by the questions projection and any call can return pending or take a late answer.
A nested call made through the tool command line is logged when it is admitted, before its body runs, so the projection can reconstruct the question even if the calling script ends first.

Upstream refuses a question from a subagent outright. In the Go design every item a child agent raises is registered for its own session and offered to whoever answers for the root session of its tree, labelled with the child's path, and settles unavailable if the root has no answerer (rule 5 of who may answer, DH-ADR-HUMAN-2; DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-6). The owner confirmed on 2026-11-19 that a subagent's request goes to whoever answers for the root session (DH-ADR-16), and both specifications now say so.
The tool renders its answer for the model as one readable line per question through the declaration's render function, while the structured value stays in the log.
A request may be made outside a turn: the turn requirement existed to tell an audit event from a crash tail, which the transactional store does not have, and an open pair found on resume is closed.
Session grants add a standing yes for one directory or one application that is logged, listed and revocable and ends with the session; nothing is stored across sessions.
The request still references the call by id, and the interaction item resolves the tool's presentation of the logged arguments, so every answerer (browser, SDK, ACP) shows what is being approved.

Upstream ships no answerer in a headless or incompletely composed deployment, so every approval there fails without anyone being asked. In the Go design each interactive profile mounts the answerer of its carrier and binds the agents it creates; the headless command registers the cli answerer when a controlling terminal can be opened and --json is not set, and asks there, also for a subagent, because the runner answers for the root session (DH-ADR-CLI-7). In every other case no answerer is registered and an approval settles unavailable and is denied, which is the stated rule, not an omission. Proven by DH-T-CLI-12, DH-T-CLI-13 and scenario DH-E-CLI-2.
A pending approval is not restored after a host restart; on resume the open audit pair is closed as unavailable and the call is denied.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-HUMAN-1 (pending approvals live in memory only) and DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-10: the interrupted turn is closed and never continued, so there is no call left to approve.

reason: An interaction's audience is an agent or a peer, so a caller without an agent (a sign-in prompt, a consent from a command) is routed to the peer that started it instead of needing a local listener.
A question is selectable options plus optional text; file pickers and diff confirmations have no interaction kind.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-HUMAN-1 (four closed kinds): each kind needs a payload type, a rendered fragment and a mapping in the SDK and ACP protocols, so a kind is added when a tool needs it.

reason: Unfinished answer text stays in the browser tab that holds it and is not stored by the host.
justification: Deliberate boundary: a draft is not a decision, and storing keystrokes of an unanswered question would add a write path and a second copy to keep consistent across tabs. DH-ADR-HUMAN-1 now states it in its tradeoff (a half-typed answer stays in the browser tab that holds it).

reason: Jobs and their in-memory output end with the host process; on resume each lost job is closed in the log and the model is told.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-1; DH-ADR-JOBS-4 and DH-D-JOBS-2 make the loss a recorded fact, and spilled output survives.

reason: A job is an effect of its owner's scope fiber, so teardown cancels it and appends job/settled inside the scope unwind, which the agent teardown order places before the final bounded flush and the lease release. A hard kill is the crash path: resume appends the settlement with cause host-exit.

Cancellation is the context of a blocking Run function. If Run has not returned after stopGrace the registry settles the job as failed with producerReported false, frees its capacity slot and lists the goroutine as detached, so a silent cancel can neither stall teardown nor hold a slot.
The job contract is in-process: live work cannot be handed to another process.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-1 (a job is owned by one session's agent and lives in the host process): a producer holds process handles, pipes and in-process state, and the design has no supervisor outside the host (DH-ADR-WEBAPP-4). DH-ADR-JOBS-4 records the loss in the session log.

reason: The model's cursor is the only consuming read of a job's output; observers read at their own offset without consuming.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-2: two consuming readers would each receive part of the output.

reason: The registry keeps at most maxSettledPerOwner settled records per owner (default 50) and removes the oldest collected one first, so the listed set is bounded without an explicit remove.

The notice is one waking steer; the sender never decides whether the owner is busy. The Go inbox makes a waking send either land in the running turn or open a new one, so there is no window in which a notice is queued and nothing wakes.
The notice peeks the unread output and the registry commits the model cursor only when the driver claims the message. Nothing is held in the tools component, so reloading it loses no output.
The wake budget refills by one wake per wakeRefillInterval as well as on a user message, and a notice held past the budget raises a live jobs.NoticeHeld notice so the UI can show that one is waiting.

The jobs projection derives from the log which settlements the model was never given (no claimed notice, no terminal job_output). On resume one notice names them, so a notice discarded at disposal is not the last word.
The model tools are the single consuming reader of a job's stream; the UI follows a job without consuming.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-2, the same as unit jobs.jobs.2.

reason: Unowned jobs are not built: every job has an owning agent reference and Start refuses a spec without one. Host work that belongs to no session is an ordinary fiber effect, not a job.
Request contributions are registered by name and listed per route, so any route may opt in; the registry is no longer tied to one vendor route.
Contributed fields are appended in name order after the base fields, so the request bytes are reproducible and can be compared with stored expectations.
The last good listing is stored in a machine-state table keyed by endpoint and credential fingerprint and is served, marked stale, when the host starts without a network.
Every listing change notifies llm.ModelsChanged, which the model picker fragment reloads on; the upstream README body already describes an announcement, so the bullet is also stale.
The vendor's version gate is evaluated in the client, so a modified client can request any model id.
justification: Fact of any client-side check: a program cannot enforce a rule on a modified copy of itself; only the vendor service can. The specification documents the gate as a compatibility guard, not a security control.

reason: The reasoning effort levels in the vendor's model listing are not read; levels come from the embedded catalogue.
justification: Still open (register entry U-K1-12): the shape of the listing field is not in the pinned upstream source. Section 10 of the spec now says that scenario DH-E-LLM-5 keeps one real listing and that a tolerant read is then added to the catalogue refresh of DH-ADR-LLM-6. What is missing: the steps and assertions of DH-E-LLM-5 do not mention the effort field, and no deliverable or test covers the read, so the fact is not obtained and the read is not designed.

reason: A listed model the build cannot drive is returned as unavailable with its reason and minimum version, so the picker can show an upgrade notice instead of a generic empty state.
Overlay fields accept an explicit none value, so an override can remove a system-prompt or tool update mode as well as set one.
