The logged request header records the credential reference name and sign-out cancels every running agent whose latest header names it, so the report and the cancellation no longer depend on the route component being loaded, and a running tool is cancelled with the turn.
An on-demand route check sends one small real request per chosen model and reports the classified result, which gives the user the remote validation the configured catalogue cannot.
One resolved model set (catalogue, listing, overlay) serves the settings page, the picker and the request, so the page and the listing cannot disagree and an edit cannot drop a listed model.
Configuration is an overlay keyed by model id, so a route with edited models still receives the ids a followed listing adds later.
Nothing compares the configured models with a built-in list any more; an overlay entry is explicit, so a new build cannot turn an old default into a customisation.
The last good listing is stored in a machine-state table and served, marked stale, on a start without a network.
Every listing change notifies llm.ModelsChanged, which the model picker fragment reloads on.
Listed models the build cannot drive are returned as unavailable with a reason, so a route with no servable model explains itself instead of offering nothing.
A route's models are an overlay keyed by model id and edited per model; there is no list to replace as a whole.
Controls gains ToolChoice, and every driver either encodes it or fails with llm/unsupported-option before any I/O.
Every provider client comes from the egress factory, so model requests follow the one proxy and certificate policy and nothing uses a default transport.

When the Messages driver cannot place an in-history system update after a user or tool-result turn it consolidates the update into the leading system slot for that request and logs a diagnostic, so placement never fails a request.
Images are input only and are sent as bytes the harness holds; a provider is never given a URL, and assistant image output is not supported.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-LLM-3 item (f): a URL the provider fetches would be model-visible content that is not in the session log. The upload-recovery half of the upstream bullet is removed by the time-based cool-down of DH-D-LLM-5.

reason: The on-demand route check probes a chosen model against the configured gateway, and a refused model fails with a classified code instead of a guess from the catalogue.
Real-provider scenarios take the key at run time in a separate credentialed workflow, and a scenario that did not run for lack of a key is reported as open, never as passed.
The harness encodes the request body itself, so the image budget is enforced on the encoded request size and not only on the base64 image payload.
Discovery follows the listing's pagination up to a bounded page count and reports when it stopped early, instead of reading one page.
A route speaks exactly one protocol and a vendor with two protocols is two routes, so a model the catalogue does not list is never ambiguous.
The on-demand route check probes each declared input type with a real request, so a wrong declaration is found before a conversation depends on it.
The harness's own drivers send no authentication header for a route that names no credential, so a keyless local server needs no placeholder key.
Reasoning level spellings, and whether a model can disable reasoning, are per-model catalogue data the Gemini driver reads, not a fixed list inside a library.
Each driver sends stop sequences where its protocol has them and fails before I/O where it does not.
System-prompt and tool update modes are overlay fields any route or model can set in configuration, not flags locked inside an installed catalogue.
Each driver states which roles can carry images, and an image in any other role is sent as the same placeholder text a text-only route receives instead of failing the request.
The shared transport keeps the HTTP status, headers, request id and original error, and failure class is a property of the code, so nothing is classified from message text.
No library is in the request path, so there is no library retry to switch off; one-shot callers that upstream leaves single-attempt get a buffered retry through Runtime.Complete.
One image policy serves every driver and removes the oldest images in byte and count quanta, so an image-adding request does not restart prompt-cache reuse every time.
The harness's own decoders forward tool-argument fragments as text and check the JSON once at the end, so there is no per-fragment re-parse and no patch to carry.
The prefix digest is computed over the request bytes actually sent, and a route may keep signed reasoning across a prefix change where its endpoint does not check.

A resolved model declares that its reasoning is bound to the request prefix, and the driver loop then holds a prefix change until the open tool round ends, which removes the cause of the rejection; this needs the agent-loop area.
Decoders keep every response member they do not model as raw JSON and replay it to the same route, so a provider-private signature survives without a patch.

A pending sign-in is an interaction in the host registry, so a page reload re-attaches to it, and sign-out calls the issuer's revocation endpoint where one exists; a host restart still abandons a pending sign-in.

OAuth routes are a later provider component that can hold an opt-in installation identifier for an issuer that requires one; whether to offer a third party's consumer sign-in is recorded as an owner question.

The four protocol drivers receive credentials only from the harness credential service, so nothing reads the environment or credential files on its own; a cloud component's vendor module that reads its own chain is stated in that deliverable.
Layers are first-class: the ownership index shows which layer supplies a route, and the writable layer can remove an inherited route explicitly instead of only resetting to it.
Routes and models merge by key across layers and removal is an explicit operation, so writing one route cannot silently drop inherited entries.
A header value is plain text or a credential reference of the redacting secret type, and a plain value under a credential-bearing header name is refused when the config loads.
A route chooses its listing mode: offer keeps adoption explicit and follow lets the endpoint's listing contribute model ids.
Runtime.Complete applies the route's retry policy to a buffered one-shot call and exposes no chunk of a failed attempt, so callers outside the agent loop are no longer single-attempt.

Retry is decided by failure class: a permanent failure such as authentication, quota or an invalid request is never retried in any mode, and the unlimited mode is replaced by one bounded by elapsed time.
One cap on attempts per step, counted from the log, binds every recovery listener, so separate budgets no longer add up.

The retry component acts on transient failures by class without first waiting for another listener, so its outcome no longer depends on listener order; a listener that never returns is bounded by the agent-loop area's dispatch deadline.
A new durable event llm/retry-abandoned records why recovery stopped, so exhaustion and cancellation are facts in the log and not inferred from later events.
Retry is a separate component by decision, a per-route concurrency cap is added to the runtime, and a response cache is deliberately absent because it would answer without an attempt.
One client identity value is the default User-Agent of every egress client, so model requests and web tools send the same identity; this needs a default hook from the egress owner.
Controls adds TopP and ToolChoice, which all four protocols can carry, and other gateway parameters are static route configuration in extraBody.
The rule that no variant exists without a producer is kept as policy; cache breakpoints are placed by the Anthropic driver itself and need no vocabulary variant.
The block set is a closed Go set and a plugin is a process that cannot add a block type, so the assembler can never meet an unknown block.

The request carries the session as an opaque label, Meta.Session, declared in the leaf package llm/vocab. Package session imports that leaf and package llm imports session, so there is no import cycle and no duplicate declaration; an import-direction test enforces it.
A loop request can only be built from the log, so the tool-update projection always receives the session-folded tool history and the missing-history fallback cannot arise for it.
Exists only because of npm: the limit is that some plugins have no npm package name and version. Go has no npm packages; a compiled-in component's identity is the binary's build version.
A compiled-in component always has the binary's identity and a plugin process cannot load without a manifest, so the opt-in installation inventory cannot be partial.
Exists only because Node can replace a mounted npm package in a running process; Go never replaces code in a running process, and a plugin process re-reads its manifest when it is restarted.
Token counts for text are a calibrated estimate, not an exact count.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-LLM-9: the meter is a deterministic fold of the log with no model call, and its tradeoff says a consumer that needs exact tokens must ask the provider. An exact local count would need a tokenizer per vendor, which not every vendor publishes.

reason: Meter state is checkpointed in the same transaction as its events, and a cold read prices only the current surface read from the session, not the whole log.
Values are immutable by ownership, so a measurement shares them instead of cloning, and context pressure is a stored total read in constant time.
When the request envelope differs from the last measured one, the estimate is scaled by the session's calibration factor instead of falling back to the raw heuristic.
The fold keeps the price of each retained system prompt and reprices a replacement in the same step, so a rewrite is no longer counted as zero until the next usage sample.
Projection state is totals plus one price per retained system prompt; the surface has one owner, the session, and is not copied into a checkpoint.

A language server starts through the host's starter under a sandbox policy: workspace-write on the workspace root and the entry's declared roots, with the configured network setting; where no backend can confine, the provider is unavailable.
A server that advertises no open and close synchronisation is queried on closed documents instead of being refused, and the real-environment scenario runs two different language servers.

Read-only queries overlap up to maxConcurrent because open documents are counted instead of opened and closed per query, and an idle process is stopped after idleTimeout so it no longer holds memory until disposal.

The process tree is owned by the host's starter, which ends it with the host on Windows and Linux, and a server in the local world is given the host's process id so that it exits by itself where the operating system gives no such owner.
A routes table in the seam's configuration names the provider for an extension that two providers claim; without an entry the overlap is a load error that names both.

Upstream offers four read-only operations. DH-ADR-CONNECT-7 now adds three more at lower priority: the symbols of one file, a symbol by name in the workspace, and the diagnostics of one file, which are fresh or marked stale (register entry U-K1-6). Built by DH-D-CONNECT-5; proven by DH-T-CONNECT-21 and by a diagnostics query after an edit in scenario DH-E-CONNECT-4. Remainder, kept as a scope boundary stated in the tradeoff of the same decision: edits (rename, code actions, formatting), because each needs a preview and a write-policy design, and the call hierarchy.
The seam has a Status query listing each provider with its extensions, running processes and last error, and a change event; the lsp tool is offered only while a provider is registered.
The model gives a column counted in characters or simply names the symbol on the line; the tool converts to the server's position encoding with the text it has just read.
A language server may return empty or partial results while it indexes, and the tool promises no completeness across servers.
justification: Third-party and protocol fact: indexing is internal to each language server and the Language Server Protocol has no completeness signal. The provider tracks the server's progress notices and the result says when the server reported that it was still indexing (DH-ADR-CONNECT-7).

reason: The account view has a phase for a grant that needs re-authorisation, distinct from an account that never connected.

Account views are derived from composed configuration and saved grants, not from a live registration, so a connector whose entry failed to load still shows an account with phase failed and the diagnostic.
MCP resources are read on demand only; a resource subscription is not followed.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONNECT-4: a changed resource is seen at the next read, and a pushed change notice is left as a later step that first needs a cap on how often a noisy server may cause a message. The other half of the upstream bullet is removed: each prompt a server offers is now a human command in the command registry (DH-D-CONNECT-3, test DH-T-CONNECT-22; register entry U-K1-7).

reason: Every operation has a harness deadline by default: startupTimeout for the whole attempt, syncTimeout for a notification-driven listing, and a page cap; nothing relies on an SDK default.

One supervisor policy covers both transports: a failed negotiation, a closed pipe and an HTTP transport failure all end the session and use the same reconnect budget, with the SDK's own retry bounded.
Audio and other non-image binary payloads from an MCP tool reach the model only as a diagnostic line.
justification: Deliberate boundary of the model vocabulary: DH-ADR-LLM-1 keeps one closed vocabulary and it has no audio block, so there is nothing to project audio into. The embedded-text and image halves are removed by DH-D-CONNECT-3. DH-ADR-LLM-1 now says so in words (audio and video never reach a model, by this decision and not by omission; recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: An MCP result that violates the protocol or the tool's advertised output schema is refused; no legacy substitute is accepted.
justification: Deliberate strictness: DH-ADR-CONNECT-2 treats a server as untrusted and DH-ADR-CONNECT-4 routes MCP tools through the pipeline's validation. The failure has its own code, mcp/invalid-result. DH-ADR-CONNECT-4 now states it (a result that does not match the protocol's shape is refused whole, never read leniently).

reason: The redirect address is a fixed path under the host's configured public address, so a browser that reaches the host through a proxy can finish authorisation, and a changed address replaces the stored client registration instead of leaving the old record.
There is no loader and no agent-owned scope: a deferred tool is an ordinary registration with summary disclosure, so allow and deny restrictions filter it like any tool.
An MCP tool that requires task-based execution cannot be used.
justification: Third-party fact: the Go MCP SDK chosen by DH-LIB-MCP has no task support and lists it as future work; implementing the extension outside the SDK would mean owning part of the protocol. Such a tool is not registered and is counted in the server status, so the model is never offered a tool it cannot call. Revisit when the SDK adds tasks.

reason: Every OAuth entry of the fleet, configured or registered, has an account view and the same authorise, cancel and sign-out operations from the settings page and the command line.
The fleet is the only way a server exists, so a server an agent preset mounts is an entry with agent scope and is listed, supervised and restartable like any other.

During a rebuild the old generation stays registered in a suspended state and is replaced in one swap when the new connection has listed its tools, so the declared tool set has no gap and two processes never overlap.
The component's overrides map lets an operator change the budgets, disclosure and enabled flag of a registered entry; the transport, command and address stay the registrant's.
A probe of an MCP server lists at most a configured number of pages and tool names and reports truncation.
justification: Deliberate bound on work done for an untrusted server (DH-ADR-CONNECT-2) and on what a management page renders, as outcome DH-O-14 requires; both numbers are configuration (DH-D-CONNECT-2). DH-ADR-CONNECT-2 now states it in its tradeoff (a probe is capped in time and in tools listed).

reason: The resource tools are offered, and a server is named in their prompt text, only while that server is connected and advertised the resources capability.
The three resource tools are registered once in the global layer with a step-time condition, so their names are always known to a restriction and a restriction always filters them.
MCP resource subscriptions and update notifications are not followed; the model lists or reads again for current content.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONNECT-4, the same as unit mcp-client.1: no subscription request is ever sent (test DH-T-CONNECT-22), and a logged resource-changed notice through the context pipeline is named there as a later step (register entry U-K1-7).

reason: A binary MCP resource that is audio or another non-image type is shown to the model as a description.
justification: Deliberate boundary of the model vocabulary, the same as unit mcp-client.4 (DH-ADR-LLM-1 has no audio block); the image half is removed by DH-D-CONNECT-3. DH-ADR-LLM-1 now states the exclusion of audio and video in words.

reason: The two listing tools need no server name and then list every visible resource-capable server in bounded sections; listing is paged under the harness page cap, not the SDK's.

Plan mode is enforced by default: a deny-only guard refuses every tool with effects, commands run only under a read-only sandbox ceiling and are denied where the ceiling cannot be applied. Guidance-only behaviour remains as a configuration choice.

A selection is appended to the log as plan/mode when it is made, with or without an open turn, and takes effect at the next proposed step. Nothing waits in process memory, so nothing is lost when the process exits.
Creation takes a plan option, and a subagent created while its creator is in plan mode starts in plan mode with origin inherited, so delegation cannot be used to write during planning.
A subagent in plan mode cannot open the plan review; it returns its plan as its result to the parent that asked.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-11: a child's plan is reviewed by its parent, which presents it to the person; a review channel per child would put several reviews before one person with no order.

reason: The review is an interaction of kind plan-review with the plan as a typed payload, so every carrier that can answer an interaction (browser, SDK, command line) can show the plan and the two choices; no client-only presentation is involved.

A preset is not a security boundary, and an old revision of a preset is not kept across a restart: a resumed session binds the definition that is current. (Removed: configuration can no longer execute host code, and a user override no longer replaces the whole child list.)
justification: Deliberate: a running revision is live component state and cannot be stored. DH-ADR-BUNDLE-6 says 'Resume binds the current definition of the recorded id' and that a resumed session can still get a different composition, which the log now records with a digest. DH-ADR-BUNDLE-4 makes children a keyed map that layers merge into. The clause 'a preset is not a security boundary' is stated in the limitations of bundle-preset.md section 10, not in a record; it is a description of what a preset is rather than a limit a person meets.

reason: The three statements stop being runtime surprises. A declaration without the registry, a duplicate preset id, an unknown base and a bad child are static issues with file, line and column, found before anything is applied. Declarations still offer no directory or file operations, which is intended: a preset is configuration and its assets are embedded and addressed by name.

The persona component can be mounted only inside a preset. Mounted at the top level it fails to load with a message that names the prompt component's persona field, which is where a deployment-wide persona is set.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-BUNDLE-4 has 'Scope boundary of this record (unit preset.persona.1): the persona component mounts only as a child of an agent preset and refuses to load at the top level, because who the agent is belongs to one composition; a global persona would silently apply to every preset and undo their differences'. Test DH-T-BUNDLE-16 checks the refusal.

reason: The persona config gains a list of context names to suppress, applied through the prompt service's suppression by name, so one optional contributor can be turned off for a preset without turning off all of them. Required contexts, such as the working directory, still cannot be suppressed, and naming one is a load error.

The limit describes how Node and its vm module load modules inside a guest program; the JavaScript guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and its seam by DH-ADR-PTC-1, so the harness evaluates no JavaScript and a script's imports are the business of whatever interpreter runs it.

The limit is about the Node provider keeping a process and heap per owner between programs; that provider is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1, and a script's process ends with its hosting call or its workflow run.

The cause was that only the already-bounded result reached the spill store. In the Go design the script's raw standard output is collected by the process starter through a bounded tail with a capped spill to storage before the model-facing text is formed, so the result carries a locator for what was cut. A hard cap remains by design: past the spill cap the stream is marked truncated.

The limit is about Node formatting guest objects before output is counted; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so no guest values exist and a script's output is bytes read through a bounded ring.

The limit is about the guest keeping a JSON snapshot beside each tool result for inspect; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so a nested call's result is printed once as JSON or text by the tool command.
A tool body called from a script runs in the host and may allocate memory while producing its result, before any size bound applies.
justification: Go runtime fact: memory cannot be limited per goroutine, so a pipeline can bound only what a body returns. Each first-party body must bound its own reads (for file tools DH-ADR-FS-8 does); the register recommends a conformance check for this beside the cancellation check of DH-ADR-TOOLS-5.

reason: The cause was a separate JavaScript bootstrap file that a remote deployment had to install and keep at the host's protocol revision by hand. In Go there is no bootstrap artifact: the tool command is the dsh binary itself, placed first on the script's search path by the spawn helper, and the endpoint request carries a wire revision so a different dsh is refused with a clear message.
The limit is about host metadata kept for every image object a retained JavaScript program acquires; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so a script holds no image objects.
A script is exactly as confined as the sandbox backend of its platform: enforcement is full or partial and reads are unconfined.
justification: Inherited operating-system facts (see the sandbox units: Windows is always partial, old Linux kernels are partial). This area cannot strengthen a backend; it reports mode, backend and enforcement in workflow/run-start and in the tool result (DH-D-PTC-2).

reason: On macOS, and on a Linux host without a delegated control group, a script's process tree has no memory or process-count limit; processor use is bounded by run time only.
justification: macOS fact: it has no facility that limits the memory of a tree of processes. Elsewhere the gap the review tracked as U-K1-2 is removed by the design: DH-ADR-PTC-5 gives a workflow run a memory and a process-count limit (maxMemoryBytes, maxProcesses), passed as Spec.Limits and carried out by the job object or control group of DH-D-EXEC-2 (test DH-T-EXEC-17, scenario DH-E-EXEC-10); the run record says enforced, partial or unavailable. No processor meter is added: the run budget of DH-ADR-PTC-5 bounds elapsed time.

reason: Cleanup of a script's process tree is as good as the tree owner of the platform; on macOS a process that leaves its process group can escape.
justification: macOS fact: process groups are the strongest owner the system offers. On Linux the gap is closed where a control group is available, which now includes a scope delegated by the user service manager (DH-ADR-EXEC-2). The run record says cleanup incomplete and names survivors instead of claiming a clean stop (DH-ADR-PTC-4).

reason: The limit describes the execution modes of the Node provider, which is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1. A script keeps state in files and the persistent shell tool is the stateful form; long work is a background job or a background workflow run.
The limit is a side effect of rewriting top-level await so that node:vm can run it; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, and the Go host neither parses nor rewrites script text.
The limit is V8 behaviour in a retained vm Script context; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so no JavaScript context exists.
The limit lists the semantics of the scoped REPL evaluator; the guest runtime and its evaluators are dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1.
The limit is about JavaScript values crossing vm realms; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, and a nested call's result crosses a process boundary as JSON text.

The cause was a seam whose only output channel was the resolved result. A workflow run is observable while it is live: standard error is read line by line into a bounded ring and a live event, member starts and endings are committed session events, and nested calls appear in the log as they happen. For a plain script the process starter's collectors can be read by offset.

The limit is about live JavaScript objects kept in a provider's memory between programs; the runtime seam is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1, and the durable record is the session log and the files a script writes.

The limit says the JavaScript runtime seam ships no container provider; the seam is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and DH-ADR-PTC-1. Where a script runs is decided by the execution world, and a container would be a world provider of the execution and sandbox areas.

The cause was that each runtime provider owned its own transport limits. In Go every nested call from every script arrives at one tool endpoint with one set of byte bounds for arguments and values. The bullet's second half, memory a body allocates before the bound applies, is carried in the row for ptc-runtime-node.14.

The Windows backend gives every write root its own capability identifier and builds each start's token with exactly that start's roots, so sandboxed processes honour extra roots like the file tools do.
On Windows hard-link aliases, unconfined reads and trees stamped by another sandbox are outside what the restricted token can govern.
justification: Windows fact: these are properties of the write-restricted Low-integrity token, the only unprivileged mechanism that does not need a read grant on every path (DH-ADR-SECURITY-2). Every start reports partial with the named effects and a policy that requires full is refused (DH-ADR-SANDBOX-3).

reason: An older Linux kernel governs only the Landlock access kinds it knows, so enforcement there is partial.
justification: Linux kernel fact: the Landlock ABI version of the running kernel decides which access kinds exist, and user space cannot add one. The state is computed per start, the missing kinds are named, and a policy that requires full is refused (DH-ADR-SANDBOX-3).

reason: The macOS backend depends on the deprecated sandbox-exec program.
justification: macOS fact: Apple offers a command-line program no supported, unprivileged successor for confining a child process (DH-ADR-SECURITY-2). The backend is probed at every start-up, so removal by Apple shows as unavailable before the first command and confined modes fail closed (DH-D-SANDBOX-5).

reason: The seam re-probes on an operator command, from the UI and automatically after a launch failure, so installing or repairing a backend takes effect without reloading the component.
A custom runner must run the launch stage as its command, passes the same functional probe and canary as built-in backends, and can never be reported full, so it is no longer an unprobed assertion.

A write-root grant is an effect registered through the agent's scope, so building the agent for a resumed or forked session registers it again without a manual step; authority is still never replayed from the session log.
The sandbox policy has a file mode and a network setting but no knob for process policy.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SANDBOX-3, whose scope sentence names this unit, and by DH-ADR-SECURITY-10 (exactly two dimensions; processes, system calls and devices are outside), the same as unit sandbox.1.

reason: Backends are probed at start, so the backend is known before the first model request and the resolver lists the real scratch and temporary paths in the model-visible section.

Diagnosis and cleanup are compiled-in owner commands: nothing is extracted to disk, and cleanup removes the labels the journal recorded; a missing WRITE_DAC is reported as a precondition only the directory's owner can fix.
A preflight before the consent step refuses a volume that stores no access-control lists and warns on a drive root or profile root; the real-Windows scenario covers a FAT-class volume.
The host, which is unconfined, classifies a preparation failure itself by reading descriptors; repairs are an owner command, so the model never needs to escalate a call to diagnose.
The read-only mode also receives the private scratch directory as its temporary area, so PowerShell can create its probe files and starts in the same language mode as under workspace-write.
There is no sandbox instance to reuse across workspaces: each start's token is built with exactly the identifiers of that start's write roots.

Every access-control change is journalled as intent before it is made, so a start-up sweep and the cleanup command find and remove a scratch directory or entry that a failed cleanup or a crash left behind.
The journal records the volume and file identity of each granted directory, so the cleanup command finds and removes entries on a workspace that was renamed.
The journal stores the original security descriptor before the first change, so revoking restores a directory that had no access list to exactly that state.
A program confined by the Windows token cannot give its own children named-pipe standard streams.
justification: Windows fact: a new named pipe gets a default security descriptor that no restricting identifier satisfies, and adding the user's own identifier to the token would remove the write restriction. Inherited and anonymous pipes work, and the model-visible policy text says so (DH-D-SANDBOX-6).

reason: The first access grant on a directory walks every descendant, which can take tens of seconds on a large tree.
justification: Windows fact: the system propagates inheritable access entries eagerly, and the confined child needs the inherited entries. DH-ADR-SANDBOX-6 moves the cost to the one-time consent step, with progress and cancellation, so it never runs inside a command's time limit.

reason: The Windows token restricts writes only; reads are unconfined and sockets cannot be restricted.
justification: Windows fact: WRITE_RESTRICTED intersects write access only and the mechanism has no socket control. A policy with the network denied fails closed on Windows instead of running unconfined (DH-ADR-SECURITY-10).

reason: A Low-integrity child cannot read objects that another AppContainer-based tool stamped with a package identifier.
justification: Windows kernel access rule outside the harness's control. The doctor command names the affected objects and offers the repair to the directory's owner, and the limit is one of the named reasons for partial enforcement (DH-ADR-SANDBOX-6).

reason: The sandbox policy expresses file effects and a network setting; it expresses no process, system-call or device restriction.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated in their own words by DH-ADR-SANDBOX-3 (Scope boundary of this record: a policy promises file effects, the network setting, the protection of the harness home and delegated-execution, and nothing about which processes a command may see or signal, which system calls it may make, or which devices it may open; a product choice, not a platform limit, because a dimension only one backend enforces would read partial on every other) and by DH-ADR-SECURITY-10 (the policy has exactly two dimensions, file effects and network).

reason: A world is one component that provides the filesystem, process and sandbox providers together, so a container or remote executor is added as a world and a mismatched trio cannot be mounted; same-world confinement stays the seam's stated scope.
A file-effect denial inside a spawned command is inferred from the command's stderr.
justification: The same claim as execution unit bash-sandbox.2, asserted without a source per backend (audit finding Q3-3); on macOS the unified system log may carry a typed violation record the user can read (inference, not verified). The seam keeps one classifier, labels its result a hint that never changes the exit code, and file tools, which run in the host, return typed denials (DH-D-SANDBOX-3). The specification now names the three scenarios that settle the claim per backend (DH-E-SANDBOX-1, -3, -4) and reads the macOS sandbox log as a hint if DH-E-SANDBOX-3 shows it names the process. What is still missing: the facts; no scenario has run.

reason: Launcher status travels on a private descriptor pair that closes before the command's first instruction, so a confined child cannot forge it and its exit code and output are never read as launcher failure.

The ordered backend chain is inside the one seam, and a world's providers mounted in one agent's scope serve that agent only, so a local and a remote sandbox coexist in one host without separate trees.
A schedule fires only while a dsh process that fires schedules is running.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-WEBAPP-4 (the host is a foreground process the user owns; no service, login item or tray is installed) and narrowed by DH-ADR-JOBS-7: any firing host on the home can deliver, a failed delivery retries with back-off, and a late delivery reports how late it is and how many occurrences were missed (DH-ADR-JOBS-6).

reason: The message id is derived from schedule, occurrence and generation and the inbox refuses a duplicate, so a send repeated after a crash is a no-op and the inbox gets the message once. The delivery row then follows the message to ran or discarded, and a message discarded by disposal is delivered once more.

Hard delete is kept as a decision, but what was delivered stays recoverable: every delivered message is a logged user message whose source names the schedule and occurrence. The part about version 1 session-log reminders does not arise, because the Go store reads no upstream data.

Every service method takes a caller. An agent caller reads and changes only schedules it created or receives; only an owner principal admitted by a carrier manages all of them; a delegated agent is refused in the service as well as in the tools.
Schedule rules are five-field cron and a bounded subset of RFC 5545, and future occurrences depend on the machine's time-zone data.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-JOBS-6 and DH-ADR-RRULE-1 for the rule subset. The zone-data half is a fact no design removes: governments change zone rules. Committed occurrences are stored as UTC and never move, and DH-ADR-TEMPORAL-1 reports the data source.

reason: Schedules are rows with indexed status, next occurrence, target and creator; history is a separate table read by page. Nothing is loaded wholesale at open, a write touches one row, and list results are summaries without prompt bodies.

The 60 second floor and latest-only catch-up are kept as stated rules. What was missing is added: maxConcurrentNewSessions caps sessions created by schedules, and each late delivery carries the missed count and its lateness.

Recovery no longer inspects the latest receipt's session: a stale claim is taken over and the deterministic message id makes the repeat a no-op. Change notices are derived, not pushed: at a turn's first step the tools component compares the session's schedules with the revisions its model last saw and injects one notice, loaded or not at the time of the change.

tool.schedule declares schedule.Key as a required service; a composition that mounts the tools without the service shows the entry as waiting on that named service in the loader's status and in the composed-tree preview, which is what outcome DH-O-2 requires.

The tool pipeline attributes every call to an agent at its first stage, and the service takes an explicit caller; a call with no agent is refused with the classified schedule/no-caller error instead of an internal error.

The tools reach only schedules the calling session created or receives, and a create or edit outside a human turn returns Ask, so a person approves or, with no answerer, it is denied. The check is in the service and the pipeline, not in a prompt sentence.

Delete and pause remove a delivered message that no turn has claimed yet from the target's inbox when this process holds the session. When another process holds it the message stays and the result says retracted false.

schedule_view returns the host's current time, the next occurrence and the last deliveries with their state (enqueued, ran with its turn, discarded, skipped, failed) and attempt count, so the model can see timing, retries and whether a delivery ran.
The refusal of a delegated caller is kept and moved to where it cannot be skipped: the service refuses an agent caller with a delegation depth above zero, whichever tool or entry made the call.
The four declarations carry a step-time condition that is false for a delegated agent, so a child's requests do not contain the schemas or the authorization section and pay no tokens for them.
There is no package to resolve a runtime from: the harness is one static binary, every client takes one explicit path or the DSH_BIN variable, and the Python wheel carries the binary inside it.

The protocol has session/cancel to stop a turn or step, session/close to dispose an agent and a $/cancel notification for an in-flight request, so stopping runtime work no longer requires closing the harness; a local timeout still never cancels work by itself.

A prompt's result is no longer a receipt-to-idle interval: the session log records which turn claimed each message, and the host reports that one turn's ending and last assistant message, so other queued work is never included.

An application's handler in the Go client is told to stop through its context; a handler that ignores the context keeps running in the application's own process after the client has stopped waiting for it.
justification: Go offers no way to stop a goroutine from outside, and the handler is the application's code, not the harness's. DH-ADR-SDK-6 bounds the effect: the late answer is never sent and the host has already settled the request as refused; Close returns after a bounded wait and names the handlers still running.

reason: initialize negotiates an integer protocol version: the client lists the versions it speaks, the host picks the highest common one or fails with sdk/version-unsupported, and only additive changes are allowed inside a version.
The protocol defines session/cancel and session/close, so a client abandons a turn or releases a session without closing the runtime process.
A pending question or approval lives in one host process: after a restart it cannot be answered, the interrupted turn is closed, and the model may ask again.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-WIRE-4 keeps one in-memory interaction registry that is settled exactly once and says 'Shutdown and transport loss settle pending items as refused', and DH-ADR-SDK-6 settles every doubt, including shutdown, as a refusal. Restoring a pending approval after a restart would let an answer apply to a turn that no longer exists; failing closed costs one more prompt.

reason: session/close disposes one agent and releases its lease while the session stays stored, and session/cancel stops a turn or a step, so agents created for a client no longer stay live until process shutdown.

The host sends session.run.completed for every accepted prompt and command, naming the turn that claimed the message, its reason, its final assistant text and its position in the log; clients no longer define and observe an interval.

Standard output is claimed once by the stdio component, which keeps the real handle private and points the process-wide os.Stdout at standard error; child processes never inherit it, and a test captures stdout with every logger forced on.
The carrier mounts no model adapter at all: a session's route is validated by exact id through the model runtime, and an unknown provider fails create or initialize with no vendor-specific fallback.
The archive and transcript functions write to any io.Writer, so a command (dsh session export --out) writes a host file atomically as well as the browser download.
An HTTP export is a host-tracked operation whose final status (complete, complete with omissions, failed) reaches the tab's event stream, and the archive ends with a manifest of omissions.
A transcript holds committed history only; stream text that has not settled into an event is absent.
justification: Deliberate boundary: a view reads committed events only (design.md section 4.6, DH-ADR-VIEW-1). The silent part of the upstream limit is removed by DH-D-VIEW-8, which states the cut and marks an open turn. DH-ADR-VIEW-9 now states the committed-only rule (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: The transcript formatter takes an option to include descendant sessions as sections, bounded by the caller's visibility.
The host streams the transcript without holding it whole; above a configured size the UI offers a file download instead of a clipboard copy and never truncates.
A copy to the clipboard that has succeeded cannot be taken back.
justification: The earlier row called this not applicable because the Go design has no client plugin to dispose of, but the limit itself arises in any design, as the debt audit found (Q3-7): the browser's clipboard interface writes and reads, and has no operation that undoes a write another program may already have read (W3C Clipboard API and events). The Go UI copies a transcript with one user gesture in the page (DH-ADR-3); what was copied stays on the clipboard.

reason: There is no per-session file whose path could lag the live log: the session id, the cut and the events of a transcript come from one read transaction of the session database.
Every Query method, search included, requires a Visibility whose zero value sees nothing, so access is enforced in the service and not left to each tool.
A search runs on its own goroutine with a cancellable context that stops the statement within the driver's bound, so nothing blocks the host.

Substring recall no longer needs a second, per-session call: one search request has a literal mode that scans the stored text of the whole corpus, and Chinese, Japanese and Korean text is prepared as overlapping two-character pieces so substrings match in ranked mode too. A token index still ranks by tokens for space-separated scripts. Provisional on measurement M3.
Index rows are written in the event's own transaction by whichever process holds the session lease, so several processes share one index in the one database.
Visibility is a required argument of every Query method and a hidden session is reported as not found, so the service itself constrains what a caller may inspect.
Search is not a separate backend to mount: it is part of the store-backed query component, and with indexing configured off it reports query/search-disabled while exact reads keep working.
Reads are ranges by seq against the store, and surface class and citation links are derived rows written with the events, so no read replays a whole log.
One search request offers a ranked mode and a literal mode over the same stored documents and the same filters, for one session or the whole corpus.
List values commit with their events, and each item carries a title_state of current, behind or pending, so a null title means only that the session has no title.

Listing is a keyset page on an index, ordered as of the first call, so work is bounded by the page size and entries do not move between calls. A session deleted or archived meanwhile is no longer returned, which is intended.
A blank flag is a list column and list_session takes include_blank, which defaults to false.
The tool test drives both the scoped and the unscoped listing through the executor in keyless replay, so neither form has unit coverage only.
Tool visibility is derived from the initiating agent and a configured policy that defaults to the caller's own workspace; mounting the tools no longer grants the whole runtime.
Only explicitly marked lines are quotes; Markdown lazy continuation is not implemented.
justification: Deliberate boundary: with lazy continuation the text a user types after a quote would be shown as part of the quote. The fenced-code half is removed by DH-D-VIEW-8. DH-ADR-VIEW-9 now states the rule (a quote is a line that carries the quote mark and nothing else is; recommended default, not confirmed by the owner), and test DH-T-VIEW-20 pins it.

reason: The log records the intent to run a tool, not the completion of its external effect.
justification: Fact of any system that acts on the outside world: a local log cannot be made atomic with an effect on another system, so after a crash the outcome of a started call is unknown. The call id is handed to tool bodies as an idempotency key and recovery reports outcome unknown (DH-D-STORE-4).

reason: Nothing is checkpointed inside a running model attempt, so a crash loses stream text that had not settled.
justification: Deliberate boundary: a disk sync per stream chunk is refused, and nothing model-visible is lost because the attempt never settled. DH-ADR-STORE-3 now states it (nothing is checkpointed inside a running model attempt), as does the failure table of design.md section 5.

reason: A tool call with no result is recorded as outcome unknown and is never retried automatically.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-10: retrying a call that may already have taken effect is the worse error, so the model is told to verify.

reason: There is no catalogue of format migrations to own or distribute: upcasters are registered together with their event type in first-party Go code.
No historical chain exists whose missing edge a plugin would need to supply; a payload version without its upcaster fails the recorded-row test at build time.
The Go store never converts a stored row, so an unknown ignorable record is kept byte for byte and nothing is refused for it. Only the upstream importer keeps the strict refusal, deliberately.
No adjacent edges and no successor files exist in the Go store, so nothing has to select later migrations or publish a result.
The Go store never converts a stored row, so an unknown ignorable record is kept byte for byte and nothing is refused for it. Only the upstream importer keeps the strict refusal, deliberately.
The Go store never renumbers events, so no sequence remap table grows with the log; reads are paged windows from the database.

No generations exist, so there is no retained predecessor that could be mistaken for a fallback. The Go rule for its own layout is forward-only migration after an automatic backup, which is the rollback.
The ambiguity of the old preset id exists only in upstream format 2 files, which the Go harness never reads.
No committed generations and no settings file are migrated: the Go store has one database whose layout is migrated in one transaction after a backup.
The store has no converter whose coverage could be incomplete. The importer reads only files already at format 4 and refuses a whole file it cannot map, writing nothing.
There is no whole-log format version to finalise or protect by a checkpoint record: each event type evolves alone, guarded by the persisted-type inventory test.
No future whole-log format needs prerequisite readers of an earlier one: an older payload version is read through its registered upcaster, and a recorded row for every version must keep decoding.
The refusal of nested historical tool-result wrappers belongs to a migration edge the Go design does not have. The importer accepts only format 4 files and refuses what its table cannot map.
The Go store has no prefixed historical extension fields. The importer maps an extension field it knows and refuses a file that carries one it does not, so none is kept without a consumer.

In the Go store a parent and its child sessions are rows of one database linked by a column, so no fact has to be recovered from child files. The importer imports a root as a whole and reports children it did not find.

Unknown historical child modes arise only when a migration reconstructs a parent catalogue from old files. The Go store reconstructs nothing; the importer carries an entry as recorded or refuses the file.
There is one store per harness home and no per-root migration scope. Bringing sessions in from elsewhere is the export and import pair, and upstream roots enter through the importer.
No migration returns a whole current history: the store serves paged windows from the database and projections open from checkpoints.
Whole-log adjacent integer versions are replaced by a payload version per event type with upcasters on read, so one type changes without touching any other event.
A session-log upload acknowledged just before a crash can be sent again.
justification: Fact of an acknowledgement over HTTP: the sender cannot record the acceptance atomically with the receiver's reply, so delivery is at least once. Each event carries the session id and sequence number so the receiver can remove duplicates, and the acceptance is committed as soon as the writer is free (DH-D-STORE-9).

reason: The Go contract states the meaning of absence: a request that is not attributed to a session this process holds carries no field and records nothing, and a test asserts it.

Upstream stalls the upload behind an event larger than the byte limit. DH-ADR-STORE-10 now sends an elision record in its place (the event's sequence number, time, type, size and digest, marked omitted), so the uploaded log stays contiguous by number and continues (register entry U-K1-11; recommended default, not confirmed by the owner). Built by DH-D-STORE-9 and proven by DH-T-STORE-15. Whether the vendor accepts such a line is settled by scenario DH-E-STORE-4, the same exit gate as the Go log format itself; if the vendor refuses, the component is not shipped.

A rejection opens a per-session breaker: the uploader stops attaching the field and reports it, and the attempt is retried without extension fields, so an optional field cannot keep failing model requests. It needs the adapter of area A04.
The Go store has one database with no per-root encoding and no catalogued chain of generations, so there is nothing whose encoding a migration must preserve.
There are no file layouts, old or new: sessions are rows, and upstream's pre-release flat layout is never read.
The export is one header line and one line per event, optionally gzip, readable by ordinary tools; the database itself is stock SQLite.
The store has a delete operation that removes a session's events, checkpoints, index rows and blob references, and an optional retention duty.

Ownership is an epoch checked inside every append transaction, so an explicit takeover from a stuck holder is safe and a removed lock file cannot corrupt a log. The Windows lock is a file lock, not a name scoped to a login session, and a home on a network filesystem is refused.
The cordis change that makes unload complete and ordered removes the cause; the store additionally stops admitting appends and runs one bounded final barrier before it releases its leases.
No file is published by hard link or rename: a session comes into existence by a transaction that inserts its row, and a second insert of the same id fails on the key.
Exists only because Node has no file-lock call and needs a prebuilt native add-on; Go reaches flock and LockFileEx through golang.org/x/sys without a native build.
Nothing is imported when a session is opened, so a read open has no hidden write of legacy history. Import is an explicit command.

There is no second live store beside the database. The importer is one-way by the owner's decision, records where a session came from and leaves the upstream files untouched, so nothing presents them as a current copy.
Every dsh process uses the one store, and the lease in its session rows excludes a second writer whichever process it is.
A change to an event type raises that type's payload version and adds an upcaster applied on read; stored rows stay as written, so no history migration of the database is needed.
Cross-process write ownership is part of the store contract, not a provider detail: the lease is specified once and the conformance tests include two-process cases.
The store is a service that sessions depend on, so they unload first and close their writers in order, and the store has no option whose change needs a reload under live sessions.

No listener path exists that could be absent: events reach storage only through the writer a session holds, so a session without a writer cannot be mistaken for a persisted one. Area A01 confirms the constructor.
Delete and retention are operations of the store contract.
Listing is a filtered, keyset-paged query on indexed columns of the session rows and never reads events.
An interrupted turn is closed with synthetic closers and never continued.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-PERSISTENCE-10 and design.md section 5: continuing would repeat a model request whose stream is lost and tools whose outcome is unknown.

reason: Checkpoint rows are deleted in the store's delete-session transaction and a prune removes rows whose key no binary registers.
There is no interval timer: checkpoints are tied to commits (every commit for list state; turn end, close and every N events for the rest).
The registry reads the store itself and folds the missing suffix inside one read transaction, so no consumer has to refold from the log.

Stored state is disposable: a version mismatch discards and refolds, so there is no record format to prove upgrades for, and one property test (checkpoint plus suffix equals full fold) replaces archived fixtures.
Every read names the keys it wants and the host renders only those; a value that grows with the session (the turn index) is stored as rows and read in pages.

Upstream's hazard was that a client could read the presence of a projection key as a statement about one session's capabilities. In the Go design no reader can do that: the host renders pages, a read names its keys and an unknown key is an error, and whether a feature is on is asked of the composition. The host-wide fold table that remains is the design, not a limit.
A definition declares the event types it consumes and the registry dispatches by type, so an event visits only the folds that asked for it.
A stored row carries the seq it covers, so a reader sees it as behind and never as current, and the next registration of the key catches up from it.

The retained definition exists because upstream hot-reloads plugin modules and lets readers outlive their owner; Go loads no code at run time and the cordis port unloads dependents first, so nothing keeps a released definition.
Fold state is checkpointed in the session database in the transaction of the events it covers, so a restart reads rows instead of refolding.
Fold functions live in leaf packages whose imports are checked (no I/O, clocks or randomness), every definition runs the equivalence and determinism tests, and a slow fold is measured and reported.
The stats view reports closed steps and steps with visible output as separate figures, so attempted work and shown work are both readable.
Every settled attempt, including a cancelled or failed one, carries its times in the hot part of its event, so all attempts are timed and model time is one figure that says what it covers.
Both scopes are offered and labelled: the fold counts the whole log, and Query counts events whose class is current from derived rows.
The projection registry is a spine service and the browser never folds events, so there is no client fallback to diverge; a composition without the stats entry simply renders no strip.
No OpenTelemetry SDK is linked; the OTLP exporter is harness code on the standard library, owned by area A18.
Collector-facing behaviour (deadlines, retry, limits) is specified and tested in the harness's own exporter instead of being inherited from an SDK.

Authorisation and delivered-through are session events, so an upload has a watermark, advances only on the collector's acknowledgement, resumes after a restart and is delivered at least once. That a sent record cannot be recalled is outside any client's power; the confirmation tells the user before sending.
With upload off no consent is asked, so there is nothing to replay; a confirmed upload is a logged fact found by a fold, not a live notification that an unloaded component can miss.
The hand-off cursor in memory is replaced by logged authorisation and delivery events: the uploader reads events after the watermark, so a crash or reload loses no authorised record.
A baseline redactor always runs last and cannot be removed or skipped: it masks secret values the credential store released and recognised secret shapes. It is pattern-based and the preview says so.
The consent event records the fingerprint of the rule set the preview was computed with; an upload under a different rule set sends nothing and asks for a new confirmation.
With the default cadence a title is generated once from the first message and can stop describing a long session.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-VIEW-6 in its own words (Scope boundary of this record: the default first-prompt cadence titles a session once and never retitles it automatically; Refresh or the every-prompt cadence is the remedy, because one bounded model call per session is the cost the product chose). The remedies are built by DH-D-VIEW-4.

reason: A fork generates a title on its first own prompt unless its inherited title is pinned by the user, so two list rows do not share one title.
One acceptance rule lives in the generator (finish stop, a non-empty first line, within the byte limit after cleaning); providers supply the prompt only.
Input over the ceiling is reduced at message boundaries (first prompt plus the newest that fit, one message clipped at a character boundary), and the request event records exactly what was sent.
Reasoning effort is one configuration field of the generator with the default lowest, not a function each provider implements.
Unpin returns a session to automatic titles, title events are search documents, and the title is a plain list column that can be filtered.
Providers register by id in a registry seam and configuration selects the one that is active, so precedence is a setting and not code in a combined provider.
The turn index is derived rows, one per turn, so a change writes and pushes one entry and the page reads a window.
An open turn's row carries the latest committed assistant text marked unsettled, which is cheap once an update touches one row.
Each entry carries a kind (text, images, files, command, tools only) and a count, so the page shows a localised label instead of a bare turn number.
The registry is a spine service and no client folds events, so there is no loaded-window fallback to diverge; a composition without the entry renders no outline.
No Go log can hold a directory the model moved, because that event type is never registered; what an imported upstream log maps to is the importer's decision (DH-ADR-11).
When the current directory and the original project are both gone, every model turn is rejected until a person chooses a directory.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-VIEW-8: the write boundary is resolved from the directory, so guessing one would not fail closed. The dead end is removed: DH-D-VIEW-10 returns a typed error on which every carrier offers the choice of an existing directory.

reason: A form addresses an entry by its id in the composed tree, and the one writable layer may hold a merge operation for any entry, whichever file or bundle supplied it; there are no separately owned include documents.
The form has two distinct operations: reset removes the user's override so the lower value is inherited, and clear writes the merge operation's null, which deletes a value a lower layer supplies.
There is no unconfined executor in Go. The one bash provider must put a launch plan from the sandbox seam on every spawn made for an agent, and the process package refuses such a spawn without one.
A persistent shell exists as its own tool on the terminal seam; the one-shot executor stays stateless on purpose.

The bash provider resolves its program by stated rules on every system, including Git for Windows on Windows while skipping the WSL launchers, and tree semantics come from the job object, so bash is no longer POSIX-only.
A start failure is an explicit Failed outcome carrying the error, separate from the output streams, so it is not served as a synthetic stderr stream that a consuming reader can lose.
Confinement governs file effects, and the network where a backend can enforce it; process visibility is not governed uniformly.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SANDBOX-3, whose scope sentence names this unit (nothing is promised about which processes a command may see or signal), and by DH-ADR-SECURITY-10 (a confined command can still see and signal other processes of the same user).

reason: A denied file operation inside a confined command is inferred from the command's stderr and reported only as a hint.
justification: Classed a platform limit before, but the fact was asserted without a source per backend, as the debt audit found (Q3-3), and it may not hold everywhere. Inference, not verified: Landlock reports a denial only through the kernel audit subsystem, which needs privileges; the Windows token reports one only through object-access auditing, which needs an administrator; but macOS writes sandbox violations to the unified system log, which the user can read, so a typed denial report may be possible there. Since the final re-check, areas/sandbox-ssh.md holds the claim as an assumption to settle per backend by three named scenarios (DH-E-SANDBOX-1 for bubblewrap and Landlock, DH-E-SANDBOX-4 for the Windows token, DH-E-SANDBOX-3 for macOS), and the macOS backend reads the sandbox log as a hint, kept only if DH-E-SANDBOX-3 shows the records name the process. What is still missing: the facts themselves; none of the scenarios has run, so no source can be named yet. Whether the launcher itself failed is no longer inferred (DH-ADR-SECURITY-3).

reason: Start returns only after the launcher status record, so a launcher that fails is a start error for a background run as well, not a fact discovered on a later read of the job.

The executor never bypasses the sandbox seam: the seam is asked for every call and itself returns the unconfined plan for danger-full-access, so one place decides and the fact is recorded on the outcome.
As for bash, there is no unconfined PowerShell executor: the one pwsh provider must carry a launch plan on every spawn made for an agent.
A persistent PowerShell exists as its own tool on the terminal seam; the one-shot executor stays stateless on purpose.
A PowerShell command is text that PowerShell itself parses, so a syntax error is a command failure and not a launch failure.
justification: Fact of PowerShell: the shell is the only parser of its language, and a second parser in the harness could disagree with it. This is what a shell tool is, and DH-ADR-EXEC-7 keeps it with no translation layer.

reason: A start failure is an explicit Failed outcome carrying the error, separate from the output streams, as for the bash provider.

The outcome records the stop cause the harness itself applied (timeout, cancelled, user, owner gone), so a stopped Windows process is classified without a signal. A kill from outside the harness still looks like an ordinary exit, which is stated as a residual.
A command whose first statement is param, using or #requires is written to a private script file and invoked after the encoding preamble, so the preamble no longer breaks it.
Non-ASCII standard input can be mis-decoded when the resolved shell is Windows PowerShell 5.1.
justification: Still open until one measurement is taken (register entry U-K1-12): scenario DH-E-EXEC-7 now passes non-ASCII text on standard input to Windows PowerShell 5.1 started with its console input code page set to UTF-8 and records the outcome. If the text arrives intact the limit is resolved by setting the code page before start; if not, it is a platform limit of that edition. What is missing: the scenario has not run, and the executor does not yet set the code page on this path. Impact is small: only the 5.1 fallback and only in-process callers that pass stdin.

reason: Reads are not confined on Windows.
justification: Windows fact: the write-restricted token that DH-ADR-SECURITY-2 keeps intersects write access only (WRITE_RESTRICTED), so it cannot deny a read. The one unprivileged alternative, an AppContainer, needs a read grant on every path the child reads, the compilers and tools included, which upstream measured and rejected (packages/sandbox/sandbox-windows-acl/README.md:125, :160). The same fact as sandbox unit sandbox-windows-acl.8; every result reports enforcement partial. The review first classed this row as a scope boundary, but no decision record states that reads are unconfined: design.md section 6 says it, outside a record.

reason: The private temp directory for workspace-write is kept as behaviour and has a defined carrier: the launch plan from the sandbox area holds the TMP and TEMP edits and the process package applies them.
Windows read-only mode is a partial boundary: hard links alias a file across paths, and trees that another sandbox stamped with a package identifier are unreadable.
justification: Windows fact: NTFS hard links give one file several paths, and the access rules for Low-integrity tokens and package identifiers are the kernel's. No unprivileged Windows mechanism removes them (DH-ADR-SECURITY-2); every start reports partial with the named effects (DH-ADR-SANDBOX-3).

reason: Built-in variables are registered as the first contributor with their descriptions, so List returns every managed variable and can feed the generated catalog.
Feeding a running program is the terminal seam's contract (Send on an owned session); the one-shot shell seam stays without it on purpose, so the vocabulary exists where the state lives.
The executor owns no timer. The caller's context carries the only deadline with a typed cause, so a caller-owned deadline is the normal mode and not a deferred one.
The persistent bash tool needs an owning agent and a real pseudo-terminal; without them it reports unavailable.
justification: Deliberate boundary: the owner gives the shell its lifetime and its access rule, and persistent shell state needs a terminal. Stated by DH-ADR-EXEC-9 items (a) and (d) (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner): where no pseudo-terminal can be allocated the tools report unavailable and never fall back to pipes.

reason: A foreground child that waits for input is recognised exactly on Linux only; elsewhere the call runs to its timeout.
justification: Operating-system fact, the same as unit terminal-bash.2: macOS and Windows cannot prove that a foreign process is blocked reading the terminal. A following command is refused while the previous one has not finished, so nothing is typed into the child (DH-ADR-EXEC-6).

reason: A timeout or cancellation first interrupts the foreground group and keeps the shell when the end line and prompt then appear; only a shell that cannot be verified is reset. An explicit exit still ends the shell, as asked.
The description stays a config field for deployment facts, and the tool adds the facts it resolved itself (shell path and edition) so they do not have to be written by hand.
The command text is written to a file and evaluated by a bootstrap function; only a fixed short line is typed, so TAB, ESC and DEL in a command never reach the line editor.

Exit code, signal and stop cause are structured fields of the logged result, and the text marker is rendered from them, so output that happens to end with a marker-shaped line cannot change the status shown.
The tool has no executor timer to opt out with: its timeout is a deadline on the call's context, the same mechanism every tool uses.

A timeout given for a background run applies to it, a deployment cap on background runtime exists, and the owner's end always stops the job, so a background command is no longer unbounded by construction.
The job registration carries the id of the tool call that is waiting on it, so a task list can mark those rows; the field is requested from the jobs area.
The persistent PowerShell tool needs an owning agent and a pseudo-terminal backend with the pwsh dialect; without them it reports unavailable.
justification: Deliberate boundary, the same as for the bash twin: the owner gives the shell its lifetime and access rule. Stated by DH-ADR-EXEC-9 items (a) and (d) (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner): where no pseudo-terminal can be allocated the tools report unavailable and never fall back to pipes.

reason: Only a short fixed line is typed, printed before the start line of the command bracket, and the result is the screen text between the bracket lines, so echoed input cannot leak into a result.
The command is read from a file by the bootstrap function and never passes through PSReadLine, so a raw ESC in a command is supported.
A command completes on the end line that carries its own nonce, printed by the bootstrap function, so redefining the prompt function does not remove the completion signal.
A new command is refused while the previous one has not printed its end line, so a child that reads input cannot consume the next call's command; the model interrupts or restarts instead.
Stop and hang-up signals are unavailable on Windows and an interrupt is a console-wide Ctrl-C, which at a prompt cancels the pending line.
justification: Windows console fact, the same as unit subprocess-local.5: consoles have no per-process-group signals. The backend refuses the unsupported signals and the result says so (DH-D-EXEC-5).

reason: The bootstrap uses core types and chcp only, so it succeeds when the read-only Windows sandbox starts PowerShell in ConstrainedLanguage. This is an inference proven by the Windows terminal scenario.
A terminal bell is not reported to the model.
justification: Deliberate boundary: nothing consumes a bell and a model-facing channel for terminal decoration would spend tokens without a use. Stated by DH-ADR-EXEC-9 item (e) (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: Under the Windows sandbox a confined command cannot open named pipes.
justification: Windows fact: a new named pipe gets a default security descriptor that no restricting identifier satisfies (see sandbox unit sandbox-windows-acl.6). The language-mode half of the upstream bullet is no longer carried: the execution spec now carries named pipes only, DH-ADR-SANDBOX-4 gives read-only mode a private scratch directory so that PowerShell is expected to start in its full mode (to be confirmed by scenario DH-E-SANDBOX-4), and nothing in the design relies on the reduced mode.

reason: The persistent PowerShell tool is part of the design and keeps one owner-scoped shell alive across calls.
The model must write PowerShell for the pwsh tool and bash for the bash tool; nothing translates between them.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-EXEC-7 (a registry by dialect, with no translation): translation between shell languages cannot be made correct in general, and both tools may be mounted on one system.

reason: Skill discovery is one directory level deep.
justification: Deliberate boundary: it bounds the scan, matches the layout other agent tools use for a shared skills directory, and keeps skill names unambiguous. DH-ADR-CONTEXT-7 now states it (discovery reads one directory level under each root).

reason: The project root comes from the shared resolver with configurable markers, the same one instruction files use, so a workspace without .git can name its own marker.
An invalid entry becomes a per-skill diagnostic in the registry; the catalogue the model sees names skipped skills, and the settings view shows the reason, so absent and invalid are distinguishable.
An unreadable skill is one diagnostic and its siblings stay listed. Only a failure to list the root itself marks the provider failed, and then its last-good catalogue is kept.
The provider holds no polling code: the shared watch service follows a path whose parent directories do not exist yet and attaches when they appear.

The digest of a loaded body is recorded on the tool result and folded; when the watched file later changes, the next step adds a one-line notice naming the skill. Old results are still not rewritten, which is correct for an append-only log.
The office skills install no authoring libraries.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by the tradeoff of DH-ADR-CONTEXT-3 (authoring libraries are the user's to install) and by owner decision DH-ADR-20: the harness downloads and bundles nothing.

reason: LibreOffice output can differ from native Microsoft Office applications.
justification: Third-party fact: LibreOffice and Microsoft Office are different layout engines, and owner decision DH-ADR-20 fixes LibreOffice as the engine. The skill text states the difference and the document area reports the engine version with each result.

reason: Legacy, encrypted and macro-enabled office files need a separate workflow.
justification: Deliberate boundary now stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-7 (the Office skills do not cover encrypted or macro-enabled documents, which the office tools refuse); legacy files are converted first through the document area's convert tool.

reason: The four skills are embedded in the binary and checked at start-up, so they cannot be missing after install; any skill problem from an override directory is a registry diagnostic shown in the settings view, not only a log line.
The embedded set is complete by construction, and an override directory that lacks one of the four fails the component's load with a diagnostic, so the router never names an absent subskill.
An override directory is served by the same watched filesystem provider code, which keeps no negative cache; restoring a file lists the skill at the next lookup without a restart.
A provider declares MaxAge: zero for one that invalidates itself, a duration for a source that cannot notify. The registry lists such a provider again once the age is exceeded.
Providers are asked concurrently, each under its own deadline, and merged in rank order; a slow provider delays only itself, and its context is cancelled at the deadline.

The registry keeps each provider's last-good catalogue and a status (ok, stale or failed, with the error). A failed provider's entries stay listed as stale, so a lower-ranked skill does not take over a name because its owner flickered.
Snapshot returns the shadowed definitions with the reason each one lost, and the settings view and the command line can list them.
A catalogue entry renders the description and, when present, whenToUse inside the length cap, and the loaded block states the skill's source class.
A body over maxBodyBytes is refused with skill/too-large, naming its size and path so the model can read it in parts; it is never truncated, because half an instruction file is worse than none.
The tool result lists up to maxResourceEntries files of the bundle directory, so the model knows what exists; contents are still read on demand with the file tools, as logged tool results.
Loading a skill returns one text result, with no partial or streaming form.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-8 (a body over the size cap is refused with its size and path, never truncated) and DH-ADR-CONTEXT-7 (providers are asked under a deadline): a larger body is read in pages with the file tools from the reported path.

reason: The catalogue state is a fold, and a change is published as a delta of added, changed and removed names when that is smaller than the list; a removal still retires a name explicitly.
The loaded body's digest is recorded with the tool result; a later change of that body is announced once by a one-line notice at the next step, so the model knows the instructions it holds are stale.

The limit describes Linux payloads that upstream's build downloads and locks for the workspace-dependencies tool. The tool is dropped by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-3, and the Go project builds and carries no payload (DH-ADR-15).

The limit describes executable permissions of a payload carried by upstream's Python wheel or desktop installer. The tool is dropped by DH-ADR-CONTEXT-3, and no payload is built or carried in the Go design.
The sweep is part of a maintenance duty that runs at start and on a timer in whichever process holds the duty lease, so a long-running host is swept without a restart.

The locator is the host path mapped through the filesystem seam, and where the active provider cannot map it the spill_read tool reads the file on the host, so retrieval does not need a co-located filesystem consumer.
The logged tool result carries a structured spill field that only the policy sets; the user interface and retention read that field and never recognise a notice by its text.
