A missing image calculator falls back to a fixed image cost and an unreadable image path omits the image with a statement, so the result is bounded in every case instead of staying inline in full.

The store reserves a fixed-size id before writing, the notice is sized first, and configuration rejects a budget smaller than the largest possible notice, so a notice always fits and no file is saved and then left unreferenced.
The Go contract includes Open, Stat and Delete beside Save, so retrieval, lifetime and deletion are defined at the seam and not left to each backend.

The store's own retrieval method checks that the calling session owns the file or was forked from the owner. Reading the path with a file tool remains possible for any session of the same user, which is the general unconfined-read gap stated in design.md section 6 and not a property of this seam.
File content travels on its own multiplexed stream instead of inside a JSON message, so a whole-file read is not bounded by the message size limit.
The helper runs the shared watch package on the remote host and streams change events to the host, so the remote filesystem provider supports watching.
The server-rendered UI never dereferences a file address itself: a host route reads through the filesystem seam of the session's world, so a remote file is shown or downloaded like a local one.
Remote confinement does not restrict process visibility, and a remote backend that is partial stays partial.
justification: The remote host runs the same operating-system backends with the same limits as a local host, so the facts of the remote kernel apply unchanged. The network setting is enforced remotely and the remote confinement state is reported on every result (DH-D-SANDBOX-9, DH-ADR-SANDBOX-3).

reason: The SSH host and the helper installed on it are trusted infrastructure.
justification: Fact of remote execution: the remote machine executes every file and process request it is sent, so no client-side design makes a hostile host safe. The digest check of DH-ADR-SANDBOX-8 detects a wrong or stale helper only; the trust statement is shown at connect.

reason: The remote helper does not run on a Windows remote host; the musl half of the upstream limit is gone.
justification: Removed: the helper is the statically linked dsh binary built with cgo off for every released target, so there is no glibc or musl split (DH-ADR-NATIVESYSTEM-3). Kept: DH-ADR-SANDBOX-8 states, as a scope boundary of that record, that the remote host is Linux or macOS (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner), because a Windows remote needs its own process-tree owner, token preparation, journal, pseudoconsole and command-line quoting on the remote machine, none of which is designed. The earlier resolved row called the Windows remote a P2 part; no deliverable carried it (audit finding Q3-2).

reason: The dsh ssh install command uploads the binary over the operator's ssh, verifies it and pins its digest in the writable config layer, and the connection state is a seam fact the UI can show.
The limit exists only because upstream's helper executable embeds a Node runtime that users might mistake for a general Node command; the Go helper embeds no interpreter.
A Windows machine cannot be the remote host, and a lost operation is never replayed; provisioning and reconnect, the other two missing pieces, now exist.
justification: Partly removed, partly kept on purpose (audit finding Q3-2). Removed: the transport needs no control master or socket forwarding, so a Windows machine can be the local end (DH-ADR-SANDBOX-7); provisioning is one command, dsh ssh install (DH-ADR-SANDBOX-8); the connection fiber reconnects for new work under a budget (DH-ADR-SANDBOX-10). Kept, each stated by its record: DH-ADR-SANDBOX-8 says, as a scope boundary of that record, that the remote host is Linux or macOS and that dsh ssh install refuses a Windows remote with ssh/unsupported-remote (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner); DH-ADR-SANDBOX-10 keeps no replay, because replaying a change that may have happened is how data is lost.

reason: UI file and workspace views are host routes that read through the filesystem seam of the session's world, so they work for a remote world without assuming host paths.

There are no per-stream keys to steal because streams are multiplexed inside the one SSH channel, and the helper marks itself non-dumpable and refuses debugger attachment; the remaining trust in the remote host is recorded as a carried limit.

Spill files live in the helper's lock-held runtime directory and are removed at close, at lease expiry, or by the next helper's start-up sweep, so they no longer wait for external temporary-file cleanup.
Each output stream belongs to its process handle and is closed with the handle or its context, and an unread stream stalls only its own sender through its own flow-control window.

The helper writes a cleanup receipt when lease-expiry cleanup ends, and the next connection reads the receipts of lost instances and logs them, so remote termination can be confirmed after a reconnect; until then the log says outcome unknown.

Every write increases a stored namespace revision in its transaction; another process compares the revision before a gating read and on a timer, reloads, and raises the change notice with origin foreign.
An update is one SQL transaction that may touch any number of records, and state that needs indexes, uniqueness or composite keys (the workspace ledger) is stored in real tables.
Each record stores the version of the type it was written with and a registered converter upgrades it when read; a change no converter can express uses the database's forward-only layout migration.
There is no whole-file JSON unit: a write changes the rows it touches in one transaction.
Writers in different processes are serialised by the database with a bounded wait and one classified busy error, so no write is lost to a later file replacement.
No machine-state file is published by rename any more. The files this area still writes (blobs and the request cache) go through the one fsx helper, which states its durability on each platform.
A batch delete is one database transaction, so a crash leaves all of it or none of it and no staging residue.
The limit exists because Node runs JavaScript on one thread and its built-in SQLite driver is synchronous; in Go a database call blocks one goroutine and the rest of the process keeps running.
Every connection to the one database uses the same bounded busy wait and returns one classified busy error when it expires, which the kv layer passes on as storage/busy.
The tables of this area are part of the one database's layout, which is migrated forward in one transaction after an automatic backup instead of being rejected.
The version is a column of every record, so a record written by an older or newer build is recognised on its own and one bad record does not decide the fate of the whole unit.
There is one database file opened by one driver package; this area has no open sequence of its own to duplicate.
There are no backend facets. The session log has its own store in the same database, and machine state uses typed tables, so a deferred log facet has nothing to wait for.
A consumer injects the store by a typed service key and is not constructed until the service is provided, so a too-early read that throws cannot happen and entry order does not matter.
Each ACP delegation starts one fresh agent process and pays the handshake; there is no process pool.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-5 (tradeoff: an external child still gets one process per run): one process per run is what lets the run own the whole process tree and prove it gone before the result is released.

reason: An ACP child receives a local path and runs on the host's own machine; a child on a remote machine is not offered.
justification: Deliberate boundary now stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-5 (a child never runs on a remote machine; recommended default, not confirmed by the owner): no area designs the mapping of paths, credentials and process ownership to a second machine, and a remote workspace is reached through the execution world of the child's tools, not by moving the child.

reason: A harness agent preset and harness model options cannot be applied inside a foreign ACP agent; a request that needs them is refused at admission.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-5 in its own words (Scope boundary of this record: a foreign product, an ACP agent, Codex or Claude Code, runs with its own operator configuration and takes no harness preset and no per-call model option, because the harness cannot compose prompts, tools or models inside another product). The output-schema and depth halves of the upstream bullet are removed by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-9 and DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-4.

reason: Only the ACP agent's final text, bounded, and a fixed-word diagnostic enter the parent's log.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-9: a child's working trace must not enter its creator's model context or log. Other updates are offered to a view as an unlogged progress event.

reason: The ACP provider gains the policy ask: the agent's session/request_permission is forwarded through the run's Ask callback to the interaction registry and shown to the root's answerer with the child's name. With no answerer the request is rejected, and reject stays the default policy.
Each Claude Code delegation is one fresh process with no saved session, continuation or pool.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-5 (one process per run) and by library decision DH-ADR-CLAUDEAGENTSDK-1, which turns session persistence off so that none of the product's state is left to clean up.

reason: One delegation tool may list several operator-declared targets (alias, provider instance, description), and the model picks one with the target argument, so a call chooses among instances without one uniquely named tool per instance. The model and the permission mode of an instance stay fixed by the operator on purpose.

The provider configuration has an explicit settings field: native (the user's Claude settings apply, as upstream) or bare (the product's bare mode, which skips settings, hooks and stored logins and needs a key in env). A hermetic mode therefore exists and the choice is written down instead of implied.
The harness does not create an account, log in or edit Claude Code settings; a sign-in failure is reported with its stage.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7 (external products run as the operator installed them) and DH-ADR-SECURITY-6: account state belongs to the vendor's product and the user.

reason: No vendor payload is installed by a package manager. The provider starts the claude executable the user installed, probes it and its version before the first run, and fails a delegation with subagent/unavailable when it is missing, so the host's own program is the path and not a missing fallback.
A Claude Code child cannot ask a person: permission prompts are denied and questions are unavailable to it.
justification: Not a platform limit, as the debt audit found (Q3-3): the vendor's SDK has prompt callbacks, and the limit follows from the driver the design chose. DH-ADR-CLAUDEAGENTSDK-1 now states it as a scope boundary of that record, in its options table: no permission callback follows from driving print mode, so the external agent has no path to ask the user. The same record names a lead to check before the first build (a flag that hands permission prompts to an MCP tool in print mode); if DH-E-CLAUDEAGENTSDK-1 shows it works, the driver uses it and the boundary narrows. A user who needs prompts reaches Claude Code through the ACP provider (DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7: Claude Code cannot ask a person).

reason: Only the final answer, bounded, and a fixed-word diagnostic enter the parent's log; reasoning, tool traffic and stderr do not.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-9: a child's reasoning, tool traffic and stderr, which may hold secrets, must not enter its creator's model context. Usage is added to the settled record when the product reports it.

reason: A harness preset and a per-call model choice are refused for a Claude Code child.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-5 in its own words (a foreign product takes no harness preset and no per-call model option); DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7 fixes the mode in the instance configuration, and tool targets give the choice among instances. The output-schema and depth halves are removed by the manager.

reason: Upstream has no time limit and restores nothing. In the Go design every external instance has maxDuration (DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7), and a target configured with isolation: worktree (DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-12, the resolution of register entry U-K1-3) runs the child, local or external, in its own checkout on its own branch, so a cancelled or failed run leaves the user's working tree untouched and the branch is the rollback. DH-T-SUBAGENT-32 covers the option and scenario DH-E-SUBAGENT-7 cancels an external run half-way and checks the user's tree. Remainder: the option is off by default, by the owner's decision DH-ADR-40, so in the default configuration a cancelled run still leaves its edits in the user's tree; effects outside the checkout are never undone, which is a fact and not debt. Built by DH-D-SUBAGENT-10.
Each Codex delegation is one fresh process, one unsaved thread and one turn, with no continuation or pool.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-5 (one process per run) and by library decision DH-ADR-CODEX-1, which keeps the thread unsaved so that nothing of the product's state is left behind.

reason: One delegation tool may list several operator-declared targets, and the model picks one with the target argument, so a call chooses among Codex instances and other providers without one uniquely named tool each. An instance's model and permission mode stay fixed by the operator on purpose.
The harness does not create an account, log in, trust a project or edit Codex settings.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7 and DH-ADR-SECURITY-6: account and project-trust state belong to the vendor's product and the user. A failure the product reports with status 401 or 403 gets the category auth.

reason: No native payload is installed by a package manager. The provider starts the codex executable the user installed, probes its version before the first run, and fails a delegation with subagent/unavailable when it is missing.

The exact-version pin is replaced by a minimum version, a tested range, and a real-product scenario that asks the installed Codex for its protocol schema and checks the fields the client relies on. An unknown server request, phase or terminal status fails closed. Each new Codex release still has to be proven by running that scenario.

A fourth permission mode, ask, takes the approval requests that upstream's client declines and forwards them through the run's Ask callback to the interaction registry and the root's answerer. With no answerer, and for an unknown request, the answer is still no. The default mode stays never.
Only the selected answer, bounded, and a fixed-word diagnostic enter the parent's log.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-9, the same as for the Claude Code child.

reason: A harness preset and a per-call model choice are refused for a Codex child.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-5 in its own words (a foreign product, Codex included, takes no harness preset and no per-call model option), the same as for the Claude Code child.

reason: Upstream has no time limit and restores nothing. In the Go design every external instance has maxDuration (DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-7), and a target configured with isolation: worktree (DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-12, the resolution of register entry U-K1-3) runs the Codex child in its own checkout on its own branch, so a cancelled or failed run leaves the user's working tree untouched and the branch is the rollback. DH-T-SUBAGENT-32 covers the option, and scenario DH-E-SUBAGENT-7 cancels a real Codex run half-way and checks the user's tree. Remainder: the option is off by default, by the owner's decision DH-ADR-40, so in the default configuration a cancelled run still leaves its edits in the user's tree; effects outside the checkout are never undone, which is a fact and not debt. Built by DH-D-SUBAGENT-10.
Each SDK delegation starts one fresh dsh runtime, which boots a whole component tree; there is no pool.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-5 (one process per run). A task that does not need process isolation uses the in-process providers.

reason: The child is the same binary, so the parent passes the preset id, the delegation depth and its creator in the SDK initialize call and the child host applies them; an output schema is validated by the parent's manager. This needs those initialize fields from area A20.

The provider's home may be set to same, which DH-ADR-12 makes safe: the child host writes its session into the parent's database under its own lease with the delegating agent as creator, so the child's transcript is listed and opened like any other child session.
The SDK child runs as a local process in a local directory; a remote runtime is not offered.
justification: The same boundary as unit subagent-acp.2, now stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-5 (a child never runs on a remote machine; recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: A fork child sees its creator's completed turns as of the fork and nothing the creator logs later.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-10 in its own words (Scope boundary of this record: a fork copies the creator's completed turns once, when it starts, and never follows the creator's later turns, because a child is its own independent log and a single copy keeps the provider's cached prefix). A creator that wants to share more sends a message.

reason: Two of the four named causes cannot arise in Go: there is no generated SDK and no restored historical override. Structured output no longer adds a child-only tool, because the manager validates the final answer. An explicit route change stays the caller's choice. A test asserts that a fork child's first request has its creator's system prompt and tool schemas byte for byte.
The shipped fork tools offer no model route fields.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-10 (fork inherits and offers no route fields by default): a provider's prefix cache is keyed by model, so a fork on another model cannot reuse the inherited prefix that fork exists for. An operator may turn the fields on.

reason: A spawn child starts with none of its creator's conversation.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-10 in its own words (a spawn starts with an empty conversation); the fork provider exists for the other case, and merging them would make every delegation pay for the inherited history.

reason: The whole tree is one projection folded from the root's log, so listing descendants is one read and needs no observation per member; a cold root needs one fold from its projection checkpoint.
A child's name cannot be changed or reused once the child was published.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-4 (names are unique for ever among one creator's children, except that a start that never published frees its name): a name appears in logged messages, notices and task owner fields, and reuse would make that history ambiguous.

reason: An ACP agent, Codex or Claude Code child runs once and accepts no follow-up message; the dsh runtime child now accepts one.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-5 (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner): a follow-up to an external child is a second run in a new process, offered where the child has a durable session. The dsh runtime provider is now Continuable (DH-D-SUBAGENT-7, test DH-T-SUBAGENT-33), which is what register entry U-K1-4 recommended. ACP children become continuable later, where the agent can load a session; Codex and Claude Code stay single-run because their library decisions turn saved sessions off.

reason: A model-authored message stays within one agent tree and reaches only the root or a local member.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-8 (tradeoff: no message crosses trees): tree membership is the only authority for a model-authored message. A person can prompt any session they may access.

reason: The agent contract of area A02 queues a waking send that arrives while a turn is being cancelled as a new turn, so nothing stays parked waiting for a second send. The manager's Send and Interrupt use that contract unchanged; the dependency on A02 is stated in section 10.

Settlement looks only at waking input. Injected context that is parked stays in the logged inbox and is restored when the child is next resumed, so it no longer has to keep the child, or its creators, in memory.

The session lease of DH-ADR-12 makes a tree belong to the one process that holds the root's lease. A second process that opens a member is refused with subagent/busy-elsewhere, and slots are counted in that one process. Nothing is delivered across processes, and a single writer needs no such delivery.

Accepting a message means its inbox splice is committed: Send returns the durable receipt of area A02, so an accepted prompt is in the child's log before the sender is told. A start is likewise recorded and flushed before anything is created.

A start passes the around event subagent.Admit, where a policy component returns Allow or Deny with a reason. Keeping a child running at its end uses the child's own TurnStopping point of area A02, which a listener on the tree's root can reach because tree events are dispatched through the root's scope.
send_message returns a receipt and never the target's reply.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-8 (a send has a receipt, never a reply): a reply cannot be attributed to one message once several messages share a step. A caller that wants a return value starts a child with wait.

reason: A member cannot be live without its root, because every activation is a fiber under the root's tree fiber. For a cold target the host resumes the root first and then only the target, so a missing root is repaired instead of reported. External and dismissed targets still cannot receive messages.

Only the holder of the root's lease can activate a member, so one projection snapshot plus that process's live registry cannot disagree with another process. A listing is still a snapshot in time; interrupt and send check authority themselves.
A wait remembers the inbox's log position it last reported, not message ids. Replacing a pending message is a new splice at a later position, so it ends the next wait.
list_agents takes a cursor and a limit (default 50, at most 200), and Dismiss removes a settled child from listings and from messaging by a ledger record without deleting its session.

The delegation tool takes wait: true. The call then blocks until settlement and returns the bounded result with caller delivery, and cancelling the call disposes the child. This is also what a workflow script calls through the tool command line.

The agent_preset choice lists each allowed preset with its description. The tool set is resolved once per step in Go, so reading descriptions at that point does not depend on declaration order. It needs a description field on presets from area A27.

Preset ids in a tool's configuration are checked against the composed preset ids when the layers are composed and again at each reload, so a misspelling is a diagnostic with file and line. The id is still resolved again at delegation.
The shipped fork tools leave model selection off.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-10, the same as unit subagent-fork-in-process.3; an operator may turn the option on under the same route authorisation.

reason: The depth cap is a value resolved at each delegation (the tool instance's live field, else the host setting), and the check applies to every provider. A different cap is a configuration edit that takes effect at the next call, not a second tool, and provider-managed is dropped.

Disposal can wait for ever upstream after SIGKILL. The Go stop ladder ends with a settle deadline: past it, Stop returns an error naming the survivors, the handle stays registered and the fiber unload completes with the leak reported.

Spill output is written through the storage area's spill store, which owns retention, instead of into an unowned directory under the operating-system temp folder, so completed spill files are collected.
The process package no longer creates a per-process spill directory once; each spill asks the storage area's store for a writer, and that store owns and recreates its directory.
A process tree is owned by the operating system on Windows and on Linux; on macOS, and on a Linux host that has neither a writable cgroup nor a user service manager, it falls back to process groups.
justification: macOS fact: the system offers no persistent owner for a range of processes. The Linux half that the review tracked as U-K1-1 is removed by the design: DH-ADR-EXEC-2 now has the host ask the user service manager once at start for a delegated scope (owner decision DH-ADR-40), built by DH-D-EXEC-2 and proven by test DH-T-EXEC-17 and scenario DH-E-EXEC-10 on a real SSH login. A Linux host with no user manager, such as a bare container, keeps the fallback and says so on every handle.

reason: Upstream probes with child processes on every eligible spawn and keeps a runner per command. The Go provider decides its owner rung once when it starts, by checking that it can create a control group or job object, and uses no child process to probe or to hold an owner.

The process is created inside its job in the same CreateProcess call through the job-list attribute, the host holds the only job handle, and the job grants no breakaway, so the create-to-assign window and the breakaway exclusion are removed. This is an inference to be confirmed by the Windows tree scenario.
On Windows an interrupt is the Ctrl-C input byte, which the console delivers to every attached process; stop and hang-up signals do not exist.
justification: Windows console fact: there are no per-process-group job-control signals, so no terminal library can deliver them. The backend refuses the unsupported signals instead of ignoring them (DH-D-EXEC-5).

reason: Go terminals use the operating system's ConPTY by default and need no file beside the binary; an operator may configure a console host directory. The reason for bundling, a byte comparison of the prompt, is removed by comparing the emulated screen.
Where only process groups own a terminal's children, a child that leaves the terminal session before it is observed can escape cleanup.
justification: macOS fact: process groups and sessions are the strongest owners the system offers, and a process-table scan sees only a moment. On Linux the gap is closed where a control group is available, which now includes a scope delegated by the user service manager (DH-ADR-EXEC-2, register entry U-K1-1). Survivors are reported, not hidden (DH-ADR-EXEC-2).

reason: Go runs no code at exit, so cleanup does not depend on an observable exit: a Windows job handle closes with the host, Linux direct children get a parent-death signal, and the host handles SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP by unloading its tree. What survives a killed host on Linux and macOS is stated per system.
Secrets are removed from a child's environment by name pattern, so a secret with an unusual name in the operator's own environment still reaches the child.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-EXEC-8 (tradeoff: the scrub is still a name heuristic for secrets the harness does not know) and accepted by DH-ADR-SECURITY-6. Deny and allow patterns are configuration, so an operator who wants a closed list can deny everything and allow named variables; names the configuration uses as credential references are removed exactly.

reason: Upstream transports that own their spawn cannot use the service. In Go no package except the process package may import os/exec or call a process-creation function, and the MCP, SDK and plugin transports are harness code that calls it; a source check enforces this.

Each upstream consumer rebuilds its own teardown ladder. The Go seam ships one stop ladder (revoke authority, ask, close input, terminate, kill, then a bounded wait) with a hook for the consumer's protocol-level request.

Consumers no longer need to know the provider to learn how strongly a tree is owned: every handle and result reports its owner kind. The weaker rungs that remain on macOS and on Linux without a control group are carried under the subprocess-local limits.

The limit is about resolving a koffi binding table that loads Windows DLLs at import time. Go selects Windows code with build constraints at compile time and has no foreign-function loader, so it exists only because of the Node binding.
The Win32 primitives become private functions of the process package, and the subprocess service around them is the only API, so no consumer has to assemble policy, limits and handle closure itself.

The null environment block is a workaround for koffi failing to marshal an explicit block. Go passes an explicit sorted UTF-16 block with CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT, so the limit exists only because of the JavaScript binding.
There is no standalone primitive package any more: streams, handles, output policy and cancellation are owned by the one process package that contains the primitives.

Creating the process inside its job in one call removes the interval between creation and assignment in which a suspended target could be left behind. The suspended-create fallback keeps the old window and is reported when used.

The architecture-specific header probe guards hand-written structure layouts for koffi. golang.org/x/sys/windows supplies typed structures per architecture, so there is no layout to probe; it exists only because of the JavaScript binding.
A task change publishes one team.TaskChanged notice that names the task and its revision, and the server-rendered board swaps that one row. The whole board is never broadcast. The view is area C5's.

Upstream gives members no worktree. In the Go design a delegation target may be configured with isolation: worktree (DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-12, the owner's resolution of register entry U-K1-3 in DH-ADR-40): the manager calls worktree.Service.ForChild before the child exists, and the child, local or external, works on its own branch in its own checkout as its only write root. It is off by default, works only in a Git repository with the worktree component mounted, and nothing is merged automatically; without it members share one checkout. Remainder: in the default configuration members still share one checkout, by the owner's decision DH-ADR-40 (off by default), not by omission. Built by DH-D-SUBAGENT-10; proven by DH-T-SUBAGENT-32, DH-T-XFORGE-13 and scenario DH-E-SUBAGENT-7.
In a shared checkout a member's write scopes only warn; a shell command, a formatter or a generator can write outside them.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-11 (tradeoff: write scopes stay advisory in a shared checkout, and the views say not enforced). The enforced alternative now exists: a member started with isolation: worktree has its own checkout as its only write root (DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-12, the resolution of register entry U-K1-3). Enforcing scopes inside a shared checkout is listed as not designed in section 10 of the spec.

reason: There are no task notices to miss: by decision a task change wakes nobody, an agent that must act is sent a message, and a message resumes a cold member. A settlement notice for a member that was away is derived from the ledger when it is next resumed.
Members cannot message another team, and only an ancestor or the user can interrupt a member.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-8: tree membership is the only authority for a model-authored message, and ancestry the only one for a model-requested stop.

reason: A member's activation is a fiber under its root's tree fiber, so a member cannot be live while its root is gone, and a cold member is reached by resuming the root first. A member therefore always has an active team.

When the ledger shows that a task owner's latest run settled as anything but completed, or that the owner was dismissed, the board appends a release revision that names the cause; the same rule runs when the root is resumed after a crash. An owner that is merely inactive keeps its task, and task views say whether the owner is resident.

The team/message/queued records exist upstream so that logs written by earlier upstream releases stay readable. Reading upstream sessions in the store is dropped by DH-ADR-11 (a separate, one-way import of the current format only) and DH-ADR-2; the Go design has no team mailbox type, so there is no historical message to leave undelivered.
The team policy text coordinates and does not confine: in a shared checkout it cannot stop a shell command or an external process from writing overlapping files.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-11: a prompt coordinates, and confinement is the sandbox's job. Members that must not collide are started with isolation: worktree, each in its own checkout (DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-12, the resolution of register entry U-K1-3).

reason: A live member always has a live root, because its activation is a fiber under the root's tree fiber. A task call still checks mode and authority again under the board's mutex when it runs, so a tool that was visible at step start cannot act after Team mode was turned off.

The Board interface takes an actor that is an agent or an owner principal, so the web board of area C5 can create, edit, reassign and release tasks through the same compare-and-set commands the tools use.

Consent is enforced by the factory: a channel cannot be created without a sharing permit and closes without a drain when the permit ends. The shutdown deadline has a default. Redaction and field selection stay with the consumer, and resource identity is evaluated lazily at the first accepted record.

The channel stays memory-only, but it now reports every batch as delivered, failed, dropped or cancelled with the sequence range it covered. A consumer with a durable source, the session upload that reads the session log, resumes after the last delivered record, so loss in the channel no longer means loss of the upload.
There is one channel type and it batches by count and by bytes, so a consumer no longer has to pick event and batch sizes that happen to fit the collector's request limit.

The model reads lines from the host-side emulated screen, which follows the alternate screen, so a full-screen program's current page is readable. This holds once the emulator gate passes; if the gate ends on the line-screen fallback the limit returns and is recorded.
That a foreign child process is waiting for terminal input can be proven on Linux only; elsewhere readiness is inferred.
justification: Operating-system fact: macOS and Windows offer no facility that proves another process is blocked reading the terminal. The Go design narrows the limit (a bracketed command completes exactly on every system) and reports the uncertain case as inferred_idle (DH-D-EXEC-7).

reason: The PowerShell bootstrap writes its prompt marker with core types only and pins the code page with chcp, both allowed in ConstrainedLanguage, so it no longer depends on Console static calls. This is an inference proven by the Windows terminal scenario under read-only mode.
The split is kept as the design and made explicit: tree teardown is one Close operation owned by the process package, and the backend only calls it and awaits it.
A host restart destroys every terminal session.
justification: The same deliberate boundary as unit terminal.terminal.1: DH-ADR-EXEC-2 ends children with the host on purpose so that nothing runs unowned, and DH-ADR-WEBAPP-4 installs nothing that outlives the host.

reason: Terminal sessions and their screen state live in the host process and end with it.
justification: Deliberate boundary: DH-ADR-EXEC-2 has the host hold every tree owner so that no child runs unowned, and DH-ADR-WEBAPP-4 says nothing is installed to keep a process alive. Surviving a restart would need a supervisor outside the host. The model's input and the returned output stay durable as tool events.

reason: A terminal session has exactly one owning agent and cannot be shared with or transferred to another agent.
justification: Deliberate boundary: owner scoping is the access rule that keeps one agent out of another agent's terminal; a person may attach a browser and take control, which the same decision governs. Stated by DH-ADR-EXEC-9 item (a) (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: A terminal session is created only on request, by an agent tool call or by a user in the web terminal; configuration cannot start one.
justification: Deliberate boundary: a session needs an owner whose end closes it, and an owner exists only once an agent or a user asks. Stated by DH-ADR-EXEC-9 item (c) (recommended default, not confirmed by the owner).

reason: Adapters, optional components, load order and teardown are no longer the caller's: compose.Start loads a named bundle and extra layers through the real loader, registers a scripted model, and unloads the tree in the test's cleanup.
The composition harness registers the scripted model on a default route unless the test supplies its own, so a test that starts the loop has an adapter without wiring one.
The process-local Inbox stub is not carried: a consumer test builds a real agent on an in-memory store, so durable events, projections and claim policy are always the production ones.
The fail-fast Inbox stub is not carried either; a test that must prove the inbox is untouched asserts that the real session log holds no inbox event.
The limit concerns generated zod Remote clients of upstream's JavaScript browser client; the Go design renders HTML on the host and has no generated client to bypass.
The limit concerns the JavaScript Gateway client's invoke path being bypassed by a test proxy; there is no Gateway client in the Go design, and UI tests call the real HTTP handlers.
The limit concerns how a JavaScript Remote proxy guesses unary or stream mode for an undeclared endpoint; the Go design has no Remote proxy.
The limit is a TypeScript compile-program detail (Node ambient types leaking into client sources); Go has one type-checked program and no ambient type sets.
The limit concerns separate fixture types for the React client's Session, Conversation and Chat stores; the Go UI has no client stores, and a page is rendered from host state.
The fault-injecting model server's random mix of failures is test pressure chosen by the test author, not an estimate of how often a real provider fails.
justification: How often a model provider fails is a property of that third-party service, which publishes no distribution; a fixture cannot know it. DH-D-UTIL-6 keeps the seeded mix and prints the seed so that a run can be repeated, and a caller with measured weights can supply them.

reason: The Go fault server keeps one script cursor per key computed from the request by a test-supplied function, so concurrent callers no longer share one arrival-ordered cursor and one server instance gives deterministic per-caller faults.

A refused connection no longer depends on overlapping a listener's start-up delay: the egress test recorder scripts a dial failure for a chosen attempt, which is deterministic and needs no real listener.

A live child session is bound to its recorded script by its lineage (the parent's script and the ordinal of the tool call that created it), not by which session calls the model first, so siblings that run concurrently bind deterministically.

A replay can derive everything the session log recorded, now including a failure before the first chunk and summariser calls, but a model call that never returns is not in the log and must be written by hand in an override file.
justification: A session export is a finite list of events, and a wait that never ended has no event to record. The Go design narrows upstream's limit to exactly that case: every attempt, failed ones included, is one logged event (DH-ADR-UTIL-7, DH-D-UTIL-7).

reason: Built mode needing a prior build exists because upstream runs either TypeScript source under tsx or bundled output under Node; go test compiles what it runs and the kit builds the dsh binary itself, once per run, from the build cache.
The binary runner caps captured output at a budget the test states and fails the test naming the cap, instead of inheriting a 100 MB default from a process library.

The binary runner starts the child through the one process package, whose operating-system job object or process group ends the whole tree at the deadline, so a tree spawned by a faulty fixture cannot outlive the test.
An in-process-only carrier is a limit of a mock for the JavaScript client's Connection object; the Go design has no such client and tests the HTTP surface with net/http/httptest.
Values crossing by reference instead of being serialised is a property of an in-realm JavaScript mock; Go UI tests go through real HTTP handlers, where everything is serialised.
Unchecked answer envelopes are a limit of the Typert Remote mock; there is no Typert result envelope in the Go design.
Endpoint-only rule matching is a limit of the Typert Remote mock, which has no Go counterpart; a Go fake is scripted per call and fails on anything unscripted.
Native stream overrides bypassing the mock's log concern Vitest mock functions over JavaScript async iterables; nothing of the kind exists in the Go design.

The replay runner harvests a session through the product's export command, which writes the line-per-event export format whatever the store's internal encoding is, so no storage mode has to be configured for tests.
Built mode needing current artifacts exists because of upstream's source-versus-bundled split under Node; the Go kit builds the binary it runs from the same packages the tests compile.

Upstream's limit was a leftover of a migration: some snapshot behaviours could not move off the ACP adapter. The Go replay runner has one driver per surface behind one interface and every scenario names the driver it needs, so a behaviour whose stimulus is an ACP client is driven through ACP by design and no adapter is a remainder.

A fixture tool is declared through the same declaration path as a product tool, with a typed output and a derived schema, so there is no special content-array fixture form that differs from production.

The kit has no way around the pipeline: a direct tool call enters the guarded pipeline's direct-caller entry on a real in-memory session, so it is logged, and batch scheduling is exercised by a scripted-model turn.
Composition and disposal belong to the composition harness, which unloads the tree in the test's cleanup and fails the test when an effect is left.
A todo list belongs to one agent session; there is no shared, subagent or team list.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-TOOLS-10: one owner per list keeps the event a last-write-wins snapshot. Shared work items are the team task board of DH-ADR-SUBAGENT-11, not this tool.

reason: A todo item is content plus one of three states, with no id, priority or active-form field.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-TOOLS-10: whole-list replacement needs no item identity and a smaller shape costs fewer tokens on every write.

reason: Replacing the whole list is the only todo operation.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-TOOLS-10: a whole-list event needs no merge and replays as last write wins, and the model already holds the list in its context.

reason: Wildcard patterns in npm package exports exist only in the npm package format that the TypeScript generator analyses; Go has no package export map and no generator runs.
Namespace re-exports across host and client faces are a TypeScript module construct between two separately compiled programs; the Go design has one program and no faces.

The Zod emitter and the conditional and mapped types it cannot emit are TypeScript constructs; no emitter exists. The Go counterpart, a Go type that reflection cannot describe, fails a test that derives every registered type instead of failing a build step.
Merging unions of named fields and index signatures into strict schemas is a property of TypeScript's structural type algebra; a Go struct has one fixed field set, so there are no operands to merge.
Generated schema imports across faces concern generated JavaScript modules for two compiled programs; nothing is generated and there is one program.
Discovery through the reachable graph of public TypeScript exports belongs to the generator's analysis; in Go a type takes part by being registered explicitly, so there is no discovery step to limit.
Importing only the host face's generated artifact is a limit of a two-program client and host build; the UI is rendered by the host, so there is no client face to discover.
Explicit package entries for nested plugins exist because loader fibers carry no resolvable npm package specifier; Go components are compiled in and nothing is located by package name.
A cached verdict about whether an npm package exports ./typert can only go stale when packages change in a running process; the Go host never loads code at run time.

There is no asynchronous registration to wait for: the method table is a Go value complete at program start, handlers are checked against it by a test, and the carrier answers initialize only when boot reports the tree ready.

A row of the method table carries the name, direction, kind, parameter and result types, capability, first version and description, and schemas come from the Go types by reflection, so full metadata needs no build pipeline.

The restrictions concern TypeScript decorators and signatures (overloads, destructuring, defaults, rest parameters); a Go handler has one form, a context and one parameter struct in, one result and an error out.
Merging host and client type graphs presupposes two faces and TypeScript references to resolve; one Go program has one set of types.
Schema keys that omit the face can only collide when two faces register into one context; there are no faces and schemas are keyed by Go type.
The schema package derives a JSON Schema once per Go type and caches the immutable result for the life of the process, and the protocol document is computed once, so no consumer has to own caching.
File replacement can be durable: the caller states it and the file and its directory are synced before success is reported (fsx.Replace with Durable, owned by area A08).
The Go replacement takes a function that writes to the staged file, so content can be streamed and need not be complete in memory.
The writer lock is a kernel file lock, released by the operating system when its holder dies; there is no lock record to be empty and no process ID to be reused, so no orphan needs an operator.
Nothing probes a process ID any more, so a different PID namespace cannot make a live holder look dead; a harness home must be on a local filesystem and one that is not is refused instead of raced.
Append-only access is a limit of a persistent list built because JavaScript state is frozen and shared by reference; a Go fold owns an ordinary slice, which has random access.
Recursive checkpoints come from the linked-chunk structure and the JavaScript runtime's nesting limits; a Go slice is stored as one flat JSON array.
The Language function matches whole file names as well as extensions, so Dockerfile, Makefile and dot files without a suffix are recognised.
A file whose name and extension are not in the language table is shown as plain text with no highlighting, even when its content is unambiguous; the table never reads content.
justification: Deliberate, so that the same file renders the same way everywhere and bytes written by the model cannot change rendering; the only content verdict is text or binary, in the filesystem area. DH-ADR-UTIL-9, added in the convergence round as a recommended default, states the rule (item a) and DH-D-UTIL-5 builds it.

reason: The double registration is gone: the host has one highlighter and a test asserts that every language id in the table is one the highlighter accepts, so adding a language is one reviewed change. The table stays curated.
Callers treat an identifier as opaque and obtain it from one function, so its form can change in one place (for example to a time-ordered form) without a second helper or dependency.
Identifiers are random and unique only with overwhelming probability; the identifier helper itself detects no collision.
justification: This is the mathematics of random identifiers with 122 random bits (RFC 9562 version 4), not something a design removes. Where uniqueness matters the store enforces it with a key constraint, so a collision would be a refused insert and never silent sharing (DH-ADR-NODECRYPTO-2).

reason: A queue without a capacity policy cannot be declared: every in-process queue is a bounded channel or bounded buffer whose declaration states what happens when it is full.
The file name offered for an exported item is derived from its declared media type, and an explicit suffix wins; the content is not inspected to guess a format.
justification: Deliberate: media types are answered from the name by one compiled-in table so that the answer is the same on every machine. DH-ADR-UTIL-9, added in the convergence round as a recommended default, states the rule (item a) and DH-D-UTIL-5 builds it.

reason: In a configured path only a bare ~ and ~/ expand to the home directory; named-user forms such as ~alice, environment variables and shell expressions are left as written.
justification: Deliberate: expanding variables or shell syntax in a path would evaluate a configuration value against the environment outside the one explicit mechanism for that, the restricted expression language of DH-ADR-LOADER-3. DH-ADR-UTIL-9, added in the convergence round as a recommended default, states the rule (item b) and DH-D-UTIL-5 builds it.

reason: Consumers no longer canonicalise a watch path themselves: the watch service accepts a path that may not exist, resolves it by file identity and follows it when parents appear or vanish; directory creation and permissions belong to the home layout.

A network whose proxy is given only by a proxy auto-configuration (PAC) file still needs the user to export the proxy variables; the launch now names the PAC address and says so. Removed in the convergence round (register entry U-K2-2): the static proxy set in the Windows or macOS system settings is read once at launch, below every environment variable. SOCKS5 proxy URLs already worked.
justification: Deliberate for the part that remains: DH-ADR-UTIL-10 states that a PAC address is reported and never fetched or evaluated, because evaluating one needs a script engine the design does not have (DH-ADR-8). The same record designs the static reader (tests DH-T-UTIL-21, scenario DH-E-UTIL-4). One fact behind it is still unverified and recorded as open in util-test-support.md section 10: that the Windows registry values can be read in a build without cgo. If they cannot, Windows has no reader and keeps the old limit; the design says so. The static reader is deliverable DH-D-UTIL-9 since the split of the fix pass.

reason: Go verifies against the operating system's trust store, and an operator setting adds certificate authority files to it; an unreadable file stops the launch with its path.
A third-party program the host starts (a Node-based MCP server, for example) goes through the proxy only if that program's own runtime reads the proxy variables it is given.
justification: How a third-party program opens its connections is that program's behaviour; a parent process can only hand over the environment. DH-D-UTIL-2 gives a trusted child the user's own values and the resolved ones for names the user left unset (DH-ADR-UTIL-5). The host itself no longer depends on any Node version.

reason: Telemetry is no longer direct: the exporter takes its HTTP client from egress, so proxy and certificate policy apply, and the client is created only for a permit holder.

The guest runtime and workflow worker do not exist; a model-written program is an ordinary command, and its environment is built for the ModelRun audience: proxy values without credentials are passed, a value carrying a password is omitted and the omission is reported once.

Register entry U-K2-3, resolved in the convergence round. util-test-support.md section 6.2 adds an import-graph gate: test DH-T-UTIL-22 lists every package in the dsh binary's import graph, dependencies included, that imports a package able to open a connection, and compares the list with a reviewed table in which each entry says how its client is supplied by egress or why it never dials. A dependency that adds such a package fails the gate until reviewed. The gate shows which packages can dial, not that they do, so the recording transport of the egress tests stays (DH-D-UTIL-2). The gate is deliverable DH-D-UTIL-10 since the split of the fix pass.

The launch environment is never written into the process environment, and the one spawn helper builds each child's environment explicitly, so a discovered project variable reaches a child only if a rule passes it on.
The launch environment is read once from the directory the harness was started in; a workspace chosen later in the web UI contributes no environment values.
justification: Deliberate, and the same boundary as unit boot.app-boot.6: DH-ADR-BOOT-4 freezes launch facts before the tree exists, because following a workspace would let a directory the model can write change the harness environment in the middle of a session.

reason: The CommonJS-only limit is a property of Node's two module systems; Go has one linker and no module loading at run time.
Dropped by DH-ADR-17 (the in-browser preview runtime is not built). The limit concerns the WebWorker packer's static discovery of JavaScript dependencies for that runtime.
The run-and-capture helper of the one process package takes an explicit output budget and offers streaming, instead of rejecting on a fixed buffer limit inherited from Node's execFile.

Dropped by DH-ADR-18 (no desktop application) and DH-ADR-UTIL-3, which records that listing the applications that can open a file is not built (also DH-ADR-UISIDE-8). The limit describes icon extraction for the application picker of upstream's desktop integration.

On Windows, opening the web UI in the default browser needs an interactive desktop session; started from a service, a scheduled task or an SSH session the hand-off can report success having opened nothing.
justification: Windows runs services and SSH sessions in a non-interactive session where the shell launches no file association; the harness cannot change that. The launch always prints the URL as well and the hand-off has a deadline, so a failed open costs only the convenience (DH-LIB-OPEN).

reason: There is no list a profile cannot extend: every compiled-in component can be named by a loader entry, so a layer can enable or add any of them without a release. Only the set of components itself changes with a release.
The item retainer supports head, tail and head-and-tail windows, each with an exact omitted count; pagination and grouping stay with the tool because they are not truncation.
Go strings are UTF-8, so there is one unit: a budget in bytes is cut on a rune boundary by the same retainer, and the separate UTF-16 surrogate helper has no counterpart.
The plugin manifest is a Go struct decoded strictly through the schema package by one reader, so parsing, validation and defaults exist once instead of in every consumer.
A declared harness version range is enforced: it is parsed strictly when the manifest is inspected and a plugin that requires another host version is refused before it starts.

Dropped by DH-ADR-13 (plugins come from local directories; nothing is discovered or downloaded). The public-npm-only limit concerns reading a package's files from npm file CDNs for a plugin detail page.
Dropped by DH-ADR-13 and DH-ADR-BOOT-11 (no plugin market). The limit concerns a generator's obligations toward an index of npm packages, which the Go design never reads.
Dropped by DH-ADR-13 and DH-ADR-BOOT-11 (no plugin market). The missing size bound concerns parsing a fetched market index document, which the Go design never fetches or parses.
Search runs inside the host in pure Go, so no executable has to be co-located and a remote provider needs no rg binary.
With in-process search there is no record stream to split and decode: a path is a Go string holding the file system's bytes unchanged, so a name with a newline or invalid UTF-8 stays usable.
The filter of a pick-list matches substrings and letters in order from a word start; a transposed or wrong letter (pluign for plugin) finds nothing.
justification: Deliberate: a filter that also guesses at typing errors returns matches the user cannot explain, and the match tiers are fixed by golden tests so that order is predictable. DH-ADR-UTIL-9, added in the convergence round as a recommended default, states the rule (item c: the filter 'tolerates no typing error'); DH-D-UTIL-12 builds it.

reason: Lists are filtered on the host, which holds the message catalogue in every language, so a label that comes from the catalogue can be matched in all languages and not only the active one.

The pick-list filter is not the ranker used for file references in the composer; that one is a separate ranker in the filesystem area's search package. Upstream's second separate index, the plugin market, is not built at all.
justification: Deliberate: ranking paths in a large tree is a different problem from filtering a short list. DH-ADR-UTIL-9, added in the convergence round as a recommended default, states the two-ranker split (item d); the market half is DH-ADR-13 (no plugin discovery).

reason: Zone names are validated and stored exactly as given and never rewritten to a canonical alias, so no answer depends on the zone data of a particular runtime build.

A schedule accepts a bounded subset of recurrence rules: five-field cron and the RRULE subset upstream accepts, with limits on density and range; anything else is refused with the cause (syntax, zone, density or range).
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-RRULE-1 says 'The accepted subset and limits of R1 to R3 are kept from upstream unchanged', because the subset is what the model was taught and the limits guarantee bounded work when occurrences are resolved after a long downtime. Built by DH-D-UTIL-11 since the split of the fix pass.

reason: The limit documents an own Duration class written because TypeScript arithmetic erases a branded number; Go's time.Duration is a distinct elapsed-time type and calendar steps are done on a time in its zone.
The limit concerns how much of the own TypeScript Duration class is published; the Go standard library's time.Duration is complete and there is no class to grow.
A span in configuration is a time.Duration field that the schema package reads from text such as 30s, and arithmetic uses that type, so no call site multiplies a bare number of seconds by a thousand.

Loading the recurrence dependencies with the package root is a cost of JavaScript module entry points and browser bundles; Go links only imported packages, caltime and recur are separate, and no time code runs in a browser.
A deadline is a notification: cancelling a context cannot stop work that ignores it, so every capability keeps its own way to end a process, a socket or a task.
justification: The Go runtime has no operation that stops a goroutine from outside. The design bounds the effect: process-owning code ends the process tree, and a conformance helper in DH-D-UTIL-6 fails any tool body that does not return when its context ends (DH-ADR-UTIL-4).

reason: There is no zero-or-negative sentinel: no deadline is expressed by not setting one, and a configured timeout is a duration field whose schema bounds reject zero.
When a cancellation from above arrives before a local timer fires, the record says cancelled and cannot also say that the timeout would have fired.
justification: Deliberate: DH-ADR-ARCH-3 records one typed cause per cancellation on turn/end and says '"First cause wins" is the standard library's behaviour', which is what makes the record unambiguous; DH-ADR-UTIL-4 makes every deadline a context.WithTimeoutCause.

reason: The idle timer on a response body measures silence on the wire only; it is not a limit on total time and does not count the consumer's own pauses.
justification: Deliberate, and stated in the record's own words since the final re-check: DH-ADR-UTIL-4 has 'Scope boundary of this record (unit util.timeout.4): egress.IdleBody bounds silence on a response body, not its total length, because a model's streamed answer may legitimately run for many minutes while bytes keep arriving; a caller that needs a total limit sets its own context deadline'.

reason: A JSON-only structural comparator exists because JavaScript has no value equality for objects; Go compares typed values directly, so there is no general comparator whose input assumptions need stating.
deepFreeze and its gaps exist because JavaScript objects are shared by reference; the Go design keeps data immutable by ownership and copying and freezes nothing.

WeakMapWithValues works around JavaScript weak references; a Go registry is owned by a fiber and each entry is an effect released on unload, which is the explicit cleanup the limit asks callers to remember.
Lexical-only resolution is a limit of code that must run in a browser, which cannot access a file system; in the Go design the host resolves paths through the filesystem seam.
Home abbreviation is POSIX-only because a browser cannot know the host's Windows home directory; the Go host knows it on every system and abbreviates before rendering.
A search request carries a budget of provider units; the tool divides searchMaxUnits among the queries of one call and a model-backed provider caps its server-side searches to its share.
A multi-query search returns the sources of the queries that succeeded and one line naming each failed query and its code; the call fails only when every query failed.
HTML that nests too deeply or fails to convert is replaced by a fixed omission marker, and table spans are not represented.
justification: Deliberate safety boundary required by the HTML-to-Markdown library specification (DH-LIB-TURNDOWN: raw markup is never the fallback and a span never multiplies work). The span half is also a format fact: Markdown tables have no spanning cell. DH-ADR-CONNECT-8 now states it (HTML that cannot be converted safely becomes an omission marker and is never passed through).

reason: web_search takes queries and an optional region, and web_fetch only a url; the result count is an operator bound and there is no format or summarising mode.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-CONNECT-8 (the two tools keep their minimal arguments beyond the ones named there), so that the tool schema stays the same under every provider (outcome DH-O-10); the full text of a truncated page is kept by the spill policy.

reason: A fetch to a loopback or private address asks a person, a metadata or link-local address is refused, an operator can require approval for every fetch, and a denied network policy also denies the fetch.

Upstream's shared request cannot pass the vendor Search API's localization parameter. The Go request has an optional region that a provider declares and honours, and the result says whether it was applied (DH-ADR-CONNECT-8, which names this parameter; register entry U-K1-9). Built by DH-D-CONNECT-6 and DH-D-CONNECT-8, proven by DH-T-CONNECT-23. The provider still does not read the service's site and ranking fields: the seam's result has no use for them, and the summary length the bullet measures is bounded by the tool's summary cap.
sendOriginalQuestion defaults to false, so the user's prompt is not sent to the search service for a signal that upstream measured as having no effect; an operator can turn it on.

A fetch result carries a status and a final URL only when the provider observed them, so this provider no longer reports an invented HTTP 200; the service's own error statuses remain retrieval failures with endpoint guidance.

There is one Check method that takes a context and may ask the credential store, so selection and step admission see the same answer and a direct caller gets the missing-credential reason before sending.

A rate-limit answer is retried once after the stated delay inside the call's deadline, a failed query no longer fails the others, and fetch shares the limiter; other clients of the same account remain uncoordinated, which no single process can change.

The provider reads a route's endpoint and credential from the model-provider area's route registry by route id, and replay there is a listener around a request, not a second adapter under the same id, so a replayed conversation keeps its route.

Every connection of a fetch, including each redirect hop and each resolved address, passes a destination guard in the egress client; private and loopback addresses need a person's approval and metadata addresses are refused.
A fetched PDF is not decoded as text: it is stored as an attachment and reaches the model as page images through the document tool; every other binary type is refused.
justification: Partly removed and partly kept on purpose. Removed: upstream refused a PDF outright; DH-ADR-CONNECT-8 now gives the fetch body a file arm, so a PDF within a size bound is stored after the same address guard and redirect rules and the result names the tool that reads it (DH-D-CONNECT-7, test DH-T-CONNECT-23; register entry U-K1-8); a missing content type is sniffed. Kept: the text decoding that upstream named as deferred work. DH-ADR-CONNECT-8 states that no text extractor is used and that every other binary type stays refused; no pure-Go PDF text extractor has been verified, so adding one is not a small cost. Consequence: a route whose model takes no images cannot read a fetched PDF. The audit (Q3-6) found that the earlier resolved row hid this remainder.

reason: Charset detection reads the header, then a byte-order mark, then an HTML meta declaration, using the x/net charset package.
When bytes are valid both as UTF-8 and as another encoding and no declaration settles it, UTF-8 is chosen.
justification: Fact of text encodings: no algorithm identifies an encoding from ambiguous bytes; a detector can only guess. The Go design reads the HTML meta declaration first, which narrows the cases, and keeps upstream's rule of never guessing a legacy encoding (DH-D-CONNECT-7).

reason: A search through the model-backed provider costs one full model request in latency and tokens.
justification: Third-party fact: it is how the vendor's server-side search tool works. The direct Search API provider (DH-D-CONNECT-8) is the alternative, and the unit budget bounds the server-side searches of this provider (DH-D-CONNECT-11). Source: upstream's own bullet (packages/web/web-search-deepseek/README.md, limit 1).

reason: Selection uses the one context-taking Check, which asks the credential store, so a provider without a key is not selected as usable.

A provider remembers that the service rejected its current credential and reports not usable until that credential changes, so a wrong key costs one failed call instead of one per attempt; no probing request is made.
With baseURL unset the search endpoint is derived from the origin of the route whose key is sent, so a gateway key goes to the gateway; an explicit baseURL still overrides.
The model-backed search service returns more sources than asked for and the seam truncates afterwards.
justification: Third-party fact: the vendor's wire has no result-count parameter, so the bound can only be applied to the response. This provider is DH-D-CONNECT-11; the direct Search API provider (DH-D-CONNECT-8) is not affected. Source: upstream's own bullet (packages/web/web-search-deepseek/README.md, limit 5).

reason: Whether a source has a snippet depends on what the endpoint returns.
justification: Third-party fact: an endpoint that returns neither an excerpt nor a citation leaves nothing to show. The provider reads structured result blocks only and never scrapes prose, a rule kept for safety; an answer with no source at all is returned as a zero-source result flagged unsourced (DH-D-CONNECT-11, test DH-T-CONNECT-24). Source: upstream's own bullet (packages/web/web-search-deepseek/README.md, limit 6).

reason: Providers lists every registered provider with a usable flag and a reason code for the given route, and a selection failure names the per-provider reasons.

Upstream's search request carries no controls. The Go request has an optional region; each provider declares which controls it honours and the result reports each control as applied or ignored, with one tool schema under every provider (DH-ADR-CONNECT-8; register entry U-K1-9). Built by DH-D-CONNECT-6 and proven by DH-T-CONNECT-23. Recency and site filters are added when a backend honours them, by the same decision.
The fetch body has a file arm that carries a stored PDF, but no arm for text extracted from a PDF.
justification: Upstream's bullet names text-extractable PDF support as the deferred work behind the missing arm. The Go body type gains a file arm that carries a stored PDF as an attachment reference with its size and the name of the reading tool (DH-D-CONNECT-6, test DH-T-CONNECT-23; register entry U-K1-8), and DH-ADR-CONNECT-8 states that no text extractor is used, so the text arm stays out by that record. The same remainder as unit web-fetch-http.2.

reason: The per-route search preference is the searchPreference list in the web component's configuration; the shipped bundle carries upstream's two rules as data.
Provider-backed page extraction (a hosted service that returns cleaned page content) is not part of the web seam.
justification: Deliberate boundary now stated by DH-ADR-CONNECT-8: no hosted page-extraction service is a provider, because it would send the page's address to a third party the user did not choose.

reason: A background run's narration and member lines go to the job's output, which the model can read before settlement, and a cancelled or timed-out run reports its partial standard output and member table as a failure instead of discarding them. The background path itself is P2 and depends on areas A03 and A13; the partial-output part also holds for foreground runs.

The args argument may be any JSON value, because it is written to a file and no longer has to satisfy a JavaScript global. A result above the model-facing bound is cut with a spill locator, so the complete output is kept behind a retrieval handle instead of being clipped away.
Subagent provider, caps and tool name of a workflow are deployment configuration; the model may lower two caps for one call and never raise them.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-PTC-5: a cap the model could raise is not a cap.

reason: The run record is written by the service that owns the run, not mirrored by the tool: a run or a member whose opening record cannot be appended does not start. Every nested call a script makes is logged by the pipeline as a start and settle pair, so nested dispatches are recorded.

The spec declares a replay-layer test in which a recorded session that contains a workflow run is replayed against the built binary and every rebuilt model request must equal the recorded one. A background run is covered by its own test and scenario with the P2 deliverable.
A workflow script's file confinement and process cleanup inherit the limits of the sandbox backend and of the process-tree owner on each platform.
justification: Inherited operating-system facts owned by the sandbox and execution areas (see units ptc-runtime-node.2 and ptc-runtime-node.4). Enforcement facts are in workflow/run-start, and an unconfirmed cleanup ends the run as cleanup incomplete with named survivors (DH-ADR-PTC-4).

reason: Upstream's counters ran inside the script's own process. In Go the host counts members started and members running in the workflow_agent tool body and the engine, where the script cannot reach them, and refuses the call that passes a cap. An optional token budget across members covers the descendant-budget half.
Every run has a budget counted by the engine's own timer, with a default and a configured maximum; when it ends the run stops with stop reason timeout and the hosting call returns after cleanup.

Cleanup now has a bound of its own: the engine waits at most settleTimeout for the process tree and every member's disposal, then appends workflow/run-end with cleanup incomplete, naming what remains, and keeps the survivors listed.

The limit is about a node:vm context whose withheld globals only guide script authors; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8 and a workflow script is an ordinary program (DH-ADR-PTC-3), confined by the operating-system sandbox and the tool pipeline, which the model is told plainly.
The limit is about JavaScript error objects from another vm realm; the guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, and a script sees a failed call as an exit status and one JSON error object with a code.

Runs are tracked by the service and can be looked up and listed, a result cut by the bound keeps a spill locator, and a background start with later collection through the job registry is a deliverable (P2, depending on areas A03 and A13). Upstream's own tool already had a background path; this bullet was stale.
A workflow run cannot be continued after a process restart; an open run is closed as interrupted.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-PTC-6: a script's direct effects are not recorded call by call, so re-running it could repeat them. Members and their outcomes are durable (DH-D-PTC-3), so the model can write a new script that skips finished members.

reason: A workflow script cannot start another workflow.
justification: Deliberate boundary stated by DH-ADR-TOOLS-6 (a command started by a nested call receives no call token, which keeps attribution to one outer call) and DH-ADR-PTC-3. The saved half of the upstream bullet is removed by the file argument of DH-D-PTC-4, and a member agent whose preset has the workflow tool can start its own run within the subagent depth limit.

reason: The run record reports token usage per member and summed for the run, and an optional maxTokens budget refuses new members once it is spent without interrupting running ones. This depends on area A12 reporting usage in a child's result, which is listed as an open question.

The service owns every run as an effect on its fiber under the owner agent's lifetime. Unloading the engine or disposing the agent cancels and settles each run; a holder has access to await and cancel, not ownership.

Session deletion now exists in the session store, and removing a workspace can cascade to it on request. The folder is never deleted by the harness, which is a recorded decision and not a missing capability.

Membership is validated once, when the session is attached and its directory resolves to the workspace, and stored as a row. Nothing is re-derived from a path later, so a missing path raises no question the store cannot answer.
Directory status is read from the filesystem when the list is rendered, with a two-second cache, so a change made outside the harness shows without a refresh or restart.
Archive and pin flags are rows that reference the sessions table and are deleted with the session, so a flag for a missing session cannot exist and both directions apply the same existence rule.

Archiving writes a pending mark first, which the step gate already treats as blocked, then asks the activity providers, then confirms or removes the mark. A turn that starts after the mark is blocked and one that started before it is reported.
Adding a workspace can adopt the ungrouped sessions whose recorded directory resolves to it, so re-adding a removed directory brings its sessions back when the user asks for that.

Dropped by DH-ADR-18 (no desktop application, so no desktop build). The marker is a dated TODO to remove legacy version-mode aliases from the script that derives the desktop CI build version; a Go release reads its version from the tag through the Go build information.
A vendor business failure is shown with its numeric code and a generic message; specific wording per code is missing.
justification: Still open (register entry U-K1-12): the list of business codes and the wording for each are not in the pinned upstream source, and the convergence round added nothing for it. The message catalogue is keyed by code, so wording can be added without a code change. What is missing: the vendor's list, and a named step (a scenario or an owner action) that obtains it.

reason: The client infers the platform path separator from the home path the host sent and marks the inference as a TODO to be replaced by a host-stamped field (packages/client/ui-directory-picker-browse/src/client/DirectoryBrowser.tsx:124-128). The Go picker never joins or splits a path in the browser: the host renders every entry's absolute path and the breadcrumb with its own path rules, so no separator is inferred anywhere.

The marker asks for a border and a literal shadow to be replaced by the elevation token. In the Go kit an elevated surface must set border 0 and an elevation token, and the stylesheet check rejects a literal colour in a shadow, so the pattern cannot be written.

A total source budget (maxTotalSourceBytes) is checked against file sizes before any read in one baseline or reconciliation batch, most specific file first, which is the aggregate bound the marker asks for.

The project root is found once per working directory, recorded in the baseline message's source and held in the fold; it is recomputed only when the session's working directory changes, so editing a marker does not reinterpret existing scope keys.
The marker asks how an image tool's result is adapted for a JavaScript program; the JavaScript guest runtime is dropped by DH-ADR-8, so no program result adaptation exists.
The marker concerns return types in the generated TypeScript SDK for programs; the guest runtime and its generated SDK are dropped by DH-ADR-8, and no TypeScript declaration is generated.
The TODO concerns placeholder paths for an installed Windows helper package. No Windows helper is built or packaged, so the layout it waits for is never needed.
The TODO asks for a run-level halt for a hook's continue false. The Go component cancels the open turn through the agent's Cancel with cause extension and records the hook's stopReason.
