Mock functions used by the remote-service test double are replaced by hand-written fakes that implement Go interfaces; no mocking library is needed.

The grep, glob and file-name searches run in process in pure Go behind a Searcher interface, so the release carries no second executable and search uses the same filesystem view and sandbox policy as file reads; the regular-expression dialect becomes Go's.

Kept with xterm.js: the add-on's proposeDimensions() is the only call used (terminal.tsx:191-200) and it reads xterm.js internals, so version 0.11.0 is vendored beside xterm.js 6.0.0 and upgraded together with it; the island clamps the result to the host limits and sends the resize.

The addon is called once, serialize() with default options, to give a newly attached browser tab the current screen. No Go emulator read for the spec exports history, screen, cursor and modes as replayable escape sequences, so the serializer is harness code above the Screen interface, tested by replaying its output into xterm.js.

Upstream runs the xterm.js emulator on the host for three things: replies to terminal queries (terminal-bash), plain-text reads with wrapped rows joined and screen marks for agents, and the state behind the browser snapshot (terminal-controller). The Go harness puts a pure-Go emulator behind its own Screen interface; the module choice is provisional until a conformance test against xterm.js passes.

Kept, not replaced: xterm.js 6.0.0 is the browser terminal widget (packages/client/ui-sidebar-terminal/src/client/terminal.tsx:3, :102-108). DH-ADR-3 allows a JavaScript island for the terminal, so the same package is vendored as its published ES module and stylesheet and wrapped in one custom element inside a same-origin frame; what changes is the packaging (no bundler, no React wrapper) and that the host emulator answers terminal queries.

It packs Node and a package tree into one executable with a virtual filesystem; go build produces one executable per target and the embed package carries assets, so no packer, archive or extraction cache exists.
It supplies a second JavaScript package manager for a generated-project test; a Go product has no npm package managers to be compatible with.

It is used only for parseShell, the grammar of the JavaScript shell that the experimental browser Preview needs because a Web Worker has no processes; a Go host runs a real shell, so no shell grammar is carried, and mvdan.cc/sh/v3 is recorded as the module to use if the owner keeps the Preview under OD-11.

Upstream parses model-written programs only to rewrite them around two limits of node:vm (no top-level await in a script, no redeclaration in a retained scope) and to rewrite ES modules for the browser Web Worker runtime; it performs no safety check. By the owner's decision the Go harness has no embedded interpreter: a script is run by whatever interpreter it names, as an ordinary sandboxed command, and the host never parses or rewrites its text, so no JavaScript parser is a dependency.

The tree walker is used by one file, the port of Node's top-level-await transform for vm scripts. That transform is dropped together with the parser because the Go harness evaluates no JavaScript at all and does not rewrite script text.

Its one runtime job, checking literal defaults against a generated JSON Schema, and its test job, validating generated documents, are done by the same module that derives the schemas, so no separate validator is needed.

Parsing terminal colour sequences in command output is own host code that also replays carriage return, backspace and erase-in-line and strips every other control sequence, because the candidate module also emits links and images from escape sequences.

It is the engine of electron-builder, also imported for its internal ASAR reader, NSIS target and signing helpers; a Go release has one executable per platform in a plain archive, no installer and no application archive to read.

The account page compares and rounds decimal balance strings exactly in the browser. The host renders that page, so the comparison and the round-down-to-two-places formatting are done with math/big.Rat from the standard library.

Upstream's two-way control pipe between the host and the program child process has no counterpart, because no guest runtime is built. Its job, carrying a script's tool calls to the host, is done by a one-request, one-reply channel between the dsh tool command and the host's tool endpoint, on the harness's own newline-delimited JSON-RPC codec, keeping every defensive rule upstream wraps around the library (bounded messages, a method allow-list, a pending call failed once on close, no transport timeouts, a revision check).

Exists only because the upstream host is JavaScript: webworker-runtime bundles this npm copy of node:buffer so that host code can run in a browser Web Worker. A Go program uses []byte from the language, including when compiled to WebAssembly.

Every consumer only needs to be told that a file or one directory level may have changed and then re-reads it; one harness watch service gives that over operating-system notifications with a stat-polling fallback, and the only recursive watch (in-process code reload) is not carried over.

Build-only source of the Chrome DevTools interface that the experimental inspector compiles and serves. Most of what it displays comes from V8 through Node's inspector, which a Go process does not have, and building it needs a JavaScript toolchain that DH-ADR-3 removes.

Upstream installs this Node MCP server beside the harness and starts it with the harness's own Node program. In Go the provider is a launch recipe for an external program the operator installs, with usage statistics always disabled, reached through the harness MCP client.
It joins CSS class names conditionally inside JavaScript component code; a host template writes the class attribute directly with its own conditionals, so no library is involved.

The two-stage command line (launcher options, then the options of the app a profile mounts) is parsed by github.com/spf13/pflag, with github.com/spf13/cobra for the fixed command tree, help and completion; apps declare options through a harness type and receive errors as values, so no library type is part of a component's contract.
Opt-in gzip response compression is kept with the same exclusions and is provided by the gzhttp handler of klauspost/compress; the event stream is never compressed.

Upload of installers and feed files to one vendor's object storage is replaced by GitHub release assets (dsh archives, checksum file, update manifest) published by GoReleaser and the release workflow, as the owner confirmed, keeping upstream's upload rules: verify before upload, manifest last, no blind retry.

No upstream source imports cross-spawn; subagent-oar declares it for the embedded third-party @botiverse/oar library, which starts vendor agent tools itself. In Go those tools are started by the harness process package, whose lookup applies PATHEXT and whose batch-file rule replaces cross-spawn's cmd.exe escaping.

It is declared only by the upstream website package, with an exact version and no import in website source, to pin a dependency of Mermaid for the site's npm bundler; it exists only because of npm resolution and the JavaScript bundler, and the Go site has neither: it vendors Mermaid's prebuilt browser file, which already contains its dependencies.

It is declared only by the upstream website package, with an exact version and no import in website source, to pin a dependency of Mermaid for the site's npm bundler; it exists only because of npm resolution and the JavaScript bundler, and the Go site has neither: it vendors Mermaid's prebuilt browser file, which already contains its dependencies.

Its one use is timeTicks() for the axis of the experimental Timeline schedule (packages/experimental/timeline/src/client/TimeScale.ts:48). The host renders that view, so round calendar marks are computed in Go with the time package and a fixed ladder of steps in the viewer's time zone.

It is declared only by the upstream website package, with an exact version and no import in website source, to pin a dependency of Mermaid for the site's npm bundler; it exists only because of npm resolution and the JavaScript bundler, and the Go site has neither: it vendors Mermaid's prebuilt browser file, which already contains its dependencies.

It is declared only by the upstream website package, with an exact version and no import in website source, as a pin for the site's npm bundler; it exists only because of npm resolution and the JavaScript bundler, and the Go site has neither, since it vendors Mermaid's prebuilt browser file.

Line diffs with three context lines are computed on the host by one package over go-udiff with a deterministic size bound; the browser-side diff disappears because the host renders the UI, and Git patch text is not parsed at all, because the code-host UI shows status only (DH-ADR-38).

Upstream sanitises only the HTML file preview in the browser; the Go host filters that document with an allow-list policy and serves it sandboxed with a policy header, and uses the same module as a last-step gate on every fragment built from untrusted text.

Electron supplied the window, native menus and dialogs, tray, single-instance lock, deep link and a bundled browser engine and Node runtime; the owner decided there is no desktop application, so the dsh command opens the web UI in the system browser and each of the 26 Electron features has a web or command-line equivalent or a recorded drop, the embedded browser pane and sign-in pages among the drops.

With no desktop application there is no bundle and no installer; what remains is signing and notarising one dsh binary per platform and archiving it, which GoReleaser does with the operating systems' signing tools, and no packaging engine is configured through hooks.

Feed check, download and installer hand-off are replaced by own code for the one dsh binary: a signed manifest verified against a compiled-in key, an optional check (off until turned on) that only shows a notice in the web UI, and the dsh update command that swaps the file; there is no desktop application to update.

Upstream source imports esbuild once, for a type in the hot-reload error handler; otherwise it is a dependency of the script runner, the front-end bundler and the test runner, and it never runs in a packaged product. Go source is compiled ahead of time by the Go toolchain, so nothing is transpiled or bundled.
Duplicate-branch and identical-expression rules are replaced by staticcheck checks of the same kind.

It exists only because of JavaScript module loading: the experimental Web Worker runtime rewrites ES modules to CommonJS and needs scope analysis to tell an imported name from a local one. A Go program has no modules to rewrite, whether that runtime is dropped or built for WebAssembly.

It is the node-field table that eslint-scope needs to walk a JavaScript syntax tree in the same ES-module-to-CommonJS transform, so it exists only because of JavaScript module loading and has no counterpart in Go.
Its one job, framing a server-sent-events response body into events for the DeepSeek adapter, is done by a small reader written in the harness on bufio and shared by every provider driver.

ExcelJS parses .xlsx workbooks in a browser Worker for the spreadsheet preview. Under DH-ADR-3 the host reads the workbook with the excelize module and renders an HTML table, so no workbook parser runs in the browser.

Four product packages and one test-support package use execa to run git, pnpm, gh and glab once and read the result, outside the subprocess service. Each option they rely on maps to os/exec or to a rule of the harness process package; a Run helper on that package replaces the library, and Windows batch files such as pnpm.cmd get an explicit safety rule instead of implicit handling.
It exists only for upstream's build process: its three call sites unpack the downloaded Node runtime, a Python wheel and the Electron runtime while packaging, and the Go release bundles none of them.
Property-based tests in five upstream suites are replaced by native fuzz targets with committed seed and crasher inputs.

The client uses it for three small reads of .xlsx parts: theme colours, relationship files and a scan for content the preview cannot draw. In the host these are token walks with encoding/xml from the standard library, which matches names by namespace and resolves no external entities.

Streaming a session export as a ZIP and reading an uploaded ZIP with per-entry limits are both covered by the standard library's archive/zip, whose pull-based reader also removes three limits upstream documents for chat import.

The library supplies one scoring function inside upstream's own 300-line search module; the Go port keeps the tiers and folding rules and replaces the call with a scorer written for the word-start rule, using golang.org/x/text for Unicode normalisation.

got is used only to make the OTLP telemetry request and its retry waits cancellable; a Go request takes a context that cancels all of that, and the client comes from the same factory so telemetry is proxied like everything else.

npm repository shorthands and the list of hosts pnpm treats specially disappear with npm packages; the remaining need, deriving host, project, clone address and web page from one full repository address, is a few string rules over net/url.
It is a development command that previews upstream's separately built static client bundle; the Go UI is rendered by the host, so there is no standalone bundle to preview (upstream build process).

It exists only because React detects change by JavaScript object identity, so client stores need a helper that produces a new immutable object per update; Go projections produce new values and the event feed says what changed.
Bind-address parsing and the wildcard and loopback checks move to net/netip, the same parser family the Go network stack binds with, which removes the upstream text-rewrite workaround.
It is the base class of a custom reporter that prints uncovered locations; go tool cover reports uncovered lines from the profile.

The second YAML parser, left in release tooling, test support and build scripts after the loader moved to yaml, has no Go counterpart: hand-written YAML is read by the one harness YAML package and machine-written files such as the update feed become JSON read by encoding/json.
Cross-file clone detection is not carried over; the static-check decision records that it is left out and can be added later as one more tool.
The simulated browser document for client component tests is replaced by rendering the Go handler and parsing its HTML, because the UI is rendered by the host.

Formulas are typeset on the host to MathML through one adapter whose first, provisional implementation is the treeblood module with a mandatory output filter; a KaTeX island is the named fallback if the coverage gate fails.

Every operating-system function upstream reaches through this foreign-function addon (write-through rename, kernel lock, permission-preserving replace, token and job process start, access-control edits, process table, process replacement) is called from Go through typed wrappers in golang.org/x/sys or the standard library, with a short list of functions bound by hand and no cgo.
The git hook manager is replaced by one checked-in pre-commit script enabled through git's core.hooksPath setting; CI remains the authority.

Kept by the owner's decision: the editor core gives the composer atomic reference chips inside plain text. The same library is vendored as its published, unpatched ES module files, embedded in the binary and loaded by one composer island through an import map; menu candidates, reference resolution, drafts and attachments move to the host.
It hashes CSS-module class names and rewrites url() references inside bundled JavaScript client packages; the Go UI serves plain embedded stylesheets and has no client bundles.
Parsing Markdown text into a tree, in the client and in root documentation scripts, is done on the host by goldmark's parser; the tree never leaves the host.
Tables, task lists, strike-through, bare links and footnotes come from goldmark's shipped extensions, with an own strike-through rule that requires two tildes.
Turning math tokens into tree nodes is the same passthrough extension's job in goldmark, which yields nodes holding the raw TeX for the typesetting adapter.

Kept for rendering diagrams in the documentation website, which the owner keeps: its published browser file (dist/mermaid.min.js of 11.17.2, MIT) is vendored into the site sources and served only by the site, never embedded in dsh. Its second upstream use, the Node gate that parses every Mermaid block, is not kept because the Go build has no Node.
Upstream imports the core emphasis construct to build its CJK-friendly bold rule; the Go renderer implements that rule as an own goldmark delimiter extension.
The GFM syntax half of the same feature set is goldmark's GFM extensions on the host; the bare-URL rule is one configured pattern, not a patched tokenizer.
Recognising dollar-delimited math in settled messages is done by the goldmark passthrough extension, configured with the dollar and backslash delimiter pairs and left out of the streaming grammar.
Its one use is whitespace handling inside upstream's tokenizer for backslash math delimiters; the passthrough extension takes those delimiters as configuration, so no tokenizer is written.
Character classification for the CJK bold rule and the math delimiters is done with Go's unicode package inside the own goldmark extensions.
Deciding whether a character is whitespace or punctuation for emphasis flanking is done with Go's unicode package in the own CJK delimiter extension.
Its one use, decoding a link destination so that a Windows path keeps its backslashes, becomes part of the own link renderer that recognises local-path destinations.
Normalising a link or image address before the scheme check is done with Go's net/url in the own link and image renderers, which apply an allow-list of schemes and fail closed on a parse error.
It is a table of numeric character codes and token names that JavaScript micromark extensions are written against; Go extension code uses rune literals and goldmark's own node kinds.
It contains only TypeScript type declarations for writing micromark extensions and has no runtime content; Go types come from the goldmark module.

Extension-to-type and type-to-extension lookups come from one media-type table compiled into the harness, because the standard mime lookup reads the Windows registry or system files and is not deterministic.
The Content-Type of a served workspace file comes from the same single media-type table as every other lookup, so the second upstream library has no counterpart.

The library's only use is the text search of the plugin market index. The owner decided that plugins are installed from local directories and that the harness downloads and discovers none (DH-ADR-13), and the boot area records that the plugin market is not built (DH-ADR-BOOT-11), so there is nothing to search and no index is built.
Its single use, choosing gzip or identity from Accept-Encoding, is done inside the chosen compression handler, so no separate negotiation library or parser is needed.

It exists only to hand upstream's JavaScript the private module-loader modules of Node, for code hot reload, profile package resolution and manifest cache clearing; a Go binary has no run-time module loader, first-party code is linked in and plugins are separate processes, so there is nothing to reach.

node-pty is used in one place, spawnTerminal in subprocess-local, for spawn, pid, onData, onExit, write, resize, pause, resume and kill. The Go harness allocates POSIX pseudo-terminals and Windows ConPTY itself on golang.org/x/sys, with no cgo and no helper executable, and keeps the master descriptor and the process handle that node-pty hides.

In product source node:assert guards internal invariants in hmr, timeline and the computer-use clients; every other import is a test, fixture or script. In Go a broken invariant is a returned error or a contained panic, and tests use the testing package.

AsyncLocalStorage carries the initiating agent in core/agent, the current query activity in the SDK server, a re-entrancy flag in hmr, the current evaluation inside the Node program runner, and a flag for an HTTP client workaround. Each use maps to a context.Context value or an explicit parameter, or exists only inside Node-specific code; none needs storage attached to a goroutine.

Buffer is used (mostly as a global) to hold and join bytes, count the bytes of a string, and encode utf8, base64, base64url, hex and utf16le; isUtf8 and the platform size constants appear in three files. Go uses []byte, len, encoding/base64, encoding/hex, unicode/utf8 and unicode/utf16, and every size limit names its unit.

125 non-test files import it: 6 in the subprocess provider, 20 product files that start programs outside the provider, 1 worker emulation, 3 test-infrastructure files and 95 build and release scripts; only spawn, spawnSync, execFile and execFileSync are used, never a shell string. Go uses os/exec inside one harness process package with operating-system owners for process trees.

The uses are random identifiers and secrets, SHA-256 content digests and derived names, one HMAC-SHA-256 cookie signature, constant-time comparison and a few algorithms fixed by outside formats; each maps to the Go standard library (crypto/rand, crypto/sha256, crypto/hmac, crypto/subtle), under one algorithm policy that an import check enforces. Upstream uses no cipher, key derivation or public-key signature, and neither does the Go design.

Exists only because of Node: the single use (experimental/liveshare relay-h2-idle.ts:85) listens to the channel on which Node's undici HTTP client announces sockets, to swallow an idle-timeout error that client reports on a socket no request owns. Go's net/http returns connection errors to the request's caller.

The only imports are a failing stub of the Node module for the browser-worker preview and its test; no product code resolves names itself, and Go dials use the system resolver implicitly (Node built-in shim).

Exists only because of Node: the single use (ptc-runtime-node scoped-repl-evaluator.ts:44) catches errors thrown later by callbacks of a model-written JavaScript program inside the Node runner process. The Go host never evaluates JavaScript in process; a program runner is a separate process and reports a failed evaluation over its connection.

Product source uses EventEmitter in two classes, once() to wait for an event in two places and addAbortListener in six. Between components the Go design uses cordis typed events; inside a component a channel closed once plus an error accessor, select on ctx.Done(), and context.AfterFunc.

Ordinary file work maps onto the Go standard library; the operations where Go and Node differ or upstream has several implementations (atomic replacement, create-if-absent, locks, file identity, containment, owner-only creation) are owned by one harness package that uses golang.org/x/sys for the missing system calls.
Listeners, route handlers, upgrades and header validation move to net/http with explicit time and size limits and owner-tracked connections, which Go does not provide by default.
The optional TLS listener uses crypto/tls with net/http; loading the certificate pair already fails on empty or mismatched files, so start-up fails closed without extra checks.

Its one use connects the experimental inspector to the host's own V8 debugger. A Go process has no V8 debugger and the DevTools interface is already dropped, so the surviving need, looking inside a running host, is met by Go's profiler and execution tracer behind owner-only loopback endpoints.

Of fifty source files, twenty-one are build scripts, fourteen do plugin and module loading that compiled-in components and plugin processes remove, and four are guest-runtime internals. Three needs survive and use the standard library: finding shipped assets (embed), finding external programs (exec.LookPath) and reading the product version (build information).
Unix sockets, half-close, IP-literal checks and inherited channels map to net, net/netip and os; Windows named pipes and Windows handle inheritance are stated gaps handed to the owning areas.

Home and temporary directories, platform, processor count and host name come from the os and runtime packages; operating-system version and memory, used only for diagnostics, come from golang.org/x/sys in build-tagged files.

Path building maps onto path/filepath for disk paths and path for forward-slash paths, with conversion at the boundary; containment tests done upstream by string comparison go through one function or a directory-rooted handle.

Three production files use the monotonic clock only to decide when to yield the single thread, which Go does not need; benchmarks and scripts use it to measure elapsed time, which time.Now with time.Since and testing.B provide. Event-loop delay measurement has no counterpart because there is no event loop.

The files that import node:process by name are governance and release scripts; the same object is a global used for arguments, environment, platform, exit and standard streams. Go reads these through os, runtime and os/signal, with process starting specified in libs/node-process-builtins.md.

The three non-test imports are release scripts that ask the operator to confirm a publish with readline.question. A Go release tool reads one line from os.Stdin with bufio and refuses when standard input is not a terminal.

ptc-runtime-node uses repl.start to evaluate model-written JavaScript while keeping variables between programs, inside a runner process. The Go host cannot evaluate JavaScript in process; under DH-ADR-4 the interpreter is a long-lived child process with piped input and output, which the process package provides. Which interpreter runs in it is left to the tool-runtime area.
isSea() tells packaged execution from script execution at four call sites; a Go program has one form, and the location of the running program comes from os.Executable through one function.

Three upstream packages use Node's built-in synchronous SQLite binding for an optional session store, the FTS5 session search and a key-value backend; they need WAL with full sync, a busy timeout, savepoints, triggers, STRICT tables, identity pragmas and FTS5 with unicode61 and highlight(). The Go store uses modernc.org/sqlite through database/sql behind one driver package, provisional until the measurements in the spec are taken.

Product source uses Node streams as the type of process and socket ends, as in-process pipes (PassThrough), for drain-based backpressure, for pipeline and finished, and to bridge Node and web streams. Go has one stream model: io.Reader and io.Writer with blocking writes, io.Pipe and io.Copy, plus stated bounds and close-on-cancel rules.

StringDecoder is imported by the SDK line transport and one release script, to decode UTF-8 that arrives split across chunks; the same need is met elsewhere by TextDecoder in streaming mode, setEncoding and hand-written trimming. The Go design splits protocols on bytes and decodes whole frames, and uses one incremental decoder where text must be shown before a frame ends.

Every import is the promise form: cancellable sleeps become a context-aware sleep helper or the cordis timer service, deadlines become context deadlines with a typed cause, and the yields to the single JavaScript thread have no counterpart because goroutines are pre-empted. Tests drive all of it in virtual time with testing/synctest.
Its only product use is TLS with a pre-shared key for forwarded SSH streams; Go's crypto/tls has no pre-shared-key suites, so the same guarantee is given by TLS 1.3 with pinned one-time certificates.

Exists only because of Node: the two importing files are stand-ins in webworker-runtime that emulate Node built-ins inside a browser Web Worker (isatty always false). No upstream product code calls the real module, so there is nothing to carry into Go.
Nearly every use locates a JavaScript module by URL, which Go does not need; the few real conversions between paths and file URLs for a named target system become a small own helper beside net/url.

Outside tests the imports are parseArgs (44 files, all scripts), promisify (25, mostly scripts), isDeepStrictEqual (18 product files), inspect (12), and single uses of parseEnv, getSystemErrorName and types. Go uses a per-type equality rule, fmt and log/slog for diagnostics, and syscall.Errno; promisify and the type predicates have no counterpart because Go calls block and values are typed.

Ten source files use it: seven evaluate model-written programs and workflow scripts in the Node child process, one evaluates model-written plugins inside the host, one compiles a config expression and one is a stub. By the owner's decision there is no embedded interpreter: a model-written program becomes an ordinary script, run as a sandboxed command, that calls tools through the dsh tool command, and every such call goes through the guarded tool pipeline and is logged. Model-written plugins become plugin processes; cross-realm test helpers have no counterpart because Go has one set of types per process.

Worker threads are used for four reasons: keeping slow work off Node's single event loop, bounding memory with a forced stop, isolating third-party code from the ambient environment, and carrying module-loader state. The first maps to goroutines with a context and a bound, the second and third to child processes because a goroutine cannot be killed, and the fourth disappears with the module loader.

gzip and DEFLATE come from the standard library; Zstandard, which Go 1.27.4 does not offer as a public package, is no longer the live session format and remains only as an optional stored-payload codec through klauspost/compress, while exports use gzip.

Handing the entry URL to the default browser is done by starting the operating system's launcher directly with a scrubbed environment through os/exec, replacing the library and the extra Node process upstream wraps it in.
The JavaScript linter is replaced by gofmt, go vet and staticcheck.
The type-aware rule backend for the JavaScript linter is replaced by go vet and staticcheck, which always analyse type-checked code.

Bounded fan-out is an errgroup with SetLimit; the two session-store limiters disappear because listing becomes a database query, and the GitLab pool keeps the idiom with cancellation on first failure.

PapaParse splits CSV and TSV text into literal string fields for the spreadsheet preview, and rewrites a file list in one build script. The host does the same with encoding/csv from the standard library, with small harness code to keep blank lines and to reject invalid UTF-16.

PDF.js draws PDF pages with selectable text in the browser, parsing in a Worker. The Go design keeps it: the prebuilt pdf.js files are vendored at a pinned version, embedded in the binary and loaded by one small JavaScript island, with the same hardened options and no network fetch.

Glob matching for watcher ignore lists, review-layer lists and sidebar address routing is done by github.com/bmatcuk/doublestar/v4 behind one helper with a single documented dialect; the call sites that exist only for the browser Preview image and npm packaging do not carry over.

Playwright is upstream's test-only driver for 249 browser test files. With server-rendered HTML most of those checks need no browser; the remaining real-browser scenarios are Go tests on chromedp, the module the product already uses, so the test lane needs no Node, no driver download and no browser cache. Firefox and Safari runs use a second back end of the same scenario helper that speaks W3C WebDriver with net/http (DH-ADR-PLAYWRIGHT-2), because the product's only UI client is the user's own browser (DH-ADR-18).
The npm package manager is replaced by Go modules with go.sum verification and a go.work workspace.
It lints the entry points of published npm packages; the Go product publishes a binary and a module tag, not npm packages.
The separate runtime distribution and its exact version pin are folded into one distribution whose platform wheels contain the Go binary, with a pure fallback wheel for platforms that have none.

hatchling and its custom hook build and tag the wheels; in the Go design a Go tool in the release job writes every wheel from the cross-compiled binaries and keeps the hook's payload, tag and size checks.
Pillow is a test-only dependency that draws and inspects images for the Office render check; Office operations leave the Python package, so nothing in it needs an image library.

pydantic validates hand-mirrored wire models at the boundary; the Go design generates frozen standard-library dataclasses with decode and encode functions from the SDK protocol schema, which keeps the boundary check and removes the dependency and the second copy of the types.

pytest runs the client's tests; the Go design's Python tests use the standard-library unittest runner so that the package needs no third-party Python package at test time, and product behaviour that upstream tests through Python is tested in Go.

The component framework that redraws a browser-side mirror of host state is replaced by HTML fragments rendered on the host and swapped by id; each job it did (incremental updates while streaming, submission feedback, kept view state, routing) is placed on the host, in the browser's own features or in a small own script.
Its job, mounting the application tree and taking over the boot DOM, has no counterpart when every page is a complete HTTP response rendered by the host and updated by fragment swaps.

Exists only because the upstream host is JavaScript: webworker-runtime bundles this npm copy of node:stream (implemented/stream.ts:9) so that host code can run in a browser Web Worker. Go's io package is part of the standard library on every target.

Interpreting the exports and imports maps of an npm package exists only because plugins are loaded as Node modules; a plugin process is started from a manifest that names its executable and assets by relative path, opened through os.Root so that no path can leave the plugin directory.

Upstream asks the rrule library only to list candidate wall times of one period and does validation, limits, time-zone mapping and end conditions in 689 lines of its own code; the Go design writes that candidate listing itself as part of one bounded evaluator on the time package, so no recurrence module is needed.
The test-only certificate fixture for the HTTPS listener is generated with crypto/x509 and crypto/ecdsa in a Go test helper; the product still never generates certificates.

Version validation, ordering, prerelease detection and range checks for plugin compatibility, plugin updates, the model-listing gate and the desktop update use github.com/Masterminds/semver/v3 behind one helper that accepts only strict spelling and always counts prereleases in ranges; the npm peer-range arithmetic and Node and pnpm version checks are not carried over.
Serving a fixed directory of files to the owner is done by net/http file serving over an embedded io/fs file system, with a thin wrapper for method, header and directory rules.

sharp binds the native libvips library to check, orient, scale and re-encode attached images. The Go attachment store does the same with the standard library image packages and golang.org/x/image, with limits read from the header before any pixel is allocated; transparent images are stored as PNG because the chosen packages have no lossy WebP encoder.

forge-session uses parse to read shell commands the agent already ran and quote to build a lookup command a shell later executes. Go reads the command with the mvdan.cc/sh/v3 syntax parser, which classifies literal and dynamic words exactly, and quotes with an own single-quote function, as upstream's dependency audit recommended for this safety boundary.

The binding carries ONNX Runtime and runs SenseVoice speech recognition in a managed Node subprocess. The Go provider runs a recognition program the operator installed (the documented example is the prebuilt sherpa-onnx runtime) as a supervised child process, so the host links no inference library; the harness downloads neither a runtime nor a model (DH-ADR-XCUA-4).
Code is tokenised on the host by chroma and written as class-named spans that the theme style sheet colours, so light and dark need no re-rendering and no highlighter runs in the browser.

Upstream uses 34 brand marks from the collection to label links to well-known hosts; the Go host keeps the fixed host table as a Go value and embeds the copied marks as one SVG sprite, with no module and no network fetch.
It reads pyproject.toml files inside the third-party notices generator; the Go notice is generated from the module graph by go-licenses.
It parses licence expressions inside the third-party notices generator; go-licenses classifies module licences instead.

Exists only because the upstream host is JavaScript: webworker-runtime bundles this npm copy of node:string_decoder (implemented/string_decoder.ts:4) so that host code can run in a browser Web Worker. The Go decoding rule is specified under node:string_decoder and needs no polyfill.

Used once, for the default colour level of the vendored console log exporter (vendor/logger-console/src/index.ts:23), which is not ported. What remains is a rule for any Go code that writes colour: only to a terminal, only when NO_COLOR is unset and TERM is not dumb, never to a protocol stream.

Reading a gzip tarball from the network with strict path, type, duplicate and size checks, and writing reproducible tarballs, are done with the standard library's archive/tar and compress/gzip plus the harness's own entry checks.
It purges one URL from the vendor's content-delivery network after a fixed installer object was replaced in place; with release assets nothing is replaced in place, so there is nothing to purge.
The per-package JavaScript bundler is replaced by go build, which links one binary from the module.
The TypeScript runner used for every repository script and for launching the CLI from source is replaced by go run and go generate.

turndown converts fetched HTML to Markdown for the web_fetch tool. The Go tool uses the html-to-markdown module on the golang.org/x/net/html parser with the same fixed style, plus harness rules that remove hidden content and neutralise table spans.

Compilation and type checking are done by the Go toolchain; the compiler-API uses (type-graph generation, persistence fingerprints, catalogs) are replaced by reflection at startup and the standard library's Go parser and type checker.
It is the real language server driven by the keyless language-server test; the Go scenario drives gopls as its real server.

undici exists to control Node's global dispatcher so that fetch honours the proxy policy; in Go every outbound client is built by one factory on net/http with the policy applied per request, and bypass matching uses the x/net httpproxy package.
It is the JavaScript hook that binds a store snapshot to a React component in one file of ui-renderer; with no React components and no client stores there is nothing to bind.
The front-end bundler and development server (three major versions installed at once) is replaced by static assets embedded in the binary with the embed package.
It maps TypeScript workspace imports to source files for the JavaScript test runner; Go resolves imports from the module graph, so the problem does not exist.

It is the static site generator that publishes docs/ as a website; the owner keeps the website, and the Go design generates it from the same Markdown with Hugo, a generator written in Go that is pinned as a docs-only tool and never linked into dsh.

It renders Mermaid diagrams inside the documentation website; in the Go site one code-block template turns a mermaid fence into an element that the vendored Mermaid script draws in the reader's browser.
The JavaScript test runner behind every upstream lane is replaced by go test and the standard testing package.
It is the component framework of the documentation website theme; the Go site's layouts are Go templates in the generator's own template language, so no component framework is needed.

No upstream source imports which; it is declared for the embedded @botiverse/oar library and is a dependency of cross-spawn. Upstream's own equivalent is resolveExecutable in subprocess-local. Go needs a short own lookup because exec.LookPath reads the harness's PATH, not the scrubbed and overridden PATH the child will receive.

The multiplexed stream socket is dropped in favour of server-sent events; the one remaining WebSocket (the terminal) and any outbound WebSocket use github.com/coder/websocket behind a harness wrapper.

SheetJS parses legacy binary .xls workbooks in the browser. The Go design has no BIFF parser: a .xls file is converted to .xlsx by the Office engine and then previewed through the same host reader, which needs the engine to be installed.

The library that parses cordis.yml, carries the !!js tag and edits files while keeping comments is replaced by go.yaml.in/yaml/v4 behind one harness package that fixes the dialect, keeps every comment on write-back and verifies each rendered file before it replaces the original.

Wire messages, persisted records, projection state and tool input are Go types; their JSON Schema, validation and strict decoding come from one harness schema package over github.com/google/jsonschema-go instead of hand-written zod schemas.

The store engine holds client copies of state and view preferences in localStorage; application state now stays on the host and view state goes to the URL, host preferences, the DOM or a small per-tab script store.
Kept as the notify event driver.StartFailed with the label, session id and error, so a consumer that buffers work for a configured identity can reject it instead of waiting.

The live event becomes the typed notify key agentpreset.Selected, a scoped event dispatched with the session's scope key after the durable agent-preset/selected event commits. Its payload is the session id, the preset, the digest and the cause; consumers drop state derived from the session's composition.
Kept as the notify event agent.StreamFrame: Start, Chunk with a dense index and exactly one End sent after the durable record is committed; frames stay live-only.
Kept as the ordered event agent.Created: listeners run one at a time, the first error fails creation and rolls it back, and no turn starts before the dispatch has settled.
Kept as the notify event agent.Disposed, sent at teardown step T7 after the final flush and after the registry entry is removed, and only when Created had begun.
Kept as the notify event agent.Failed, which reports a step or turn failure also when it has no position in the log, for example a failed append.
Kept as the notify event agent.InboxClaimed, one per message, sent after the claim splice is committed in the turn-opening batch.
Kept as the notify event agent.InboxDiscarded, which now also carries the cancel cause recorded on the discard splice.
Kept as the notify event agent.InboxInserted with the message and the seq of its splice, queued under the inbox mutex and delivered outside it.
Kept as the around event agent.PreStep with a request type and the closed decisions Enter and Reject; Reject now carries a reason that is logged on turn/end.
Upstream marks the waterfall deprecated and forbids new listeners. It is the one place a request could differ from the log, so it is not built; each of its four uses has a named replacement.
Kept as the around event agent.AttemptFailed with the closed decisions GiveUp and Retry; the driver, not the listener, waits the back-off and caps attempts per step.
Kept as the notify event agent.StatusChanged with the two values idle and running; a separate lifecycle state says whether the agent accepts input.

Kept as the around event agent.TurnStopping behind a merging helper, with the closed decisions AllowStop and KeepOpen; a listener can only keep the turn open, so listener order cannot change the outcome.

No Go event carries list activity to a browser. The hub's shell source re-renders the affected row and its order when area A06 announces a change of the list summary, and sends it as a state replacement.

The shell source re-renders the session row for each reader when an agent is created or a workspace membership changes; the row is rendered through the access filter, so no summary payload is forwarded.
A failure outside a durable turn position becomes a notice event on the stream, raised from area A02's agent.Failed; it is declared lossy, and a failure that matters is in the session log.
The shell source replaces the affected region when an agent is disposed or a session is removed; a tab that connects later gets the current list as its baseline.
The running mark of a session row is a state region replaced when area A02 raises agent.StatusChanged; the status is in every baseline, so a missed change cannot leave it wrong.

Replaced by the typed notify event loader.Reloaded, raised after every settled reconciliation whatever caused it. Unlike upstream's event it carries the ids created, updated, restarted and removed and the issues found, so listeners need not re-read the tree to learn what changed.
No waterfall event is dispatched: the approval service asks the interaction registry, which delivers the item to the one answerer bound to the agent, so listener order cannot decide who answers.
Replaced by the notify-form key authz.Settled carrying the record key and the outcome, sent after the key is released.
Replaced by the notify-form key command.Changed carrying the scope, sent after a registration or removal commits.

Replaced by the typed around key compact.SummaryFailed with the closed results GiveUp and Repaired; the image-offload component is its first listener and must record a durable change before asking for another request.

The waterfall let a plugin refuse or hold authenticated requests before the body was read; upstream's desktop used it to lock new work during an approved installation. There is no desktop installer, and area A18's admission pipeline deliberately has no middleware seat, so no Go event replaces it.

The event is emitted inside upstream's browser application when its gateway connects. The Go UI has no client runtime; a reconnecting tab resumes the event stream by sequence number or receives a reset from the host.
The typed notify key plugin.StateChanged carries a value copy of the plugin's descriptor when its status becomes running; listeners cannot hold up the supervisor, which is why emit becomes notify.

The same key, plugin.StateChanged, carries the descriptor with a stopped status (closed, disabled, failed) or announces its removal; a durable plugin-host/detached event records it for an attached plugin.

The event asks a browser page to answer an inspect query from client-side providers; every Go inspect provider lives in the host and is called directly, and there is no client plugin runtime to describe.
The event tells pages that a client inspect query settled; with no page-side providers there is no cross-page query to settle.

No event of this area is needed: a request to attach a plugin is a pending consent item in area A17's interaction registry, delivered by the registry to the bound answerer with the inspection report as its display.
The interaction registry's own settlement notice tells every view that the consent item is no longer answerable; this area adds no event of its own.
Replaced by the notify-form key secret.RecordChanged carrying the record key and the operation; a deletion also fires the revocation signal of every lease on that record.
Replaced by the notify-form key secret.ReferenceChanged carrying the reference name and whether the change was local or made by another process.
No event is needed: a model request on the account route without a sign-in settles as an attempt record with the code llm/sign-in-required, which the user interface already renders.
Replaced by the notify-form key account.Expired, sent after a 401 from the vendor cleared the local grant.
Replaced by the notify-form key account.SignedOut, sent after the local grant was removed and before its leases are closed.

Replaced by the typed notify event kv.Changed, raised after commit in commit order per namespace with namespace, key, operation, revision and origin; it also reports writes made by another process, which upstream's in-process event cannot.

The event existed so that an uploader could send the session when feedback was committed; recording now sends nothing and an upload starts only from the user's confirmed preview, so no hook is needed.

Replaced by the typed live key forge.ProvidersChanged in the notify form, carrying the family whose provider registered or withdrew; a failing listener is logged and contained, as upstream's parallel mode did.

The event announces a review write the code host accepted through the forge service. The Go forge seam is read-only: no review write, pending review or viewed mark exists, so there is nothing to announce.
Folded into the one around event fs.Intent, whose request names the operation (delete) and whose result is a closed decision where the strictest answer wins.
Folded into the one around event fs.Intent, whose request names the operation (edit, patch or move-source) and whose result is a closed decision where the strictest answer wins.
Kept as the notify event fs.Observed, which contains listener failures, and additionally written as a log-only durable fs/observed session event so that observations survive a restart.
Folded into the one around event fs.Intent, whose request names the operation (write or move-destination) and whose result is a closed decision where the strictest answer wins.
Replaced one for one by the typed notify key goal.ActivationChanged with the session, the goal reference and whether it is armed; the goal panel's live fragment consumes it.
Replaced one for one by the typed notify key goal.Changed, dispatched through the agent's scope after the goal/change append, carrying the operation, the reference and the view.

The event reports a watched file that is neither a module nor a configuration file. The Go host watches layer files only and reloads no code, so no general file-change event exists; template and asset edits during UI development are a build concern.
The event announces finished module replacements. No module is replaced in Go; the one notification after a reload settles is loader.Reloaded, which also covers an entry restarted on request.
A cordis internal event used to see a fiber's config candidate. The Go port offers the owned OnConfig hook for the same purpose; it is not an agent event.

A cordis internal hook that sees every dispatch. Its one upstream user vetoes an event by throwing from an observer; in Go an event that may be vetoed has a closed decision type, so the hook is not provided.
A cordis internal event that upstream components use to learn that a fiber is leaving. In Go each fiber has a cancellation context, and the remaining uses get an owned subscription.
A cordis internal event about service availability. The Go port already has the subscription and gives it a form owned by the subscribing fiber.

A cordis internal event about fiber state changes. The Go port already has the subscription and gives it an owned form; the agent registry's own use disappears because the initiator is a context value.

Replaced by the ordered key llm.PrepareHeaders, which applies to every route instead of one adapter; credential headers and the client identity are applied afterwards and an error fails the call before any I/O.
Replaced by the payload-free notify key llm.RoutesChanged; a failing observer is contained and cannot veto a registry change, as upstream.
Replaced by the notify key llm.ModelsChanged carrying the route id, which the model picker fragment reloads on.

Replaced by the around key llm.StreamAround, whose listeners may proceed or substitute the stream with the substitution recorded in the attempt record; rerouting a request to another provider is no longer possible.
A loader event that tells a component one of its live config fields changed. In Go a component accepts an in-place update through its update hook.
The event is emitted and consumed inside upstream's browser application when the user changes language. The Go host renders HTML in the chosen language, so there is no client event.
The typed notify key mcp.StatusChanged carries the server name and its status after the status cell changes; listeners cannot hold up lifecycle work, which is why the parallel form becomes notify.
Replaced by the notify-form key preset.CatalogChanged, sent when the live preset table or the reserved auto entry changes.

Kept as the typed notify event plugins.Changed with the entry ids whose listing changed. It is derived from loader.Reloaded, so a change made by a hand edit of a layer file is announced too, which upstream's event does not do.
The event streams the output of a pnpm run. No package manager or other child process runs during a management operation; an operation's diagnostic is in its result.

The event reports the phases of an installation across registries (installing, cancelling, applying). Adding a plugin is one validated write followed by reconciliation, with no phases and nothing to cancel.

Kept as the typed notify event plugins.Operation with an operation id, action, target id, phase and outcome, raised on the manager's own goroutine after the caller has its result so that a listener never delays an operation. It carries no directory path, grant list or error text.
The event reports the steps of a bundle update (checking, removing, installing, restoring). DH-ADR-13 excludes updates: an operator replaces the directory.
The event announces a change to the configured market index sources. There are no index sources.
Replaced by the typed notify key schedule.Changed, which carries the changed ids and whether the change was made by this process or seen from another through the revision counter.

Upstream lets the embedding activate a target session through a waterfall. Go uses a service interface, schedule.Activator, provided by the carrier that keeps sessions loaded, with a fallback in the schedule component; a service cannot be shadowed by listener order and returns a release function.

The redaction waterfall is replaced by upload.Redactors, an ordered registry of functions that may change or withhold a record; unlike a waterfall listener, a redactor cannot skip the others, and the built-in baseline always runs last.
Replaced by the typed scoped event session.Created in the ordered dispatch form: the first listener error stops the dispatch and vetoes publication, as a synchronous throw does upstream.
Replaced by the typed scoped event session.Closed in the notify form, sent after the deliverer has delivered every event and carrying the id, header, final length and cause as values.

Replaced by the typed scoped event session.Committed in the notify form. One deliverer goroutine per session reads forward from a cursor and notifies in commit order outside the append lock, so a listener cannot fail or block an append.
No Go event: storage is no longer a set of listeners, so the durability barrier is the method Session.Flush, which calls the session's storage writer directly and returns the new durable offset.
Replaced by the typed notify event settings.FormChanged with the entry id and the entry revision of the boot area, raised when the loader announces a settled reload and a form's revision differs.
Replaced by the typed notify key skill.Changed carrying the scope and a revision, sent after a provider invalidation or registration commits; listener failures are contained.
The event is emitted by upstream's client UI renderer when a slot registration changes and has no consumer. The Go UI composes templates on the host and has no client slot registry.

Replaced by the typed notify event subagent.Settled, dispatched through the same scope after cleanup and after the settled record is in the root's log; it carries the stop reason, the cleanup state and the record's sequence number.

Folded with provider-removed into one typed notify event, subagent.ProvidersChanged, with a name and an added flag. The delegation tool no longer listens: tool visibility is resolved per step from the registry.

The 22 skills are working instructions for contributors to the upstream repository, not part of the product; the test-isolation rules worth keeping are restated in the test decisions and the rest is not copied.

The 35 workflows are replaced by harness jobs added to this repository's ci.yml and release.yml plus one credentialed scenario workflow; weighted approval, issue lifecycle and stale-pull-request automation are dropped as repository governance, not product.

The one launcher is kept as cmd/dsh plus internal/cli: two-stage parsing, profile launch, bounded shutdown and a start-up failure report all survive. Changed: launcher options come before the command or profile name, the three dump switches and profile creation become fixed commands, dsh plugin manages local directories instead of forwarding to pnpm, shutdown goes through one stop function that ends the turn in the log before a configurable deadline, and every command shares one output contract and one closed exit-status table. The package's 91 workspace dependencies are a composition list that the boot and bundle areas own.

The owner decided that there is no desktop application (DH-ADR-18). The Electron shell is not built in any form. Each of the 44 duties found in apps/desktop and apps/desktop-host has one answer in section 6.4 of the spec (web, command line, not applicable, or dropped with a decision), the table is enforced by test DH-T-WEBAPP-14, and section 6.5 states what a user loses.

The package is the child process Electron starts in Node mode to run the web profile and answer the shell over private IPC. In Go the host is the dsh process that dsh web starts, so the IPC ends (credential receipt, readiness, platform session, file drag, Windows console signals through a native binding) have no counterpart. Two of its duties survive in another form: the quit inspection becomes the work summary shown before a stop from the UI or the terminal, and the bounded fatal diagnostic becomes the host's crash report. Update admission (lock, drain, re-check) is not built because an update never stops a host.

The tool uploads desktop packages to one cloud vendor's object storage, raises a rollout percentage and refreshes website installers. The owner dropped the vendor release publisher: releases are GitHub release assets produced by the release workflow, and there are no installers. Its durable rules (separate credentials for building and publishing, verify before upload, artifacts before manifest) are kept as requirements DH-LIB-COS-R1 to R5 of the library specification.

The tool writes a plugin market index from a list of npm packages and Git repositories for the Discover page. The owner decided that plugins are installed from local directories with no download or discovery, so there is no market and no index to generate. If a registry is added later, the generator's safety rules (read only, bounded sizes, integrity checks, Git hooks disabled) are recorded as the starting point in DH-ADR-WEBAPP-8.

The package is a Vite build entry over the client shell library plus the browser test suite. There is no separate front-end build in Go: pages are rendered by the host and every file a page loads is embedded in the dsh binary (C1's ui/assets tree). What the entry itself contributed is carried by this area: the start sequence of dsh web and the check that the shipped web profile loads completely (DH-D-WEBAPP-1), the product files and size budget of the embedded tree (DH-D-WEBAPP-2), the install manifest and icons (DH-D-WEBAPP-4) and the keyless real-browser lane that replaces apps/web/tests (DH-D-WEBAPP-6).

Budgeted user-path performance gates are kept as Go tests that run the built binary in a fresh child with synthetic inputs and constants held in source; the eight upstream benchmark directories name the paths to measure.

The upstream docs tree (1,268 files) is read as input and not ported: the Go project keeps hand-written design documents under docs/harness and generates its reference catalogues (tools, events, config, services, commands, persisted event types) from Go source with a freshness check; the upgrade guides and persistence change records describe upstream release and format history that DH-ADR-2 does not carry, and the Chinese translations are not carried.

The workspace exists to compile two C programs per operating system, processor and C library and to publish them as npm packages; the Go design compiles the launch stage and the lock into the harness binary with go build, so the C sources, the platform packages, the build matrix and the release procedure are not carried, while the launcher and lock behaviour they tested is kept as requirements.

The Landlock launcher becomes a hidden launch stage of the dsh binary that builds its ruleset with go-landlock, enforces it on one locked thread and then replaces itself with the command, reporting status on a separate descriptor instead of exit code 125; the flock binding becomes a direct syscall.Flock call from the standard library.

System-browser sign-in with state and PKCE, authoritative local cancel, origin-bound release of request headers and local-first sign-out are kept; desktop embedding is dropped with the desktop application and notification polling becomes an opt-in setting.

Choosing the credential kind for one vendor request and releasing ready headers becomes the Authorizer interface of the account package; the presence-ordered auto billing is not carried because it changes who is billed without a record.

The automation-only ACP v1 agent on stdio is kept as component wire.acp behind the acpwire wrapper, with truthful capabilities, settlement at quiescence and rollback of a failed setup; changed are the stop-reason mapping for failed turns and support for additional directories.

The typed call dispatcher, the Typert descriptors, the multiplexed stream socket and the client face are not built, because the Go host renders HTML and its handlers call services directly. What the gateway guaranteed is restated as rules: only declared routes are callable, input is decoded strictly before a handler runs, access is checked on every route, cancellation reaches the work, and live data flows on one event stream with three recovery classes.

The two Remote streams and the reference-counted client job service become three routes and two stream interests (roster, output tail) over area A13's job registry; the human kill keeps its reason and its access is the session in the URL.

The model is kept: principals, resources, roles, bindings, one policy per non-owner kind, one decision point that fails closed. Changed: every route and stream source must declare its rule or it cannot register, decisions take no request arguments, and the client-side snapshot and hooks are replaced by rendering with the same Allows function that enforces.

The build-time assembly of remote namespaces and the allowlist of forwarded host events are replaced by run-time registration: a route or a stream source is an effect of the component that owns the feature, and no host event is forwarded to a browser.

The Remote namespace, the follow stream and the whole client half (session manager, journal stream, submission echoes, retain references) are replaced by session routes, the stream's journal class and a small host component, conversation, that keeps the ordering rules: blank reuse under the lease, a prompt admitted once per request id, fork and manual continuation.

The settings and credentials Remote namespaces become owner-only form routes over area A07's settings forms and area A17's credential store. The rule that no call returns a secret value is kept and tested by scanning every response. Opening the settings file in a native editor is dropped with the desktop application; the page shows the path.

The person's terminals are kept as the userterm service: session-owned, unconfined, capped, reattached from a screen snapshot and reclaimed after confirmed idleness. Changed: the terminal session, emulator and agent terminals are area A09's service, the duplex Remote stream becomes one WebSocket per terminal, and nothing is kept in browser storage.

Create, rename, remove, reorder, archive, pin, the first-use workspace and directory picking are kept as routes over area A07's workspace registry. The follow stream becomes the shell state region of the event stream, and the client workspace model is not built.

The bounded file service is kept as wsfiles over the filesystem seam: text pages, byte reads, listing, search and watching, with reads following the backend's authority. Changed: bytes are plain HTTP with Range, the change feed becomes stream interests, and the client resource provider is replaced by host rendering.

The attachment seam is kept as a Go contract package: opaque identifiers, references in events, all-or-none batch admission, stable error codes and verify-on-read. It gains size limits for generic files, a Touch step before an event cites a stored reference, and streaming reads.

The local provider keeps content-addressed files under the harness home, staged, synced and published by exclusive link, with the image pipeline rewritten on pure-Go decoders. The content-address mechanics become a blob service other areas also use, and it gains reference rows, garbage collection and a per-process decoded-pixel budget.

The boot library's product duties are kept as Go package internal/boot: layered launch environment with the launch-only name rule, profile and layer composition, best-effort start with a required-entry audit, the fatal exit path and the config dump. Its Node duties (runtime module resolution, version ranges, worker bootstrap, plugin display metadata read from package.json) have no subject because components are compiled in.

The three launcher facts are kept as services provided before the tree mounts: the app's words in launch.Data, and readiness and the exit request in launch.App. The commander adapter becomes the harness-owned command-line Spec of the commander library spec, so no component sees a parsing library.

Its result (validate a candidate, write the profile layer keeping comments, reconcile, refuse an edit a higher layer shadows) is given by config.Service over the loader's one writable layer. The file is no longer parsed a second time by this package, a merge operation replaces the whole-config override, and a cross-process lock and a revision check are added.

Configuration reload is kept: the loader's layer source watches the layer files and applies changes on one serial loop, gated by this area's static check and switched on by the boot.reload component after readiness. JavaScript module replacement, module file comparison and package-cache invalidation are not built because the Go host never replaces code in process.

The management surface is kept (list, inspect, enable, disable, add, remove, one service shared by the command line, the web page and a model-facing tool, protected management entries) but over loader entries and operator-placed plugin directories. Every pnpm, registry, Git, update, build-approval and version-exemption operation is gone under DH-ADR-13.

The package reads plugin indexes so that a user can discover and install npm bundles. DH-ADR-13 decides that plugins come from local directories with no download or discovery, so there is no index to read; the reader's safety rules are recorded in DH-ADR-BOOT-11 for a later registry design.

The exclusive provider slot is kept: one provider, a second registration fails even under the same name, and the slot is held until the provider's resources close. The Go service adds what upstream left to each provider: a provider interface of plain actions, one fixed tool catalogue, the session-to-browser table, isolation and approval per origin.

The patch becomes acp.yml, which mounts area A20's wire.stdio and wire.acp components, disables the title model call and removes from the standard preset the children ACP cannot express. The start-up provider is folded into A20's stdio component. The second model default of the upstream row is dropped; the default in the core layer applies.

The 101-row base patch becomes embedded layer files: admin.yml and core.yml (the kernel every profile stacks first) and base.yml (product host-plane services). Its 22 model-facing rows move into the shipped presets, so no host-plane layer mounts a model-facing component. Telemetry, vendor log upload and account sign-in are mounted off or gated.

The package is split. Its runner, flag parser and JSON stream are specified by area A24 as the component cli.headless in areas/app-cli.md and are not redefined here. This area keeps the 46-line patch as headless.yml: it mounts that runner, limits the secret store to environment sources, disables the authorization entry and removes the question tool from the presets.

The patch becomes sdk.yml, which mounts area A20's wire.stdio and wire.sdk components and disables the title model call. The start-up provider that accepted the command line and bound end of input to shutdown is folded into A20's stdio component and A21's launch data. The office-kit, runtime-download and client rows are not carried: office tools are preset children that work only where LibreOffice is installed.

A minimal SDK profile is kept, but as a subset and not as a second complete tree: profile sdk-minimal stacks the core bundle, the minimal bundle and the sdk bundle. The same capability set also ships as the preset minimal in every other profile, which is what area A24 asked for. Sandbox mode stays workspace-write by default and the vendor session-log row is not carried.

The browser layer becomes web.yml, which mounts the listener, authentication, routes, stream and page components and the reload entry. The 65 client rows, the gateway rows and the desktop-only analytics rows have no Go counterpart, the 22 disabling overrides are not needed because the agent plane is only in presets, and the glue plugin that prints the URL and opens the browser is area A18's host.launch component.

The package is types for live host config fields handed to browser plugins. No plugin code runs in the page: a Go component reads its own typed config struct, renders from the current value, and calls Shell.Touch when a live field changes so that open pages refresh their regions. The guarantee kept is that a config change shows without a reload and a secret never reaches the browser.

The host half (source check, authentication provider registry, request bridge) is area A18's admission pipeline, used as written. The browser half (generations, jittered reconnect, offline handling, a reconnect command) becomes the stream and conn modules of the first-party script on top of A19's cursor resume. Kept guarantees: nothing falls between baseline and live updates, the page reconnects by itself and shows its state, and typed input is not lost.

Upload when picked, one first-in-first-out queue, progress, cancellation and a reference that a later prompt cites are kept. The carrier is a plain multipart form to A19's upload route with an optional island; the Worker is not needed because the browser streams a File body from disk, and staged references become durable through A07's draft record.

Hot replacement of plugin code has no subject: code changes only with the binary. The other half of the package, keeping open pages in step when a plugin is enabled, disabled or reconfigured, is kept by the composition epoch: a change is published in a state region and open pages re-fetch their regions. The development loop is DevDir, which re-reads templates and assets on each request.

The catalogue with Chinese and English as required baselines, a host-stored preference, browser-language fallback and language packs are kept. Text is resolved on the host per request instead of in the browser, plural forms and direction are added, and the six further shipped languages and packs are P2 data files.

The host half composed a boot graph of plugin bundles and served them; the browser half was a lazy module table. Both exist to load plugin code into the page. The Go replacement is the page shell with embedded, content-addressed assets and a small island table: the only modules a page loads are the first-party script, htmx and islands that are on the page.

Upstream reports desktop interactions by default with account and device identity and machine facts. The Go design records usage events in the route handlers on the host, from a closed typed catalogue, through area A18's reporting channel, and sends nothing without a permit from the sharing gate, which is off by default. Machine sampling and identity are removed.

Addressable shared live data is kept as a contract, with other parts: an address is the URL of a fragment route, a holder is an interest of the tab registered through A19's Tab.Watch, and the live helper gives every such region an id and the ability to fetch itself. The browser-side registry, cache and hook disappear because there is one host state rendered per reader.

A registry of named script environments for optional client extensions; upstream does not mount it by default and states it is not a sandbox. With no client plugin runtime there is no code to place in an environment. Where a separate browser environment is needed the design uses a framed island with its own policy.

The only provider for the script-realm registry: a hidden same-origin iframe that shares object references with the page. It serves the client plugin runtime, which is not carried. The Go design's frames are real document boundaries with their own Content-Security-Policy and a closed postMessage set, declared per island.

The command registry, physical key codes, per-platform defaults, conflict checks at registration, device-local overrides with save-before-activate and the double-Escape sequence are kept. Commands are registered on the host and dispatched by the first-party script from a rendered table. Desktop profiles, native interception and two-key chords are gone with the desktop application.

The store engine (Zustand and Immer snapshots with optional localStorage) kept view state and mirrors of host state in the browser. Host state is no longer mirrored, and view state goes to four named places: the URL, host preferences, the DOM and a small per-tab store in the first-party script.

Notice cards become a host-rendered contribution to the shell's notice region, fed by area A17's poll, which is a setting that is off by default and obeys the off-switch. The browser polls nothing and reports nothing; the host reports an interaction only while the setting is on.

The preset picker, roster with default and read-only configuration viewer are rendered on the host over area A27's preset service. The viewer shows each child with the layer that supplied it instead of YAML text; the roster is no longer filtered by the Coding Tools setting; the analytics event becomes one opt-in usage event.

The Shared tasks section and the teamwork switch are rendered on the host from area A12's task board fold and updated as a state region. The confirmation before switching teamwork off is kept; owner forms to create, reassign, complete and delete a task are added because the board accepts an owner principal as actor.

The approval card that took over the composer becomes a host-rendered card in the interaction region above the composer. It shows what the interaction area lists for a request, offers a session grant only as an explicit non-default choice for an owner and a grantable subject, and is the same item in every tab with the first valid answer winning. Upstream's always-allow button, which was the primary action, is not carried.

The React rail, drop overlay, gallery factory and lightbox are replaced: a staged upload becomes an attachment chip inside the composer's text, as the owner decided in DH-ADR-21, with its progress, failure, retry and remove inside the chip; one gallery partial called from four views, and a native modal dialog with fit and actual-size views and a download link. Picking, drop, paste and progress are area C1's upload control placed in the composer form.

The package exists to show the DeepSeek mark and name and to play a whale animation derived from a vendor video. The Go project is not upstream's product and upstream's brand guidelines ask others not to use its official materials in a way that suggests endorsement, so no asset is carried; the product's name and mark are configuration with a neutral default, and the decoration is not built.

The React chat target is not built. Its reading rules (replies stay visible, the process folds, hidden rows, the retry receipt, one row per tool call, the inherited-history divider) become one pure host plan that area C4's renderer places nodes by; the turn rail, usage row and statistics are server-rendered fragments from host projections; scroll following is the first-party script's job and older history loads under browser scroll anchoring. Folding on the next message, the exchange rule and the fold animation are dropped by decision.

The client-side command directory cache and the three client command kinds are not built. The menu lists area A17's command catalogue and area A14's skills through one host completion source, matched by name or translated title; a command with arguments becomes a leading chip, a picker or form is a host fragment opened from the menu, and the plus button opens the same menu without script. A command line is still never sent to the model.

The host registry, its remote and the browser half are not built. Area A15's account view is already the host-computed display, and the connections section renders its phase and actions as given; an authorization page is a link in the answer to the Connect form.

Typed targets, registered contributions, capture of the target when the gesture begins, resolution under a timeout with failed contributors left out visibly, and one shared menu are kept. Changed: the registry is a host service, the menu is a fragment the host renders, an item is a request to a declared route instead of a browser callback, and a menu is resolved once per opening.

The browser-side assembly engine, its view-target and group registries, the retain facet and the React shell are not built. What they did is done on the host: a node registry folds session events into nodes keyed by (kind, id), an index committed with the events finds a node's start, and the same pure functions draw a page and a stream fragment.
